meta.title: GHG Standards Tracker
meta.subtitle: Weekly-updated reference on revisions to corporate emissions reporting standards and regulations
meta.disclaimer: Independent, non-commercial reference compiled from official sources for sustainability professionals. Not legal or compliance advice. Verify deadlines against primary sources before acting.

audit.clean: Most of the site held up. The EU material came through strongest: the revised reporting standards' entry into force on November 10, 2026 and application to financial years from January 1, 2027 were confirmed word for word against the Official Journal, as were the employee and turnover thresholds, the removal of the reasonable-assurance obligation, the non-EU parent tests and dates, the deletion of the corporate due-diligence transition-plan duty, and the finding that the green claims proposal is blocked rather than withdrawn — a contrarian call that the legislative tracker supports. On the GHG Protocol side, roughly eighty quoted passages from the consolidated development plan, the Scope 2 and Scope 3 progress updates, the market-instruments white paper and the land sector standard matched the sources exactly, including every consultation response count and the land standard's January 1, 2027 effective date. The ISSB amendments to the climate standard checked out in full, down to the paragraph numbers and the January 1, 2027 effective date with early application permitted. SBTi's own numbers — the hourly-matching recognition thresholds, the ten-gigawatt-hour significance pool, the fifteen-year generator limit, the five percent Scope 3 test, the company-category tests and the whole target-maintenance cycle — were all exact, and the February 1, 2027 validation date is now used consistently. The California reporting regime was re-verified end to end: thresholds, penalties, acceptable formats, the fee calendar, the assurance timing, and the fact that the climate-risk law remains enjoined while the emissions law does not. No dead links were found among the sources spot-checked.

audit.intro: Once a month every factual claim on this site is re-checked against primary sources, independently of the weekly refresh. The weekly run only adds; this one re-reads what is already here. Seven parallel reviewers each took one framework — GHG Protocol, ISO, SBTi, ISSB, EU, US — plus the glossary, crosswalk and landscape material, and worked through every date, deadline, threshold, percentage, criterion or article number, status label and confidence rating in their section, including the specifics behind every Details drawer. A finding only counted if the reviewer could cite the document and say what it states; surprising claims had to check out against a second source. Where an earlier audit had softened a line and the standard's own text said otherwise, the standard won. Three flags were dropped on cross-check: a reviewer read the timeline axis starting in July 2022 as inconsistent with the November 2022 revision window, but a background span legitimately predates the window this tracker covers; a reviewer suspected the SBTi removals figure was mis-numbered, but two reviewers reading different documents confirmed that both criterion C45 and criterion C40.3 carry an at-least-1% figure, so the line stands; and one ISO page showing the net-zero draft back at an earlier ballot stage turned out to be a rendering artefact of iso.org, contradicted by the committee mirror and by the absence of any recirculated draft.
audit.backup_note: The dataset was copied to a dated backup table before any edit, and backups older than three months were dropped after this run.

changes.intro: What the new or proposed rules actually change, framework by framework: today's rule on the left, the new one on the right. Final = adopted text. Proposed = official draft, can still change. Open = direction genuinely undecided.

frameworks.note: V2.0 is final (June 11, 2026) and takes effect February 1, 2027, when V2.0 validation opens. Companies may still submit under V1.3.1 until January 31, 2028; V2.0-only after that.

rows.new: Category A (large companies from all countries + medium companies in high-income countries) gets the strictest requirements; Category B gets lighter ones. The SME route is replaced.
rows.old: Broadly uniform requirements, with a separate SME route.

detail.timing: Category is set at registration and fixed for the five-year cycle. V2.0 validation opens February 1, 2027; the old rules (including small-company requests) stay open until January 31, 2028; the Category A removals duty starts in 2035.

detail.applies_to: Everyone validating under V2.0. Category A is large companies everywhere (€450 million+ turnover or 1,000+ employees) plus medium-sized companies with a high-income-country parent; Category B is everyone else.

sub_changes.new: Any company with €450 million+ revenue or 1,000+ employees is Category A, wherever it is based. Medium-sized companies count too if their parent is in a high-income country.
sub_changes.old: One rulebook for everyone, with a lighter route for small companies.
sub_changes.topic: Who counts as Category A
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: no company categories; one set of criteria for every company plus an optional streamlined SME route. V2.0: net turnover ≥ €450 million or ≥ 1,000 FTE, any country; in high-income countries also companies with scope 1+2 ≥ 10,000 tCO2e, or at least two of balance sheet ≥ €25 million / net turnover ≥ €50 million / ≥ 250 FTE (Table 2, Standard and System Overview).

sub_changes.new: Category B is everyone who fails the Category A tests: small companies everywhere, and medium-sized companies whose parent is in a lower-income country. The country that counts is where the ultimate parent is incorporated.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable — the only size-based split was whether you qualified as a small company.
sub_changes.topic: Who counts as Category B
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: Category B = any company that does not meet the Category A tests (small companies everywhere; medium companies in lower-income countries). Geography follows the World Bank income classification of the ultimate parent company's jurisdiction of incorporation (Standard and System Overview).

sub_changes.new: The size tests use the whole group's consolidated numbers, whichever part of the company the target covers. A subsidiary that runs as a distinct business can set its own target but must name its ultimate parent — and the parent's country decides the income test, so a US-parented subsidiary is judged as high-income.
sub_changes.old: Targets were set at parent or group level, not by subsidiary, and a subsidiary of a large parent could not use the small-company route.
sub_changes.topic: Groups, parents and subsidiaries
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: targets submitted at parent or group level, not subsidiary level; a subsidiary of a corporate-route parent could not use the SME route (C1). V2.0: thresholds assessed on consolidated figures for the group as a whole regardless of where the target boundary sits; boundary set at the ultimate parent (CNZS-C3.2); a subsidiary operating as a distinct business may set its own boundary; any subsidiary setting targets submits the full legal name of its ultimate parent (CNZS-C3.4); a US-parented subsidiary therefore takes the high-income test.

sub_changes.new: Your category is set when you register, confirmed when your target is validated, and then stays fixed for the whole five-year target cycle.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: When your category is locked in
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: category determined at registration, reconfirmed at Target Validation, and applies for the duration of the five-year target cycle (Standard and System Overview).

sub_changes.new: The small-company route is gone, replaced by the Category A/B split; the old small-company size limits now work in reverse to define which medium-sized companies are Category A. During the transition, a company that would be Category B can still ask for small-company status under the old rules.
sub_changes.old: Small companies could use a simplified route if they were under 10,000 tonnes of scope 1 and 2 emissions and met size tests such as under 250 employees or under €50 million turnover. For near-term targets they only had to measure and reduce scope 3, though their net-zero targets did include it.
sub_changes.topic: What happened to the small-company route
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: SME route (from Jan 1, 2024) required under 10,000 tCO2e scope 1 + location-based scope 2; not a financial institution or oil & gas company; no sector-specific criteria; not a subsidiary of a corporate-route parent; plus three of: under 250 employees, turnover under €50 million, assets under €25 million, not in a mandatory FLAG sector; SME near-term targets covered scope 1+2 with a commitment to measure and reduce scope 3; SME net-zero targets included scope 3. V2.0: replaced by the Category A/B split (Main Changes, p.6); the old SME size thresholds reappear inverted as the Category A 'medium company' test; during the transition, companies meeting Category B may still request SME status under V1.3.1.

sub_changes.new: Required for Category A: report scope 3 in the base-year inventory, work out which categories are significant, and set near-term scope 3 targets. Optional for Category B.
sub_changes.old: Everyone had to build a scope 3 inventory, and had to set a scope 3 target if scope 3 was 40% or more of total emissions.
sub_changes.topic: Scope 3 duties by category
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: all companies completed a scope 3 inventory (C10) and set scope 3 targets when scope 3 was 40% or more of total emissions (C4). V2.0: only Category A must report scope 3 in the target base-year inventory (CNZS-C5.2) and determine its significant categories (CNZS-C5.7); scope 3 near-term targets (CNZS-C14, C15) required for Category A, optional for Category B.

sub_changes.new: Required for Category A: an independent check of the base-year inventory, and again whenever the base year is recalculated. Optional for Category B.
sub_changes.old: No independent checking of emissions data was required.
sub_changes.topic: Assurance by category
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: no third-party assurance requirement. V2.0: base-year inventory assurance (CNZS-C7) and assurance of recalculated base years (CNZS-C8.6) required for Category A, optional for Category B. The required level is limited assurance at a minimum (CNZS-C7.2; see the Assurance row).

sub_changes.new: Long-term scope 2 and scope 3 targets are optional for everyone. A long-term scope 1 target is required only for Category A companies whose near-term scope 1 target is an intensity or asset-transition target.
sub_changes.old: Every net-zero target needed long-term targets covering at least 90% of scope 3, with a target year of 2050 or sooner.
sub_changes.topic: Long-term targets by category
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: every net-zero target needed long-term targets covering at least 90% of scope 3 (C7), target year no later than 2050 (C17). V2.0: long-term scope 1 targets (CNZS-C11) required for Category A only when its near-term scope 1 target is an intensity or asset-transition target; long-term scope 2 (CNZS-C13) and scope 3 (CNZS-C16) targets optional for everyone.

sub_changes.new: Category A must publish a transition plan within 15 months of validation; Category B must prepare one but need not publish it. From 2035, Category A must also support carbon removals — optional for Category B.
sub_changes.old: No requirement to publish a transition plan; funding climate action outside your own value chain was only recommended.
sub_changes.topic: Transition plans and removals by category
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: no transition-plan publication requirement; beyond-value-chain mitigation a recommendation (R12). V2.0: Category A publishes a transition plan within 15 months of completing Target Validation (CNZS-C2.4); Category B develops one under CNZS-C2 but need not publish; from 2035 Category A must support eligible carbon removals under CNZS-C45 (optional for Category B).

implications: Test your whole group on consolidated numbers: €450 million+ turnover or 1,000+ employees makes the group — and every subsidiary it validates — Category A wherever it is based.
If a subsidiary wants its own targets, be ready to show it runs as a distinct business and to name its ultimate parent, whose country still decides the income test.
Budget the Category A package as one program: scope 3 inventory and significance screen, base-year assurance, a transition plan within 15 months, and separate scope 1, 2 and 3 targets.
Expect less from smaller or lower-income-country partners: Category B suppliers are not required to set scope 3 targets or get assurance.
Treat the category as fixed for the five-year cycle once validated, and plan reorganizations and divestitures around that window.

rows.new: Separate targets for scope 1, scope 2, and scope 3, each with its own rules.
rows.old: One near-term target usually covering scope 1 and 2 together; a scope 3 target required when scope 3 is 40% or more of total emissions.

detail.timing: V2.0 validation opens February 1, 2027; the old rules run alongside until January 31, 2028. The first V2.0 near-term period may be shorter than five years; later cycles are five-year blocks; long-term targets reach 2050 at the latest.

detail.applies_to: Everyone validating under V2.0. Separate scope 3 targets and the 20% electricity-growth rule apply to Category A only; long-term scope 1 targets apply to Category A companies using intensity or asset-transition near-term targets.

sub_changes.new: Required for everyone: scope 1 and scope 2 each get their own target. Category A also sets a separate scope 3 target.
sub_changes.old: Scope 1 and 2 were usually covered by one combined target with a single ambition test.
sub_changes.topic: Separate scope 1 and scope 2 targets
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: targets covered company-wide scope 1 and 2 (C3), normally as one combined target with a single 1.5°C ambition test (C19). V2.0: Category A sets separate scope 1, scope 2 and scope 3 targets; Category B sets separate scope 1 and scope 2 targets (CNZS-C9.1); each scope has its own criterion (CNZS-C10, C12, C14/C15).

sub_changes.new: No trigger any more. Every Category A company must set near-term scope 3 targets; which categories they cover is decided by a 5% significance test.
sub_changes.old: You only needed a near-term scope 3 target if scope 3 was 40% or more of your total emissions.
sub_changes.topic: The 40% scope 3 trigger is gone
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: scope 3 in near-term targets only when scope 3 was 40% or more of total scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions (C4). V2.0: no trigger; scope 3 near-term targets required for every Category A company (CNZS-C14, C15), with the boundary set by the 5% significance test (see 'Scope 3 boundary').

sub_changes.new: Cover 100% of scope 1 and cut it in a straight line to a small residual by 2050. There is no fixed yearly percentage — the slope is simply base year to residual by 2050. Three routes are allowed: absolute cuts, an intensity target, or an asset decarbonization plan.
sub_changes.old: Scope 1 and 2 together had to fall at least 4.2% a year in a straight line.
sub_changes.topic: Scope 1 ambition
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: minimum ambition a linear reduction of 4.2% per year for scope 1 and 2 on the cross-sector 1.5°C pathway (Standard p.18; C19). V2.0: 100% of scope 1 covered (CNZS-C10.1); three routes (CNZS-C10.2): absolute reduction on a linear trajectory to residual levels by 2050, intensity reduction from applicable sector activities to residual levels, or a trajectory defined by an Asset Decarbonization Plan; no fixed %-per-year stated — the slope is the straight line from base year to residual by 2050.

sub_changes.new: Cover 100% of scope 2, measured on grid-average numbers. Choose an absolute reduction target or a low-carbon electricity target. Category A companies expecting electricity use to grow more than 20% a year must set an emissions target.
sub_changes.old: Same combined 4.2%-a-year test; you picked grid-average or contract-based accounting and stuck with it.
sub_changes.topic: Scope 2 ambition
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: same combined 4.2%/yr test; location- or market-based accounting chosen and used consistently (C9). V2.0: 100% of scope 2 covered (CNZS-C12.1), ambition set on the location-based inventory (CNZS-C9.4); options: absolute scope 2 reduction target or low-carbon electricity alignment target (CNZS-C12.2); Category A companies projecting average electricity-consumption growth above 20% a year over the cycle must set an emissions target (CNZS-C12.4). Details under 'Scope 2 accounting for targets'.

sub_changes.new: Scope 3 now follows the same rule as scope 1: a straight line to about 10% or less of base-year emissions by 2050 or sooner. There is no slower rate for scope 3.
sub_changes.old: Near-term scope 3 targets only had to meet a 'well-below 2°C' pace of 2.5% a year.
sub_changes.topic: Scope 3 ambition
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: near-term scope 3 targets only had to meet 'well-below 2°C' (C22), a 2.5% per year linear rate (Standard p.18). V2.0: absolute scope 3 targets run on a linear trajectory to a residual level consistent with an eligible net-zero pathway (CNZS-C15.1), about 10% or less of base-year emissions in a net-zero year of 2050 or sooner (Executive summary, p.8); no separate, slower rate for scope 3.

sub_changes.new: Gone. No target option is pegged to 'well-below 2°C'; everything points to net-zero pathways that reach residual levels by 2050 or earlier.
sub_changes.old: Accepted as the minimum ambition for near-term scope 3.
sub_changes.topic: 'Well-below 2°C' option removed
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: well-below 2°C accepted as the minimum for near-term scope 3 (C22). V2.0: no criterion offers a well-below 2°C target option and the phrase does not appear in the V2.0 criteria or Key Terms; all targets point to residual levels on net-zero pathways consistent with net-zero by 2050 or earlier.

sub_changes.new: Long-term scope 2 and scope 3 targets are optional for everyone, and so is the net-zero target itself. A long-term scope 1 target is required only for Category A companies using an intensity or asset-based near-term scope 1 target. Any long-term target covers 100% of its scope and reaches residual levels by 2050 at the latest.
sub_changes.old: A net-zero target required long-term targets covering at least 95% of scope 1 and 2 and 90% of scope 3, cutting emissions at least 90% by 2050.
sub_changes.topic: Long-term targets (mostly optional)
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: long-term targets covering at least 95% of scope 1+2 and 90% of scope 3 (Standard p.24), reaching an economy-wide reduction of at least 90% by 2050 (Standard pp.18–19; C17 target year no later than 2050). V2.0: long-term scope 1 targets (CNZS-C11) required only when the near-term scope 1 target is intensity- or asset-based (Category A); long-term scope 2 (C13) and scope 3 (C16) optional for all; where set, cover 100% of the scope and reach residual levels by 2050 at the latest (C9.3); the net-zero target itself optional for all (Executive summary table).

sub_changes.new: Near-term targets now cover a fixed five-year period starting from your latest reporting year, with a shorter first period allowed once. The base year must be your most recent year with full data and is reset every cycle. Companies with 2030 targets set their 2030–35 targets under the new rules from 2028.
sub_changes.old: Near-term targets ran 5 to 10 years from submission, the base year could be no earlier than 2015, and targets were reviewed at least every 5 years.
sub_changes.topic: Target period and base year
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: near-term targets 5–10 years from submission (C17); base year no earlier than 2015 (C16); review all targets at least every 5 years (C32). V2.0: near-term targets cover a five-year period starting at the most recent reporting period at submission (CNZS-C9.2), a shorter period allowed once at first validation under V2.0 (C9.2a); base year is the most recent year with comprehensive data (CNZS-C4.1), reset every cycle (C4.2); companies with 2030 targets set their 2030–35 targets under V2.0 from 2028. Because the base year resets to the most recent year each cycle while the 2050 endpoint is fixed, a later base year shortens the runway and raises the implied annual reduction rate.

sub_changes.new: Both still exist. Targets must use SBTi-approved methods and pathways; intensity targets use sector activities, sector pathways drive some scope 3 options, and any SBTi sector standard that applies to you must be followed.
sub_changes.old: You could use the cross-sector pathway (4.2% a year) or an approved sector pathway for intensity targets.
sub_changes.topic: Sector vs cross-sector pathways
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: cross-sector pathway (4.2%/yr) or approved 1.5°C sector pathways for intensity targets (C21). V2.0: targets use applicable and eligible SBTi metrics, methods and pathways (CNZS-C9.5); intensity targets use applicable sector activities (C10.2b); sector pathways drive the Group A scope 3 options (C15.3); targets conform to any applicable SBTi Sector Standard (C20).

implications: Split your scope 1 and 2 target into a scope 1 target (absolute, intensity or asset-transition) and a scope 2 target on grid-average numbers, each covering 100% of its scope.
Recalculate ambition as a straight line from your most recent base year to roughly 10% residual by 2050, and model the implied annual rate before you commit.
Drop any plan built on the old 2.5%-a-year scope 3 pace — scope 3 absolute targets now use the same straight-line-to-residual construction as scope 1.
Decide early whether scope 1 takes the intensity or asset-transition route, because that alone makes a long-term scope 1 target mandatory and requires a published transition plan at validation.
Plan in five-year cycles: if you hold 2030 targets, prepare your 2030–35 targets under the new rules from 2028 with a fresh base year.

rows.new: Category A companies must obtain at least limited assurance over the GHG inventory and the data behind target-setting, plus assured end-of-cycle performance assessments. Category B: encouraged, not required.
rows.old: No third-party assurance requirement — inventories and progress were self-reported.

detail.timing: V2.0 validation resources publish October 1, 2026; validation opens February 1, 2027. Base-year assurance is due at validation; progress assurance at each end-of-cycle assessment, which is completed within 12 months of the end of the target period.

detail.applies_to: Required for Category A; optional or recommended for Category B. Anyone joining the removals recognition program or the hourly-matching recognition program must get that claim checked regardless of category.

sub_changes.new: Required for Category A: an independent third party must check the base-year inventory for scope 1, 2 and 3, plus the low-carbon electricity figures, emissions-intensive activities and any other numbers used to set targets. Optional for Category B.
sub_changes.old: No independent check was required — companies reported their own numbers and only had to publish the inventory and progress each year.
sub_changes.topic: Base-year inventory must be checked (Category A)
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: no assurance criterion — companies self-reported; C30 only required public annual reporting of the inventory and progress. V2.0: Category A obtains independent third-party assurance covering scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions for the target base year, low-carbon electricity calculations, emissions from significant emissions-intensive activities, and any other metrics used for target setting (CNZS-C7, C7.1); optional for Category B.

sub_changes.new: Limited assurance is enough — the lighter of the two standard levels — but it must come from an accredited independent provider using a recognized assurance standard. SBTi accepts an accreditation-body listing or an ISO 14065 certificate as proof. The stricter 'reasonable assurance' level was rejected because of cost and auditor availability.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: How rigorous, and who can do it
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: limited assurance at a minimum (C7.2) from an accredited independent third party using internationally recognized assurance standards (C7.3); SBTi's preliminary evidence list accepts IAF or national accreditation-body directory listings, or ISO 14065 accreditation certificates, as proof; reasonable assurance not adopted, citing cost and access to qualified auditors (Basis for Conclusions, Minor Issue 5).

sub_changes.new: Required: publish what period, scopes and methods the check covered, the type of assurance and a summary of findings, in the first reporting cycle after validation. You also consent to the assurance level appearing on SBTi's public dashboard within six months.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Publishing the assurance result
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: publicly report the time period, scope and boundary, methodology and standards, type of assurance, and a summary of findings (C7.4); in the next reporting cycle after Target Validation, with consent to show the assurance level on the SBTi Dashboard within six months (C7.5).

sub_changes.new: Required for Category A: whenever the base year is recalculated, the new figures must get at least limited assurance too.
sub_changes.old: Big changes forced a base-year recalculation (the threshold was 5% or less), but the recalculated numbers were never checked.
sub_changes.topic: Recalculated base years
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: C33 triggered base-year recalculation (significance threshold of 5% or less) but no assurance of the recalculated figures. V2.0: Category A obtains at least limited assurance of the recalculated GHG inventory and other metrics (CNZS-C8.6), in accordance with CNZS-C7.

sub_changes.new: Required for Category A: the data behind the end-of-cycle progress assessment gets at least limited assurance; recommended for Category B. Every annual progress report must also say whether the inventory has been independently checked.
sub_changes.old: Progress was self-reported every year.
sub_changes.topic: Checking progress at the end of each cycle
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: progress self-reported annually (C30, C31). V2.0: Category A obtains at least limited assurance of the data and calculations substantiating the end-of-cycle progress assessment (CNZS-C37.7); recommended for Category B (R37.1); every annual progress report states the third-party assurance status of the inventory (C36.7).

sub_changes.new: If a Category A company counts certificates, power purchase agreements or supplier contracts toward its targets, the end-of-cycle check must confirm each instrument met the rules on timing, project eligibility, instrument type and registry retirement — not just the emissions math. The hourly-matched percentage Category A reports for big electricity pools must be checked too, as must the percentage of anyone who joins the optional hourly-matching recognition program, including Category B.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Certificates, PPAs and hourly matching
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: where a Category A company counts market instruments (certificates, PPAs, supplier contracts) toward targets, end-of-cycle assurance checks that each instrument met the rules on timing of use (C25), qualifying projects (C26), eligible instrument types (C27) and registry retirement without double counting (C28), not just the emissions math (C28.2); the hourly-matched percentage Category A reports for large electricity pools must be assured (C32.4); any company joining the optional hourly-matching recognition program, including Category B (which otherwise has no assurance duties), must have its percentage assured (C34.3).

sub_changes.new: Anyone who joins the voluntary removals recognition program must report and get an independent check showing they met their chosen level.
sub_changes.old: Funding climate action beyond your own value chain was recommended only, with no checking.
sub_changes.topic: Removals recognition program
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: beyond-value-chain mitigation a recommendation (R12) with no assurance. V2.0: any company participating in the Ongoing Emissions Responsibility recognition program reports and obtains independent assurance showing conformance with its selected recognition level (CNZS-C44).

sub_changes.new: Not stated. SBTi has not said whether an assurance engagement done for European (CSRD) or ISSB reporting is accepted; what matters is that the provider is accredited, uses a recognized standard, and covers the full scope 1–3 base-year inventory plus the target-setting numbers. SBTi and its validators do not check emissions data themselves.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Does CSRD or ISSB assurance count?
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: not specified; the V2.0 documents do not say whether an assurance engagement done for CSRD or ISSB reporting is accepted; the test is C7.1–C7.3 — accredited provider, recognized standard, and a scope covering the full scope 1–3 base-year inventory plus the target-setting metrics; neither SBTi nor its validation bodies independently verify emissions data.

implications: If you are Category A, budget a limited-assurance engagement over the full scope 1–3 base-year inventory before submitting — it is a prerequisite for validation, not a follow-up.

Extend any existing CSRD or ISSB assurance scope to cover the SBTi target-setting numbers (grid-average scope 2, hourly matching, emissions-intensive activities), since SBTi has not ruled on equivalence.
Check your provider's accreditation evidence (an ISO 14065 certificate or an accreditation-body listing) — SBTi asks for it at submission.
Plan a second assured data set at the end of each five-year cycle, including checks on the certificates, PPAs and hourly-matching claims used toward targets.
Prepare the public assurance disclosure alongside the target announcement and consent to dashboard display within six months.

rows.new: Targets sit on location-based (grid-average) numbers; a separate optional 'low-carbon electricity' alignment target covers procurement — with hourly accounting intervals for significant electricity users.
rows.old: Market-based accounting (contracts and certificates) could carry the target.

detail.timing: V2.0 published June 11, 2026; effective February 1, 2027 when validation opens; old rules accepted until January 31, 2028 and existing targets stay valid for their cycle; the 15-year-rule exceptions are proposed to move into the Standard itself, and four electricity-criteria interpretations and limited-scope revisions went out for public comment on November 5, 2026 for at least 30 days, for implementation in January 2027 via a Basis for Conclusions effective on publication; recognition thresholds step up in 2030 and 2035; the low-carbon intensity threshold tightens in 2035. The comment period on the four proposed electricity interpretations and revisions closes December 4, 2026 at 23:59 Pacific — a date stated on the comment survey and on SBTi's take-part page, and on neither the blog post nor the terms of reference, which give only 'a minimum of 30 days'. SBTi's take-part page records that the Technical Council approved the four items for release to public comment.

detail.applies_to: Everyone setting or renewing targets under V2.0 (Category A and B) for the grid-average basis, grid-region pools, the 15-year rule and the instrument list; hourly reporting for 10 GWh pools, electricity forecasts and the 20% growth rule apply to Category A only.

sub_changes.new: Required for everyone: the target is set on grid-average, location-based scope 2. Certificates and contracts can still help you deliver the target, but they are tracked and reported separately from the physical inventory.
sub_changes.old: You could set and track your scope 2 target on either grid-average (location-based) or contract-and-certificate (market-based) numbers. Most companies with certificates used the market-based number.
sub_changes.topic: Targets sit on grid-average numbers
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: location-based or market-based accounting under the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance, one method used for setting and tracking the target (Near-Term Criteria C8; Net-Zero Criteria C9); most companies holding certificates set the target on the market-based number. V2.0: target ambition set only on the physical inventory — the location-based method for scope 2 (CNZS-C9.4) — for Category A and B alike; market instruments may still implement the target but are accounted for and reported separately from the physical inventory (CNZS-C5.4).

sub_changes.new: Required for everyone: a stand-alone target covering 100% of scope 2, either an absolute cut in a straight line to a residual level or a low-carbon electricity target with no fixed percentage milestones. Long-term scope 2 targets are optional. Category A must also submit an electricity forecast, and an emissions target is required if use grows more than 20% a year on average.
sub_changes.old: Scope 2 could be folded into the scope 1 target, or replaced by a renewable-electricity target with fixed milestones of 80% by 2025 and 100% by 2030.
sub_changes.topic: Scope 2 target options
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: scope 2 target combined with scope 1 (Near-Term C20) or replaced by a renewable-electricity procurement target with fixed milestones of 80% by 2025 and 100% by 2030, near-term and long-term alike (Near-Term C21; Net-Zero C27). V2.0: stand-alone near-term target covers 100% of scope 2 (CNZS-C12.1); either an absolute reduction on a linear trajectory to a defined residual level or a low-carbon electricity (LCE) alignment target raising the share of LCE used, contracted or matched along an eligible net-zero pathway (CNZS-C12.2), no fixed % milestones; long-term scope 2 targets optional (CNZS-C13); Category A submits projected electricity consumption, and if average annual growth exceeds 20% over the cycle an emissions target is mandatory with LCE alignment only as an add-on (CNZS-C12.3–12.4). Plain-cell detail moved here: the LCE option raises the share of clean power along an SBTi-approved pathway.

sub_changes.new: You now group your electricity use into 'pools' by grid region — the area a connected power plant can realistically serve. Certificates and contracts must come from the same pool unless you can show transmission rights, or you sign a power purchase agreement within a wider interconnected grid you operate in, with delivery starting within 36 months of the plant being commissioned. Contracts signed before the new rules keep their old geography; renewals do not. Out for comment since November 5, 2026: a proposed interim interpretation would require the generator to sit in the same wide-area synchronous grid as the consuming facility, with exceptions where a regulator draws a tighter boundary and where the grid is not a country's main supply method, and SBTi has published a proposed list of regions.
sub_changes.old: SBTi set no rule of its own; it relied on GHG Protocol guidance that certificates come from the 'same market' as the electricity use — in practice a national or regional certificate market.
sub_changes.topic: Where your certificates can come from
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: no SBTi geographic rule; C8 deferred to the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Quality Criteria, requiring instruments sourced from the same market as the consuming operations, 'market' undefined — in practice a national or regional certificate market. V2.0: scope 2 'activity pools' defined by deliverability region (CNZS-C30.1), a geographical area throughout which all generation connected to a synchronous grid can reasonably be expected to serve consumption on that grid (Key Terms); instruments beyond a pool only with demonstrated transmission rights, or where the company operates in two or more interconnected pools on a wide-area synchronous grid and covers that load with a PPA from an LCE project in one of those pools with offtake starting within 36 months of commissioning (CNZS-C30.3); long-term contracts signed before V2.0's effective date keep their old deliverability, load-weighted by pool; renewals do not (CNZS-C30.5). Proposed interpretation out for public comment November 5, 2026 (Electricity Criteria: Proposed interpretations and limited-scope revisions, Draft for Public Comment, Version 1.0, November 2026): CNZS-C30.1 deliverability region interpreted so that generation behind a low-carbon electricity project or contractual instrument must be in the same wide-area synchronous grid as the consuming facility, with exceptions for stricter regulatory boundaries and for countries where the grid is not the main supply method, plus a proposed region list; CNZS-C30.3.b revised for load aggregation under project-specific long-term contracts with delivery starting within 36 months of commissioning or re-powering, attributes allocable across the activity pool or the national boundary, whichever is larger; CNZS-C30.5 interpreted so that contracts fully executed and legally binding before the February 1, 2027 effective date are eligible regardless of when delivery starts. Comment is limited to clarity, practical application and region-list accuracy; original intent and other criteria are out of scope. Implementation January 2027 via a Basis for Conclusions effective on publication. The exact close date is not stated — only a minimum of 30 days.

sub_changes.new: Optional for meeting your target. Large Category A electricity users must publish how much of their power was matched hour by hour, but it is a disclosure, not a pass/fail test. A voluntary recognition program rewards companies that reach 50% now, 75% by 2035 and 90% after.
sub_changes.old: No hourly rule of any kind — certificates just had to be from roughly the same year.
sub_changes.topic: Hourly matching (optional for targets)
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: no hourly or interval requirement; GHG Protocol Quality Criteria only required certificates issued and redeemed as close as possible to the consumption period; V1.3.1 never mentions hourly matching. V2.0: target progress uses annual matching — actions correspond to activities within 12 months unless a longer period is justified (CNZS-C25.5); pools of 10 GWh or more per year are 'significant' (CNZS-C32.1) and Category A must calculate, have assured and publicly report the hourly-matched LCE share (CNZS-C32.2, 32.4, 32.5) — a reporting requirement, not a pass/fail test; Category B may report voluntarily; one temporal accounting interval per pool (CNZS-C32.3); every company states at validation whether it joins the optional Hourly Matching recognition program, with an explanation if not (CNZS-C33); recognition thresholds at least 50% hourly matching in each reporting year until 2030, 75% until 2035, 90% from 2035 (CNZS-C34.1), assured even for Category B participants (CNZS-C34.3).

sub_changes.new: 'Renewable' is replaced by 'low-carbon electricity', defined by emissions intensity rather than technology: at or below 0.048 kg CO2 per kWh, tightening to 0.024 in 2035. Six kinds of instrument qualify, including physical and virtual PPAs, supplier contracts and unbundled certificates — but only from plants commissioned or re-powered within the last 15 years and tracked in a secure registry. Guidance on exceptions to the 15-year rule is promised by Q4 2026.
sub_changes.old: Targets talked about 'renewable electricity' with no SBTi list of eligible instruments; quality relied on GHG Protocol rules, and the age of the power plant was only an optional disclosure.
sub_changes.topic: 'Renewable' becomes 'low-carbon'
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: targets framed around 'renewable electricity procurement' with no SBTi list of eligible instruments; integrity rested on the GHG Protocol Quality Criteria (tracking, no double counting, vintage, same market); facility age only an optional disclosure. V2.0: 'low-carbon electricity' defined by intensity not technology — generator direct emissions at or below 0.048 kg CO2/kWh, tightening to 0.024 in 2035 (Key Terms); six eligible instrument types — physical PPAs, financial (virtual) PPAs, supplier LCE contracts, unbundled energy attribute certificates, default-delivered LCE backed by certificates, and default-delivered LCE in pools at least 95% low-carbon with no certificate registry (CNZS-C31.1); only from generators commissioned or re-powered within fifteen years of the consumption period (CNZS-C31.3), recorded in a secure registry (CNZS-C28.1); guidance on exceptions to the 15-year rule promised by Q4 2026.

sub_changes.new: Power you generate on site, or receive by a direct line without touching the grid, must be cleaned up at the source; certificates from behind-the-meter generation cannot be used to cover grid electricity.
sub_changes.old: Not covered by SBTi rules; GHG Protocol rules applied.
sub_changes.topic: On-site and direct-line power
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: not addressed in SBTi criteria; GHG Protocol rules applied. V2.0: electricity from on-site generation, or off-site generation delivered by direct line without grid transfer, decarbonized through activity-level actions (CNZS-C29.2); certificates from behind-the-meter generation cannot be applied to grid consumption (CNZS-C31.2).

sub_changes.new: The new rules take effect February 1, 2027, when validation opens (one SBTi document says January 31). You can still submit under the old rules until January 31, 2028, though some SBTi texts say 'end of 2027'. Companies with 2030 targets set their 2030–35 targets under the new rules from 2028. A proposed legacy clause out for comment since November 5, 2026 would let any power contract fully executed and legally binding before February 1, 2027 keep its eligibility regardless of when delivery starts.
sub_changes.old: The old rules (V1.3.1 and Near-Term Criteria V5.3.1, April 2026) are still current, and targets validated under them stay valid for their full cycle.
sub_changes.topic: Timing and existing targets
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1 and Near-Term Criteria V5.3.1 (April 2026) remain the current rules; targets validated under them stay valid for their full cycle. V2.0: takes effect February 1, 2027 (the Main Changes document says 31 January — a one-day inconsistency), when validation opens; V1.3.1 stays open for new or updated targets until January 31, 2028 (the executive summary and launch blog round this to 'end of 2027'); companies with 2030 targets set their 2030–35 targets under V2.0 from 2028; SBTi also plans a Call for Evidence on hourly matching to inform future revisions.

implications: Rebuild your scope 2 baseline and target on grid-average figures now, and quantify how much higher that number is than your certificate-adjusted one.
Map each site into a grid-region pool and screen your certificates and PPAs against it: out-of-pool instruments stop counting unless transmission rights, a multi-pool PPA or the legacy clause apply.
Collect commissioning or re-powering dates for every plant behind your PPAs and certificates, since anything older than 15 years at the time of use is ineligible.
Category A: set up hourly consumption and certificate data for every pool using 10 GWh or more a year, and decide before validation whether to join the hourly-matching recognition program.
Category A: prepare an electricity demand forecast for the cycle, because average growth above 20% a year makes an emissions reduction target mandatory.

rows.new: Significance-based: address every category that is ≥5% of category 1–14 emissions; new alignment-target options (supplier engagement, revenue-based); long-term scope 3 targets largely optional.
rows.old: Cover 67% of scope 3 near-term / 90% long-term.

detail.timing: Applies to targets submitted under V2.0 from February 1, 2027; mandatory for all submissions from February 1, 2028 (the old 67% / 90% tests remain usable until January 31, 2028). Exclusion and significant-category reporting fall due in the first reporting cycle after validation.

detail.applies_to: Category A (scope 3 inventory, significance screening and near-term scope 3 targets required); optional for Category B. Category 15 sits outside the 1–14 tests and is covered by a recommendation to use the financial-sector standard.

sub_changes.new: Cover every scope 3 category that is 5% or more of your scope 3 emissions across categories 1–14, measured on the physical inventory. There is no overall coverage floor like 67% any more, and categories under 5% can be left out.
sub_changes.old: Near-term targets had to cover at least 67% of scope 3, you could leave out up to 5% of the inventory, and none of it applied unless scope 3 was 40% or more of your total emissions.
sub_changes.topic: Which scope 3 categories must be covered
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: near-term reduction and/or engagement targets covered at least 67% of total scope 3 emissions (C6); inventory exclusions capped at 5% of total scope 3 (C5); the whole obligation triggered only at 40% of total emissions (C4). V2.0: near-term targets cover at least every scope 3 category that individually represents 5% or more of the company's scope 3 emissions in categories 1–14, based on the physical inventory (CNZS-C14.1); no overall coverage floor such as 67% is specified; categories below 5% may be left out.

sub_changes.new: Scope 3 is reported to the GHG Protocol's minimum boundaries, with all transport counted on a full fuel life-cycle basis. Anything you account for beyond those boundaries is reported separately and does not count in the 5% test. Category A must work out and report every category at 5% or more.
sub_changes.old: Everyone built a scope 3 inventory covering all relevant sources.
sub_changes.topic: The inventory behind the test
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: all companies completed a scope 3 inventory of all relevant sources (C10). V2.0: scope 3 reported to the GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard minimum boundaries (Table 5.4), with all transport on a well-to-wheel / well-to-wake basis; emissions accounted outside the minimum boundary reported separately and excluded from the significance determination (CNZS-C5.6); Category A determines and reports every category at 5% or more of categories 1–14 (CNZS-C5.7).

sub_changes.new: A named list of exclusions is allowed whatever their size: second-hand goods, fuel-related emissions already cut through your own energy savings, all employee commuting, leased assets and transport you have no way to influence, processing steps you cannot know or contract for, and independent franchisees. Each exclusion must be reported with its reason, tonnes, share of scope 3 and planned mitigation.
sub_changes.old: Exclusions were capped at 5% of the total scope 3 inventory.
sub_changes.topic: What you may leave out of a significant category
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: exclusions limited to 5% of the total scope 3 inventory (C5). V2.0: named exclusions regardless of significance (CNZS-C14.2) — cradle-to-gate emissions of second-hand goods (cat. 1–2); cat. 3 where mitigated through scope 1/2 energy cuts; all of cat. 7 commuting; cat. 8 leased assets with no operational control and no contractual or practical means to influence them; cat. 9 transport with no contractual means to influence fuel type; cat. 10 where processing steps are unknown or there is no contractual relationship; cat. 14 franchisees operating as independent businesses or leasing space; each exclusion reported with its condition, tonnes, share of scope 3 categories 1–14, and intended mitigation actions (CNZS-C14.3).

sub_changes.new: Three routes: an overall absolute reduction target in a straight line to residual levels; an overall supplier or customer alignment target that raises the share of tier 1 partners (by emissions, spend or revenue) that are in transition or net-zero aligned; or targets set category by category.
sub_changes.old: Absolute or intensity reduction targets at a 'well-below 2°C' pace, or supplier and customer engagement targets that had to be met within five years.
sub_changes.topic: Ways to set a scope 3 target
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: absolute or intensity reduction targets (well-below 2°C minimum, C22), or supplier/customer engagement targets fulfilled within a maximum of five years (C23). V2.0: three routes under CNZS-C15 — an overarching absolute reduction target on a linear trajectory to residual levels (C15.1); an overarching supplier and/or customer alignment target raising the share of tier 1 suppliers or customers, by emissions, spend or revenue, that are in transition or net-zero aligned (C15.2); or category- or activity-specific targets (C15.3).

sub_changes.new: Upstream categories with sector or commodity pathways (purchased goods, capital goods, upstream transport, business travel) can use a sector pathway, a volume target for lower-carbon purchases, or supplier alignment. Other upstream categories use emissions reduction or supplier alignment. Downstream categories use emissions reduction, product-use or end-of-life alignment, or customer alignment.
sub_changes.old: Not structured this way — one coverage test across all of scope 3.
sub_changes.topic: Category-by-category menu
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0 (C15.3): Group A (upstream categories with sector or commodity pathways — cat. 1, 2, 4, 6, 9): emissions reduction on a sector pathway, volume alignment (share of purchased commodities or transport that is lower-carbon or net-zero aligned), or supplier alignment by emissions or spend. Group B (other upstream): emissions reduction or supplier alignment. Group C (downstream, cat. 9–14): emissions reduction, product-use alignment by volume or revenue, product end-of-life alignment, or customer alignment by emissions or revenue.

sub_changes.new: If no target option realistically fits the emissions from customers using your products, you may tackle the same amount of emissions in another category instead, or apply for an exception — which then requires a long-term target for those emissions by 2050, a plan with milestones, and annual reporting.
sub_changes.old: Treated like any other category under the 67% coverage test.
sub_changes.topic: Use of sold products (category 11)
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: category 11 included under the 67% coverage test like any category. V2.0: if no eligible option can reasonably apply to category 11, a company may address an equivalent amount of emissions from a different category through any eligible option, or apply for an exception — which requires a long-term category 11 target to residual levels by 2050, a plan with actions and interim milestones, and annual reporting of category 11 emissions and progress (CNZS-C15.4).

sub_changes.new: Optional for everyone. If you set one, it covers 100% of scope 3 and reaches residual levels, and an alignment target only counts as met when your partners reach zero or near-zero emissions.
sub_changes.old: Required for any net-zero target, covering at least 90% of scope 3 with a target year of 2050 or sooner.
sub_changes.topic: Long-term scope 3 targets (optional)
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: required for net-zero targets, covering at least 90% of scope 3 (C7), target year no later than 2050 (C17). V2.0: optional for all companies (CNZS-C16); if set, cover 100% of scope 3 (C16.1), reach residual levels on applicable net-zero pathways (C16.2), and alignment targets count as met only when partners reach zero or near-zero emissions (C16.3).

sub_changes.new: Category 15 sits outside the 5% test, which runs over categories 1–14 only. Companies with investment emissions below the threshold for the financial-sector standard are recommended — not required — to use that standard when setting targets for them.
sub_changes.old: Counted as part of scope 3 for the 40% trigger and the 67% and 90% coverage tests.
sub_changes.topic: Investments (category 15)
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: category 15 part of total scope 3 for the 40% trigger and the 67% / 90% coverage tests. V2.0: significance and exclusion tests expressed over categories 1–14 (CNZS-C5.7, C14.1, C14.3); Recommendation R9.2: companies with category 15 emissions below the revenue threshold for mandatory use of the Financial Institutions Net-Zero Standard are recommended to apply that Standard when setting targets for them — a recommendation, not a requirement.

sub_changes.new: Required for Category A, optional for Category B. Category B does not even have to report scope 3 in its base-year inventory.
sub_changes.old: Any company whose scope 3 was 40% or more of total emissions; small companies on the near-term route only committed to measure and reduce it.
sub_changes.topic: Who must set scope 3 targets
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: any company whose scope 3 was 40% or more of total emissions (C4); SMEs on the near-term route only committed to measure and reduce scope 3. V2.0: CNZS-C14 and C15 bind Category A and are optional for Category B; Category B not required to report scope 3 in the target base-year inventory (CNZS-C5.2).

implications: Rebuild the scope 3 inventory to the GHG Protocol minimum boundaries, then rank categories 1–14 by share: every category at 5% or more goes into the near-term target.

For each significant category, choose a route deliberately: sector-pathway reduction or volume alignment where commodity pathways exist, supplier alignment elsewhere upstream, and product-use or customer alignment downstream.
Document each exclusion with its reason, tonnes, share of categories 1–14 and mitigation actions, now that the 67% floor and flat 5% exclusion cap are gone.
Define what 'in transition' and 'net-zero aligned' mean for your tier 1 suppliers and customers before choosing an alignment target.
Decide whether to keep a now-optional long-term scope 3 target, and if product-use emissions dominate, prepare the evidence that no eligible option reasonably applies to category 11.

rows.new: Offsets still never count toward targets. New Ongoing Emissions Responsibility framework: voluntary recognition at three levels (Engaged, Advanced, Leadership) covering from 1% to 100% of ongoing emissions; from 2035 Category A companies must support carbon removals equal to at least 1% of ongoing emissions, including a rising share of long-lived removals that is still to be defined.
rows.old: Beyond-value-chain mitigation encouraged but voluntary; offsets never count toward targets.

detail.timing: Recognition is available from V2.0 validation (opens February 1, 2027); participation details are due in the second half of 2026 and the framework launches in 2027; mandatory removals for Category A start in 2035; neutralization applies at the company's net-zero year (2050 at the latest) and after.

detail.applies_to: The credits-never-count rule and net-zero neutralization: all companies. The recognition program: voluntary for all, but everyone must state their intent at validation. Mandatory removals from 2035: Category A only.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged in effect: removals and credits cannot replace real cuts or count toward target progress. Anything used for the new 'ongoing emissions responsibility' program is tracked separately from the inventory and from target progress.
sub_changes.old: Carbon credits could not count as emission reductions toward targets; they were allowed only to neutralize leftover emissions at net-zero or as extra action beyond your own value chain.
sub_changes.topic: Credits still never count toward targets
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: carbon credits must not count as emission reductions toward near-term or long-term targets (C12); permitted only to neutralize residual emissions (C28) or as beyond-value-chain mitigation (R12). V2.0: removals cannot substitute for direct reductions and are prohibited from counting toward target progress (Basis for Conclusions, Minor Issue 18); OER outcomes accounted for separately from the inventory and target progress (C43); reductions, removals or credits used for OER excluded from target implementation (C26.2b).

sub_changes.new: A voluntary recognition program replaces it. Everyone must say at validation whether they will join — a 'no' needs an explanation, and the answer appears on SBTi's dashboard within six months. Recognition is awarded at the end of the cycle, based on progress against targets and the climate contributions delivered at your chosen level.
sub_changes.old: Acting or investing outside your value chain was a recommendation with no defined scale and no SBTi recognition.
sub_changes.topic: From 'beyond value chain' to 'ongoing emissions responsibility'
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: R12 recommendation to act or invest outside the value chain, in addition to targets; no defined scale, no SBTi recognition. V2.0: voluntary OER recognition program (C38–C44); every company states at Target Validation whether it will participate (C38), non-participants submit an explanation (C38.1), intent shown on the SBTi Dashboard within six months (C38.2); recognition assessed and awarded at the End-of-cycle Assessment based on progress against validated targets and delivery of climate contributions under the chosen level (C39).

sub_changes.new: Three levels — Engaged, Advanced and Leadership — differ by how much of your ongoing emissions you cover with climate contributions. The criteria print the percentages: at least 1% of total ongoing scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions (Engaged), 100% of ongoing scope 1 and 2 plus enough scope 3 to reach at least 10% of the total (Advanced), and 100% of all three scopes at Leadership for the largest companies, with everyone else's Leadership level set at 100% of scope 1 and 2 plus scope 3 to reach at least 10%.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: The three recognition levels
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: three levels — Engaged, Advanced and Leadership — 'distinguished by the volume of emissions covered' (Chapter 6); companies pick one and deliver contributions over the near-term target period at the coverage that level requires (C40); the percentages are in the criteria themselves: at least 1% of total ongoing scope 1, scope 2 and scope 3 emissions (Engaged, CNZS-C40.3); 100% of ongoing scope 1 and 2 plus additional scope 3 as necessary to reach at least 10% of the total (Advanced, C40.4); 100% of total ongoing scope 1, 2 and 3 for Category A (Leadership, C40.5), with Category B's Leadership level at 100% of scope 1 and 2 plus scope 3 to reach at least 10% (C40.6); the Executive Summary describes the range as 'from 1% to 100% of ongoing emissions'.

sub_changes.new: Everything you still emit each year, across all scopes, while you are on your reduction pathway — not just what is left at net-zero.
sub_changes.old: Not defined; guidance just spoke of action 'in addition to' targets.
sub_changes.topic: What 'ongoing emissions' means
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: not defined; guidance spoke of emissions 'in addition to' targets. V2.0 Key Terms: 'the GHG emissions across all scopes that continue to be released into the atmosphere within the target timeframe' — what the company still emits each year while on its reduction pathway, not just the residual left at net-zero.

sub_changes.new: Contributions must be verified mitigation outcomes or other eligible climate actions that meet recognized high-integrity criteria and SBTi's own minimum criteria. Both reductions and removals qualify, durable or not, and outcomes must be independently checked after the fact. Further participation details are promised in the second half of 2026.
sub_changes.old: Companies were pointed to SBTi's beyond-value-chain guidance; there were no SBTi integrity criteria.
sub_changes.topic: What contributions qualify
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: R12 pointed to the BVCM guidance; no SBTi integrity criteria. V2.0: climate contributions support only eligible verified mitigation outcomes and/or other eligible climate actions (C41), meeting recognized third-party high-integrity criteria where applicable and SBTi minimum integrity criteria (C42); reductions and removals both qualify, long-lived or not (Executive Summary); a 'verified mitigation outcome' is by definition independently assured ex post (Key Terms); further participation details to follow in the second half of 2026 (FAQ 12).

sub_changes.new: Required for Category A from 2035: support carbon removals equal to at least 1% of your ongoing scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, including a rising share of long-lived removals. The 1% floor is fixed; the long-lived share and how fast it grows are not yet defined. Optional for Category B.
sub_changes.old: Nothing was mandatory before the net-zero year.
sub_changes.topic: Mandatory removals from 2035 (Category A)
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: nothing mandatory before the net-zero year. V2.0 CNZS-C45: 'From 2035, companies shall support eligible carbon removals equal to at least 1% of ongoing scope 1, scope 2, and scope 3 emissions, including a defined and increasing share of long-lived removals'; applicability Category A, optional for Category B; the 1% floor is the published figure and the long-lived share and its growth path are not yet defined; SBTi also marks C45 as an illustrative requirement it will review in the next major revision (Version 3).

sub_changes.new: Required for everyone: at your net-zero year and after, cut all scopes to residual levels and neutralize 100% of what remains with eligible removals delivered in the same year, inside or outside your value chain. Long-lived gases like CO2 must be balanced with long-lived storage (centuries or more); other gases may use short-lived, long-lived or a mix.
sub_changes.old: At the net-zero date and every year after, remove and permanently store carbon to balance any remaining emissions; long-term targets had to cut emissions at least 90%.
sub_changes.topic: Neutralizing what is left at net-zero
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: remove carbon from the atmosphere and permanently store it to counterbalance any unabated emissions at the net-zero target date and every year after (C28); long-term targets cut emissions at least 90% (Standard p.18). V2.0 CNZS-C46 (all companies): at the net-zero target year and thereafter, reduce scope 1–3 to zero or residual levels and neutralize 100% of residual emissions with eligible removals that deliver verified outcomes in the same reporting period and meet the C42 integrity criteria, inside or outside the value chain (C46.1); residual long-lived GHGs neutralized with long-lived removals (storage for centuries to millennia); other residuals may use short-lived, long-lived or a mix (C46.2).

sub_changes.new: You are directly responsible for all your scope 1 residuals, and share responsibility for scope 3 residuals with the partners who report the same emissions — or take it on yourself if they cannot show they have neutralized them. A removal cannot be used twice, and you must report whether the credits are authorized by the host country and adjusted in its national accounts.
sub_changes.old: Not specified.
sub_changes.topic: Who is responsible, and no double use
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: companies take direct responsibility for all scope 1 residuals (C46.3) and for scope 3 residuals jointly with value-chain partners that report the same emissions — or directly where partner neutralization is not demonstrated (C46.4); removals cannot be reused against another residual source (C46.5); companies report whether removal credits are host-country authorized and subject to corresponding adjustments (C46.6).

implications: Keep credits out of your inventory and target-progress numbers — run a separate ledger for the recognition program with volumes, vintages, integrity standard and double-claiming checks.
Decide your answer on joining the recognition program before submitting: a yes or no with reasons is required at validation and appears on SBTi's dashboard.

If you go for recognition, model contribution volumes against the three levels (Engaged at least 1%, Advanced at least 10%, Leadership 100% for Category A and at least 10% for Category B) over the five-year cycle and budget for the independent check.
Category A: start a removals procurement roadmap now, because at least 1% of ongoing scope 1–3 emissions in eligible removals is mandatory from 2035.
Classify residual emissions by gas: long-lived residuals such as CO2 will need long-lived removals at net-zero, which changes the instrument mix compared with the old 'permanent storage' wording.

rows.new: The mandatory five-year review is retired. Instead every target runs on a five-year cycle, with a progress assessment at the end of each cycle and new targets set for the next one. Updated review guidance for V1 targets published August 13, 2026.
rows.old: Mandatory review and re-validation every 5 years.

detail.timing: Review guidance updated August 13, 2026 and extended to financial institutions on October 7, 2026 (V2.1); dashboard statuses effective September 24, 2026, with Commitment and Target Statuses V2.1 (October 7, 2026) defining when a target becomes Expired; about 300 companies' review triggers land by end-2026, with financial-institution triggers deferred to December 31, 2026; V2.0 validation opens February 1, 2027; old-standard submissions close January 31, 2028; next-cycle V2.0 targets for 2030–35 set from 2028.

detail.applies_to: All companies with validated targets. The five-year review rules bind old-standard target holders until they move to V2.0; annual reporting and the end-of-cycle assessment bind all V2.0 users, with the assurance step for Category A only.

sub_changes.new: The mandatory review is retired because every target now runs on a five-year cycle. Near-term targets cover five years from your latest reporting period, with a shorter first period allowed once. Instead of a scheduled review, you must revise targets whenever a significant change makes them non-compliant.
sub_changes.old: Every active target had to be reviewed at least every five years against the latest rules, and updated and revalidated if it no longer complied.
sub_changes.topic: Five-year review becomes five-year cycles
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: review all active targets at least every five years for consistency with the latest criteria; update and revalidate if they no longer conform (C32; Near-Term Criteria C26). V2.0: mandatory review retired because all targets are set on a five-year basis (Main Changes p.8); near-term targets cover five years from the start of the most recent reporting period, shorter first period allowed once (C9.2); in place of a scheduled review, CNZS-C20 requires targets to be revised whenever significant changes (the C8 recalculation triggers) leave them non-conforming.

sub_changes.new: Those rules continue for companies holding old-standard targets, with new flexibilities added in August 2026: companies waiting for V2.0 or a sector standard can ask, case by case, for up to 18 extra months beyond the original update deadline; scope-3-only extensions are allowed; and the review form can be skipped if you already know an update is needed.
sub_changes.old: Your review was triggered at the end of the month five years after your target was last published; the review form was due within 6 months, updated targets within 12 months, and you could skip it if a target year fell within 24 months of the trigger.
sub_changes.topic: Review rules still in force for old targets
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: trigger date = end of the month five years after the latest validated-target publication; review form due within 6 months; updated targets within 12 months; waiver if a target year falls within 24 months of the trigger. Same rules continue for V1.3.1 target holders (Mandatory Five-Year Review Manual V1.1, Aug 2026), plus: companies waiting to move to V2.0 or a Sector Standard may apply, case by case, for an extension until that Standard is published — up to 18 additional months from the original update due date; scope-3-only extensions allowed; review form can be skipped if an update is already known to be needed.

sub_changes.new: Required for everyone: at the end of each cycle, assess and report progress on each target and overall, using your full inventory, the change since the base year, the actions you took and the barriers you hit. Category A must also get the progress data independently checked (recommended for Category B). An SBTi-recognized body runs the assessment within 12 months of the cycle ending.
sub_changes.old: Only annual public progress reporting; no formal assessment of whether you hit the target.
sub_changes.topic: End-of-cycle assessment
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: annual public progress reporting only (C30, C31); no formal assessment of achievement. V2.0 CNZS-C37 (all companies): assess and report progress against each target and in aggregate at cycle end, using the full scope 1–3 inventory, the base-year-to-target-year change, actions taken and material barriers (C37.1–C37.10); Category A obtains at least limited assurance of the progress data (C37.7; recommended for Category B, R37.1); an SBTi-recognized validation body conducts the End-of-cycle Assessment, completed within 12 months of the target timeframe.

sub_changes.new: Still annual, but more prescribed: report the period, your validated targets, progress per target and overall, scope 1 and 2 emissions, actions, barriers and whether the data was independently checked — starting the reporting cycle after validation.
sub_changes.old: Publish your inventory and progress every year.
sub_changes.topic: Annual reporting
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: publish inventory and progress annually (C30). V2.0 CNZS-C36: annual reporting of the period, validated target information, progress per target and in aggregate, scope 1–2 emissions, actions, material barriers and assurance status (C36.1–C36.8), starting in the next reporting cycle after Target Validation.

sub_changes.new: New targets every cycle, with a fresh base year equal to your most recent full-data year. Submit them no earlier than 24 months before and no later than 12 months after the current cycle ends; SBTi strongly encourages submitting before it ends to avoid a gap.
sub_changes.old: You only revalidated if the review found a problem; otherwise targets ran unchanged to the target year.
sub_changes.topic: Setting the next cycle's targets
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: re-validation only if the review found non-conformance; otherwise targets ran unchanged to the target year. V2.0: new base year equal to the most recent year with comprehensive data (C4.2); next-cycle targets submitted no earlier than 24 months before and no later than 12 months after the current timeframe ends (System Overview); SBTi 'strongly encourages' submitting before the current timeframe ends to avoid gaps between targets (Chapter 5).

sub_changes.new: You still set new targets, even when you fell short. Higher emissions at the end of a cycle mean steeper cuts in the next one, and any reduction claim must rest on real changes in your physical inventory. Minimum progress rules for later cycles are still to come.
sub_changes.old: No consequence was defined beyond the five-year review.
sub_changes.topic: What happens if you miss a target
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: no consequence defined beyond the five-year review. V2.0: companies set new targets 'including where there are gaps between emissions and targets'; higher target-year emissions mean steeper cuts next cycle; companies expected to use all available levers and address barriers (Executive Summary); minimum progress criteria for later cycles to be set out in the SBTi Assurance Manual; emissions-reduction claims must rest on changes in the physical inventory (C37.10).

sub_changes.new: Old-standard submissions close January 31, 2028; V2.0 is mandatory from February 1, 2028. If your target year is 2030 or later, keep your targets through the cycle and set V2.0 targets for 2030–35 from 2028. Just over 300 of the 11,600+ companies with validated targets hit their review trigger by end-2026 and can ask for the up-to-18-month extension to land on V2.0.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Moving existing targets to V2.0
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: V1.3.1 stays open for submissions until January 31, 2028; V2.0 mandatory for submissions from February 1, 2028; companies with 2030-or-later target years keep their targets through the cycle and set V2.0 targets for 2030–35 from 2028; just over 300 of the 11,600+ companies with validated targets hit their review trigger by end-2026 and may apply for the up-to-18-month extension to land on V2.0.

sub_changes.new: A new status system went live on SBTi's dashboard on September 24, 2026, with three headline groups — committed to set targets, commitment removed, validated targets — and sub-statuses. 'Target Expired' applies if 12 months pass after your review trigger with no review form or new submission, if a review deadline lapses, or one year after a target year with no new targets.
sub_changes.old: Your public status followed the old Commitment Compliance Policy.
sub_changes.topic: Dashboard statuses (from September 24, 2026)
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: statuses under the Commitment Compliance Policy. V2.0: Commitment and Target Statuses V2.0 (Aug 2026) superseded the Commitment Compliance Policy and went live with the SBTi Dashboard update on September 24, 2026; V2.1, effective October 7, 2026, now governs; three headline categories (Commitment to Set Targets; Commitment Removed; Validated Targets) with sub-statuses; 'Target Expired' applies when 12 months pass from the review trigger date without a completed form or new submission, when a review-set deadline lapses, or one year after a target year with no new targets submitted.

implications: Work out your review trigger date now; if it falls before end-2027 and you plan to move to V2.0, file the review form and apply for the up-to-18-month extension.
If any target year is within 24 months of the trigger date, consider the waiver and go straight to new targets instead of a review.
Start building the end-of-cycle data pack now (progress per target and overall, base-year changes, actions and barriers) and, if Category A, line up assurance with the 12-month assessment window.
Plan on a new base year and fresh targets every five years, and watch the recalculation triggers continuously rather than at a five-year checkpoint.
Check your company's status on the SBTi dashboard under the September 24 changes and confirm nothing is drifting toward 'Target Expired'.

rows.new: V2.0 was published June 11, 2026 and takes effect February 1, 2027, when V2.0 validation opens; V1.3.1 submissions close January 31, 2028. Existing validated targets stay valid for their full cycle and move to V2.0 at the next renewal. Companion policies (Renewal Policy, interpretation and interim accounting guidance, and the Claims Policy, all expected Q4 2026) are published plans, not yet released.
rows.old: V1.3.1 (effective April 14, 2026) was the only route, with no sunset date; validated targets ran on a mandatory five-year review.

detail.timing: V2.0 published June 11, 2026; validation resources October 1, 2026; V2.0 effective and validation opens February 1, 2027; old-standard validations close January 31, 2028 (some SBTi texts say 'end of 2027'); V2.0 mandatory from February 1, 2028; companion policies expected Q4 2026.
