detail.applies_to: Every company in the SBTi system — new submitters and companies with validated old-standard targets; the dates do not differ by category or sector.

sub_changes.new: V2.0 was released June 11, 2026 and takes effect February 1, 2027, the day V2.0 validations open. SBTi documents disagree by one day: the summary of changes says January 31, 2027.
sub_changes.old: The old standard (V1.3.1) was released April 14, 2026 as a minor revision that updated the reduction method to work with more recent base years.
sub_changes.topic: Publication and effective date
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: released April 14, 2026 as a non-substantive revision (updated absolute-contraction method to accommodate more recent base years). V2.0: released June 11, 2026; effective February 1, 2027 per the Standard's version history, the day SBTi Services opens V2.0 validations; the Main Changes document says 'in effect as of 31 January 2027' — a one-day inconsistency.

sub_changes.new: SBTi Services published the V2.0 validation pack on October 1, 2026 and said validation slots open to book from February 1, 2027. From then until January 31, 2028 you can submit under either version.
sub_changes.old: Until January 31, 2027 you can only submit under the old near-term criteria or V1.3.1.
sub_changes.topic: When V2.0 validation opens
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: until January 31, 2027 companies can submit only under Near-Term Criteria V5.3 or CNZS V1.3.1. V2.0: SBTi Services published six V2.0 validation resources on October 1, 2026 (preliminary submission form, preliminary target-setting tool data points, validation schedule, standard operating procedure, validation procedures and a services glossary) and stated that validation slots open to book from February 1, 2027; between February 1, 2027 and January 31, 2028 companies may submit under either version.

sub_changes.new: SBTi documents disagree on the exact date. The formal transition documents close V1.3.1 on January 31, 2028, with V2.0 mandatory from February 1, 2028; the standard's own summary and launch blog say 'until the end of 2027'. Plan for December 31, 2027 to be safe; January 31, 2028 is the formal close.
sub_changes.old: No closing date; V1.3.1 was simply the current standard.
sub_changes.topic: When the old standard closes (SBTi disagrees)
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: no sunset; V1.3.1 was the current standard. V2.0: the formal transition documents (Transition PDF, SBTi Services guide, Main Changes document, SBTi web pages) close V1.3.1 on January 31, 2028, with V2.0 mandatory from February 1, 2028; the Standard's own executive summary and the June 11 launch blog say 'until the end of 2027'; treat December 31, 2027 as the conservative planning date, January 31, 2028 as the formal close.

sub_changes.new: No forced migration: existing targets stay valid for their whole cycle, still subject to the five-year review rules. If your target year is 2030 or later, or your review falls in 2028, SBTi advises keeping current targets and setting V2.0 targets for 2030–35 from 2028. Revalidation is due at the end of the year after your target year (a 2026 target year means December 31, 2027), and anything submitted from February 1, 2028 must use V2.0.
sub_changes.old: Old targets were subject to the mandatory five-year review, triggered at the end of the month five years after last validation, with the review done within six months.
sub_changes.topic: Existing validated targets
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: targets validated under V1 subject to the mandatory five-year review — trigger date at the end of the month five years after the last validation publication, review completed within six months. V2.0: no forced migration; existing targets remain fully valid throughout their cycle, subject to the five-year review provisions; companies with 2030-or-later target years, or a review falling in 2028, advised to keep current targets and set V2.0 targets for the 2030–35 cycle from 2028; re-validation due at the end of the year after the target year (e.g., 2026 target year → due December 31, 2027) or at the review trigger; any submission on or after February 1, 2028 must use V2.0.

sub_changes.new: Companies below the Category A thresholds can ask to be treated as small companies under the old rules. SBTi recommends, but does not require, that old-standard companies get independent assurance of end-of-cycle progress. Company categories, the implementation hierarchy, progress assessment and the removals program are to be opened to old-standard companies through a Renewal Policy expected in Q4 2026.
sub_changes.old: The small-company route was only for companies under the small-company thresholds; no assurance was expected.
sub_changes.topic: Flexibilities for companies staying on V1
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: SME route only for companies meeting SME thresholds; no assurance expectation. V2.0 transition: companies that do not meet the V2.0 Category A thresholds may request SME categorization under V1; SBTi recommends (not requires) that V1 companies adopt third-party assurance for end-of-cycle progress reporting; company categorization, the implementation hierarchy, progress assessment and OER to be made available to V1 companies, with a Renewal Policy (expected Q4 2026) setting out how.

sub_changes.new: Required for everyone: the near-term base year is your most recent year with complete emissions data, and you set a new one at every cycle renewal. No maximum age is stated.
sub_changes.old: A historical base year was allowed as long as it was 2015 or later, though the April 2026 revision already pushed companies toward the most recent data.
sub_changes.topic: How recent the base year must be
sub_changes.specifics: V1.3.1: historical base year permitted (no earlier than 2015); V1.3.1 (April 2026) already updated the absolute-contraction method so targets are set from a base year reflecting the most recent emissions data. V2.0: the near-term base year is the most recent year with comprehensive emissions data (C4.1, all companies); a new base year is set at each cycle's renewal (C4.2); no maximum base-year age stated.

sub_changes.new: All 'expected', none released: final target-setting methods and pathways in Q4 2026 (feedback closed July 31, 2026); a Renewal Policy, interpretation guidance and interim guidance on certificates and contracts, all Q4 2026; a Claims Policy in Q4 2026; recognition of removals-program instruments expected Q4 2026, with that program launching in 2027.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Companion policies still to come
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: all 'expected', not committed — final target-setting methods and pathways in Q4 2026 (feedback closed July 31, 2026); a Renewal Policy in Q4 2026 setting out how V2.0's implementation, end-of-cycle assessment and OER elements become accessible to all companies; V2.0 interpretation guidance in Q4 2026; interim accounting and reporting guidance on market instruments in Q4 2026; a Claims Policy in Q4 2026; recognition of OER instruments expected Q4 2026, with the OER framework launching in 2027.

sub_changes.new: Optional. Since July 14, 2026 SBTi Services offers a structured, evidence-based review of where you stand and what you need to do to submit under V2.0, open to any company with validated targets under a previous version.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: V2.0 Readiness Assessment (optional)
sub_changes.specifics: V2.0: announced July 14, 2026 by SBTi Services; a structured, evidence-based assessment and report of where a company stands and the steps needed to submit under V2.0; open to companies with validated targets under any previous version; optional.

implications: Anything submitted before February 1, 2027 must use the old rules, so run V2.0 preparation in parallel rather than waiting for the portal.
Use December 31, 2027 as your internal deadline for any old-standard submission; the formal close is January 31, 2028, but SBTi's own summaries say 'end of 2027'.
Work out your five-year review trigger date and target-year revalidation dates now — those, not V2.0's effective date, decide when you must move.
Hold decisions that depend on the Renewal Policy, interpretation guidance or interim certificate guidance until Q4 2026, but start scoping assurance now.
If you hold validated targets, consider the Readiness Assessment before the Q4 2026 guidance lands so gaps are known ahead of the February 1, 2027 opening.

rows.new: V2.0 itself changes little: FLAG targets stay separate (C9.8), the inventory must follow the GHG Protocol Land Sector and Removals Standard (C5.5; effective January 1, 2027), and FLAG Guidance V1.2 still decides who must set them. The substantive change will come from FLAG Standard V2.0 — call for evidence open until October 8, 2026, publication expected by or before Q1 2028.
rows.old: Under FLAG Guidance V1 (mandatory since April 30, 2023; V1.2 from March 2026), companies in FLAG-designated sectors or with FLAG emissions of 20% or more of scopes 1–3 must set separate FLAG targets plus a public no-deforestation commitment.

detail.timing: FLAG Guidance V1.2 effective March 19, 2026; GHG Protocol Land Sector and Removals Standard effective January 1, 2027 (per SBTi); V2.0's FLAG rules apply to V2.0 submissions from February 1, 2027; FLAG V2.0 call for evidence closes October 8, 2026; FLAG V2.0 publication expected by or before Q1 2028; existing FLAG guidance valid alongside the old standard until end of January 2028.

detail.applies_to: Companies in FLAG-designated sectors or with land-related emissions of 20% or more of scopes 1–3; the land-sector accounting rule binds all Category A and B companies with any land, bioenergy or removals in their inventory.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged by V2.0. The same sector list and 20% threshold apply, though SBTi says all FLAG thresholds will be reconsidered in the FLAG revision now under way.
sub_changes.old: Since April 30, 2023: companies in land-heavy sectors — forestry and paper, food production, food and beverage processing, food retail, tobacco — or any company whose land-related emissions are 20% or more of its total scopes 1, 2 and 3, must set a separate FLAG target when they submit.
sub_changes.topic: Who must set land-based (FLAG) targets
sub_changes.specifics: FLAG-C1: companies in FLAG-designated sectors (forest and paper products; food production — agricultural and animal source; food and beverage processing; food and staples retailing; tobacco), or in any sector with FLAG-related emissions of 20% or more of total scopes 1, 2 and 3, must set a FLAG target upon (re)submission — required since April 30, 2023. V2.0: unchanged; the FLAG V2.0 Terms of Reference keep the same sector list and threshold but note that the appropriateness of all FLAG thresholds will be considered during the revision.

sub_changes.new: Now you must add the FLAG target no later than your mandatory five-year review submission, and should do it as soon as possible. This came from an urgent update to the FLAG guidance effective March 19, 2026, not from V2.0.
sub_changes.old: If you already had validated targets and crossed the FLAG threshold, you had six months after the GHG Protocol's land-sector standard was published to add a FLAG target.
sub_changes.topic: Deadline when you already hold non-FLAG targets
sub_changes.specifics: FLAG V1.1: a company with validated non-FLAG targets that met FLAG-C1 had to add a FLAG target within six months of the GHG Protocol Land Sector and Removals Standard's publication. FLAG V1.2 (effective March 19, 2026, via an urgent revision, not V2.0): such companies 'shall set a FLAG target at the latest as part of their mandatory five-year review submission, and should set it as soon as possible'.

sub_changes.new: In effect now for new submissions. The commitment's target date must be within two years of submitting your FLAG target and no later than December 31, 2030, with a cutoff date of 2020 or earlier (or at most three years before your first FLAG submission). It covers seven commodities, and within 12 months of validation you publish the commitment, your commodity assessment and your delivery plan.
sub_changes.old: A public no-deforestation commitment with a 2025 target date was required; a cutoff date of 2020 or earlier was recommended.
sub_changes.topic: No-deforestation commitment
sub_changes.specifics: FLAG V1.0/V1.1 (FLAG-C4): public no-deforestation commitment with a 2025 target date; 2020-or-earlier cutoff recommended. FLAG V1.2: target date no later than two years after FLAG target submission and never later than December 31, 2030; cutoff recommended 2020 or earlier and, if later, no more than three years before the FLAG submission; commodities per Appendix A (cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soy, timber); within 12 months of validation the company publishes the commitment, its commodity assessment and how it will deliver; in effect immediately for new submissions.

sub_changes.new: Required for everyone: account for land-based emissions, bioenergy emissions, and both natural and technological removals under the GHG Protocol Land Sector and Removals Standard, keeping emissions and removals separate. SBTi puts that standard's effective date at January 1, 2027.
sub_changes.old: Until the GHG Protocol's land-sector standard took effect, FLAG companies could use either its 2022 draft or the final version.
sub_changes.topic: Land-sector accounting in the inventory
sub_changes.specifics: Before: until the GHG Protocol Land Sector and Removals Standard took effect, FLAG companies could use either the 2022 draft guidance or the final Standard. V2.0 C5.5 (all companies): account for and report FLAG emissions, bioenergy emissions, and biogenic and technological removals in line with the GHG Protocol Land Sector and Removals Standard, keeping emissions and removals separate; SBTi states the Standard's effective date as January 1, 2027 (FLAG Guidance V1.2; FLAG sector page).

sub_changes.new: Same rule in V2.0: FLAG targets are set and reported separately and never merged with other targets. Scope 3 activities already covered by a FLAG or other sector target need no extra V2.0 scope 3 target, and sector standards take precedence where they modify V2.0.
sub_changes.old: Land-based and energy/industry targets and accounting were kept separate.
sub_changes.topic: FLAG targets stay separate
sub_changes.specifics: FLAG Guidance V1: keep FLAG and energy/industry (non-FLAG) targets and accounting separate. V2.0: same rule carried in as C9.8 (FLAG targets set and reported separately, never aggregated with non-FLAG targets); scope 3 activities already covered by FLAG (or other Sector Standard) targets need no additional V2.0 scope 3 target (§3.4); applicable Sector Standards take precedence where they modify V2.0 requirements (§B.2).

sub_changes.new: SBTi is rewriting the FLAG standard: a call for evidence runs until October 8, 2026, and publication is expected by or before Q1 2028. It aims to bring V2.0 concepts into FLAG, add commodity pathways and revisit all thresholds, with at least one 60-day public consultation along the way.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: FLAG Standard V2.0 revision (in progress)
sub_changes.specifics: FLAG V2.0: Terms of Reference V1.0 published July 30, 2026; call for evidence open from July 30 to October 8, 2026 (10 weeks); scope: bring V2.0 concepts into FLAG (alignment targets, implementation hierarchy), enable long-term FLAG targets, ensure interoperability with the Land Sector and Removals Standard, add at least five commodity pathways, explore action-based targets, and reconsider all FLAG thresholds; at least one 60-day public consultation with parallel pilot testing; publication expected by or before Q1 2028.

sub_changes.new: Not stated. SBTi says existing sector guidance including FLAG stays valid alongside the old rules until the end of January 2028, and FLAG companies keep following FLAG Guidance V1.2 while the revision runs (12 months or more). How FLAG V1.2 attaches to V2.0 submissions from February 2027, and what governs FLAG after January 2028 if FLAG V2.0 is not out, is an open question.
sub_changes.old: The existing FLAG guidance sat alongside the old standard and near-term criteria.
sub_changes.topic: Which FLAG rules apply under V2.0 (open point)
sub_changes.specifics: Before: FLAG Guidance V1.x applied alongside V1.3.1 and the Near-Term Criteria. V2.0: SBTi says existing sector guidance including FLAG remains valid alongside V1.3.1 and the Near-Term Criteria until the end of January 2028, and FLAG companies continue under FLAG Guidance V1.2 while the revision runs (12 months or more); how FLAG V1.2 attaches to V2.0 submissions from February 2027, and what governs FLAG after January 2028 if FLAG V2.0 is not yet out, is not stated — an open point.

implications: Run both FLAG tests (the sector list, and whether land-related emissions are 20% or more of scopes 1–3) on your current inventory, noting the threshold is under review.
If you hold non-FLAG targets and cross the threshold, add the FLAG target as soon as possible and no later than your five-year review submission.
Move land-sector, bioenergy and removals accounting onto the GHG Protocol Land Sector and Removals Standard, mandatory under V2.0 and effective January 1, 2027, for the FY2027 inventory.

If FLAG applies, recheck your no-deforestation commitment: 2020 cutoff, target date within two years of submission and by December 31, 2030, delivery documentation published within 12 months of validation.
Respond to the FLAG V2.0 call for evidence by October 8, 2026, and do not assume FLAG rules will be settled before the new standard lands by Q1 2028.

detail.applies_to: Every company reporting a corporate inventory under GHG Protocol, all sectors and sizes; no thresholds proposed.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: no. Equity share would be removed as a consolidation option for everyone. Stakes in companies you control financially are counted in full; stakes you do not control move to your scope 3 investments category in proportion to your ownership.
sub_changes.old: Yes. You could consolidate emissions by your percentage ownership in each operation (equity share) or by control. Few companies did: about 2% of those reporting to CDP in 2023.
sub_changes.topic: Can we still use the equity share approach?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Corporate Standard (2004) Chapter 3 lets companies consolidate under either the equity share approach or a control approach (financial or operational). Proposed (Corporate Standard Phase 1 Progress Update, December 2025): eliminate equity share; rationale cites that only 2% of companies disclosing to CDP in 2023 used it. Equity in entities under financial control consolidates at 100%; equity in entities not under financial control is reported in scope 3 Category 15 (investments) by percentage ownership. Provisional: 'subject to change prior to public consultation' (consolidated draft estimated Q2 2027).

sub_changes.new: Proposed: financial control becomes the recommended default for everyone, defined simply as whatever you consolidate in your financial statements. Operational control stays as an alternative with a rewritten definition based on the 'power or practical ability' to direct an operation's day-to-day activities, particularly those affecting emissions.
sub_changes.old: Your choice between financial control (you direct financial and operating policies for economic benefit) and operational control (you have full authority to set operating policies). Neither was preferred.
sub_changes.topic: Which control approach should we use?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Chapter 3 defines financial control as the ability to direct financial and operating policies with a view to economic benefit, and operational control as 'full authority to introduce and implement its operating policies'; no approach is preferred. Proposed: companies 'should apply the financial control consolidation approach'; 'A company has financial control over an entity or operation if it consolidates the latter in its financial statements' (GAAP-agnostic). Operational control retained: 'the power or practical ability to direct or implement the latter's policies, processes, or day-to-day activities of the operation, particularly those that impact the operation's greenhouse gas emissions', regardless of legal ownership; in multi-party arrangements the entity with the greatest such power holds operational control. Key terms unfinalized.

sub_changes.new: Proposed recommendation: if the financial-control inventory does not fairly present your emissions, you should also account for operations you run but do not consolidate financially, and report those figures on their own, outside your inventory totals.
sub_changes.old: Not addressed. You picked one approach and reported under it.
sub_changes.topic: What if financial control misses operations we run?
sub_changes.specifics: Proposed (December 2025 Progress Update): 'when financial control fails to provide a [fair presentation / sufficient representation] of their GHG emissions, companies should separately account for and report on all required emissions from entities, operations, and assets under the reporting company's operational control that are not under financial control.' These additional emissions are presented separately and not included in total inventory figures. The bracketed wording signals that the test itself is unsettled. Current standards: no equivalent recommendation.

sub_changes.new: Proposed requirement for everyone: disclose the approach chosen. Companies that do not follow the financial-control recommendation, or do not add the operational-control figures, must disclose their rationale, including the results of a screening comparison between what they control financially and what they control operationally.
sub_changes.old: You had to state which approach you used. No justification was needed for choosing one approach over another.
sub_changes.topic: Do we have to explain our choice?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Corporate Standard Chapters 3 and 9 require disclosure of the consolidation approach used; no rationale required. Proposed: 'Companies shall disclose the chosen consolidation approach. Companies choosing not to apply the recommendations to consolidate emissions based on financial control and/or separately report emissions under operational control (not already included under financial control) shall disclose their rationale for choosing a different approach'; 'The rationale should include the outcomes of a screening assessment comparing the entities, operations, and assets under the reporting company's financial control and operational control.'

sub_changes.new: Open. The working group still has to write rules for investment entities, redo the leased-asset guidance and produce examples for joint operations and associates under the new financial-control definition. Expect this text in the consultation draft.
sub_changes.old: Leased assets were classified using worked examples tied to the chosen approach; joint ventures and associates followed the equity-share or control rules.
sub_changes.topic: Leases, joint ventures and investment entities
sub_changes.specifics: Pending items listed in the December 2025 Progress Update — financial control: 'Requirements/guidance for investment entities will be developed'; 'Guidance on categorizing leased assets will be revised'; examples of how accounting categories such as joint operations and associates are consolidated under U.S. GAAP and/or IFRS will be developed, plus reporting requirements; operational control: definitions of 'greatest power' and 'ability' to be finalized, leased-asset guidance revised, examples developed. Current: Corporate Standard Chapter 3 and its leasing appendix govern. Nothing final; text expected in the consolidated draft (estimated Q2 2027).

sub_changes.new: The stated aim is alignment with financial reporting, so your emissions boundary matches your consolidated accounts and becomes comparable across companies. GHG Protocol has also asked its board to consider stating that companies under other mandatory regimes follow those regimes' requirements.
sub_changes.old: Disclosure regimes generally accepted whatever boundary you chose, so companies on different approaches were hard to compare.
sub_changes.topic: How this lines up with disclosure rules
sub_changes.specifics: Rationale in the December 2025 Progress Update: alignment between GHG and financial accounting, enhanced comparability, standardization, and interoperability with external programs (IFRS S1 and S2, ESRS E1 and SBTi are named). Pending for the ISB: a program applicability statement that 'reporters for other programs should follow the requirements of those programs (e.g., mandatory preparers for IFRS S2, ESRS E1).' ISO experts joined the Technical Working Groups in Q1 2026; the Phase 1 text predates that integration.

implications: Map your financial consolidation perimeter against your current emissions boundary and quantify the gap; that is the inventory you would report under the proposed default.
If you use equity share today, plan a full rebase: controlled entities move to 100%, minority stakes move to scope 3 investments.
If you prefer operational control, start documenting the 'power or practical ability' test for each site so the rationale disclosure is ready.
List joint ventures, associates and leased assets now; the rules for them are still being written and will shape your consultation response.
Hold formal comments until the consolidated consultation opens; GHG Protocol will not process feedback submitted before then.

detail.applies_to: Every company claiming conformance with the corporate standard, all sectors; a lighter tier for smaller companies outside mandatory disclosure regimes is proposed but undecided.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: yes, required for every company claiming conformance with the corporate standard. The change would bring the corporate rulebook into line with the major disclosure regimes and target-setting programs, which already expect scope 3.
sub_changes.old: No. Scope 3 (value-chain emissions) was optional under the corporate inventory rules; only companies that chose to follow the stand-alone value-chain standard had to report it.
sub_changes.topic: Do we have to report scope 3 at all?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Corporate Standard Chapter 4 — 'Scope 3 is an optional reporting category'; 'Companies shall separately account for and report on scopes 1 and 2 at a minimum'; the Scope 3 Standard (2011) requires scope 3 only of companies conforming to it. Proposed (Corporate Standard Phase 1 Progress Update, December 2025): require scope 3 accounting and reporting for Corporate Standard conformance, aligning with IFRS S2, ESRS E1, ISO 14064-1:2018, GRI and SBTi. Provisional; subject to change before the consolidated consultation draft (estimated Q2 2027).

sub_changes.new: Proposed requirement: at least 95% of your required scope 3 emissions. You may leave out whole categories or activities as long as everything excluded adds up to no more than 5%, and tiny sources count toward that same 5%.
sub_changes.old: All of it in principle. You had to account for every scope 3 emission and disclose and justify anything left out, using judgement about relevance rather than a number.
sub_changes.topic: How much of scope 3 must we include?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Scope 3 Standard Table 3.1 — 'Companies shall account for all scope 3 emissions and disclose and justify any exclusions'; per-category minimum boundaries in Table 5.4. Proposed (Corporate Standard Progress Update, December 2025; Scope 3 Progress Update, March 2026, Revision B1): 'Companies shall account for and report at least 95% of total required scope 3 emissions'; 'Companies shall not exclude more than 5% of required scope 3 emissions (the 5% exclusion threshold)'; exclusions may be a category or activities within a category; de minimis exclusions count within the 5%. Recorded support for B1: 87%. Companies 'should' include relevant emissions within the 5% and optional emissions where relevant.

sub_changes.new: Proposed requirement: every year, estimate 100% of your required scope 3 emissions so you can show the excluded part is under 5%. A rough 'hotspot' screen using any estimation method is allowed for this purpose, and exclusions must carry a standard notation.
sub_changes.old: A written justification was enough; no number had to be put on what was left out.
sub_changes.topic: How do we prove our exclusions are small enough?
sub_changes.specifics: Proposed (Scope 3 Progress Update, March 2026): Revision B2 — companies 'shall quantify total required scope 3 emissions to justify exclusions', annually, using any method (87% support); Revision B3 defines hotspot analysis as 'high-level quantification' to identify relative magnitude, permitting 'any calculation or estimation method' (98% support in the post-meeting survey); Revision B6 — 'Companies shall use specific notation to identify exclusions in disclosures' (mark a wholly excluded category 'excluded' or 'X'; partial exclusions within a category shall not use that notation; 100% TWG support). Current: Scope 3 Standard requires disclosure and justification of exclusions but sets no quantification duty.

sub_changes.new: Proposed requirement: break scope 3 down by data type (for example supplier-specific activity data versus spend-based estimates) using set classification rules, and label scope 3 data 'verified', 'partially verified' or 'not verified'. The verification label applies only to companies that have some verification done.
sub_changes.old: You described your data types, sources and quality in words for each category and could state the share calculated from supplier data. No verification label existed.
sub_changes.topic: Must we label data quality and verification?
sub_changes.specifics: Proposed (Scope 3 Progress Update, March 2026): Revision A1 — 'Companies shall disaggregate scope 3 emissions using the classification rules' (80% support); Annex A Option 1 differentiates specific activity data and/or specific emission factors from spend-based calculations with an 'Unclassified' tier, Option 2 combines data source and calculation method; rules 'still pending finalization'. Revision A2 — report whether scope 3 data was third-party verified using labels (1) Verified, (2) Partially verified, (3) Not verified (87% support); applies only to companies that verify some or all emissions; alignment with ISO 14065:2020 under consideration. Current: Scope 3 Standard Chapter 11 requires a description of data types, sources and quality per category and the percentage of emissions calculated from supplier data.

sub_changes.new: Proposed requirement: report required and optional scope 3 emissions as two distinct figures. 'Minimum boundary' is renamed 'required scope 3 emissions'; the 95% test applies only to the required part, and optional emissions never count toward the 5% allowance.
sub_changes.old: Each of the 15 categories had a 'minimum boundary' of what you had to include plus optional extras; required and optional amounts could be mixed in one figure.
sub_changes.topic: Required versus optional scope 3 emissions
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Scope 3 Standard Table 5.4 sets a minimum boundary per category with optional elements. Proposed (Scope 3 Progress Update, March 2026): Revision B7 — 'Companies shall report required scope 3 emissions separately from optional scope 3 emissions' (100% TWG support); terminology 'required (formerly minimum boundary) scope 3 emissions'; the 95% threshold applies to required emissions only and optional emissions sit outside the 5% exclusion cap; Revision B9 keeps the justified exclusion for downstream emissions of intermediate products where end use is unknown. Category-by-category required boundaries are under Phase 2 review.

sub_changes.new: Open. The working group recommended that eligible smaller companies not subject to mandatory climate disclosure report at least their three most relevant scope 3 categories, but the board has not yet decided whether to allow different reporting levels by company type.
sub_changes.old: No size-based tiers; the same optional status applied to everyone.
sub_changes.topic: Is there relief for small and medium companies?
sub_changes.specifics: December 2025 Progress Update, pending ISB review: 'Eligible SMEs shall report at least the three most relevant scope 3 categories'; 'Eligible SMEs should report all scope 3 categories'; eligibility limited to companies not subject to mandatory climate disclosure rules; the ISB 'is considering broader questions about the role of GHG Protocol in defining different levels of reporting for different types of organizations'. No SME definition or size threshold has been proposed. Current standards contain no SME tier.

implications: Treat scope 3 as a required part of the inventory from now; budget for annual estimation of all categories, including those you intend to exclude.
Tag every scope 3 data point with its data type and verification status so the proposed classification and labels can be produced without rework.
Rebuild exclusion documentation around a quantified 5% test rather than a relevance narrative, and keep the hotspot calculations as evidence.
Split required from optional scope 3 figures in your systems now; the two would be reported as distinct totals.
If you are a smaller company outside mandatory disclosure rules, watch for the board's decision on a reduced scope 3 tier before scoping work.

rows.new: Proposed hard caps: at most 1% of scope 1 and 1% of scope 2 may be excluded (scope 2 cap still under review).
rows.old: Qualitative 'completeness' principle.

detail.timing: Provisional (December 2025); scope 2 cap under review by the electricity working group; consultation estimated Q2 2027; publication estimated Q4 2028; no effective date.

detail.applies_to: Every company reporting under the corporate standard; the caps apply per scope with no size exemption proposed.

sub_changes.new: Proposed requirement for everyone: exclude no more than 1% of scope 1 and no more than 1% of scope 2, so roughly 99% of each must be in the inventory. The scope 2 figure is still being checked with the electricity working group.
sub_changes.old: No number. The completeness principle asked you to cover all sources within your chosen boundary and to disclose and justify any specific exclusions.
sub_changes.topic: How much of scope 1 and 2 can we leave out?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Corporate Standard Chapter 1, completeness principle — 'Account for and report on all GHG emission sources and activities within the chosen inventory boundary. Disclose and justify any specific exclusions.' Proposed (Corporate Standard Phase 1 Progress Update, December 2025): a '1% quantitative exclusion threshold for scope 1 and a 1% quantitative exclusion threshold for scope 2' for justifiable exclusions; the scope 2 threshold is 'under review with the Scope 2 TWG'. Rationale: move from a qualitative, principles-based approach to a 'more prescriptive and quantitative approach'. Provisional, subject to change before the Q2 2027 consultation draft.

sub_changes.new: Proposed requirement: estimate your total scope 1 and total scope 2 emissions so the excluded share can be shown to sit under 1%, using any estimation method. Each exclusion must still be disclosed and justified.
sub_changes.old: A qualitative justification; no estimate of the excluded amount was required.
sub_changes.topic: How do we show an exclusion is under 1%?
sub_changes.specifics: Proposed (December 2025 Progress Update): companies must quantify total emissions to justify exclusions but 'may use any method to estimate total emissions to justify exclusions'; must 'disclose and justify any exclusion'; companies 'should report total scope 1 emissions and total scope 2 emissions'. The thresholds apply per scope, not to a combined scope 1 plus scope 2 figure. Current: no quantification duty; narrative justification only.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: the word 'chosen' is dropped, so completeness refers to the inventory boundary the standard prescribes. This reflects the move to fixed rules on scope 3 and exclusion caps rather than company judgement. Four other principles get clarifying edits.
sub_changes.old: Completeness referred to all sources 'within the chosen inventory boundary', leaving the boundary itself to company choice.
sub_changes.topic: Completeness principle wording
sub_changes.specifics: Current text (2004): 'Account for and report on all GHG emission sources and activities within the chosen inventory boundary. Disclose and justify any specific exclusions.' Proposed: 'Account for and report on all GHG emissions, from sources and activities within the inventory boundary' — 'chosen' removed because 'proposed updates to requirements for defining the inventory boundary are moving in the direction of more prescriptiveness (e.g., required scope 3 emissions reporting)'. Other proposed principle edits: consistency expanded to comparisons 'over time, between divisions within the company, and across multiple companies where relevant'; transparency reorganized around an audit trail for internal reviewers and external verifiers; accuracy gains guidance on conservative estimates where uncertainty is high; relevance gains materiality guidance.

sub_changes.new: No. Proposed guidance will explain how materiality is used by disclosure regimes, but the standard would not set accounting or reporting requirements based on materiality. The quantitative caps, not materiality, decide exclusions.
sub_changes.old: The relevance principle guided what to include; materiality as used by disclosure regimes was not addressed.
sub_changes.topic: Does 'materiality' now decide what we report?
sub_changes.specifics: December 2025 Progress Update: working draft revisions to the relevance principle guidance 'including supplemental text on materiality' are underway for the consultation draft; no change to the principle's definition; 'The current proposed revisions under development to the relevance principle do not imply the establishment of any accounting or reporting requirements on the basis of materiality (nor do they preclude them).' Materiality in the verification context is deferred to Phase 2 (verification and assurance, current Chapter 10).

sub_changes.new: Not yet proposed. Tracking emissions over time and the verification chapter are Phase 2 topics; nothing on recalculation thresholds or mandatory assurance has been published.
sub_changes.old: You set your own significance threshold for recalculating the base year; external verification was encouraged, not required.
sub_changes.topic: Base years, recalculation and assurance
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Corporate Standard Chapter 5 leaves the significance threshold for base-year recalculation to the company; Chapter 10 describes verification without requiring it. December 2025 Progress Update: 'Updates related to the topic of verification and assurance (current Corporate Standard chapter 10) will be considered during phase 2 of revisions'; 'Tracking emissions over time' is assigned to Phase 2 (Subgroup 1). Not stated: any recalculation threshold or assurance requirement.

implications: Quantify every scope 1 and scope 2 source you currently exclude, including small sites and refrigerants, and test the totals against a 1% cap per scope.
Replace qualitative exclusion notes with a documented estimate of the excluded share and the method used.
Review de minimis policies that rely on a percentage above 1%; they would no longer be defensible under the proposal.
Keep base-year and assurance policies unchanged for now but flag them for the Phase 2 proposals.

rows.new: The technical working group has now agreed to put forward a SINGLE proposal rather than two competing methods. The proposed market-based method uses hourly matching but explicitly not 24/7 certificate matching, with deliverability defined as a plausible physical connection and incrementality recommended but not required (though you would disclose your incremental share). Whether market-based reporting is required or optional is still open, and reporting would be optional below a size or load threshold. The standards board considers the recommendations on December 15, 2026.
rows.old: Report both location-based and market-based figures; annual-basis certificates support market-based claims.

detail.timing: Consultation closed January 31, 2026; feedback summaries published July 29 and August 25, 2026; GHG Protocol published a two-method direction of travel on October 16, 2026; a technical working group workshop was held October 20-22, 2026 in Washington DC and its outcomes were published with a newest document dated November 10, 2026. Decision calendar from those outcomes: subgroup recommendations to the full working group November 23-24, 2026, materials to the standards board by December 1, and the board considering the secretariat's recommendations December 15, 2026. A second workshop is expected in early 2027 and public consultation on the combined draft is targeted for Q2 2027. All switchover dates remain to be determined; the phase-in years in the outcomes document are bracketed and illustrative, not adopted.

detail.applies_to: Any company buying electricity and using certificates, supplier contracts or power purchase agreements in its market-based scope 2 figure; exemptions for smaller users were proposed but no threshold was set.

sub_changes.new: Undecided. The consultation draft proposed that every contractual instrument match consumption in the same hour, with exemptions for smaller users. Support was low in GHG Protocol's own summary; its own summary records 22% of all respondents and 12% of companies in support, with 82% of companies giving it low or no support. The board has asked for further work on multiple market-based reporting approaches instead of one rule.
sub_changes.old: No. Certificates and contracts only had to be issued and retired as close as possible to the period of consumption, which in practice meant annual matching.
sub_changes.topic: Must certificates match our use hour by hour?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Scope 2 Guidance (2015) Chapter 7 Quality Criteria — instruments 'issued and redeemed as close as possible to the period of energy consumption'. Consultation draft (October 20, 2025 to January 31, 2026) Quality Criterion 4, section 5.1.1: 'All contractual instruments used in the market-based method for scope 2 accounting shall be issued and redeemed for the same hour as the energy consumption to which the instrument is applied'; load profiles may estimate hourly data. Feedback: executive summary (July 29, 2026) reports 'low support' overall; the full summary itself records these: 22% support overall (n=909) and 12% among companies with 82% low or no support (section 10.2, Question 71), and 84% of those who raised concerns preferring 'may' over 'shall' (section 10.4, Question 74). ISB 'called for further work on multiple market-based method reporting approaches that reflect different theories of change.'

sub_changes.new: Undecided. The draft proposed that smaller users — below a consumption threshold per grid region of 5, 10 or 50 GWh a year, or qualifying as a small or medium enterprise — could keep monthly or annual matching. Most reporting companies would have been exempt while most grid load would be covered.
sub_changes.old: No exemptions needed; there was no hourly rule.
sub_changes.topic: Who would be exempt from hourly matching?
sub_changes.specifics: Draft section 5.3.1 and section 6: four exemption options — (1) 'Companies with annual consumption up to [X] GWh/year in a deliverable market boundary may use a monthly or annual accounting interval'; (2) SME categorization (pending SBTi definition); (3) threshold OR SME; (4) threshold AND SME; Question 70 offered 5, 10 or 50 GWh. Pre-consultation overview: 'a majority of CDP reporting companies would be exempt from requirements to hourly match, while the vast majority of electricity load on the grid would still be subject to the hourly matching requirement.' Executive summary: 'broad support' for exemptions and the legacy clause. No threshold decided.

sub_changes.new: Undecided. The draft proposed that instruments come from generation deliverable to your load, using defined market boundaries (for example zonal price markets in Europe, provinces in Canada, grid regions in China), with three options still open for the United States. Support was low among companies (media tallies put it near 19%) and higher among NGOs and governments.
sub_changes.old: Certificates had to come from the 'same market' as the consuming operations, with 'market' left undefined.
sub_changes.topic: Must the power plant be able to deliver to us?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Scope 2 Guidance Quality Criteria — instruments sourced from the same market as the consuming operations. Draft Quality Criterion 5, section 5.1.2: 'All contractual instruments used in the market-based method shall be sourced from generation that is deemed deliverable to the consuming load'; boundaries listed for zonal markets (Australia, Brazil, ENTSO-E Europe), Canada (provincial grids), China (grid company territories), Africa (regional power pools), elsewhere the smaller of country or synchronous grid; US options (Question 69): eGRID regions, DOE 45V regions, or wholesale market/balancing authority. Alternates: nodal price ratio below 1.05, or contracted exclusive transmission. Feedback: executive summary 'low support' among companies, 'plurality support' among NGOs, government, GHG programs, academia, consultants and data providers; media-reported figures 30% overall, 19% companies.

sub_changes.new: Proposed and broadly supported: where no residual mix exists you would use a fossil-only grid factor or a default fossil fuel factor; a plain grid-average factor would no longer be allowed in the market-based figure. Residual mix is redefined to strip out claimed certificates and allocated public supply.
sub_changes.old: Companies without instruments used the residual mix where available; otherwise a grid-average factor was commonly used.
sub_changes.topic: What if no residual mix factor exists?
sub_changes.specifics: Draft section 5.1.4 (Quality Criterion 9): residual mix is 'a residual emission factor characterizing the GHG intensity of electricity, within the relevant market boundary and time interval, not claimed through contractual instruments or allocated via Standard Supply Service'. Section 5.1.5: 'In cases where a residual mix is not available, reporting organizations shall use a fossil-based emission factor that reflects electricity generation within the relevant market boundary'; failing that, an authoritative default (IPCC or government coal, gas or oil factor); 'Generic location-based average grid emission factors shall not be used.' New Criterion 6: reporters may claim up to their pro rata share of Standard Supply Service generation. Executive summary: 'many respondents expressed support' for these updates.

sub_changes.new: Proposed and contested: a hierarchy that prioritises the most precise location, then the finest time interval, and consumption-based over production-based factors, with a duty to use the most precise 'accessible' factor — free, public and credible. Respondents split about 40% for and 42–44% against the hierarchy and the duty; 80% backed the definition of 'accessible'.
sub_changes.old: Use the most representative grid-average factor; no fixed hierarchy of location or time precision.
sub_changes.topic: Which grid factor for the location-based figure?
sub_changes.specifics: Draft section 4: 'use the most precise location-based emission factor accessible for which activity data is also available'; spatial precision first, then temporal granularity (hourly, monthly, annual); consumption-based factors prioritized because they 'account for imported and exported power between regions'. Full feedback summary v1.1 (August 25, 2026): hierarchy (Question 23) 40% support, 17% neutral, 44% low or no support; most-precise-accessible requirement (Question 44) 40% / 18% / 42%, with companies 30%, industry groups 25%, governments 82%; definition of 'accessible' (Question 35) 80% / 13% / 7%; 84% of opponents cited administrative, data-management and audit burden. Dual reporting of location- and market-based figures is retained.

sub_changes.new: Not set. The draft spoke of publication in late 2027 followed by a multi-year phase-in, asking companies which reporting year from 2027 to beyond 2030 they could be ready for. Scope 2 now moves into the consolidated standard consulted on in Q2 2027 and published around Q4 2028, so any effective date comes later still. Existing contracts were promised a legacy clause whose terms are unwritten. The November 2026 workshop outcomes put illustrative — explicitly bracketed and NOT adopted — phase-in years of 2031, 2033 and 2035 for the largest, middle and smaller electricity users, with the 2015 guidance remaining available until roughly 2035-2039.
sub_changes.old: The 2015 rules apply today, with dual reporting of location-based and market-based figures wherever contractual instruments exist.
sub_changes.topic: When would any new scope 2 rule apply?
sub_changes.specifics: Draft sections 4.1.4 and 5.1.6: publication 'anticipated late 2027', 'implementation could phase in over multiple years' with 'staged effective dates'; Question 67 offered readiness options from 'earlier than reporting year 2027' to 'later than reporting year 2030'. Section 7: 'A legacy clause is under consideration to recognize investments made under existing scope 2 accounting rules' — no dates or duration proposed. Superseding timeline (SDP, July 29, 2026): Scope 2 TWG engages with consultation feedback and ISO WG4 in Q3–Q4 2026 at the ISB's direction; consolidated consultation estimated Q2 2027; publication estimated Q4 2028; effective date not stated. Pre-consultation overview: 'no new LBM or MBM requirements will take effect before those AMI outcomes are available.' Scope 2 Workshop Outcomes (November 2026): illustrative bracketed phase-in of 2031 / 2033 / 2035 for largest / middle / smaller load tiers, with the 2015 Guidance remaining available until roughly 2035-2039. These figures appear in brackets in a document marked draft and subject to change; they are not adopted and no effective date is set. The same document targets Q2 2027 for public consultation on the combined draft GHGP-ISO Corporate Standard incorporating the Scope 2 outcomes, and Q4 2028 for ISB decisions is not stated — the next board decision point is December 15, 2026.

sub_changes.new: Not in the inventory. A parallel consultation on methods for estimating the grid emissions avoided by electricity actions drew 185 responses, with only 37% backing the proposed formula; that work now feeds the planned 'impact statement' in the market-instruments part of the new standard, reported apart from scope 2.
sub_changes.old: No standard method. Claims about the grid impact of power purchases sat outside scope 2 with no agreed rules.
sub_changes.topic: Do avoided emissions from clean-power deals count?
sub_changes.specifics: Electricity-sector consequential methods consultation (October 20, 2025 to January 31, 2026): 185 valid responses (88% organizations); 37% of 133 respondents supported the proposed quantification formula, 63% did not; topics were the formula, additionality, marginal emission rates and build/operating margin weighting. GHG Protocol: 'Outputs from this consultation will be incorporated into AMI's ongoing work on reporting the emissions impacts of actions.' The October 2025 release: 'reporting these actions separately from Scope 2 would not determine whether or how they count toward specific goals or targets.' Current standards: no consequential method.

sub_changes.topic: One rule, or a choice between two?
sub_changes.old: One set of rules: the 2015 guidance, with dual reporting of location-based and market-based figures.
sub_changes.new: One proposal, not two. The working group has agreed to develop a single proposal rather than competing alternatives — an informal poll recorded 22 members able to support that, with none opposed. Written alternatives can still go to the standards board, so the design is not locked.
sub_changes.specifics: Scope 2 Workshop Outcomes Overview (document dated 2026.11.10) and full draft summary (dated 2026.10.30), from the October 20-22, 2026 in-person workshop logged in the repository as 'Scope 2 TWG Meeting #24 (In person sessions)': 39 of 46 TWG members participated, daily attendance 36-39, poll responses 17-31, held under the Chatham House Rule. Informal poll: 22 could support a single TWG proposal, none opposed; written alternatives may still be submitted to the ISB. Proposed elements: an improved location-based method using a ranked emission-factor hierarchy (order unresolved, votes split evenly between recency-first and spatial-first); a market-based method using hourly matching but explicitly NOT 24/7 certificate matching; deliverability as plausible physical connection; incrementality recommended not required with disclosure of the incremental share, qualifying via a long-term offtake contract or an asset-age limit (~15 years discussed); consequential impact metrics; key indicators including hourly, monthly and annual carbon-free-electricity matching scores. Open: whether market-based reporting is required or optional; reporting optional below a size or load threshold (broad support); treatment of long-term contracts signed under the 2015 guidance undecided; 'Standard Supply Service' unresolved with no direction indicated. Both documents are marked draft and subject to change and the outcomes are described as 'an interim step towards a final standard' still requiring public consultation.

implications: Scenario-plan both outcomes: keep annual certificate matching workable while building hourly consumption and certificate data for large sites.
Map each site to a plausible deliverability region and check where your existing certificates and power contracts originate.
Check which markets lack a residual mix factor; under the proposal those sites would fall back to a fossil factor, not the grid average.
Keep your location-based figure robust by collecting the most granular public grid factors available; that duty drew more support than hourly matching.
Record signature dates and terms for all long-term clean power deals in case a legacy clause is adopted.
Do not sign long-dated annual-matching certificate contracts on the assumption they stay eligible — their treatment is undecided.

rows.new: Narrowed to financed emissions, aligned with industry standards such as PCAF.
rows.old: All investment-related emissions in one broad category.

detail.timing: Provisional (March 2026 scope 3 update; December 2025 corporate update); consolidated consultation estimated Q2 2027; publication estimated Q4 2028; no effective date.

detail.applies_to: Banks, asset owners and insurers for the core category; any company holding stakes it does not financially control once equity share is removed.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: the category is narrowed to investments only — commonly called financed emissions — and every investment type left in it becomes required. Insurance underwriting, issuance and other financial services move out to a proposed new category.
sub_changes.old: Investments covered the operation of equity and debt investments and project finance; managed investments and client services were optional and loosely defined, so banks and insurers reported very differently.
sub_changes.topic: What stays in the investments category?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Scope 3 Standard Table 5.4 — Category 15 'Operation of investments (including equity and debt investments and project finance) in the reporting year, not included in scope 1 or scope 2', with required and optional boundaries in section 5.5. Proposed (Scope 3 Progress Update, March 2026, Series C): Revisions C2–C4 restrict Category 15 to 'investments (commonly known as financed emissions)' and move insurance-associated activities, underwriting, issuance and other financial services to Category 16; Revision C5 makes all investment types in the narrowed category required. No support percentage is recorded for Series C. Provisional.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: the share is calculated against both the investee's equity and its debt, so shareholders and lenders carry proportionate responsibility. This mirrors the banking-sector financed-emissions method.
sub_changes.old: By your equity share of the investee, which weighted shareholders more heavily than lenders.
sub_changes.topic: How do we share out an investee's emissions?
sub_changes.specifics: Proposed Revision C10 (March 2026): 'Equity proportionality now includes both equity and debt in the denominator'; the update states this 'aligns with industry standards like PCAF, ensures equal-weighting of accountability between equity and debt holders, and improves the comparability of category 15 emissions between equity and debt holders.' Revision C11 adds references to third-party, industry-specific accounting and reporting standards. Current: Scope 3 Standard section 5.5 allocates investee emissions by equity share.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: into this category. Stakes in entities you do not control financially would be reported here in proportion to ownership, which makes investments a required category for many non-financial groups too.
sub_changes.old: Companies using the equity share approach folded minority stakes into scopes 1 and 2 by ownership percentage.
sub_changes.topic: Where do minority stakes go once equity share is scrapped?
sub_changes.specifics: Corporate Standard Phase 1 Progress Update (December 2025): with equity share eliminated, equity in entities without financial control is 'reported under Scope 3, Category 15 (investments) based on percentage ownership'; entities under financial control consolidate at 100%. Investment-entity requirements under financial control are still to be developed. Combined with Revision C5 (all investments required), joint ventures and associates outside financial control would appear in required scope 3 rather than in scopes 1 and 2.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: the category is defined around 'financed emissions', the term the banking methodology uses, and the standard would point to recognised industry methods rather than rewrite them.
sub_changes.old: The standard spoke of 'investments' without using the term 'financed emissions', and left room for interpretation on managed assets and client services.
sub_changes.topic: 'Financed emissions' as the defining term
sub_changes.specifics: Scope 3 Progress Update (March 2026): Category 15 restricted to 'investments (commonly known as financed emissions)'; Revision C1 addresses applicability; Revision C11 references third-party, industry-specific standards (PCAF named in the C10 rationale). The Scope 3 TWG (65 members, three subgroups, 42 meetings September 2024 to end-2025) ran Category 15 in Group C; boundaries of the other categories are Phase 2 work. Current: Scope 3 Standard section 5.5 does not use the term 'financed emissions'.

implications: Financial institutions: align financed-emissions calculations to the equity-plus-debt denominator and prepare to report every investment type as required.
Insurers and arrangers: plan to move underwriting and facilitated activity out of investments into the proposed new category.
Non-financial groups: list every non-controlled stake; under the proposal these become required scope 3 investments rather than consolidated emissions.
Keep ownership percentages and investee emissions data current, since the allocation would rest on them every year.

rows.new: Proposed Category 16 'other value chain activities' (e.g. facilitated deals, licensing) — optional for most, mandatory for oil & gas distributors.

detail.applies_to: Optional for most companies; proposed as required for oil and gas distributors; most relevant to licensors, insurers, underwriters and deal arrangers.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: a sixteenth category, 'other value chain activities', for 'facilitated' emissions — emissions from third-party activity on which you earn direct transactional income without buying, selling or owning it. Examples named are licensing and many financial services.
sub_changes.old: Fifteen categories, fixed since 2011. Income from activities you neither buy, sell nor own — licensing, underwriting, arranging deals — had no clear home.
sub_changes.topic: What is the proposed Category 16?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Scope 3 Standard Table 5.3 lists 15 categories (upstream 1–8, downstream 9–15). Proposed (Scope 3 Progress Update, March 2026, Revision B11): 'A new category is proposed, to account for other value chain activities, which includes facilitated emissions (i.e., emissions generated by third-party activities from which the reporting company earns direct, transactional income but never buys, sells, or owns the activity)'; subcategories set out in Annex C; rationale 'modernizes the scope 3 boundary to account for current and new business models'. No TWG vote percentage is given for B11.

sub_changes.new: Proposed as optional for most companies: the majority of its subcategories are 'may' items. The one named exception is oil and gas distributors, for whom the category would be required.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable; the category did not exist.
sub_changes.topic: Is Category 16 mandatory?
sub_changes.specifics: Scope 3 Progress Update (March 2026): 'The majority of subcategories within category 16 are optional to promote feasibility'; the named exception is oil and gas distributors. Optional emissions are reported apart from required emissions (Revision B7) and do not count toward the 5% exclusion allowance. The Annex C subcategory list was not reproduced in the text this tracker could read; exact subcategory boundaries and the definition of 'oil and gas distributor' remain to be set in the consolidated draft (estimated Q2 2027).

sub_changes.new: Proposed: insurance-associated activities, underwriting, issuance and other financial services move from investments into this new category, leaving investments as financed emissions only.
sub_changes.old: Insurance underwriting, issuance and other financial services sat uneasily in the investments category as optional items.
sub_changes.topic: What moves here from investments?
sub_changes.specifics: Revisions C3 and C4 (Scope 3 Progress Update, March 2026): move insurance-associated activities and other financial activities out of Category 15 into Category 16; Category 15 restricted to investments. Interaction with Category 14 (franchises) is not stated in the summary text read. Current: Scope 3 Standard section 5.5 treats some of these as optional Category 15 items.

sub_changes.new: Open. The category-by-category required boundaries for the other fourteen categories, and how recycled or circular products are treated, are Phase 2 work with no published text yet.
sub_changes.old: Category minimum boundaries unchanged since 2011.
sub_changes.topic: What else might change in the categories?
sub_changes.specifics: Scope 3 Progress Update (March 2026): 'required (formerly minimum boundary) scope 3 emissions, by category, are currently being reviewed by the Scope 3 TWG as part of Phase 2 considerations'; pending topics include 'category-specific boundary updates, and circularity considerations for recycled products'; Revision B9 retains the justified exclusion for intermediate products whose end use is unknown. Draft text expected in the consolidated consultation (estimated Q2 2027).

implications: Identify revenue streams where you earn fees or royalties on activity you do not own; these are candidate Category 16 emissions.
Oil and gas distributors: assume the new category would be required and start estimating facilitated downstream emissions.
Financial institutions: keep underwriting and arranging data apart from lending and investment data in preparation for the split.
Treat Category 16 as optional disclosure for now and avoid hard-coding category structures into reporting systems before the consultation draft.

rows.new: Proposed separate statements: physical inventory, market-based/contractual inventory, and an impact statement — reported side by side, never netted.
rows.old: Instruments blend into the market-based scope 2 figure; no standard for claiming 'impact.'

detail.applies_to: Any company using certificates, supplier contracts, commodity certificates, carbon credits or making avoided-emissions claims; whether the new statements will be required is undecided.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: a multi-statement report. A physical inventory based on physical flows; a market-based inventory for contractual claims; an impact statement for the real-world effect of your actions; and an optional non-GHG indicators statement. 84% of 437 valid respondents supported the structure.
sub_changes.old: Certificates and supplier contracts changed your market-based scope 2 number; carbon credits were reported apart from the scopes with no standard for claiming 'impact'.
sub_changes.topic: How will market instruments be reported?
sub_changes.specifics: AMI Phase 1 White Paper (March 31, 2026) sections 8.2–8.5: physical GHG inventory (attributional, physical flows); market-based GHG inventory (attributional, 'based on qualified contractual arrangements for the purchase of goods and services'); GHG impact statement (consequential: 'emissions avoided, reduced, or removed' inside and outside the value chain); non-GHG indicators (metrics 'not expressed in CO2 equivalent'). RFI Summary of Responses (September 2026): 437 valid of 487 responses; 84% support the structure; 87% want the market-based statement, 80% the impact statement; non-GHG indicators 33% support, 44% neutral, 25% opposed. Current: Corporate Standard Chapter 8 reports project-based reductions and instrument trades apart from the inventory.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: never. Each statement is reported on its own with no adding, netting or combining into one figure. Whether a target program lets you count market-based or impact figures toward a goal is that program's decision, not GHG Protocol's.
sub_changes.old: Within scope 2, certificates effectively lowered the reported market-based figure; outside scope 2, netting credits against the inventory was discouraged but common in 'net' claims.
sub_changes.topic: Can statements be netted against each other?
sub_changes.specifics: White Paper section 6.1: 'transparent and disaggregated reporting of unique reporting statements and elements, without netting'; p. 28: 'Whether to include one or more accounting categories within a target boundary and whether to net one category against another is a policy decision' for target-setting programs. RFI summary p. 14: results should not be 'added, netted, or combined into a single undifferentiated result'. Interim guidance (FAQ, July 29, 2026): 'report physical inventory emissions, market-based emissions, and the impacts of climate actions separately and transparently, without netting between categories.'

sub_changes.new: Undecided. GHG Protocol has not decided whether any new statement is required or optional; many respondents asked that they start optional while data and methods mature.
sub_changes.old: Only the two scope 2 figures were required; impact claims were voluntary and unregulated.
sub_changes.topic: Will the new statements be mandatory?
sub_changes.specifics: White Paper p. 4: 'Decisions have not yet been taken as to whether any newly proposed statements should be required or optional.' RFI summary p. 4: 'many stakeholders recommended that they remain optional, at least initially', citing evolving methodologies, SME capacity and data readiness. Phase 2 priorities: quality criteria and safeguards, double-counting prevention, alignment with existing standards and target programs, implementation guidance. The ISB has not yet been asked to approve a draft for consultation.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: in the impact statement, using consequential accounting, never inside the physical inventory. Respondents want clear distinctions between avoided emissions, reductions, credits and removals, each with its own evidence rules.
sub_changes.old: Reported apart from the scopes, with no GHG Protocol rules on how to present their effect.
sub_changes.topic: Where do carbon credits and removals go?
sub_changes.specifics: White Paper Table 1 and section 8.4: credits and project-based reductions sit in the GHG impact statement, with subcategories — within organizational boundary, value-chain associated, sector associated, beyond value chain and sector (global), and impacts of sold products (section 5.4). RFI summary p. 29: respondents asked for distinction between 'avoided emissions, emissions reductions, credits, and removals' as 'different physical realities, time horizons, and evidence requirements'; p. 36: eligibility, quality and evidence criteria covering 'traceability, uniqueness, retirement, verification, registry controls' and chain-of-custody models including mass balance and book-and-claim.

sub_changes.new: The market-based scope 2 method is expected to become part of the market-based statement, and similar contractual approaches are proposed for scope 1 and scope 3 — for example certificates for low-carbon fuels, steel or cement. The electricity rules themselves are decided by the scope 2 working group, not this one.
sub_changes.old: The market-based scope 2 method was the only place contractual instruments were recognised.
sub_changes.topic: Does this change scope 2 certificates and PPAs?
sub_changes.specifics: White Paper p. 5: 'The market-based GHG inventory may incorporate the existing scope 2 market-based method and is expected to introduce new approaches for scope 1 and scope 3'; examples 'mitigation-related contractual agreements or commodity certificates for the purchase of low-carbon fuels/commodities'; footnote 3: 'No changes will be made in the AMI TWG regarding the requirements for scope 2 location-based and market-based reporting.' The consolidated standard places AMI in Part 2 'Actions and Market Instruments' (SDP section 6), with an AMI Guidance Version 1.0 to follow publication.

sub_changes.new: A draft for public consultation is planned for 2027 — GHG Protocol's FAQ and feedback summary say Q2 2027, while its market-instruments web page says Q3 2027. Final publication is targeted for Q4 2028 as the second part of the consolidated standard.
sub_changes.old: No standard existed; the workstream began with a white paper and request for information in March 2026.
sub_changes.topic: When will there be draft text?
sub_changes.specifics: White Paper RFI opened March 31, 2026 with an original 60-day window to May 31, 2026, which GHG Protocol extended to June 15, 2026; Summary of Responses published September 23, 2026. Timeline conflict: FAQ (July 29, 2026) and Summary of Responses p. 4 — 'A draft standard is expected to be released for public consultation in Q2 2027'; AMI standard web page — public consultation 'planned for Q3 2027'. SDP: Part 2 publication estimated Q4 2028. AMI TWG held its second in-person meeting June 30 to July 2, 2026 and moved to standard drafting (Pulse, August 2026).

implications: Design reporting so physical, contractual and impact figures live in distinct ledgers that never net; this direction now has documented majority support.
Keep certificate and contract evidence — vintage, geography, registry, retirement — clean enough to pass eligibility criteria still being written.
Stop presenting a single 'net' emissions number that blends credits or avoided emissions with your inventory.
List your non-electricity contractual instruments such as low-carbon fuel or commodity certificates; they are candidates for the market-based statement.
Decide which target programs you report to and watch their rules, since GHG Protocol will not decide what counts toward targets.
