detail.applies_to: Companies with significant agricultural land activities in operations or value chain, and any company choosing to report CO2 removals or geologic storage; forestry is excluded for now.

sub_changes.new: Required for any company reporting in conformance with GHG Protocol that has significant land-sector activities in its operations or value chain — including producers, buyers and sellers of agricultural products — or that chooses to report CO2 removals or captured CO2 with geologic storage, now or in past years.
sub_changes.old: Not covered. The corporate rules had no requirements for land emissions, biogenic products or removals.
sub_changes.topic: Who must use the land and removals standard?
sub_changes.specifics: LSR Standard v1.1 Requirement 1: 'Companies reporting a corporate- or organization-level GHG inventory in conformance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol shall follow the Land Sector and Removals Standard and Guidance if the company has significant land sector activities in its operations or value chain and/or if the company chooses to account for and report CO2 removals or CO2 capture with geologic storage in the current year or has done so in previous years.' FAQ: applies across sectors to 'producers, buyers, and sellers of agricultural products'. Version 1.0 published January 30, 2026; v1.1 (administrative and non-substantive edits) June 30, 2026.

sub_changes.new: Effective January 1, 2027: the first reports that must conform are 2028 reports covering 2027 data. The twenty-chapter Guidance, a reporting checklist and a template were published June 30, 2026 to support it.
sub_changes.old: No rules, no date.
sub_changes.topic: When does it take effect?
sub_changes.specifics: v1.1 cover: 'Effective date 01 January 2027'; announcement June 30, 2026: 'The LSR Standard and Guidance take effect on January 1, 2027'. FAQ: compliance required in 2028 GHG reports covering 2027 data; 2026 to update internal processes, 2027 to begin collecting data. Guidance published June 30, 2026, organized into the same 20 chapters as the Standard with worked examples, calculation guidance and 10 corporate case studies; a reporting requirements checklist and sample reporting template published alongside. Early adoption: not stated.

sub_changes.new: No. Version 1 applies to agriculture and CO2 removal technologies and does not apply to companies that own or control forest land or are in forest product value chains. Forest carbon accounting is out for a request for information until February 1, 2027; companies disclosing forest carbon meanwhile should be transparent about their method.
sub_changes.old: Not covered.
sub_changes.topic: Does it cover forests?
sub_changes.specifics: v1.1: 'Version 1 of this Standard and Guidance applies to agriculture and CO2 removal technologies. Version 1 of this Standard and Guidance does not apply to forestry, as it does not provide comprehensive requirements for companies that own or control forest land or are in forest product value chains.' Forest Carbon Accounting RFI (June 30, 2026): closes February 1, 2027; seeks input on activity-based accounting (30-year projection), managed land proxy plus, non-zero reference levels and spatial/temporal boundaries; the ISB will recommend whether to proceed with standard development or defer to the next scheduled LSR revision 'within five years of version 1.0'. FAQ interim: 'be transparent about their chosen methodology'.

sub_changes.new: Required: emissions from converting land (for example forest or grassland to cropland) are spread over a 20-year assessment period for annual crops, weighted so that crops grown closer to the conversion year carry more of the emissions, and are calculated either for the specific land directly or statistically by sourcing region.
sub_changes.old: No corporate rule; companies used assorted product-footprint conventions.
sub_changes.topic: How are land-clearing emissions counted?
sub_changes.specifics: v1.1 Chapter 7: 'For annual crops or other land-based products or services with a cultivation cycle or rotation period less than or equal to 20 years, the LUC assessment period is 20 years'; 'Companies shall allocate the LUC emissions to each year in the LUC assessment period using linear amortization' per the Guidance section 7.5 formula, or disclose and justify another method; use either direct land use change (dLUC, 'LMU-level' or 'jurisdictional') or statistical land use change (sLUC) for a given product type by sourcing jurisdiction; sLUC applies the product expansion allocation method unless the shared responsibility method is justified (section 7.3).

sub_changes.new: Required: land emissions broken into land use change, net biogenic CO2 from land management, land management production emissions and biogenic product emissions, each shown alongside fossil emissions, plus land occupation and related metrics. Biogenic CO2 from products such as biofuels is reported gross, not netted against land removals.
sub_changes.old: Only fossil and industrial emissions by scope.
sub_changes.topic: What else must land-exposed companies report?
sub_changes.specifics: v1.1 Figure 4.1 required physical inventory categories: fossil fuel and industrial emissions; land emissions (land use change; land management net biogenic CO2; land management production; biogenic product emissions); removals if applicable. Additional categories: land use, land carbon leakage, gross CO2 fluxes, product carbon storage, reversals. Requirement 17: companies that purchase, consume, process or sell biogenic products account for biogenic product emissions; Guidance 11.4.2: that subcategory 'is not additive with the emissions category' (double counting with land management net biogenic CO2 or removals); FAQ: reported apart only if all lifecycle GHG emissions and leakage are reported, otherwise gross biogenic product CO2 from biofuel combustion goes in the physical inventory. Requirement 14 (clarified in v1.1) sets required versus optional carbon pools.

sub_changes.new: Optional, with conditions. You may report removals from land management, technological capture or captured biogenic CO2 with geologic storage only if you follow the conservativeness and permanence principles: physical traceability through chain of custody, ongoing monitoring of storage, reporting of reversals, leakage assessment and lifecycle emissions.
sub_changes.old: No rules; removals were not part of the inventory.
sub_changes.topic: Can we count carbon removals in our inventory?
sub_changes.specifics: v1.1 Part 2.2 (requirements for companies choosing to report CO2 removals) applies 'only if relevant to business goals' — removals reporting is optional. Requirement 2: 'Companies shall also follow the principles of conservativeness and permanence if accounting and reporting for removals'; Table 3.1 permanence: 'monitor the continued storage of reported removals and captured CO2, account for reversals, and report emissions from associated carbon pools'; Chapter 12: storage 'for a defined time period, which varies by accounting category' with monitoring plans. FAQ: physical traceability via identity preservation, segregation, controlled blending and some mass balance; leakage assessment; lifecycle emissions; no double counting. Section 15.3 (v1.1) clarifies digital tracking methods.

sub_changes.new: No. The standard sets no rules for credit projects or certification and does not let credited reductions or removals be used as inventory results; companies must disclose land where credits were issued and avoid double counting against targets.
sub_changes.old: Credits sat apart from the scopes; no land-specific rules.
sub_changes.topic: Do carbon credits count?
sub_changes.specifics: v1.1 Chapter 1 (Introduction): 'This Standard does not provide requirements or guidance on project accounting, GHG credit certification, or GHG credit verification' but includes requirements on avoiding double counting with GHG credits. Requirement 22: disclose 'any lands where emission reductions or removals were issued as GHG credits to be used as an offset or for compensation' within the scope 3 spatial boundary. Requirement 30: avoid double counting when setting targets where reductions or removals are accounted for 'by other companies or GHG programs as GHG credits used toward GHG targets.'

sub_changes.new: Not for now. GHG Protocol says the land standard is outside the ISO partnership but may be brought in later; if the corporate standard's revised consistency principle is adopted, a future land-standard update would align its comparability principle to it.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Will it merge into the new corporate standard?
sub_changes.specifics: FAQ: the LSR Standard 'builds on the Corporate Standard (2004) and Scope 3 Standard' and is currently 'outside the scope of the GHG Protocol and ISO partnership but may be brought into this partnership in the future.' Corporate Standard Phase 1 Progress Update (December 2025): if the comparability approach is adopted, future LSR updates will align its comparability principle with the revised consistency principle. Next scheduled LSR revision: within five years of v1.0 (Forest Carbon Accounting RFI, p. 2).

implications: Screen scope 1 and scope 3 for agricultural land, biogenic products and removals exposure before January 1, 2027; food, beverage, retail and bioenergy supply chains are most affected.
Set up data collection for land use change by sourcing region in 2026 so 2027 data can be reported in 2028.
If you intend to report removals, build monitoring, reversal and chain-of-custody evidence first; without it the removals cannot be included.
Forestry and forest-product companies: respond to the forest carbon request for information by February 1, 2027 and document any interim method transparently.
Keep carbon credits out of inventory results and record where credits were issued on land in your supply chain.

rows.new: Probably still not required, but genuinely undecided. GHG Protocol's secretariat reports that neither its technical working group nor its Independent Standards Board supports mandating verification, leaving a recommendation, an option, or silence as the live choices. ISO's representative argued it should be mandatory, and the ISO draft being merged in already assumes verification, so the two sides are openly apart.
rows.old: The current corporate standard treats verification as optional good practice. It devotes a chapter to it and recommends it, but nothing in the standard requires a company to obtain it.

detail.timing: Discussed at the Corporate Standard full technical working group meeting of October 27, 2026, with the item shortened and no votes taken. The working group's feedback survey closes November 13, 2026 and the next full meeting is November 24, 2026. Any outcome would surface in the consolidated draft going to public consultation, estimated Q2 2027, with publication estimated Q4 2028. No effective date.

detail.applies_to: Every company that would report under the merged corporate standard. Note that none of your binding assurance duties come from GHG Protocol: those come from California, the EU, and SBTi for its most stringent company category.

sub_changes.new: Not as things stand. The secretariat told the working group there is no support for requiring verification from either the working group or the Independent Standards Board, and that the choice is between recommending it, making it an explicit option, or saying nothing about it. No decision was taken and no vote was held.
sub_changes.old: No. Verification is recommended and explained but never required by the standard itself.
sub_changes.topic: Is verification mandatory?
sub_changes.specifics: Current: Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (2004 revised edition), Chapter 10 'Verification of GHG Emissions', which sets out the purpose, scope and process of verification and recommends it, with no requirement in the standard's reporting requirements. Position reported October 27, 2026 (Full TWG Meeting 11 minutes, Verification and Assurance item): the Secretariat stated there is no support for requiring verification from either the TWG or the ISB, and that the options are a recommendation, an option, or silence. The item was shortened for time and no live polls were held, so nothing is settled. GHG Protocol has published no draft text on assurance.

sub_changes.new: The reporting clause in the second working draft of ISO 14064-1 is conditional on verification having been obtained, while GHG Protocol is heading towards not requiring it. Because the merged standard has to be approved by both sides, this has to be resolved before a consultation draft can go out.
sub_changes.old: Not an issue: the two documents were separate, and ISO 14064-1 set its own terms.
sub_changes.topic: GHG Protocol and ISO disagree
sub_changes.specifics: Reported October 27, 2026 (Full TWG Meeting 11 minutes): the ISO representative argued that verification should be mandatory, and the minutes record that the ISO 14064-1 WD2 reporting clause is conditional on verification being obtained. Approval requires both GHG Protocol's ISB and Steering Committee and a two-thirds majority of ISO/TC 207/SC 7 participating members with no more than a quarter of votes cast against (partnership governance). No reconciliation has been published, and neither the clause text nor a resolution date is public. Not stated: whether the condition would survive into the merged text.

sub_changes.new: Some working group members argued GHG Protocol should stay out of it, because whether a company must have its numbers checked is a legal and regulatory question rather than an accounting one. That view is part of why the outcome may be silence.
sub_changes.old: Not raised. Assurance requirements came from regulators and programmes, not from GHG Protocol.
sub_changes.topic: Should GHG Protocol decide this at all?
sub_changes.specifics: Reported October 27, 2026 (Full TWG Meeting 11 minutes): some TWG members argued GHG Protocol should not decide the assurance question because it intrudes on legal and regulatory matters. No count of members holding this view is given and no poll was taken. Not stated: whether the ISB has expressed a view on the jurisdictional point as distinct from the substantive one.

implications: Do not build an assurance budget around a GHG Protocol mandate; plan against California, the EU and SBTi instead.
If you already obtain limited assurance, nothing here changes it — the direction of travel is towards no new requirement.
Watch the November 24, 2026 meeting and the consultation draft for whether assurance is recommended, optional or absent.
Companies relying on ISO 14064-1 verification statements should track whether that draft keeps its verification condition.
Treat this as open: a single Independent Standards Board decision could still move it either way.

rows.new: One co-branded corporate standard: consolidated draft for public consultation estimated Q2 2027, publication estimated Q4 2028, approved by GHG Protocol's board and a two-thirds ISO vote; no effective date announced. Current standards remain the rules until then.
rows.old: Three GHG Protocol documents plus ISO's corporate inventory standard, each revised on its own timetable; a December 2025 plan aimed for consultation in mid-2026 and a final text by end-2027.

detail.applies_to: Every company using GHG Protocol or ISO's corporate inventory standard; no company is required to change anything before the consolidated standard is adopted.

sub_changes.new: Confirmed: one jointly published, co-branded corporate standard combining all three GHG Protocol documents, the new market-instruments work and ISO's corporate inventory standard, in two parts — general requirements and physical inventory, and actions and market instruments. The working title is Corporate Standard Version 3.0.
sub_changes.old: Companies followed the 2004 corporate standard, the 2015 scope 2 guidance and the 2011 scope 3 standard, and some also certified against ISO's corporate inventory standard — two rulebooks with differences.
sub_changes.topic: What exactly is being merged?
sub_changes.specifics: Announcement (July 29, 2026): GHG Protocol and ISO will 'combine their corporate carbon accounting standards into a single, harmonized global accounting standard'. SDP (July 29, 2026): title 'Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (Corporate Standard), Version 3.0' — 'draft and to be determined in conjunction with ISO'; Part 1 'General Requirements and Physical GHG Inventory', Part 2 'Actions and Market Instruments'; 'The part structure is subject to change; either part can be subdivided into multiple parts' (section 6, p. 10). Consolidates the Corporate Standard (2004 revised), Scope 2 Guidance (2015), Scope 3 Standard (2011), AMI outputs and ISO 14064-1. Partnership announced September 9, 2025; ISO experts joined the TWGs in Q1 2026.

sub_changes.new: Published plan, not a commitment: one consolidated public consultation estimated Q2 2027 and publication estimated Q4 2028. A pilot-testing phase may be added, which would push the dates out. GHG Protocol will not accept comments before the consultation opens.
sub_changes.old: The December 2025 plan said a complete draft would be consulted on in mid-2026 and the third edition finalized by the end of 2027.
sub_changes.topic: When can we comment, and when is it final?
sub_changes.specifics: SDP section 9, p. 13: 'Consolidated draft standard for public consultation (estimated Q2 2027)'; 'Published revised standard (estimated Q4 2028)'; 'If a pilot testing phase is added, the timeline would be extended'; p. 14: 'The workplan and timeline are subject to change during the standard revision process'. Superseded: December 2025 Corporate Standard Progress Update — complete draft for public consultation mid-2026, final third edition end of 2027. Scope 3 Progress Update: the Secretariat 'will not accept or process any feedback submitted prior to this formal consultation period.' Guidance documents (Corporate Standard Guidance v1.0, Scope 2 Guidance v2.0, Scope 3 Guidance v2.0, AMI Guidance v1.0) follow publication.

sub_changes.new: Both. GHG Protocol's Independent Standards Board approves the draft, which then goes at the same time to GHG Protocol's Steering Committee for ratification and to the ISO technical subcommittee, where it passes if two-thirds of permanent members vote in favour and no more than a quarter of votes cast are negative. The result is published under both logos.
sub_changes.old: GHG Protocol's own governance approved its standards; ISO standards went through national-body ballots.
sub_changes.topic: Who approves the final text?
sub_changes.specifics: SDP section 8, p. 11: the ISB 'reviews and approves GHG Protocol standards according to the Standard Development and Revision Procedure' and 'makes decisions related to the content of standards'; section 9, p. 15: after ISB approval the draft goes concurrently to the GHG Protocol Steering Committee for ratification and 'to ISO/TC 207/SC 7 for approval through the ISO enquiry stage. The standard is approved by ISO if a two-thirds majority of permanent members of ISO/TC 207/SC 7 are in favor and no more than one quarter of the total number of votes cast are negative'; 'Adopted standards will be published under a dual logo.' ISB membership call closed August 8, 2026.

sub_changes.new: Not stated. No effective date or transition period has been published for the consolidated standard, and GHG Protocol has not said when or whether the current documents will be withdrawn. Until the new text is adopted, the existing standards are the rules.
sub_changes.old: Current standards have no sunset date; nothing obliges a change.
sub_changes.topic: When would we have to switch?
sub_changes.specifics: SDP: no effective date or transition provisions; publication estimated Q4 2028 only. FAQ (July 29, 2026): does not address effective date or the validity of current standards. The Scope 2 consultation draft had envisaged 'implementation could phase in over multiple years' with 'staged effective dates' after a late-2027 publication — now superseded. ISO 14064-1:2018 withdrawal or revision timing: not addressed in the SDP. Treat Q4 2028 as the earliest possible publication, with an effective date later and unknown.

sub_changes.new: Keep reporting under the existing standards. GHG Protocol's only interim guidance applies to companies that choose to start using the multi-statement approach: report physical inventory emissions, market-based emissions and the impacts of climate actions separately, without netting. The land and removals standard, effective January 1, 2027, is the one final new text.
sub_changes.old: Report under the existing standards.
sub_changes.topic: What should we do now?
sub_changes.specifics: FAQ (July 29, 2026), interim guidance pending the consolidated standard: 'report physical inventory emissions, market-based emissions, and the impacts of climate actions separately and transparently, without netting between categories.' The LSR Standard v1.1 (effective January 1, 2027) sits outside the ISO partnership for now. Product-level accounting is a separate ISO–GHG Protocol joint working group (finalized April 9, 2026) with no published timeline, and the Project Protocol is being revised by a separate GHG Protocol–ISO working group with no published timeline; its replacement date is not stated.

implications: Budget a gap assessment against the proposed changes for early 2027 so a consultation response and an implementation plan are ready together.
Do not retire current-standard processes; plan for them to run at least through 2028 reporting.
Nominate owners for the Q2 2027 consultation now, since one integrated window will cover boundaries, scope 2, scope 3 and market instruments at once.
If you certify to the ISO corporate standard, track the ISO ballot stage; dual approval means the ISO vote can change or delay the text.

detail.applies_to: Any company reporting scope 3 category 15 (investments) under the ISSB climate standard may use the limit; the extra financed-emissions detail applies only to asset management, commercial banking and insurance activities.

sub_changes.new: Optional for any reporter, not only financial firms: you may limit what goes into your category 15 figure to financed emissions alone. The extra financed-emissions detail is still required only for companies with asset management, commercial banking or insurance activities.
sub_changes.old: Scope 3 category 15 (investments) had to be measured in full, with no carve-out written into the standard. Asset managers, commercial banks and insurers also had to give extra detail on their financed emissions, meaning the emissions of the companies they lend to or invest in.
sub_changes.topic: Who can use the financed-emissions limit
sub_changes.specifics: 2023: paragraph 29(a)(i)(3) required absolute gross Scope 3 emissions and 29(a)(vi)(2) required additional financed-emissions information for asset management, commercial banking or insurance activities (application guidance B58–B63). The Basis for Conclusions (BC127, BC129) suggested a narrower reading, which stakeholders found conflicted with the standard (BC121B–BC121C). 2026: new paragraph 29A — 'an entity is permitted to limit what it includes in its measure of Scope 3 Category 15 greenhouse gas emissions to only its financed emissions'. The permission is drafted for 'an entity', not restricted to financial-sector activities; 29(a)(vi)(2) and B58–B63 continue to apply only to asset management, commercial banking and insurance.

sub_changes.new: Loans, project finance, bonds, equity investments and undrawn loan commitments count as 'loans and investments'. For asset managers, the emissions attributed to assets under management are financed emissions too.
sub_changes.old: Financed emissions were defined as the share of an investee's or borrower's emissions attributed to your loans and investments, but the standard did not spell out which instruments that meant.
sub_changes.topic: What 'financed emissions' now covers
sub_changes.specifics: Definition (Appendix A, unchanged): 'the portion of gross greenhouse gas emissions of an investee or counterparty attributed to the loans and investments made by an entity to the investee or counterparty'. 2026: paragraph 29A states that 'Loans and investments' include loans, project finance, bonds, equity investments and undrawn loan commitments, and that for an entity participating in asset management activities, financed emissions include emissions attributed to assets under management. Asset-class lists in B62A(b) (banking: loans, project finance, bonds, equity investments, undrawn loan commitments) and B63A(b) (insurance: loans, bonds, equity investments, undrawn loan commitments) must be covered; additional asset classes require an explanation of why they are relevant.

sub_changes.new: Permitted: when using the financed-emissions limit you may exclude emissions attributable to derivatives, but you must explain what you treated as a derivative, for example by pointing to the definition in your accounting standards.
sub_changes.old: Not stated. The standard did not define derivatives or say whether emissions attributed to them belonged in category 15.
sub_changes.topic: Can we leave derivatives out?
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: paragraph 29A — 'For the purpose of the limitation, an entity is permitted to exclude greenhouse gas emissions attributable to derivatives.' Paragraph 29B(a): the entity shall 'explain what it has treated as a derivative', for example items meeting the definition of a derivative under IFRS Accounting Standards or other applicable GAAP used for its financial statements. BC121F: 'In the absence of a definition of derivatives in IFRS S2, an entity could determine what it treats as a derivative.' The exposure draft (April 28, 2025; comments to June 27, 2025) had proposed this relief; 179 comment letters and survey responses were received (BC80D).

sub_changes.new: Not required: facilitated emissions and insurance-associated emissions are described as other types of category 15 emissions that a reporter using the limit may leave out. Insurers' financed emissions cover their own loans and investments, not the emissions of the businesses they insure.
sub_changes.old: Unclear whether emissions linked to deals a bank arranges (facilitated emissions) or to insurance policies it writes (insurance-associated emissions) had to be included in category 15.
sub_changes.topic: Investment-banking and underwriting emissions
sub_changes.specifics: 2026 Basis for Conclusions BC121D–BC121E: 'Financed emissions are a type of Category 15 greenhouse gas emissions, distinct from other types… Examples of other types… are facilitated emissions that are associated with investment banking activities, and insurance-associated emissions that are associated with insurance and reinsurance underwriting activities.' BC129 footnote: IFRS S2 requires Category 15 disclosure 'for only financial activities associated with an insurer's loans and investments', not the associated emissions of underwriting portfolios. The Basis does not commit the ISSB to revisit facilitated or insurance-associated emissions later (not stated). BC121H: the limitation does not relieve an entity from other requirements, including information about targets that cover Category 15 emissions beyond financed emissions.

sub_changes.new: Required for anyone using the limit: describe the financial activities you left out, including derivative-related activities, and, if category 15 is in your scope 3 figure at all, disclose the category 15 total and the financed-emissions subtotal inside it.
sub_changes.old: No specific disclosure existed because the limit did not exist; the general rules on explaining your measurement approach, inputs and assumptions applied.
sub_changes.topic: What we must say if we use the limit
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: paragraph 29B(b) — describe 'the financial activities it has excluded from its measure of Scope 3 Category 15 greenhouse gas emissions as a result of applying paragraph 29A, including activities associated with derivatives'. Paragraph 29C — if Category 15 emissions are included in the Scope 3 measure, disclose 'the total Category 15 greenhouse gas emissions and the subtotal of financed emissions included in that total' (applies whether or not the 29A limit is used). BC121I–BC121K explain that the ISSB required only a qualitative description of excluded activities rather than quantification, because users said that would meet their needs, and address the undefined term 'financial activities', concluding that entities identify them using the Category 15 descriptions in the GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard. The general measurement-approach disclosure in 29(a)(iii) is unchanged.

sub_changes.new: Required unless impracticable: if you already reported scope 3 including category 15, present last year's category 15 total and financed-emissions subtotal on the new basis when you first apply the amendments.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable before the amendments.
sub_changes.topic: Restating last year's category 15 figure
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: paragraph C6(b) — if the entity disclosed Scope 3 emissions in the preceding period and the measure included Category 15, it 'shall adjust the comparative information to provide the total Category 15 greenhouse gas emissions and the subtotal of financed emissions included in that total as if it had applied the requirement in paragraph 29C in that preceding period', 'unless it is impracticable to do so' (BC175–BC177). C6 applies only to entities that 'previously applied IFRS S2'; first-time appliers use the ordinary first-year reliefs in C3–C5 instead.

sub_changes.new: The amendments apply to annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027. Earlier use is allowed if you say so. The matching changes to the three financial-sector industry standards take effect on the same date.
sub_changes.old: The original standard applied to annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2024, where a jurisdiction required it.
sub_changes.topic: When the relief starts
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: paragraph C1B — apply the amendments listed in C1A 'for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. Earlier application is permitted. If an entity applies these amendments earlier, it shall disclose that fact.' BC164A–BC164B: the date gives jurisdictions time to incorporate the changes. Consequential amendments (version 2025-12) to the SASB Standards for Asset Management & Custody Activities (FN-AC-410b.1, .3, .4), Commercial Banks (FN-CB-410b.1–.4) and Insurance (FN-IN-410c.1–.4) are 'effective for all entities for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027'. Jurisdictions set their own mandatory dates (Japan's profile notes early application of the amendments is permitted).

implications: Decide now whether to limit category 15 to financed emissions for 2027 reporting, and document which activities, including derivatives, you are leaving out.
Pick and record a working definition of 'derivative', ideally the one your accounting policies already use, because you must explain it.
Build the new category 15 total and financed-emissions subtotal into your inventory template, and prepare the prior-year figures on the same basis.
Check that any emissions target covering investment-related emissions still has the data it needs; the relief does not shrink your target disclosures.
If you report under a local version of the standard, confirm whether and when it picks up the 2027 amendments before applying them early.

rows.new: Other classification systems permitted with justification.
rows.old: GICS required when disaggregating financed emissions.

detail.timing: Effective for annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027; early application permitted with disclosure; comparatives restated unless impracticable.

detail.applies_to: Companies with commercial banking or insurance activities that disclose financed emissions by industry; asset managers are not affected by the classification change.

sub_changes.new: No. Required instead: choose any industry classification that lets investors understand your exposure to transition risk, the risk that policy, technology and market shifts hurt the companies you finance.
sub_changes.old: Banks and insurers breaking down financed emissions by industry had to use one specific commercial classification system, the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS).
sub_changes.topic: Is the GICS system still required?
sub_changes.specifics: 2023: B62(a) and B63(a) required disaggregation 'by industry' using the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) six-digit industry-level code. 2026: B62(a) and B63(a) amended; new B62A(a)(i) and B63A(a)(i) — 'select an industry-classification system that enables it to classify investees or counterparties in a manner that results in information that enables users of general purpose financial reports to understand the entity's exposure to climate-related transition risks'. BC129A–BC129F: the GICS requirement was replaced with a principle-based approach because of 'legal and cost implications' and 'duplicative reporting'; users confirmed information remains decision-useful without a single standardised system.

sub_changes.new: Required: prefer a system that other companies in your industry or country commonly use over one you built yourself, as long as it still gives useful transition-risk information. All else being equal, the commonly used system wins.
sub_changes.old: No choice to make.
sub_changes.topic: How to choose a classification system
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: B62A(a)(i) / B63A(a)(i) — 'A system that is commonly used by other entities such as those operating in the same industry or jurisdiction (commonly used system) is more likely to support the comparability of information than a system used only by the entity (entity-specific system). If a commonly used system enables the entity to provide useful information about its exposure to climate-related transition risks—with all else being equal—the entity shall prioritise that system.' BC129D refers to a system 'used to meet a jurisdictional or exchange requirement' as an example of a system entities may already use; the standard names no specific system and does not state which systems qualify (not stated).

sub_changes.new: Permitted: a group that does both commercial banking and insurance may use different classification systems for the two activities.
sub_changes.old: One prescribed commercial classification system for everything.
sub_changes.topic: Groups with both banking and insurance
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: B62A(a)(i) and B63A(a)(i) each state that 'An entity that participates in both commercial banking and insurance activities need not use the same system to classify investees or counterparties for its commercial banking and insurance activities', cross-referring to each other. Asset management (B61) has no industry disaggregation requirement, so no classification choice arises there (not stated).

sub_changes.new: Required: name the classification system you used and explain how that choice gives investors a view of your transition-risk exposure.
sub_changes.old: Nothing beyond naming the prescribed system.
sub_changes.topic: What to disclose about the choice
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: B62A(a)(ii) / B63A(a)(ii) — disclose '(1) the industry-classification system it used to classify investees or counterparties; and (2) information that enables users of general purpose financial reports to understand how the entity's selection of that system fulfils the requirements in paragraph B62A(a)(i)' (or B63A(a)(i)). This is in addition to the existing B62/B63 disclosures of gross exposure by industry and asset class, the percentage of gross exposure included, and the methodology used.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: banks must still cover loans, project finance, bonds, equity investments and undrawn loan commitments; insurers the same list without project finance. Adding other asset classes is allowed if you explain why they are relevant.
sub_changes.old: Financed emissions had to be broken down by named asset classes.
sub_changes.topic: Asset classes are still fixed
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: B62A(b) — 'the disclosure shall include loans, project finance, bonds, equity investments and undrawn loan commitments'; B63A(b) — 'loans, bonds, equity investments and undrawn loan commitments'. Both add: 'If the entity calculates and discloses financed emissions for other asset classes, it shall include an explanation of why the inclusion of those additional asset classes provides relevant information to users of general purpose financial reports.' Disaggregation remains by Scope 1, 2 and 3 of the investee for each industry by asset class (B62(a), B63(a)).

sub_changes.new: Required unless impracticable: if you previously disclosed financed emissions by industry, re-present last year's breakdown using the classification system you now select.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Restating last year's industry breakdown
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: C6(c) — if the entity disclosed disaggregated financed-emissions information by industry in the preceding period under B62 or B63, it 'shall adjust the comparative information to reflect the industry-classification system it selected in accordance with paragraph B62A(a) or B63A(a) as if it had used that system in that preceding period', unless impracticable. Effective with the rest of the package: annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, early application permitted (C1B).

implications: Decide which industry classification your lending and investment books will use for 2027 reporting, and prefer the one your peers or regulator already use.
Write down the reasoning for the choice; you will publish a short explanation of why it shows transition-risk exposure.
If you run both banking and insurance, decide whether one system or two serves investors better, and keep the decision consistent year to year.
Re-map last year's financed-emissions breakdown to the new system so comparatives are ready.

detail.applies_to: Every company applying the ISSB climate standard; the partial relief matters for groups with operations in jurisdictions that mandate their own GHG method.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: the 2004 Corporate Standard remains the required method. The amendments did not move the reference to any newer or revised GHG Protocol text.
sub_changes.old: Emissions had to be measured using the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard as published in 2004, unless a government or stock exchange required a different method.
sub_changes.topic: Which GHG Protocol version is required
sub_changes.specifics: 2023 and 2026: paragraph 29(a)(ii) and B24 require measurement 'in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (2004)'. The December 2025 amendments did not alter the version referenced; the Basis for Conclusions does not discuss the GHG Protocol's ongoing revision (not stated). Scope 3 category definitions continue to reference the GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard (2011) (29(a)(vi)(1), B32).

sub_changes.new: Clarified: the relief applies 'in whole or in part'. You may use the other method for the part of the company covered by the requirement, for as long as that requirement lasts.
sub_changes.old: If a government or stock exchange required a different measurement method, you could use that method instead. The wording did not say what happened if the requirement only touched part of your business.
sub_changes.topic: When a government requires another method
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: 29(a)(ii) — '...unless the entity is required, in whole or in part, by a jurisdictional authority or an exchange on which the entity is listed to use a different method'. B24 — 'the entity is permitted to use this different method for the part of the entity to which that requirement applies, rather than using the Greenhouse Gas Protocol… for as long as the jurisdictional or exchange requirement applies to that part of the entity'. BC97A–BC97D: relief continues 'for as long as any such jurisdictional or exchange requirement applies'. The relief is triggered by a requirement, not by a permission to use another method (B24 wording).

sub_changes.new: Permitted: the part of the group subject to the local rule uses the local method; the rest keeps using the GHG Protocol. The result is one inventory built on two methods, which you must explain.
sub_changes.old: Not stated.
sub_changes.topic: Mixing methods inside one inventory
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: BC97B — 'if only part of an entity is subject to a jurisdictional or exchange requirement, the entity is permitted to use this relief but only for the part of the entity to which that jurisdictional or exchange requirement applies. The remaining part of the entity is required to measure its greenhouse gas emissions using the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard'; 'part' can be a subsidiary, a branch or an asset such as an energy-production facility. B28 (as amended): for each alternative method applied under 29(a)(ii), B24–B25 or C4(a), disclose the method and measurement approach, the reasons, and how it relates to the paragraph 27 disclosure objective. C6(a): if measurement changed because of the relief, adjust the preceding period 'as if it had changed how it measures greenhouse gas emissions in that preceding period', unless impracticable.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged in substance, now applying to each alternative method you use: name the method and approach, give the reasons, and explain how it meets the disclosure objective.
sub_changes.old: Disclose the method and measurement approach used, the reasons for choosing it and how it relates to the aim of giving investors useful emissions information.
sub_changes.topic: What to disclose when using another method
sub_changes.specifics: B28 (2026 wording, listed as amended in C1A): 'When an entity discloses its greenhouse gas emissions measured in accordance with another method, applying paragraphs 29(a)(ii), B24–B25 or C4(a), the entity shall disclose for each alternative method: (a) the applicable method and measurement approach the entity uses to determine its greenhouse gas emissions; and (b) the reason, or reasons, for the entity's choice of method and measurement approach and how that approach relates to the disclosure objective in paragraph 27.' Paragraph 29(a)(iii) separately requires the approach, inputs and assumptions used, including changes in the period and the reasons.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: the first-year relief stays. It is a one-year bridge, separate from the open-ended jurisdictional relief.
sub_changes.old: A company already using a method other than the GHG Protocol could keep using it in the first year it applied the standard.
sub_changes.topic: First-year relief for an existing method
sub_changes.specifics: C4(a): in the first annual reporting period of applying IFRS S2, an entity that used a method other than the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard (2004) in the immediately preceding period 'is permitted to continue using' that method. C5: a relief used in the first year may continue to be applied in comparative information presented in later periods. The IFRS Foundation preparers' guide (September 2024) confirms the method and Scope 3 reliefs apply to 'the first year' only. Jurisdictions may extend reliefs (Jurisdictional Guide, May 2024, paragraphs 25 and 136).

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: the amendments do not touch the boundary choice. You still pick a GHG Protocol approach and disclose it, with the reasons and any change in the year.
sub_changes.old: Not fixed by the standard: you choose the GHG Protocol consolidation approach (equity share, financial control or operational control) and disclose it.
sub_changes.topic: Equity share or control boundary
sub_changes.specifics: B26–B27 (UK SRS S2 reproduction of IFRS S2 text): the entity discloses its measurement approach, such as the equity share or control approach under the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard (2004), the rationale, and any changes during the reporting period. The ESRS–ISSB interoperability guidance (May 2024, section 4.1(vii)) notes that IFRS S2 B27 'permits an entity to choose the equity share or control approach', while ESRS mandates inclusion of operationally controlled entities. Note the GHG Protocol revision proposes removing equity share (see the GHG Protocol block); that proposal does not change IFRS S2 unless the ISSB amends the reference.

sub_changes.new: Nothing changes automatically. Once GHG Protocol publishes revised standards, the ISSB must assess whether they serve the climate standard's objective, study the likely effects and run a public consultation before changing the 2004 reference.
sub_changes.old: A June 2024 agreement gave the ISSB an observer seat on the GHG Protocol's standards board and a commitment to keep the two bodies' work compatible.
sub_changes.topic: When GHG Protocol finishes its revision
sub_changes.specifics: SSAF staff paper AP4 'Working with the GHG Protocol' (September 2025): memorandum of understanding signed June 2024 'to ensure ongoing compatibility'; ISSB holds 'an observer seat on the GHG Protocol's Independent Standards Board' (p. 9); before proposing changes to IFRS S2 the ISSB must assess 'whether the revisions serve the objective of IFRS S2', evaluate 'likely effects of those changes' (p. 8, citing BC90) and conduct public consultation. GHG Protocol's consolidated draft is estimated for Q2 2027 and the revised standard for Q4 2028 (see GHG Protocol block). The paper does not state what happens to the 2004 reference in the interim (not stated).

implications: List every government or exchange rule that forces a non-GHG Protocol method on any part of your group, and map which legal entities it covers.
Decide whether to use the partial relief or convert the local figures to the GHG Protocol method; either way, document the method and reasons for publication.
Keep your 2004-basis inventory as the master; do not switch to draft GHG Protocol revisions for ISSB reporting until the ISSB changes the reference.
Prepare prior-year comparatives on the same mixed-method basis when you first apply the relief.
Record your consolidation approach and reasons; it is a disclosure, and investors will compare it with your financial statements.

rows.old: Latest IPCC global warming potential values required.

detail.timing: Effective for annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027; early application permitted with disclosure.

sources.ref: B21–B22 as amended; C1A, C1B, C6(a); BC97E–BC97H

detail.applies_to: Every company applying the ISSB climate standard; the relief matters for companies whose regulator or exchange mandates specific warming potential values.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged as the default: latest-IPCC, 100-year values remain required for everyone not covered by the new relief.
sub_changes.old: To add up different gases into one CO2-equivalent number you had to use the 100-year global warming potential values from the most recent IPCC assessment report available at your reporting date.
sub_changes.topic: Which warming values are required
sub_changes.specifics: B21 (2023 and 2026): convert the seven Kyoto Protocol greenhouse gases to CO2 equivalent 'using global warming potential values based on a 100-year time horizon, from the latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assessment available at the reporting date'. The standard does not name a specific assessment report; 'latest… available at the reporting date' moves automatically when the IPCC publishes a new one (B21 wording).

sub_changes.new: Permitted: if a government or stock exchange requires different warming values for all or part of your company, you may use those values for that part, for as long as the requirement applies.
sub_changes.old: No relief: a company required by a local rule to use older or different values had to recalculate to the latest IPCC values for ISSB reporting.
sub_changes.topic: The new relief
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: B21–B22 amended — '...unless the entity is required, in whole or in part, by a jurisdictional authority or an exchange on which it is listed to use different global warming potential values', in which case the entity is permitted to use them 'for the part of the entity to which that requirement applies, for as long as that requirement applies'. BC97E–BC97H: the relief 'does not significantly affect comparability' because GWP is 'only one of the inputs'. As with the method relief, a requirement (not a permission) is the trigger.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: factors already expressed in CO2-equivalent need not be recalculated; otherwise you apply the IPCC values (or the jurisdiction-required values under the relief).
sub_changes.old: If an emission factor you use already expresses the result in CO2-equivalent, you did not have to re-derive it with the latest values.
sub_changes.topic: Supplier factors already in CO2-equivalent
sub_changes.specifics: B22 (2026 wording): an entity using emission factors that already convert gases to CO2 equivalent 'need not recalculate' using the latest IPCC values, unless required in whole or in part by a jurisdictional authority or exchange to use different global warming potential values. The standard does not require disclosure of the vintage of factors used (not stated), but 29(a)(iii) requires the approach, inputs and assumptions, which would ordinarily cover emission-factor sources.

sub_changes.new: No new dedicated disclosure is added for the relief. The general requirement to explain inputs and assumptions applies, and if the relief changes your numbers you adjust last year's figures unless impracticable.
sub_changes.old: Approach, inputs and assumptions had to be disclosed; no dedicated warming-value disclosure existed.
sub_changes.topic: What to disclose and restate
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: no paragraph specific to GWP disclosure was added (B28 covers alternative measurement methods under 29(a)(ii), B24–B25 and C4(a), not B21–B22; BC97G notes a description of the GWP values used is required under 29(a)(iii)(1) where material). 29(a)(iii) requires disclosure of the measurement approach, inputs and assumptions, including changes and reasons. C6(a): if the entity 'has changed how it measures greenhouse gas emissions as a result of applying the relief in… paragraphs B21–B22', it adjusts comparative information for the preceding period unless impracticable. The proposed IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Taxonomy update (July 29, 2026; comments closed September 28, 2026) carries digital tags for the amended disclosures.

sub_changes.new: Annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, with early application permitted if disclosed.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: When the relief starts
sub_changes.specifics: C1A lists B21–B22 among the amended paragraphs; C1B: 'annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. Earlier application is permitted. If an entity applies these amendments earlier, it shall disclose that fact.' The exposure draft (April 28, 2025) proposed the relief; the final text was issued December 11, 2025.

implications: Inventory which regulators or exchanges require specific warming values for any part of your group, because only a requirement unlocks the relief.
Keep two conversion tables ready if you report the same gases under a local rule and under the ISSB default.
Re-check supplier and database emission factors for the warming values embedded in them; those already in CO2-equivalent need no recalculation.
Disclose the values and sources used as part of your inputs and assumptions, and restate last year if the relief changes your numbers.

rows.new: A voluntary practice statement built on the TNFD framework. The exposure draft was published on October 22, 2026 and comments close February 19, 2027. It is not a new mandatory standard, and applying it is not required to claim compliance with IFRS Standards - though a jurisdiction may choose to require it, and the ISSB is consulting on whether to issue the content as a full standard instead.
rows.old: Not covered.

detail.timing: Exposure draft published October 22, 2026; the 120-day consultation closes February 19, 2027. Both dates were announced by the ISSB on October 6, 2026 and the draft published on the announced date. No date is stated for final publication.

detail.applies_to: Any company applying the ISSB standards with material nature-related risks or opportunities; use of the practice statement itself would be optional unless a jurisdiction requires it.

sub_changes.new: No. Proposed: a 'Practice Statement', which is how-to guidance a company can choose to use, not a new standard. The ISSB says this leaves the door open for a standard later and will ask in the consultation whether this form is right.
sub_changes.old: No nature-specific standard or guidance existed. Nature-related risks fell under the general requirement to disclose any material sustainability-related risk.
sub_changes.topic: Is a new mandatory nature standard coming?
sub_changes.specifics: April 22, 2026 ISSB decision (12 of 12 members): 'to propose requirements and guidance for nature-related disclosures in the form of an IFRS Practice Statement'; the exposure draft will invite comment 'on the proposed form of an IFRS Practice Statement—with reference to alternative forms' (12/12). Sue Lloyd, June 29, 2026: 'a tool that companies can choose to use when providing nature-related information to investors, although a jurisdiction could decide to require companies to use it'; 'by developing these proposals in the form of a Practice Statement, we are leaving the door open for a Standard in the future'. IFRS S1 and S2 are not amended.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged and emphasised: material nature-related information is already required of anyone applying the ISSB standards. The practice statement would explain how to provide it.
sub_changes.old: Yes, if material: the general standard already covers all sustainability-related risks and opportunities that could affect your prospects.
sub_changes.topic: Do we already have to disclose nature risks?
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS news release, April 22, 2026: 'The ISSB's existing Standards already require companies to provide material information about all sustainability-related risks and opportunities, including nature-related risks and opportunities that could reasonably be expected to affect a company's prospects.' Emmanuel Faber: 'Providing material nature-related disclosures is not optional; IFRS S1 already requires that. A Practice Statement will guide companies on how to provide such disclosures.' The release also states applying the Practice Statement 'would have the full effect of an ISSB Standard for companies applying it'.

sub_changes.new: Proposed content agreed so far: location-specific information, definitions of nature-related physical and transition risks, the amount and share of assets or business activities exposed to nature risks or aligned with nature opportunities, and information on engagement with Indigenous Peoples, local communities and affected stakeholders, all with a 'reasonable information without undue cost or effort' proportionality cushion.
sub_changes.old: Nothing specific.
sub_changes.topic: What the practice statement would contain
sub_changes.specifics: ISSB Update April 2026: location-specific information about nature-related risks and opportunities; information about interactions and engagement with Indigenous Peoples, Local Communities and affected stakeholders (10/12); 'the amount and percentage of assets or business activities' vulnerable to nature risks or aligned with opportunities, with proportionality based on 'all reasonable and supportable information… without undue cost or effort' (12/12); governance, strategy, risk management and connected information built on IFRS S1. ISSB Update June 2026 (meeting June 24–25): use 'environmental resources' rather than 'environmental assets' (12/12); define 'nature-related transition risks' and 'nature-related physical risks' (8/12); first application: no comparatives in the first period, compliance statements required (12/12).

sub_changes.new: Proposed: the practice statement draws on the TNFD framework, including its stakeholder categories, and would let companies refer to TNFD metrics where they help meet the ISSB objective and do not conflict with the standards. Existing TNFD work should carry over.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable; many companies used the voluntary TNFD recommendations directly.
sub_changes.topic: How it uses the TNFD framework
sub_changes.specifics: April 2026 decision: reference the TNFD framework for stakeholder categorisation (9/12). June 2026 decision (11/12): entities may refer to TNFD metrics 'if they assist in meeting IFRS S1 objectives and don't conflict with IFRS standards or the Practice Statement'; IFRS S1 retains the reference to the CDSB Framework Application Guidance as a source of guidance (12/12). TNFD announced support for the ISSB's nature work in November 2025 (IFRS news). In April 2026 the ISSB also decided 'to consider the findings of the nature-related disclosures project as part of its work on enhancing the SASB Standards' (12/12). Which TNFD components (LEAP approach, core global metrics) are reproduced is not stated in published decisions.

sub_changes.new: Yes, in principle: companies choose whether to use the practice statement, but a government or regulator could require it when adopting the ISSB standards. No jurisdiction has announced such a requirement in the sources read.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Can a jurisdiction make it mandatory?
sub_changes.specifics: Sue Lloyd, IFRS Foundation Conference, June 29, 2026: 'a tool that companies can choose to use when providing nature-related information to investors, although a jurisdiction could decide to require companies to use it.' The IFRS Foundation's Jurisdictional Guide (May 2024) frames adoption as 'adopt, apply or otherwise be informed by' ISSB Standards (paragraph 16). No jurisdictional profile or snapshot read for this research mentions mandating the nature Practice Statement (not stated).

sub_changes.new: Published: exposure draft issued October 22, 2026, comments close February 19, 2027; final text later, date not stated. Once issued, the practice statement would be usable immediately, with no comparatives required in the first period.
sub_changes.old: Research project only, started after the 2023 agenda consultation; the ISSB moved it to standard-setting in November 2025.
sub_changes.topic: Timeline and first-time use
sub_changes.specifics: ISSB Update July 2026 (meeting July 21–22, 2026): all 12 members satisfied with due process; no member intends to dissent; 'The ISSB decided to set a 120-day comment period for the exposure draft' (12/12); 'plans to publish the exposure draft in October 2026'. The exposure draft was published on October 22, 2026; the project page now shows the project open for comment to February 19, 2027, with 'Exposure Draft Feedback' as the next milestone. June 2026 decision (12/12): Practice Statement available from issuance date; no comparative information required for the first period; exemptions consistent with IFRS S1 paragraph 73 apply. Final publication date: not stated.

implications: Do not wait for the practice statement to assess nature-related risks: if they are material to your prospects, the general standard already requires disclosure.
Keep any TNFD-based assessment and metrics; they are the expected starting point and should carry over.
Prepare location-level data on sites and supply chains exposed to nature risks, since location-specific information is in the proposals.
Plan to review the exposure draft when it lands and decide whether to comment within the 120-day window.
Watch the jurisdictions you report in for any move to make the practice statement compulsory.

rows.new: Unchanged by the amendments: all three scopes remain required for everyone applying the standard, scope 3 may be omitted only in the first year, and the only new scope 3 relief is the category 15 financed-emissions limit.
rows.old: Scope 1, 2 and 3 all required; scope 3 could be skipped in the first year of applying the standard; location-based scope 2 required.

detail.applies_to: Every company applying the ISSB climate standard, whether voluntarily or under a local mandate; local versions may lengthen the reliefs.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: scope 3 is required for everyone applying the climate standard after the first year. You must consider all 15 categories and say which ones your figure includes. The 2027 amendments add only the category 15 financed-emissions limit.
sub_changes.old: Yes, required: gross scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions in tonnes of CO2-equivalent, with scope 3 covering upstream and downstream and the 15 GHG Protocol categories considered.
sub_changes.topic: Is scope 3 mandatory under the ISSB?
sub_changes.specifics: Paragraph 29(a)(i): absolute gross Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions in metric tonnes of CO2 equivalent. 29(a)(vi)(1) and B32: consider the 15 Scope 3 categories of the GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard (2011), include upstream and downstream, and disclose the categories included. B34–B35: reassess scope on a significant event or change in circumstances; more frequent reassessment permitted. Jurisdictions diverge: UK SRS S2 makes the Scope 3 relief indefinite on a comply-or-explain basis (UK snapshot, June 18, 2026); Canada's CSDS extends it to three years; Australia requires Scope 3 from the second year (Group 1 from periods beginning January 1, 2026).

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: the same five first-year reliefs remain, and you can still state full compliance while using them. The 2027 amendments add a separate transition rule for companies already reporting who switch to a relief.
sub_changes.old: First-year reliefs: no comparatives, keep an existing non-GHG Protocol method, skip scope 3 (including financed emissions), report climate only, and publish sustainability disclosures later than the financial statements.
sub_changes.topic: What you can skip in year one
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS S2 C3: no comparative information required in the first annual reporting period. C4(a): continue a non-GHG Protocol method used in the preceding period. C4(b): 'An entity is not required to disclose its Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions', including financed emissions for asset managers, banks and insurers, in the first period. C5: reliefs may continue in comparatives presented later. IFRS S1 Appendix E (per the IFRS preparers' guide, September 2024): climate-only reporting in year one; publication after the financial statements in year one. Preparers' guide: a company using these reliefs 'may state that it has complied with ISSB Standards provided it has otherwise met all of the requirements'. 2026: new C6 governs comparatives for entities already applying IFRS S2.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: location-based scope 2 is required; a market-based figure is not required but you must give information about contractual instruments such as renewable power contracts and unbundled certificates where needed to understand scope 2.
sub_changes.old: Location-based (grid-average) scope 2 required, plus information about any contracts or certificates that investors need to understand your scope 2 position.
sub_changes.topic: Scope 2: which number to report
sub_changes.specifics: Paragraph 29(a)(v): disclose 'location-based Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions, and provide information about any contractual instruments that is necessary to inform users' understanding of the entity's Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions'. B30–B31: contractual instruments include 'any type of contract between an entity and another party for the sale and purchase of energy bundled with attributes about the energy generation or for unbundled energy attribute claims'. No market-based total is required (not stated). Contrast: ESRS requires both location- and market-based figures (interoperability guidance, section 4.2, ESRS E1.AR24). The GHG Protocol Scope 2 revision (see GHG Protocol block) does not alter this requirement unless the ISSB amends the standard.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: disclose scope 1 and 2 separately for the consolidated group and for associates, joint ventures and unconsolidated subsidiaries. The split is not required for scope 3.
sub_changes.old: Scope 1 and 2 had to be shown separately for the consolidated accounting group and for other investees such as associates and joint ventures.
sub_changes.topic: Splitting group companies from investees
sub_changes.specifics: Paragraph 29(a)(iv): for Scope 1 and Scope 2, disaggregate between (1) the consolidated accounting group (parent and consolidated subsidiaries) and (2) other investees excluded from the consolidated group (associates, joint ventures and unconsolidated subsidiaries). ESRS E1.50 uses a different split (operational control), so a company reporting under both may need two disaggregations (interoperability guidance section 3.1(iv), p. 17). Scope 3: not stated.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: the measurement framework and the two percentage disclosures stay as they were.
sub_changes.old: Use all reasonable and supportable information available without undue cost or effort; prefer direct measurement, primary data, timely data and verified data; disclose how much of scope 3 came from specific suppliers' data and how much was verified.
sub_changes.topic: How good must scope 3 data be?
sub_changes.specifics: B39: use 'all reasonable and supportable information that is available to the entity at the reporting date without undue cost or effort' in selecting approach, inputs and assumptions. B40: prioritise inputs with four characteristics — direct measurement over estimation (B43–B45), primary data from specific value-chain activities over secondary data (B46–B49), timely data representing the activity's jurisdiction and technology (B50–B52), verified data (B53–B54). B56: disclose the extent measured 'using inputs from specific activities within the entity's value chain' and the extent 'using inputs that are verified'. B19: value-chain data from a different reporting period may be used if the periods are the same length and significant events between the dates are disclosed.

sub_changes.new: Several adopting jurisdictions give longer or open-ended scope 3 relief, so the year-one answer depends on where you file. Check the local text, not only the ISSB's.
sub_changes.old: The one-year reliefs were the standard's own; adopting jurisdictions were encouraged to limit phasing to those reliefs.
sub_changes.topic: Local versions stretch the reliefs
sub_changes.specifics: Jurisdictional Guide (May 2024) paragraph 25: jurisdictions 'might choose to consider providing brief extensions of the transition standard reliefs'; paragraph 136: phasing 'should be limited only to transition standard reliefs'. IFRS Foundation snapshots and profiles: UK SRS S2 (February 25, 2026) — Scope 3 relief with 'no specified time limit', proposed comply-or-explain for listed companies; Canada CSDS 2 (December 2024) — Scope 3 relief extended to three years; Australia AASB S2 — Scope 3 mandatory for Group 1 from periods beginning January 1, 2026; Singapore — Scope 3 mandatory FY2026 for STI constituents only, voluntary for others (profile updated June 26, 2026); Hong Kong — Scope 3 follows the New Climate Requirements timeline (LargeCap mandatory from January 1, 2026).

implications: Treat scope 3 as mandatory from your second ISSB reporting year unless the jurisdiction you file in extends the relief in writing.
Decide early which scope 3 categories your figure includes and be ready to publish the list with reasons for exclusions.
Build the two percentages, share from supplier-specific data and share verified, into your scope 3 workpapers now.
Report location-based scope 2 as the headline and prepare a plain description of your contracts and certificates alongside it.
If you use a first-year relief, say so and still make the compliance statement; keep the relief consistent in later comparatives.

rows.new: The ISSB cannot mandate anything itself. More than 45 jurisdictions are using the standards (IFRS Foundation, August 2026), with first mandatory reports already filed in Australia and due in Hong Kong (2026), Japan (fiscal years ending March 2027) and the UK (accounting periods from January 1, 2027, on a comply-or-explain basis, confirmed by FCA PS26/19 on September 30, 2026); the US and EU are not on the list. Brazil revoked its 2026 mandate in May 2026 and moved to a voluntary, justify-if-you-don't regime from 2027.
