sub_changes.new: Unchanged: each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt the standards as issued, build local standards designed to deliver the same outcomes, or only draw on them. Your obligation comes from local law or listing rules, not from the ISSB.
sub_changes.old: The standards took effect for annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2024, 'subject to jurisdictional adoption'; nothing was mandatory until a government or exchange made it so.
sub_changes.topic: Who decides whether we must report
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS S2 paragraph C1: effective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after January 1, 2024, earlier application permitted (IFRS navigator page). Jurisdictional Guide (May 2024) paragraph 16: 'adopt or otherwise use' covers approaches to 'adopt, apply or otherwise be informed by' ISSB Standards, including 'local sustainability-related disclosure requirements (or standards) designed to deliver functionally aligned outcomes'. Paragraphs 110–111: full adoption means a legal requirement for all or most publicly accountable entities to apply IFRS S1 and S2 'as issued by the ISSB'. Paragraphs 142–145: modifications removing requirements 'could conflict with the objective' of comparable information.

sub_changes.new: August 2026: the IFRS Foundation counts more than 45 jurisdictions using the standards and says companies in 18 jurisdictions will be issuing reports by 2027. Its jurisdiction page (updated September 24, 2026) lists 24 jurisdictional profiles (one marked forthcoming) and 13 in-progress snapshots; the page gives no official totals.
sub_changes.old: June 12, 2025: 36 jurisdictions adopting or finalising steps; 17 published profiles, of which 14 aimed at full adoption, 2 climate-only, 1 partial.
sub_changes.topic: How many jurisdictions, as of now
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS news, June 12, 2025: 36 jurisdictions 'have adopted or otherwise used… or are in the process of finalising steps'; 17 profiles (Australia, Bangladesh, Brazil, Chile, Ghana, Hong Kong SAR, Jordan, Kenya, Malaysia, Mexico, Nigeria, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Chinese Taipei, Tanzania, Türkiye, Zambia), 14 targeting full adoption, 2 climate requirements only, 1 partial. IFRS news, August 18, 2026 (Trustees' five-year plan): '45+ jurisdictions' using ISSB Standards; '18 jurisdictions will have companies issuing reports by 2027'. Use-by-jurisdiction page, last updated September 24, 2026: 24 jurisdictional profiles listed as of the page's September 24, 2026 update (Oman marked forthcoming, so 23 published) and 13 snapshots; the IFRS Foundation's own September 2026 World Standard-setters deck counts 22 finalised profiles and 14 snapshot jurisdictions, so counts differ between IFRS Foundation sources (in progress, including Canada, China, South Korea, Switzerland, United Kingdom). Counting methods differ between sources; cite the as-of date.

sub_changes.new: Required for the largest Tokyo Prime Market companies: ISSB-based Japanese standards apply from fiscal years ending March 2027 for companies above 3 trillion yen market value, March 2028 above 1 trillion, March 2029 above 500 billion. Limited assurance starts in the second year, initially on scope 1 and 2, governance and risk management.
sub_changes.old: Japan's standards board was consulting on local standards based on the ISSB's.
sub_changes.topic: Japan: the first big market with hard dates
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS jurisdictional profile: Japan (updated July 16, 2026): Financial Services Agency and Sustainability Standards Board of Japan (SSBJ); mandatory for Prime Market listings with market capitalisation of ¥500 billion or more on a five-year average; phase-in: FY ending March 2027 for ¥3 trillion+, March 2028 for ¥1 trillion+, March 2029 for ¥500 billion+. 'Limited assurance is required from the second annual reporting period', restricted for the first two years to Scope 1 and 2 emissions, governance and risk management. SSBJ Standards contain 'jurisdiction-specific alternatives' and deliver 'functionally aligned outcomes'; early application of the December 2025 S2 amendments is permitted. Scope 3 mandatory status: not explicitly stated in the profile.

sub_changes.new: Required: Group 1 (meets at least two of: revenue of at least A$500 million, assets A$1 billion, 500 employees, or is registered under the national emissions reporting scheme) from financial years beginning January 1, 2025; Group 2 from July 1, 2026; Group 3 from July 1, 2027. Scope 3 from the second year. Assurance phases from limited on scope 1 and 2 to reasonable assurance on everything for financial years beginning on or after July 1, 2030.
sub_changes.old: Legislation passed in 2024 made ISSB-based climate reporting mandatory in three waves from January 1, 2025.
sub_changes.topic: Australia: already reporting, assurance ramping up
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS jurisdictional profile: Australia (updated June 12, 2025): Corporations Act 2001 amendments (2024); AASB S2 mandatory, AASB S1 voluntary. Group 1: at least two of revenue ≥ A$500m, assets ≥ A$1bn, ≥ 500 employees, or NGER-registered corporations (same two-of-three test for Groups 2 and 3), periods from January 1, 2025; Group 2: A$200m / A$500m / 250, from July 1, 2026; Group 3: A$50m / A$25m / 100, from July 1, 2027. Scope 3 mandatory from periods beginning January 1, 2026 for Group 1. Assurance: year 1 limited over governance, strategy, Scope 1 and 2; years 2–3 limited over all; reasonable over all for financial years commencing on or after July 1, 2030 (ASSA 5010; ASSA 5000 engagements). Industry-based disclosures not required until finalised (target 2030). Scenario analysis: a high-warming and a Paris-aligned scenario (s.296D(2B)).

sub_changes.new: Proposed: UK versions of both standards were published February 25, 2026 and are voluntary until mandated. The listing regulator consulted (closed March 20, 2026) on requiring them for listed companies from January 1, 2027, with final decisions expected autumn 2026; a Companies Act route is deferred.
sub_changes.old: The UK was consulting on endorsing the ISSB standards with modifications.
sub_changes.topic: United Kingdom: standards final, mandate pending
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS snapshot: United Kingdom (June 18, 2026): UK SRS S1 and S2 issued February 25, 2026; UK amendments remove the delayed-publication relief, make the non-climate and Scope 3 reliefs open-ended, add compliance-assertion wording, let financial entities omit financed emissions where 'impracticable to reliably estimate' (B59A), and change industry guidance from 'shall' to 'may'. FCA consultation published January 30, 2026, closed March 20, 2026; 'final decisions on the application of UK SRS are expected in the autumn of 2026'. FCA CP26/5 proposes UK SRS S2 climate disclosures (excluding Scope 3) for accounting periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, Scope 3 comply-or-explain from January 1, 2028, non-climate UK SRS S1 comply-or-explain from January 1, 2029; assurance 'to be determined'. UK SRS S2 reflects the December 2025 amendments. FCA Policy Statement PS26/19, published September 30, 2026, finalises the rules: UK SRS applies to in-scope listed issuers on a comply-or-explain basis for accounting periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, with one year of transitional relief for Scope 3 and two years for the wider UK SRS S1 disclosures.

sub_changes.new: Required in Singapore for straits-index companies from FY2025 (scope 3 from FY2026), other listed issuers from FY2028 or FY2030 by size, large private companies from FY2030. Required in Hong Kong for large-cap issuers from January 1, 2026, comply-or-explain for other main-board issuers from 2025, with full local standards targeted for 2028.
sub_changes.old: Both exchanges had announced ISSB-aligned climate reporting roadmaps.
sub_changes.topic: Singapore and Hong Kong: listed companies first
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS profile: Singapore (updated June 26, 2026): STI constituents FY2025 for Scope 1 and 2 and other ISSB climate disclosures, Scope 3 mandatory FY2026 (STI only); non-STI issuers with market cap ≥ S$1bn FY2028, under S$1bn FY2030; large non-listed companies (revenue ≥ S$1bn and assets ≥ S$500m) FY2030; limited assurance on Scope 1 and 2 from FY2029 (listed) and FY2032 (non-listed). IFRS profile: Hong Kong SAR (updated June 12, 2025): HKFRS S1/S2 issued December 2024, voluntary from August 1, 2025; HKEX New Climate Requirements mandatory for LargeCap issuers from January 1, 2026, comply-or-explain for Main Board from January 1, 2025; Scope 1 and 2 mandatory for all listed issuers from 2025; full HKFRS S1/S2 targeted for January 1, 2028.

sub_changes.new: Canada: voluntary standards since January 1, 2025 with longer reliefs; the securities regulators paused their mandatory rule in April 2025, while the banking supervisor's guideline aligns with them. Brazil: no longer required. A May 29, 2026 resolution revoked the mandate that would have applied from fiscal years beginning January 1, 2026; reporting under the translated ISSB standards is now voluntary, companies that do not file must justify that choice from January 1, 2027, and those that opt in must continue for at least three consecutive years. Assurance rules for voluntary reporters are unchanged (law-firm summaries; the IFRS profile is under review).
sub_changes.old: Canada's standards board was consulting; Brazil's securities regulator had set a voluntary-then-mandatory path.
sub_changes.topic: Canada and Brazil
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS snapshot: Canada (June 12, 2025): CSDS 1 and 2 issued December 2024, voluntary from January 1, 2025; Scope 3 relief three years; climate-first two years; quantitative scenario-analysis relief three periods; CSA 'pausing work on a climate-related disclosures rule' (April 2025); OSFI Guideline B-15 updated February 2025. IFRS profile: Brazil (June 12, 2025; 'updated 25 June 2026 pending review'): CVM Resolution 193 (October 2023) — voluntary from January 1, 2024, mandatory for publicly held companies from January 1, 2026 using CBPS 01 and 02 (IFRS S1 and S2 translations); limited assurance voluntary period, 'reasonable assurance' mandatory period. CVM Resolution 244 (May 29, 2026) 'revoga a obrigatoriedade' of the sustainability report; from January 1, 2027 a company that opts out 'deverá justificar essa opção'; voluntary reporters continue at least three consecutive fiscal years and pre-announce discontinuation; assurance of any published report retained (Mattos Filho, Demarest alerts; official text at conteudo.cvm.gov.br).

sub_changes.new: In practice most adopters modify something: open-ended scope 3 relief (UK), three-year relief (Canada), no industry metrics until 2030 (Australia), jurisdiction-specific alternatives (Japan). Read the local standard you actually file under, including whether and when it picks up the December 2025 amendments.
sub_changes.old: The ISSB encouraged adopting as issued, allowing only brief extensions of the transition reliefs.
sub_changes.topic: Local versions differ from the ISSB text
sub_changes.specifics: Jurisdictional Guide paragraphs 25, 136, 142–145 (brief extensions only; modifications removing requirements may conflict with the objective). Observed modifications in IFRS Foundation profiles and snapshots: UK — Scope 3 and non-climate reliefs with no time limit, 'shall' to 'may' for industry guidance, B59A impracticability relief; Canada — Scope 3 relief three years, climate-first two years; Australia — industry-based disclosures not required until the AASB finalises them (target 2030), AASB S1 voluntary; Japan — 'jurisdiction-specific alternatives'. Amendment uptake: UK SRS S2 reflects the December 2025 amendments; Japan permits early application; the AASB S2 compilation dated December 2025 includes C6; Australia's June 2025 profile does not mention them.

sub_changes.new: Still neither: the US and the EU do not appear among the IFRS Foundation's adopting profiles or snapshots as of September 24, 2026. US obligations come from state law (see US block) and EU obligations from its own standards (see EU block and the interoperability row).
sub_changes.old: Neither had adopted the ISSB standards.
sub_changes.topic: United States and European Union
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS Foundation use-by-jurisdiction page (last updated September 24, 2026) lists 24 profiles (one forthcoming) and 13 snapshots; the United States and the European Union are not among them. The EU's revised sustainability reporting standards (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563, Official Journal September 21, 2026, entering into force November 10, 2026, applying to financial years beginning on or after January 1, 2027) do not name the ISSB but recital 2 refers to 'interoperability with global sustainability reporting standards'. For US state requirements and the SEC position, see the US block; this row makes no further claim.

implications: Map every listed entity and large subsidiary to the jurisdiction list and record its first mandatory reporting period and assurance start date.
Set your group inventory to the strictest timetable you face, which today is likely Australia or Japan rather than your home market.
For each jurisdiction, note which local variant applies and whether it has incorporated the December 2025 amendments.

Read FCA PS26/19 (September 30, 2026) and plan UK SRS comply-or-explain reporting for FY2027 and note that Brazil has withdrawn its 2026 mandate (voluntary with a justification duty from 2027) before locking 2027 plans.
Do not assume ISSB compliance satisfies EU or US rules; those are separate regimes with their own rows.

rows.new: Still not stated by the ISSB: assurance is decided by each adopting jurisdiction, and most adopters phase it in, starting with limited assurance over scope 1 and 2.
rows.old: Not stated: the standards contained no requirement for independent assurance.

detail.timing: Global sustainability assurance standard effective for periods beginning on or after December 15, 2026; Australia requires reasonable assurance over all disclosures for financial years beginning on or after July 1, 2030; Japan limited assurance from the second reporting year; Singapore from FY2029; UK and Hong Kong undecided.

detail.applies_to: Companies with mandatory ISSB-based reporting; assurance obligations attach through local rules, not the ISSB standards.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: no assurance requirement exists in the ISSB standards or the 2027 amendments. Whether, when and at what level your disclosures are assured is set by the jurisdiction or exchange that mandates reporting.
sub_changes.old: Not stated. The standards describe what to disclose, not whether an auditor must check it; the IFRS Foundation told jurisdictions to consider assurance when adopting.
sub_changes.topic: Does the ISSB require assurance?
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS S1, IFRS S2 and the December 2025 amendments contain no assurance requirement (not stated). Jurisdictional Guide (May 2024) paragraph 80: materials will assist regulators with 'effectively phasing in supervision. Consideration will also be given to the introduction of assurance and related supervision.' IFRS preparers' guide (September 2024): 'Assurance by a third party could be possible. In cases of partial application, assurance would give users… a better understanding of and confidence in the basis for the information presented.' The IFRS S1 compliance statement (paragraph 72, per the preparers' guide) does not depend on assurance (not stated).

sub_changes.new: A dedicated global standard now exists: it works with any reporting framework including the ISSB's, covers both limited and reasonable assurance, and applies to periods beginning on or after December 15, 2026, with early use permitted.
sub_changes.old: Sustainability assurance was performed under general assurance standards; a dedicated global standard was in development.
sub_changes.topic: Which assurance standard practitioners use
sub_changes.specifics: IAASB: 'International Standard on Sustainability Assurance 5000, General Requirements for Sustainability Assurance Engagements' (ISSA 5000), approved September 2024 and published November 2024; 'Effective for periods beginning on or after December 15, 2026', early application permitted; framework-neutral, 'applicable across various sustainability topics and frameworks'; accommodates limited and reasonable assurance; usable by accountant and non-accountant practitioners. Australia applies the local equivalent ASSA 5000; Brazil's profile lists ISSA 5000, NBC TO 3000 (ISAE 3000 equivalent) and IESSA ethics standards.

sub_changes.new: Varies by market: Australia phases from limited to reasonable assurance over everything for financial years beginning on or after July 1, 2030; Japan requires limited assurance from the second reporting year; Singapore requires limited assurance over scope 1 and 2 from FY2029 for listed companies; Brazil's reporting mandate was revoked in May 2026, so its reasonable-assurance rule now applies only to companies that report voluntarily; the UK and Hong Kong have not decided.
sub_changes.old: Few mandates existed.
sub_changes.topic: What adopting jurisdictions actually require
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS profiles and snapshots: Australia (June 12, 2025) — year 1 limited assurance over governance, strategy, Scope 1 and 2; years 2–3 limited over all; reasonable over all from the fourth year, the Corporations Act requiring reasonable assurance over all disclosures for years commencing on or after July 1, 2030 (ASSA 5010; ASSA 5000 engagements). Japan (July 16, 2026) — 'Limited assurance is required from the second annual reporting period', first two years restricted to Scope 1 and 2, governance and risk management. Singapore (June 26, 2026) — limited assurance on Scope 1 and 2 from FY2029 (listed) and FY2032 (large non-listed). Brazil (June 12, 2025, pending review) — limited in voluntary period, reasonable from 2026; CVM Resolution 244 (May 29, 2026) revoked the mandate, so assurance attaches only to reports published. UK (June 18, 2026) — 'to be determined'. Hong Kong (June 12, 2025) — AFRC consultation planned; HKEX review in 2027.

sub_changes.new: Where phased, assurance starts with scope 1 and 2 emissions, governance and risk management, then widens to strategy and scope 3, and only later moves from limited to reasonable assurance.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: What gets assured first
sub_changes.specifics: Japan profile: limited assurance in years one and two of assurance covers 'Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions, governance and risk management'. Australia profile: year 1 limited assurance over governance, strategy, Scope 1 and 2; years 2–3 limited over all disclosures (including Scope 3 and scenario analysis); reasonable assurance over all from the fourth reporting year and, by law, for years commencing on or after July 1, 2030. Singapore profile: Scope 1 and 2 only at first. No jurisdiction read requires reasonable assurance from the first mandatory year; Brazil, which did, revoked its mandate by CVM Resolution 244 (May 29, 2026) and the profile is pending review.

implications: Ask the question jurisdiction by jurisdiction: the ISSB will not tell you whether assurance is required, your regulator or exchange will.
Get scope 1 and 2 data, governance and risk-management descriptions assurance-ready first; that is where every phased regime starts.
Plan for reasonable assurance within a few years in Australia (and for any voluntary report you publish in Brazil), and budget for the dedicated sustainability assurance standard.
Keep evidence trails for scope 3 estimates and scenario analysis now, since they fall into scope in year two or three of most regimes.

rows.new: The 2024 guidance still stands, but it was written against the 2023 EU standards. The EU adopted revised, slimmer standards in 2026 (entering into force November 10, 2026) and no updated joint ISSB–EU guidance had been published as of October 1, 2026, so the map must be re-checked against the new EU text.
rows.old: Joint guidance (May 2024) mapped the ISSB standards to the EU's 2023 sustainability standards: a company starting from the EU rules could meet the ISSB climate standard with 'a very limited number of points to consider', and an ISSB reporter needed a defined list of extra EU disclosures.
rows.topic: Reporting under both the ISSB and EU rules

detail.timing: Joint guidance dated May 2, 2024; revised EU standards enter into force November 10, 2026 and mandatory for financial years beginning on or after January 1, 2027; no updated joint guidance as of October 1, 2026.

detail.applies_to: Groups with EU reporting obligations (in scope of the EU directive at the revised thresholds) that also report under the ISSB standards voluntarily or in another jurisdiction.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: the two financial-materiality definitions are aligned, so a company applying both should reach the same financial-materiality conclusions. The EU adds impact materiality on top, which the ISSB does not require.
sub_changes.old: The EU rules use 'double materiality' (impacts on people and planet as well as financial effects); the ISSB uses financial materiality only.
sub_changes.topic: Materiality: one test or two
sub_changes.specifics: ESRS–ISSB Standards Interoperability Guidance (May 2, 2024, 33 pages), introduction and section 1.1: 'The financial materiality assessment in ESRS 1 corresponds to the identification of information that is material for primary users of general purpose financial reports' (ESRS 1 paragraph 48; IFRS S1 paragraph 18); ESRS assesses impact and financial materiality, ISSB focuses on primary users of general purpose financial reports; on financial materiality, outcomes are expected to align. The IFRS Foundation's webcast slides on the guidance note 'ESRS has a complementary yet broader scope than the ISSB Standards.' Whether the revised ESRS (2026) changed the materiality wording is addressed in the EU block; the 2024 guidance has not been re-issued (not stated).

sub_changes.new: Per the 2024 map, an EU reporter needs to add or check seven climate items: transition-plan assumptions, scenario analysis done the ISSB way, industry-based metrics, the group-versus-investee emissions split, quantified climate opportunities, capital deployed, and carbon-credit credibility; financial firms also need financed emissions.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable before the guidance.
sub_changes.topic: Starting from EU rules: what to add for the ISSB
sub_changes.specifics: Interoperability Guidance section 3.1: (i) key assumptions and dependencies of the transition plan (IFRS S2.14(a)(iv)); (ii) scenario analysis 'commensurate with entity's circumstances' (S2.22, B1–B18), ESRS E1 only requires disclosing whether used (E1.21); (iii) refer to and consider the Industry-based Guidance (S2.12, 23, 32, 37), ESRS lacks sector standards (ESRS 1.131(b) relief); (iv) Scope 1–2 disaggregation (S2.29(a)(iv) vs ESRS E1.50); (v) amount and percentage of activities aligned with climate opportunities (S2.29(d)); (vi) capital deployment (S2.29(e)); (vii) carbon-credit credibility and integrity (S2.36(e)(iv)). Section 3.2(i): financed emissions (S2.29(a)(vi)(2), B58–B63) have no ESRS equivalent. Written against ESRS Set 1 (2023).

sub_changes.new: Per the 2024 map, an ISSB reporter must add, among others: a market-based scope 2 figure, energy consumption and mix, gross (not net) reduction targets with a base year, an operational-control boundary, carbon credits actually cancelled, locked-in emissions and EU taxonomy links in the transition plan, plus governance and strategy items with no ISSB equivalent.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable before the guidance.
sub_changes.topic: Starting from the ISSB: what to add for EU rules
sub_changes.specifics: Interoperability Guidance section 4.1–4.2: scenario disclosures including a Paris-aligned scenario (E1.AR12(c)) and high-emission scenarios (E1.AR11(d)); single amounts rather than ranges except where ESRS allows (AR70(a), AR73(a), AR74(a)); gross exposure before adaptation (E1.66–67); GHG reduction targets gross only, intensity targets need an absolute companion (E1.AR23); operational-control boundary (E1.46, 50(b)); mandatory market-based Scope 2 (E1.AR24); energy consumption and mix (E1.35–43); credits cancelled in period (E1.59); internal carbon pricing detail (E1.63); transition-plan detail (E1.16(a)–(j)). Table 4.2.1 lists ESRS 2 governance and strategy items (board composition, due diligence, internal controls, SBM-1 to SBM-3). The revised ESRS (2026) cut mandatory datapoints (see EU block), so this list is likely shorter now; not re-mapped by the standard setters (not stated).

sub_changes.new: Under the 2024 map: the ISSB lets you disclose planned credit use and set net targets if you also show the gross target; the EU rules allow only verified credits, require credits cancelled in the year, and forbid counting credits toward a reduction target.
sub_changes.old: Both frameworks asked about credits, but with different rules.
sub_changes.topic: Carbon credits and 'net' targets
sub_changes.specifics: Interoperability Guidance section 4.1(iii) and (vi): IFRS S2.36(e) permits disclosure of planned carbon-credit use without a verification requirement; ESRS E1 restricts to credits 'verified according to recognised quality standards' (Annex II) and E1.34(b) prohibits using credits to claim achievement of GHG reduction targets; ESRS requires credits cancelled in the reporting period (E1.59, AR61–63). IFRS S2 allows net or gross targets, with gross disclosed separately if net (S2.36(c), B68–B69); ESRS defines GHG reduction targets as gross only and 'net zero' as roughly 90–95% reduction plus removals (Annex II). Based on ESRS Set 1 (2023).

sub_changes.new: Unchanged in the 2024 map: a company reporting under both may need two boundary presentations, and the group-versus-investee split differs between the frameworks.
sub_changes.old: The ISSB lets you follow whichever GHG Protocol consolidation approach you choose; the EU rules require emissions from operations you control operationally even if not in your financial consolidation.
sub_changes.topic: Whose emissions are in the boundary
sub_changes.specifics: Interoperability Guidance section 4.1(vii), pp. 23–24: IFRS S2 B27 'permits an entity to choose the equity share or control approach' under the GHG Protocol (an IFRS S2 reporter moving to ESRS 'could elect to retain the financial control option'); ESRS E1.46 and 50(b) mandate inclusion of emissions 'under operational control' including associates, joint ventures, unconsolidated subsidiaries and contractual joint arrangements. Section 3.1(iv), p. 16: IFRS S2.29(a)(iv) splits consolidated group vs other investees; ESRS E1.50 splits consolidated group vs operationally controlled entities — 'two different disaggregations would need to be provided' if they differ (p. 17).

sub_changes.new: Partly. The EU's revised standards were adopted July 3, 2026, published September 21, 2026 and apply from financial years beginning January 1, 2027. They promise interoperability with global standards and mention the ISSB's industry guidance only as an optional source for entity-specific disclosures, without naming the ISSB itself, and the two standard setters have not reissued their joint guidance in the sources read.
sub_changes.old: It matched the EU standards in force at the time.
sub_changes.topic: Is the 2024 guidance still current?
sub_changes.specifics: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 of July 3, 2026 amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772: Official Journal September 21, 2026; entry into force November 10, 2026; applies to financial years beginning on or after January 1, 2027; recital 2 refers to 'interoperability with global sustainability reporting standards' without naming the ISSB. EFRAG news (2026) on the revised ESRS makes no mention of updated ISSB interoperability guidance. The ISSB Updates for April, June, July and September 2026 record no decision on ESRS interoperability (not stated). Reporting-year choice for FY2026 (revised or 2023 ESRS with reliefs) is covered in the EU block.

implications: If you report under both regimes, keep the 2024 joint guidance as your working map but re-test every line against the revised EU text before FY2027.
Run one financial-materiality assessment for both frameworks and layer the EU impact-materiality step on top.
Produce both location-based and market-based scope 2 figures and reconcile your boundary if the two frameworks' control tests differ.
Structure emissions targets as gross absolute reductions with a base year, and track carbon credits cancelled, not only planned.
Watch for a reissued ISSB–EU interoperability document; none had appeared by October 1, 2026.

rows.new: Unchanged by the amendments. The IFRS Foundation's June 2025 guidance and its implementation group (July 2026) clarify that 'targets' are not limited to emissions targets, nor to things labelled targets or approved by the board, and that the standard still does not require you to have a transition plan.
rows.old: Each climate target had to be disclosed with its metric, scope, period, base year, milestones, how the Paris Agreement informed it and, for emissions targets, whether it is gross or net; a transition plan was not required, but any plan you have had to be described with its assumptions and dependencies.

detail.timing: Core requirements effective where adopted since annual periods beginning January 1, 2024; transition-plan guidance published June 2025; implementation-group clarification on targets July 23, 2026, reported to the board September 24, 2026.

detail.applies_to: Every company applying the ISSB climate standard that has climate-related targets or a transition plan; no company is required to adopt either.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: not required. If you have one, you must describe it, the key assumptions behind it and what it depends on, alongside how you plan to meet your targets and resource the plan. The 2025 guidance is non-binding help, not a new rule.
sub_changes.old: No. The standard required disclosure of any transition plan you have, with its key assumptions and dependencies, but did not require you to make one.
sub_changes.topic: Do we have to have a transition plan?
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS S2 paragraph 14(a)(iv): disclose 'any climate-related transition plan the entity has, including information about key assumptions used in developing its transition plan, and dependencies on which the entity's transition plan relies'; 14(a)(i)–(iii), (v) and 14(b) cover business-model changes, mitigation and adaptation, achieving targets and resourcing. Appendix A: a transition plan is 'an aspect of an entity's overall strategy that lays out the entity's targets, actions or resources for its transition towards a lower-carbon economy'. IFRS Foundation guidance (June 2025), p. 2: 'not part of IFRS Standards and does not add to or otherwise change the requirements'; p. 6: 'IFRS S2 does not require an entity to have a transition plan nor require an entity to publish a transition plan'.

sub_changes.new: Clarified (staff view agreed by the implementation group, July 2026): targets are not limited to emissions targets and need not be labelled 'targets' or approved by a particular body. Anything used to manage climate risk or seize climate opportunities whose progress can be measured may need to be disclosed, which can pull in energy, water or resilience goals.
sub_changes.old: The standard asked for climate-related targets you set or must meet by law, including emissions targets, without saying whether non-emissions goals counted.
sub_changes.topic: What counts as a 'target'
sub_changes.specifics: Transition Implementation Group meeting July 23, 2026 (summary in ISSB agenda paper AP9, September 2026): staff view that climate-related targets required by IFRS S2 'are not limited to GHG emissions targets' (paragraph 6) and 'are not limited to things that are explicitly referred to or labelled as "targets", or targets that have been approved by a particular governance or management body' (paragraph 7); judgement considers whether the item '(a) is used to mitigate or adapt to its climate-related risks or take advantage of its climate-related opportunities' and '(c) progress toward the "target" can be monitored or measured' (paragraph 9); members 'expressed agreement with the staff analysis and staff view' (paragraph 17). TIG summaries are not authoritative amendments.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged.
sub_changes.old: For every target: the metric, the objective, where it applies, the period, the base year, milestones, and whether it is absolute or intensity-based; plus how it was set, whether a third party validated it, how it is reviewed and tracked, and performance against it.
sub_changes.topic: What to disclose about each target
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS S2 paragraph 33: for each target disclose the metric; the objective (mitigation, adaptation or conformance with science-based initiatives); the part of the entity covered; the period; the base period; interim milestones; absolute or intensity; and how the latest international agreement on climate change (including jurisdictional commitments) informed the target (33(h)). Paragraph 34: approach to setting and reviewing the target — third-party validation of target and methodology, review process, monitoring metrics, revisions with explanations. Paragraph 35: performance against each target and trend analysis. Paragraph 37: metrics should be cross-industry metrics from paragraph 29 or industry-based metrics from the SASB Standards or other sources meeting IFRS S1. (Text read in the UK SRS S2 reproduction.)

sub_changes.new: Unchanged. Reporters comparing with EU rules should note the EU does not recognise net reduction targets (see interoperability row).
sub_changes.old: For emissions targets: which gases, which scopes, whether gross or net (with a separate gross target if net), whether a sector pathway was used, and planned use of carbon credits.
sub_changes.topic: Extra detail for emissions targets
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS S2 paragraph 36: for GHG emissions targets disclose (a) the greenhouse gases covered; (b) whether Scope 1, 2 or 3 emissions are covered; (c) whether the target is gross or net, and if net, the associated gross target separately; (d) whether derived using a sectoral decarbonisation approach; (e) planned use of carbon credits — (i) the extent of reliance on credits, (ii) the third-party verification or certification scheme, (iii) the type of credit (nature-based or technological; carbon reduction or removal), (iv) other factors needed to understand credibility and integrity. Interoperability Guidance section 4.1(vi): ESRS defines reduction targets as gross only (ESRS E1 Annex II) and requires an absolute target where an intensity target is disclosed (E1.AR23).

sub_changes.new: No. The June 2025 guidance is educational material that builds on the TPT disclosure framework, which the IFRS Foundation took over in 2024, and maps the standard's requirements to TPT elements. It does not change what is required.
sub_changes.old: No ISSB guidance existed; many companies used the UK Transition Plan Taskforce (TPT) framework.
sub_changes.topic: Is the transition-plan guidance binding?
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS Foundation transition-plan guidance (June 2025), p. 2: the Foundation assumed responsibility for Transition Plan Taskforce materials in 2024 'to reduce fragmentation in disclosures and enhance the quality and comparability of information'; p. 7: the guidance 'builds on the disclosure-specific material authored by the Transition Plan Taskforce'; Appendix B maps IFRS S2 requirements to TPT framework elements; pp. 22–23: dependencies are 'critical factors and conditions for an entity's transition plan to be implemented' (workforce, ecosystem services, technologies, resources) and key assumptions may cover policy and regulatory action, technological developments, demand shifts, physical climate impacts and adaptation effectiveness.

implications: Inventory every measurable climate-related goal in your strategy, including energy, water and resilience commitments, and decide which must be disclosed as targets.
Do not create a transition plan solely for the standard; if you have one, document its assumptions and dependencies in disclosure-ready form.
For each emissions target, be explicit about gases, scopes, gross versus net and any planned credit use with the verification scheme.
Record whether a third party validated each target and how often you review it; both are disclosures.
Map an existing TPT-style plan to the standard using the guidance's appendix rather than rewriting it.

rows.new: Proposed: nine SASB industry standards comprehensively rewritten and 41 given targeted updates (consultation closed November 30, 2025; being redeliberated), three more proposed in March 2026 (closed July 24, 2026), six technology and communications standards to follow; the three financial-sector standards were already amended for financed emissions, effective January 1, 2027. Decided tentatively on October 29, 2026: when the SASB standards are used to prepare disclosures under the ISSB standards, the IFRS S1 requirements apply, the IFRS S1 reliefs for legally prohibited and commercially sensitive information are available, and the proportionality mechanism applies. A proposal to rename the SASB standards was discussed but not decided. Published for the November 18-19, 2026 meeting: staff recommend RETAINING the Scope 1 metrics in the industry-based materials, on a design principle that duplication with IFRS S2 is not by itself a reason to exclude content, with Scope 2 and Scope 3 left open and selective addition possible. Staff also set April 2027 as the planned publication of the digital tagging rules for the amended GHG disclosures.
rows.old: Companies applying the ISSB standards must refer to and consider the SASB industry standards and the industry-based guidance when identifying risks and choosing metrics.

detail.timing: Phase 1 consultation closed November 30, 2025 (redeliberation ongoing); three-standard consultation closed July 24, 2026; technology exposure draft to come; financial-sector amendments effective January 1, 2027; taxonomy comments closed September 28, 2026. Three tentative decisions taken October 29, 2026 and recorded in the October 2026 ISSB Update, all subject to formal ballot under the Due Process Handbook; feedback summaries on three industry standards and the first discussion of greenhouse gas taxonomy feedback are scheduled for the November 18-19, 2026 meeting. Agenda papers for the November 18-19, 2026 meeting are published and readable but carry no posting date beyond 'November 2026'. Paper AP6E asks the board to agree or disagree with three staff recommendations; papers AP6, AP6C, AP6D and AP7 state that no decisions are requested. Per AP7, balloting on the taxonomy update begins at the end of November 2026 with a pre-ballot review, with publication planned for April 2027 — dates that appear nowhere on the public project page. No date is given for redeliberation or finalisation of the three industry standards.

detail.applies_to: Every company applying the ISSB standards must consider the SASB standards for its industries; the financial-sector changes bind asset managers, banks and insurers reporting financed emissions.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged at ISSB level. Adopting jurisdictions vary: Australia does not require industry-based disclosures until it finalises its own by 2030, and the UK version turns the industry guidance from 'shall' into 'may'.
sub_changes.old: You must 'refer to and consider the applicability' of the SASB standards when identifying risks and metrics; you are not bound to report every metric. Some jurisdictions switch this off.
sub_changes.topic: Are the SASB industry standards mandatory?
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS news (July 3, 2025): under ISSB Standards companies must 'refer to and consider the applicability of' the SASB Standards to 'identify sustainability-related risks and opportunities applicable to its business activities and operations'. IFRS S2 paragraphs 12, 23, 32 and 37 refer to the Industry-based Guidance on Implementing IFRS S2 (per the interoperability guidance, section 3.1(iii)). Australia profile (June 12, 2025): AASB S2 'does not currently require industry-based disclosures'; 'The AASB intends to finalise mandatory requirements for industry-based disclosures by 2030'. UK snapshot (June 18, 2026): industry-specific guidance changed from 'shall' to 'may'.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: comprehensive amendments to nine standards, all eight extractives and minerals-processing industries plus processed foods, and targeted amendments to 41 more on common topics such as water management and workforce health and safety. Consultation closed November 30, 2025; the board discussed feedback in May 2026 without decisions.
sub_changes.old: SASB standards as inherited by the ISSB in 2022 (77 industries); no comprehensive review since.
sub_changes.topic: Which industries are being rewritten
sub_changes.specifics: Exposure Draft 'Proposed Amendments to the SASB Standards' (July 3, 2025): 'comprehensive amendments to nine SASB Standards' (the eight Extractives & Minerals Processing industries and Processed Foods) and 'targeted amendments to a further 41 SASB Standards' to 'maintain consistent disclosures for common topics across industries' (water management, workforce health and safety); related Exposure Draft on the Industry-based Guidance on Implementing IFRS S2 covering the nine priority industries and 37 of the 41. Comment period closed November 30, 2025. Project page: May 13, 2026 meeting discussed feedback on extractives and processed foods; 'The ISSB was not asked to make any decisions.' Original aim: 'issue the enhancements in 2026, subject to stakeholder feedback'.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: amendments to the Agricultural Products, Meat, Poultry & Dairy, and Electric Utilities & Power Generators standards, consulted March 26 to July 24, 2026, to align language and concepts with the ISSB standards and improve international applicability.
sub_changes.old: Not in the first batch.
sub_changes.topic: Agriculture, meat and power generation
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS news (March 26, 2026): second Exposure Draft proposing amendments to three SASB Standards — Agricultural Products; Meat, Poultry & Dairy; Electric Utilities & Power Generators; 120-day comment period to July 24, 2026; aims to 'align the language and concepts in the SASB Standards with ISSB Standards' and 'improve the international applicability and decision-usefulness of the disclosures', keeping climate content aligned with IFRS S2 industry guidance. Finalisation timing: not stated.

sub_changes.new: Proposed next: the board decided in July 2026 to enhance the six technology and communications standards and will prepare an exposure draft; no date yet.
sub_changes.old: Not scheduled.
sub_changes.topic: Technology and communications sector
sub_changes.specifics: ISSB Update July 2026: 'The ISSB decided to enhance the six SASB Standards in the Technology & Communications sector of the Sustainable Industry Classification System (SICS)' (12/12); 'The ISSB will begin preparing an exposure draft of proposed amendments to the six SASB Standards in the Technology & Communications SICS sector.' Exposure draft date: not stated.

sub_changes.new: Final: the three financial-sector standards were amended in December 2025 to match the new financed-emissions rules, effective for annual periods beginning January 1, 2027.
sub_changes.old: Financed-emissions metrics in the asset management, commercial banking and insurance standards referenced GICS and the pre-amendment category 15 scope.
sub_changes.topic: Financial-sector metrics already changed
sub_changes.specifics: Consequential Amendments to Align with Amendments to Greenhouse Gas Emissions Disclosures (December 2025): Asset Management & Custody Activities (FN-AC-410b.1, .3, .4), Commercial Banks (FN-CB-410b.1–.4), Insurance (FN-IN-410c.1–.4); 'This version 2025-12 of the Standard is effective for all entities for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027.' EFRAG commented on the SASB enhancement proposals calling for greater interoperability (EFRAG news, 2025–2026), not read in full for this research.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: a taxonomy update adding tags for the December 2025 amendments was consulted July 29 to September 28, 2026; finalisation date not stated. Expect updated tags for 2027 reporting if finalised in time. Timing now stated, in an agenda paper only: balloting begins at the end of November 2026 with a pre-ballot review, and publication of the final update and taxonomy files is planned for April 2027. The narrative explaining how a company limited its Category 15 disclosure will change so the full passage can be tagged as a block of text, and staff confirm financed emissions are a subtotal within Category 15 rather than an additional component.
sub_changes.old: The digital taxonomy tagged the original emissions disclosures.
sub_changes.topic: Digital tagging of the new disclosures
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS news (July 29, 2026): Proposed IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Taxonomy Update reflecting the Amendments to Greenhouse Gas Emissions Disclosures; comment deadline September 28, 2026. Project page: next milestone 'Proposed IFRS Taxonomy Update Feedback'; finalisation timing not stated. Element-level changes are not itemised on the public pages read (not stated). ISSB agenda paper AP7, November 2026: the proposed taxonomy update was published July 2026 reflecting the IFRS S2 amendments issued December 2025; the 60-day comment period closed 28 September 2026; ten comment letters were received (2 regulators, 2 standard-setters, 3 'other', 1 each investors, preparers, accounting profession/auditors; by region 3 Africa, 2 each Asia-Oceania, Europe, North America, 1 South/Latin America). Quoted: 'The balloting process for the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Taxonomy Update will begin with a pre-ballot review at the end of November 2026'; final update and taxonomy files 'planned for publication in April 2027', forming the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Taxonomy 2027. Neither date appears on the public project page. Changes staff will make: Category 15 narrative element data type changed to text block with refined labels. Under consideration: documentation that financed emissions are a subtotal within Category 15, and a 'financial activity types' axis distinguishing financed emissions from commercial banking, insurance or both. Industry-classification modelling: three options with no staff preference — finalise unchanged as narrative only; add an empty extensible enumeration with preparer-created extensions and a later common-practice review; or add a pre-populated list (Appendix A). No new elements proposed for the measurement-method and conversion-factor reliefs. The ISSB is not asked to make decisions on AP7 at this meeting.

sub_changes.new: Not yet: the board aimed to issue the first batch in 2026 but had not done so by October 1, 2026, and no effective date has been announced. Until then the current SASB standards remain the ones to refer to.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: When the industry updates become final
sub_changes.specifics: IFRS news (July 3, 2025): 'aims to issue the enhancements in 2026, subject to stakeholder feedback'. Project page (read October 1, 2026): next milestone 'SASB Standards Amendments', no date; ISSB Updates for April, June, July and September 2026 record no final decisions on Phase 1 beyond the July 2026 technology-sector decision. Effective date of amended standards: not stated.

sub_changes.new: Tentatively yes, where you use the SASB standards to report under the ISSB standards. The SASB standards will say that the IFRS S1 requirements apply; you may omit information that law or regulation prohibits you from disclosing and commercially sensitive information about a sustainability-related opportunity; and you need only use reasonable and supportable information available without undue cost or effort. Whether extra relief applies to particular metrics, and whether any of this applies when the SASB standards are used on their own, is still undecided.
sub_changes.old: Not addressed. The SASB standards did not say how the IFRS S1 reliefs and proportionality mechanism interacted with them.
sub_changes.topic: Do the IFRS S1 reliefs apply to SASB metrics?
sub_changes.specifics: Tentative decisions of 29 October 2026 (ISSB Update October 2026, Enhancing the SASB Standards): (1) the SASB Standards will include an explanation that IFRS S1 requirements apply when an entity uses them to prepare IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards disclosures — agreed 10 of 10; (2) the IFRS S1 paragraph 73 reliefs will be available in that context, covering information whose disclosure is prohibited by law or regulation and commercially sensitive information about a sustainability-related opportunity, subject to the IFRS S1 conditions — agreed 9 of 10; (3) the proportionality mechanism (all reasonable and supportable information available at the reporting date, without undue cost or effort) will apply — agreed 9 of 10. Carried forward and not decided: an additional proportionality mechanism for particular SASB metrics based on an entity's circumstances including skills, capabilities and resources, and whether these measures apply to stand-alone use of the SASB Standards. Renaming was discussed and the ISSB was not asked to decide. All preliminary and subject to formal ballot.

sub_changes.topic: Do the duplicate Scope 1 metrics get deleted?
sub_changes.old: Industry metrics and the IFRS S2 requirements both ask for Scope 1 emissions information, with no stated principle on the overlap.
sub_changes.new: Staff recommend keeping them. A November 2026 staff paper proposes that duplication with IFRS S2 is not by itself a reason to exclude content from the industry-based materials, and that the Scope 1 metrics should be retained. Scope 2 and Scope 3 are left open, and staff say selective addition could be justified.
sub_changes.specifics: ISSB agenda paper AP6E, 'Determining the content of industry-based materials', November 2026, for the 18-19 November 2026 meeting. Three recommendations put to the board: (1) design principle at paragraph 56, question 2 — information specified elsewhere in the ISSB literature does not on its own determine whether it appears in industry-based materials; (2) basis for determining content at paragraph 70, question 3 — assess whether characteristics of business models, activities or other common features characterise participation in an industry, informed by six considerations at paragraph 63, stated not to be a formulaic test; (3) paragraph 82, question 4 — 'retain the Scope 1 greenhouse gas emissions metrics in the industry-based materials', including those in the Phase 1 exposure drafts, 'unless applying the basis for determining industry-based content' supports amending or removing particular metrics, applying also to Phase 2 and future work (paragraph 81). Scope 2 and Scope 3: no recommendation; staff say selective addition 'could' be justified in principle (paragraphs 83, 85), with analysis focused on energy-management topics for Scope 2 and upstream/downstream value-chain topics for Scope 3 in a separate later analysis (paragraph 86). Paragraphs 66-69: industry-based metrics are not exhaustive and absence does not mean information is immaterial. Status: staff recommendation in a published agenda paper, not a board decision — the board has not met.

implications: Check whether your industries are among the nine rewritten, the 41 targeted, the three agriculture and power standards or the six technology standards, and read the proposed metrics.
Keep using the current SASB standards for 2026 reporting; nothing in the industry batch is final yet.
Financial groups: update financed-emissions metric mappings to the December 2025 versions before 2027 reporting.
Confirm whether your jurisdiction requires industry metrics at all; Australia and the UK have loosened this.
Digital filers: watch for the final taxonomy update and plan tag changes for the 2027 reporting cycle.
Map which SASB metrics you omit or estimate, and document the relief or proportionality basis, ready for the final text.

frameworks.title: ISSB — what changed, and what is proposed next

frameworks.note: The Omnibus directive is law, and the revised ESRS are now law too — published in the Official Journal on September 21, 2026 and in force November 10, 2026, mandatory for financial years beginning in 2027.

rows.new: Required for companies already in scope: for a financial year beginning in 2026 you choose either the revised standards in full or the 2023 standards with specified reliefs, and you must state in the sustainability statement which version you applied. From financial years beginning on or after January 1, 2027 the revised standards are mandatory with no election.
rows.old: In-scope companies applied the 2023 standards, as last amended in 2025.

detail.applies_to: Undertakings already within CSRD scope and reporting for a financial year beginning between January 1 and December 31, 2026. Companies newly in scope under Omnibus I first report on FY2027, where the revised standards are mandatory.

sub_changes.new: Three options, and you must disclose which you took — the revised standards in full, or the 2023 standards with reliefs for materiality-assessment flexibility, undue cost or effort, and the timing of acquisitions and disposals.
sub_changes.old: No choice: the 2023 standards as last amended applied to the financial year.
sub_changes.topic: The FY2026 election
sub_changes.specifics: Article 2 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 covers reporting periods starting between 1 January and 31 December 2026: an undertaking may apply the standards as amended by this Regulation, or Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 as last amended by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1416 with the specified reliefs, and must clearly state in the sustainability statement which version it applied. Article 3 sets entry into force at 10 November 2026 — a fixed calendar date in the instrument, not publication plus twenty days, which would have been 11 October 2026 — and application to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027.

sub_changes.new: Optional for companies that stay on the 2023 standards for FY2026: eight named reliefs can be bolted on — the top-down materiality approach, estimates instead of supplier data, deferring newly acquired businesses, dropping insignificant activities from metrics and joint operations you do not operationally control from pollution, water, biodiversity and circular-economy metrics, partial value-chain coverage, a separate taxonomy appendix and an executive summary.
sub_changes.old: The 2023 standards had no menu of optional reliefs; the only flexibilities were the phase-ins written into the standards themselves.
sub_changes.topic: Which reliefs the hybrid option carries
sub_changes.specifics: Article 2 of C(2026) 5010 / Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 lists the reliefs available with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772: revised ESRS 1 paragraph 27 (top-down approach); paragraphs 32–33 (undue cost or effort; value-chain limitation); paragraphs 74–75 (new acquisitions and disposals); paragraph 90 (metrics for non-significant activities); paragraph 91 (partial reporting scope of the value chain); paragraph 92 (joint operations); paragraph 106 (Taxonomy disclosures in a separate appendix); paragraph 110 (executive summary). Whichever option is used, the undertaking must 'clearly state in their sustainability statement which version they apply' (Article 2(2) of Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 and recital 9; also explanatory memorandum to C(2026) 5010). Revised ESRS 2 BP-1 paragraph 6 separately requires disclosure of any relief applied.

sub_changes.new: In force since September 24, 2026: the VSRS is published, so the ceiling on what you can demand from smaller value-chain partners is now a real document. Its cap article applies to financial years beginning on or after January 1, 2027.
sub_changes.old: The value-chain cap pointed at a standard that had not yet been adopted.
sub_changes.topic: The voluntary standard and the value-chain cap
sub_changes.specifics: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 establishes sustainability reporting standards for voluntary use by undertakings protected by the value chain cap. Article 4: entry into force on the third day following Official Journal publication of 21 September 2026, i.e. 24 September 2026. Article 3 (the value-chain-cap provision) applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027. Note that an automated reading of the EUR-Lex summary page reports entry into force as 1 January 2027, conflating the application date of Article 3 with the Article 4 entry into force; the published text governs.

sub_changes.new: Required: a company that first reports on a financial year beginning in 2027 applies the revised standards only; the FY2026 election never applies to it because it has no FY2026 reporting duty. First-year comparatives are not required.
sub_changes.old: Companies due to start reporting in later waves would have applied the 2023 standards when their turn came.
sub_changes.topic: Companies newly in scope: no election
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 Article 3: applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027. Directive (EU) 2026/470 (recital 30; amended Article 5(2)(b) of Directive (EU) 2022/2464): undertakings exceeding EUR 450 million net turnover and 1,000 employees that were not first-wave reporters apply the rules 'for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2027'. Revised ESRS 1 paragraph 124: 'other undertakings' (paragraph 122: first reporting for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2027) need no comparative information in their first year; paragraph 127 phase-ins run from their first reporting year — E4, S2, S3, S4 omitted for two years (FY2027–2028); anticipated financial effects omitted for two years; quantitative anticipated financial effects omitted for four years (through FY2030). Annex, revised ESRS 1 paragraphs 124-127 (Official Journal text).

sub_changes.new: Optional relief in two layers for first-wave companies that fall under the new size test: your Member State may exempt you from reporting altogether for FY2025 and FY2026, and if it does not, the revised standards let you drop every topical standard for FY2026 and give only the general disclosures plus a short account of your material topics.
sub_changes.old: Every first-wave company (large listed companies, banks and insurers above 500 employees) reported in full from FY2024 with no way out.
sub_changes.topic: First-wave companies now below the new thresholds
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 31: 'Member States should be able to exempt such undertakings from reporting obligations as regards the financial years beginning between 1 January 2025 and 31 December 2026.' Revised ESRS 1 paragraph 126 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 Annex): wave-one undertakings not exceeding EUR 450 million net turnover and 1,000 employees may omit 'all the DRs of all topical standards for their financial years prior to financial year 2027, subject to the provisions of ESRS 2 General Disclosures, paragraphs 7 to 10' (statement of the materiality outcome and brief description of material topics). 'Wave-one undertakings' are defined as those reporting for financial years starting 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2026.

implications: Decide your FY2026 version election now and get the required statement of which version you used into the reporting plan.
If you elect the 2023 standards with reliefs, document which reliefs you relied on, because each has its own conditions.
Do not treat November 10, 2026 as provisional any more — it is a date in the published regulation and no further step precedes it.
Cap what you ask of sub-threshold suppliers at the VSRS content, which has been in force since September 24, 2026.

EFRAG's draft datapoint list review closed October 23, 2026 and a final list is due by end-2026; comment on the draft XBRL taxonomy before November 11, 2026 and wait for the final list before hard-coding a datapoint inventory into systems.

detail.applies_to: EU companies and parent companies of groups exceeding both 1,000 average employees and 450 million euros net turnover; non-EU parents with more than 450 million euros of EU turnover and an EU subsidiary or branch above 200 million euros. Listed SMEs are out.

sub_changes.new: Required only for companies, and parent companies of groups, that exceed both 1,000 average employees and 450 million euros net turnover. Both conditions must be met, so a 5,000-person group with 300 million euros of turnover is out.
sub_changes.old: Any 'large' company caught the duty by meeting two of three tests — more than 250 employees, more than 50 million euros turnover or more than 25 million euros balance sheet (40 and 20 million before the 2023 inflation uprating) — plus all companies listed on an EU regulated market, including small and medium-sized ones.
sub_changes.topic: The size test for EU companies and groups
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 amends Directive 2013/34/EU: Article 19a(1) now covers 'undertakings which, on their balance sheet dates, exceed a net turnover of EUR 450 000 000 and an average number of 1 000 employees during the financial year'; Article 29a(1) applies the same two cumulative tests to parent undertakings on a consolidated basis. Recital 7 confirms only undertakings exceeding both thresholds report individually. Previous regime: 'large undertaking' under Directive 2013/34/EU Article 3(4) (two of three: 250 employees, EUR 50 million turnover, EUR 25 million balance sheet as uprated in 2023) plus listed SMEs under Directive (EU) 2022/2464. The Commission reviews the thresholds for inflation every five years (Article 3(13) as amended).

sub_changes.new: Unchanged in principle: the test is applied to the consolidated group, the parent reports, and an EU subsidiary that is covered by a parent's consolidated sustainability report prepared under the EU standards or equivalent standards is exempt — including when that parent sits outside the EU.
sub_changes.old: Group reporting at the EU parent exempted EU subsidiaries, provided the parent's consolidated report followed the EU standards or equivalent ones and the subsidiary cross-referenced it.
sub_changes.topic: Groups: parent reports, subsidiaries can lean on it
sub_changes.specifics: Directive 2013/34/EU Article 29a(1) as amended by Directive (EU) 2026/470: parent undertakings of a group exceeding, on a consolidated basis, EUR 450 million net turnover and 1,000 employees. Articles 19a(9) and 29a(8) (inserted by Directive (EU) 2022/2464, retained): a subsidiary or exempted parent is exempted where included in the consolidated management report of a parent — including one 'established in a third country' — drawn up in accordance with ESRS or 'in a manner equivalent' under a Commission equivalence decision, provided the consolidated report is published and the subsidiary's management report names the parent, links to the report and states the exemption. Financial holding undertakings with independently operated subsidiaries may omit consolidated sustainability reporting (recital 17).

sub_changes.new: Removed: listed SMEs are out of the mandatory regime entirely, as are small non-complex banks and captive insurers that were in the same wave. They may use the voluntary standard if customers or lenders ask.
sub_changes.old: Small and medium-sized companies with shares or bonds on an EU regulated market were to report from FY2026, later pushed to FY2028, under a lighter standard.
sub_changes.topic: Listed small and mid-sized companies
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2025/794 Article 1 had moved the third wave (listed SMEs, small and non-complex institutions, captive insurance and reinsurance undertakings) to 'financial years starting on or after 1 January 2028'. Directive (EU) 2026/470 removes them: the Council's 9 December 2025 press release records the agreement to 'remove listed SMEs from the scope of the directive', and the amended Articles 19a(1)/29a(1) contain no listing-based trigger below the 1,000-employee / EUR 450 million test. Recital 32 applies the same threshold logic to issuers under Directive 2004/109/EC. The voluntary standard in Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 Article 2 is available to 'undertakings not subject to mandatory reporting requirements under Articles 19a and 29a'.

sub_changes.new: Three dates matter now. First-wave companies above the new thresholds carry on. Every other EU company or group above the thresholds starts with the financial year beginning in 2027 (first reports in 2028). Non-EU parents above the EU-turnover test start with the financial year beginning in 2028 (first reports in 2029).
sub_changes.old: Four waves: large listed companies, banks and insurers above 500 employees from FY2024; all other large companies from FY2025; listed SMEs from FY2026; non-EU parents from FY2028. A 2025 'stop-the-clock' law pushed waves two and three back two years.
sub_changes.topic: The waves as they now stand
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2022/2464 Article 5(2) as amended: point (a) — first-wave undertakings (large public-interest entities above 500 employees) from financial years starting 1 January 2024, limited to 'three financial years from 1 January 2024' for those outside the new scope (recitals 30–31); point (b) — undertakings exceeding EUR 450 million and 1,000 employees 'for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2027'; Article 40a third-country undertakings from financial years starting 1 January 2028 (EFRAG: first ESRS-40a reports 'cover financial year 2028, with publication in 2029'). Directive (EU) 2025/794 had set wave two at FY2027 and wave three at FY2028 before wave three was deleted. Source note: Article 5(2) read only via secondary summaries (Deloitte); recitals read on EUR-Lex.

sub_changes.new: Optional exit, decided country by country: Member States may exempt first-wave companies that miss the new 1,000-employee / 450-million-euro test from reporting on FY2025 and FY2026. Where the national law does not, the revised standards let those companies drop all topical standards for FY2026.
sub_changes.old: Once in, a first-wave company stayed in; there was no exit short of shrinking below the large-company tests for two years.
sub_changes.topic: Companies that reported for FY2024 but now fall out
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 31: 'Member States should be able to exempt such undertakings from reporting obligations as regards the financial years beginning between 1 January 2025 and 31 December 2026.' Council press release 9 December 2025: 'transition exemption for companies... falling out of scope for 2025 and 2026'. Revised ESRS 1 paragraph 126 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1563): wave-one undertakings below the thresholds may omit all topical disclosure requirements for financial years prior to 2027, subject to ESRS 2 paragraphs 7–10. Transposition is due 19 March 2027 (Latham & Watkins; entry into force 18 March 2026, the twentieth day after Official Journal publication on 26 February 2026), so national exemptions depend on each Member State acting in time.

sub_changes.new: Still required from FY2028, but for far fewer groups: more than 450 million euros of EU net turnover in each of the last two years, plus at least one EU subsidiary or branch above 200 million euros. The report is published by the EU subsidiary or branch and covers the whole non-EU group. See the separate row on the non-EU parent standard.
sub_changes.old: A non-EU parent with more than 150 million euros of EU turnover and either a large or listed EU subsidiary or an EU branch above 40 million euros had to publish a group-level report from FY2028.
sub_changes.topic: Non-EU parents: a separate test
sub_changes.specifics: Directive 2013/34/EU Article 40a(1) as amended by Directive (EU) 2026/470 (recital 26): net turnover threshold for the third-country undertaking raised 'from EUR 150 million to EUR 450 million'; subsidiary and branch thresholds set at EUR 200 million (originally EUR 40 million for branches under Directive (EU) 2022/2464). EFRAG ESRS-40a project page: 'net turnover in the Union exceeding EUR 450 million in each of the last two consecutive financial years' and EU branches or subsidiaries with net turnover exceeding EUR 200 million in the preceding financial year. Reporting entity: the EU subsidiary or branch publishes the report, which 'covers the ultimate non-EU parent undertaking or group' (Article 40a(2)–(3)). Financial holding undertakings whose subsidiaries operate independently may omit consolidated reporting (recital 26).

sub_changes.new: The final law carries no percentage. The Commission's own impact document counts about 6,750 companies remaining in scope after the Omnibus; the same document puts the reduction in companies in scope at about 85%, which is the basis for the 80–90% figure; the directive itself states no percentage.
sub_changes.old: The Commission's 2021–2023 estimates put roughly 50,000 companies in the original scope once all waves were in.
sub_changes.topic: How many companies are left
sub_changes.specifics: Commission Staff Working Document SWD(2026) 500 accompanying the revised ESRS: 'circa 6 753 companies remaining in scope' after the Omnibus I amendments; projected reporting cost savings 'EUR 3.7 billion' cumulative over 2027–2031 excluding trickle-down effects, 'EUR 4.7 billion' including them. Directive (EU) 2026/470 states no removal percentage; SWD(2026) 500 states the Omnibus I thresholds reduce 'the number of companies in scope by about 85%' (the Commission's February 2025 proposal had estimated roughly 80%). Commission news of 3 July 2026 expects reporting costs 'over 30% per company' lower from the revised standards.

implications: Re-run the size test on each EU entity and on the consolidated group: both 1,000 employees and 450 million euros must be exceeded.
If you were a first-wave reporter now below the thresholds, check whether your Member State has enacted the FY2025–2026 exemption before stopping.
Map which EU subsidiaries can rely on the group report exemption and make sure each one cross-references the parent report.
Plan FY2027 as the first mandatory year for newly scoped EU entities and FY2028 for a non-EU parent-level report.
Stop building toward listed-SME requirements; offer the voluntary standard to lenders or customers who still ask.

rows.new: Mandatory datapoints cut by ~60% (total by ~70%); simpler materiality approach.
rows.old: ESRS Set 1: 1,100+ datapoints across 12 standards.

detail.timing: Revised standards in force November 10, 2026, mandatory for financial years from January 1, 2027. EFRAG datapoint list review closes October 23, 2026; XBRL taxonomy consultation closes November 11, 2026; tagging not required until the Commission adopts rules.
