detail.applies_to: Everyone reporting under the revised standards: companies in scope for FY2026 that elect the revised standards, and all companies in scope from financial years beginning in 2027.

sub_changes.new: Required-if-material datapoints are cut by about 61% and every voluntary datapoint is deleted, so the total falls by more than 70%. The exact count for systems work is in EFRAG's draft 2026 datapoint list, under review until October 23, 2026.
sub_changes.old: The 2023 standards carried roughly 1,100 datapoints: about 160 always required, about 625 required if the topic was material, and almost 280 voluntary 'may disclose' items.
sub_changes.topic: How many datapoints are left
sub_changes.specifics: Set 1 (EFRAG Draft IG 3 explanatory note, April 2024): '162 datapoints are mandatory irrespective of the materiality assessment; a further 625 datapoints are subject to the materiality assessment', plus '277 voluntary datapoints'. EFRAG exposure drafts, July 2025: 57% fewer mandatory datapoints, total reduced by 68%, text shortened by over 55%. EFRAG final technical advice, December 2025: '61% reduction of datapoints that are required if material', 'deletion of all voluntary disclosures'. Commission explanatory memorandum C(2026) 5010 p. 3: 'reducing the mandatory datapoints by 61%'; Commission news 3 July 2026: 'over 60%' mandatory, 'more than 70%' total. EFRAG draft 2026 datapoint list: review closes 23 October 2026 (DRSC); draft XBRL taxonomy consultation to 11 November 2026 (XBRL International).

sub_changes.new: Required: you shall not report a datapoint if the information is not material, apart from a few items demanded by other EU law. Material means omitting or misstating it could reasonably be expected to influence investors or other users looking at your material impacts, risks and opportunities.
sub_changes.old: You were 'not required' to report datapoints on immaterial matters, so many companies reported them anyway to be safe, and reports grew.
sub_changes.topic: Immaterial information must now be left out
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS 1 paragraph 23 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 Annex): 'Information is material when omitting, misstating or obscuring that information could reasonably be expected to influence: (a) decisions that primary users of general-purpose financial reports make...'. Paragraph 24: 'the undertaking shall not disclose information prescribed by an ESRS DR or datapoint if that information is not material', with limited exceptions. Commission explanatory memorandum p. 3: the text 'specifies that undertakings "shall not" report information that is not material... rather than stating that the undertaking "is not required to"'. This is one of the Commission's changes to EFRAG's advice (IBR-IRE comparison, difference 1).

sub_changes.new: Optional shortcuts, now written into the standard: conclude at topic level from your strategy, business model, sectors and geographies without itemising every impact; focus on areas where material matters are likely; use sector or regional data instead of asking suppliers; and update the assessment only when something significant changes.
sub_changes.old: Companies were expected to screen every possible impact, risk and opportunity across their own operations and whole value chain, usually with direct input from suppliers, and to redo the exercise each year.
sub_changes.topic: A lighter materiality assessment
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS 1 paragraph 27: the undertaking 'may derive a conclusion... on the basis of an analysis of its strategy and business model' at topic or sub-topic level (top-down approach), with AR 9–10. Paragraph 32: use 'reasonable and supportable information available to the undertaking... without undue cost or effort'. Paragraph 33: value-chain assessment may be conducted 'without direct input from value chain actors'. Paragraph 34: at each reporting date 'consider whether significant changes have occurred that could affect the conclusions'. Commission change versus EFRAG (IBR-IRE, difference 2): no assessment 'at the level of each individual impact, risk or opportunity (IRO), unless it can reasonably be expected' to change the outcome. Double materiality (impact and financial) is retained.

sub_changes.new: Required: the sustainability statement, taken as a whole, must fairly present your material impacts, risks and opportunities; applying the standards is deemed to achieve that, and using a relief does not break it if you explain. You must state that the statement follows the standards and list every relief or option you used.
sub_changes.old: The 2023 standards were applied datapoint by datapoint; there was no overarching test that the statement as a whole gave a fair picture, and the compliance statement was a simple sentence.
sub_changes.topic: Fair presentation and the compliance statement
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS 1 paragraph 3 (fair presentation objective) and paragraph 21 with AR 6: applying ESRS 'results in a fair presentation', and using the reliefs in Chapters 5.4, 7.3, 7.4 or 7.7 'is not detrimental to fair presentation provided that the undertaking gives explanations enabling users to understand the consequences on reported information and resulting limitations' (Commission wording, firmer than EFRAG's 'presumed to result' — IBR-IRE difference 3). Commission explanatory memorandum: fair presentation 'applies to the overall sustainability statement and does not apply to each datapoint'. Revised ESRS 2 BP-1 paragraph 5: 'The undertaking shall state that its sustainability statement has been prepared in accordance with ESRS as applicable at the end of the reporting period'; paragraph 6: disclose 'any relief, option or other specific provision prescribed in ESRS 1 General Requirements that it applies'.

sub_changes.new: Optional reliefs for every metric except gross greenhouse-gas emissions: drop activities that are not significant sources of the impact; report only the objectively defined part of operations or value chain for which you have reliable data; exclude joint operations you do not control; and, for the first three years, report partial or no value-chain data with an explanation.
sub_changes.old: Metrics had to cover the whole consolidated group and the value chain, with a stated preference for primary data from suppliers.
sub_changes.topic: Metrics you may leave out or estimate
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS 1 paragraph 90: exclude activities 'not a significant driver of the impacts'. Paragraph 91: 'Except when reporting ESRS E1-8 metrics Gross scope 1, 2, 3 GHG emissions', where reliable direct or estimated data is available without undue cost or effort 'only for an objectively defined part of its own operations or its upstream or downstream value chain', report that part. Paragraph 92: exclude non-operationally-controlled 'joint operations' from environmental metrics. Paragraph 123: for 'the first three financial years', where value-chain information is unavailable 'the undertaking shall explain the efforts made'. Each relief used must be disclosed (ESRS 2 BP-1 paragraph 6). EFRAG advice: 'elimination of the preference for direct data in the value chain'.

sub_changes.new: Rewritten around two groups. First-wave companies above the new thresholds may skip biodiversity, value-chain workers, communities and consumers standards through FY2026, most anticipated-financial-effects figures through FY2027 and the quantitative ones through FY2029. Companies starting in FY2027 get similar reliefs counted from their first year: the four nature and social standards for two years, anticipated financial effects for two years and the quantitative figures for four years. No new scope 3 phase-in exists.
sub_changes.old: Phase-ins in the 2023 standards ran from FY2024 and were tied to a 750-employee cut-off, with scope 3 emissions and several social standards deferrable for one year.
sub_changes.topic: Phase-ins for the years ahead
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS 1 paragraph 125 (wave-one undertakings exceeding EUR 450 million and 1,000 employees): omit all DRs of ESRS E4, S2, S3, S4 until FY2026; anticipated financial effects (ESRS 2 paragraph 27; E1-11 except paragraphs 39(a)–(b) and 40(a)–(b) on assets at physical and transition risk) until FY2027; quantitative anticipated financial effects and quantitative substances-of-concern data (E2-5) until FY2029; substances of very high concern for article users until FY2027; listed S1 datapoints until FY2026. Paragraph 124: 'other undertakings' (first reporting FY2027) need no comparatives in year one. Paragraph 127: E4/S2/S3/S4 omitted for two years (FY2027–2028); anticipated financial effects omitted to FY2028; quantitative anticipated financial effects omitted to FY2030 — para 127 not directly readable on EUR-Lex, years per Mayer Brown. E1-8 gross GHG emissions, including scope 3, carries no phase-in (Set 1 allowed a one-year scope 3 deferral).

sub_changes.new: Not required until the Commission adopts the tagging rules: companies need not mark up their sustainability statement in the meantime. EFRAG's draft taxonomy for the revised standards is out for consultation to November 11, 2026, so tagging will come.
sub_changes.old: Sustainability statements were to be tagged in machine-readable format under the EU electronic reporting rules from the first reports.
sub_changes.topic: Digital tagging is parked
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 24: 'Until such rules on the marking-up of sustainability reporting are adopted by means of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/815, undertakings should not be required to mark up their sustainability reporting.' EFRAG released a draft 2026 list of datapoints (review to 23 October 2026, per DRSC) and a draft revised ESRS XBRL taxonomy for consultation 'until 11 November', intending to 'submit the final taxonomy to the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) and the European Commission by year end' (XBRL International). The ESEF amendment date is not stated in any text read here.

implications: Rebuild your disclosure inventory from the revised datapoint list, deleting voluntary items and anything your materiality assessment does not support.
Reframe the materiality exercise top-down and document why topic-level conclusions were reasonable, since you now must leave immaterial datapoints out.
Record every relief you use with the reason, because each one has to be listed in the general disclosures.
Keep greenhouse-gas inventories complete: the partial-scope relief does not apply to gross emissions and scope 3 has no phase-in.
Pause tagging projects for the revised standards until the taxonomy is final, but comment on EFRAG's drafts before the November deadline.

rows.new: Limited assurance made permanent — the upgrade is deleted.
rows.old: Limited assurance, with a planned upgrade to reasonable assurance.

detail.timing: Reasonable assurance deleted with effect from March 18, 2026 (entry into force of the Omnibus directive); the Commission opened a targeted consultation on the limited assurance standard on November 12, 2026, closing January 18, 2027 at 23:59 Central European Time; the delegated act setting the standard is due by July 1, 2027 at the latest; third-country auditor simplified registration runs 2025-2030. The reporting year from which the standard becomes mandatory is reported to be in play — 2027, 2028 or later.

detail.applies_to: All companies filing a sustainability statement under the EU rules; the transitional registration regime concerns non-EU auditors assuring the sustainability reports of non-EU companies listed on EU regulated markets.

sub_changes.new: Required: limited assurance, permanently. The empowerment to raise the level to reasonable assurance has been deleted to avoid higher assurance costs, so no EU-wide step-up is scheduled.
sub_changes.old: Limited assurance — a review-style engagement giving a negative-form conclusion — was the starting point, with the law telling the Commission to move everyone to reasonable assurance, the audit-style level, after assessing feasibility.
sub_changes.topic: The level of assurance you must buy
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 5: 'To avoid an increase in the costs of assurance for undertakings, the requirement to adopt reasonable assurance standards should be removed'; the second subparagraph of Article 26a(3) of Directive 2006/43/EC (empowering reasonable assurance standards, previously due by 1 October 2028) is deleted. The limited assurance requirement itself in Directive 2013/34/EU Article 34(1) remains. Member States may still impose stricter national requirements only within the directive's framework; the texts read here do not address national gold-plating.

sub_changes.new: Postponed: the Commission's deadline for adopting limited assurance standards is now July 1, 2027. Until they exist, your assurance provider applies national standards, procedures or requirements, which differ by country. Moving now: on November 12, 2026 the Commission opened a targeted consultation on the standard, closing January 18, 2027. It does not reopen whether assurance is required or that limited assurance is the level — but it does ask from which reporting year the standard should be mandatory.
sub_changes.old: The Commission was to adopt limited assurance standards by October 1, 2026; until then national standards or procedures applied.
sub_changes.topic: When the EU-wide assurance standard arrives
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 4: 'To allow adequate time to develop the limited assurance standards, the deadline for their adoption should be postponed to 1 July 2027.' Amended Article 26a(3) of Directive 2006/43/EC: Commission to adopt limited assurance standards by delegated act by 1 July 2027 (previously 1 October 2026). Directive 2006/43/EC Article 26a(2) (unchanged): until the Commission adopts standards, Member States may apply national assurance standards, procedures or requirements. Whether the Commission will issue interim targeted assurance guidelines is not stated in the recitals read here. Targeted consultation on limited assurance standard, opened November 12, 2026, deadline January 18, 2027 23:59 CET, online questionnaire only; built on technical work by CEAOB; the Commission states it does not reopen the requirement for assurance, the choice of limited assurance as the level, or the content of ESRS. Audience includes preparers, auditors and independent assurance providers, investors, standard-setters and oversight bodies. Secondary coverage (ESG Today, November 12, 2026) reports the draft is based on ISSA 5000 with EU-specific departures — the EU Taxonomy treated as applicable assurance criteria with eligibility and alignment procedures, procedures for digital tagging requirements, and rules on using third-party verification reports — and that the consultation asks whether the standard should be mandatory from 2027, 2028 or later. A national standard-setter's note (DRSC, November 13, 2026) states the standards would be adopted as a delegated act under Directive 2013/34/EU by 1 July 2027 at the latest, supplementing Directive 2006/43/EC; the Commission page does not state that deadline. Not stated on the Commission page: the mandatory start year, or whether interim guidance will issue.

sub_changes.new: Simplified: an audit firm that wants to provide sustainability assurance need only designate at least one key sustainability partner who meets the approval requirements and is an approved statutory auditor in that Member State. Independent assurance providers remain a national option.
sub_changes.old: Audit firms needed a full set of approvals for sustainability assurance, with every partner meeting sustainability-specific training and examination requirements.
sub_changes.topic: Who may sign the assurance report
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 3: 'Audit firms that wish to carry out the assurance of sustainability reporting should only need to ensure that they designate at least one key sustainability partner who meets the requirements for the purposes of approval and who is approved as statutory auditor in the Member State concerned' (amending Directive 2006/43/EC Article 3). The option for Member States to allow independent assurance services providers (Directive 2013/34/EU Article 34(4)) was introduced by Directive (EU) 2022/2464 and is not changed by the recitals read here.

sub_changes.new: Lighter transitional regime: from 2025 to 2030 a third-country auditor providing sustainability assurance needs only to register basic information, with no equivalence assessment. Relevant to non-EU companies with securities listed on an EU regulated market whose sustainability assurance is done by a home-country auditor; a non-EU parent-level group report may instead carry an opinion from an auditor authorised in its own country.
sub_changes.old: Third-country auditors issuing sustainability assurance reports on EU-listed non-EU companies faced full registration and equivalence requirements from the start.
sub_changes.topic: Assurance by non-EU auditors
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 6 and new Article 45(5b) of Directive 2006/43/EC: a 'transitional simplified registration regime' for third-country auditors and audit entities issuing sustainability assurance reports, covering 2025–2030, requiring submission of basic information rather than equivalence assessments. For Article 40a parent-level reports, the original CSRD text (Directive 2013/34/EU Article 40a(2)) requires the report to be accompanied by an assurance opinion or a statement that one was not provided; the revised wording after Omnibus I was not read directly here.

implications: Budget for limited assurance only; drop any roadmap item that assumed a move to reasonable assurance.
Agree with your assurance provider which national standard or procedure governs engagements before the EU standard arrives in 2027.
Confirm your audit firm has designated an approved key sustainability partner in each Member State where you file.

If you have EU-listed securities, ask your auditor about the simplified EU registration route through 2030; for a non-EU group report, choose a home-country assurance opinion or state none was obtained.
Respond to the Commission's assurance consultation by January 18, 2027, above all on the mandatory start year.

rows.new: Abandoned; optional guidance instead.
rows.old: Mandatory sector standards planned.

detail.timing: Empowerment deleted on March 18, 2026 with the Omnibus directive; no date for optional sector guidance has been published.

detail.applies_to: All companies reporting under the revised standards, including non-EU parents under the proposed Article 40a standard.

sub_changes.new: Removed: the power to adopt sector-specific standards is deleted, so no mandatory sector datapoints will be added. The Commission may instead publish non-binding guidance illustrating how the general standards apply in a sector.
sub_changes.old: The Commission was empowered to adopt sector-specific standards by delegated act, adding datapoints for high-impact sectors such as oil and gas, mining, road transport, agriculture and textiles; adoption had already been pushed to 2026.
sub_changes.topic: Mandatory sector standards
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 20: the empowerment in Directive 2013/34/EU Article 29b(1), third subparagraph, to adopt sector-specific standards 'should be deleted' to avoid prescribing additional datapoints; the Commission may provide 'sector-specific guidance' illustrating ESRS application per sector. Directive (EU) 2024/1306 had previously postponed sector-standard adoption from 30 June 2024 to 30 June 2026 (not re-read here). Recital 27: the Commission is to set up a dedicated online portal with templates and guidance for applying the standards.

sub_changes.new: Required: that duty stays. If a material impact, risk or opportunity is not captured, or not captured in enough detail, by the general standards, you must add entity-specific information; the revised standards say applying the standards alone is then not sufficient for a fair presentation.
sub_changes.old: Where the general standards did not cover a material sector issue, companies had to add their own entity-specific disclosures, pending the sector standards.
sub_changes.topic: Entity-specific disclosures still apply
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS 1 Chapter 2 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 Annex): fair presentation requires 'entity-specific information when applying ESRS is not sufficient' (ESRS 1 paragraph 20(b), with paragraph 11 requiring entity-specific disclosures where the ESRS do not sufficiently cover a material matter). EFRAG's ESRS-40a exposure draft takes the same line for non-EU parents: entity-specific disclosures are required where standard topics do not adequately capture material impacts, and the draft 'contains no sector-specific standards' (Conventus Law summary of the exposure draft). Where optional sector guidance will be published and when is not stated in the texts read.

sub_changes.new: Optional and not yet published: the Commission may issue sector guidance, and EFRAG's technical advice work on sectors was stopped. Nothing in the adopted texts obliges a company to follow any future sector guidance.
sub_changes.old: Draft sector standards had reached early exposure stage at EFRAG for several sectors before work was paused in 2024.
sub_changes.topic: Sector guidance, if it comes
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 20: the Commission 'could support undertakings by providing sector-specific guidance that illustrates and facilitates the application of ESRS within a given sector', the empowerment being deleted 'to avoid an increase in the number of prescribed datapoints'. Revised ESRS (Regulation (EU) 2026/1563) contain no sector standards; EFRAG's December 2025 technical advice covers only the cross-cutting and topical standards. The Commission's Article 29b(1) duty to adopt the revised cross-cutting and topical standards 'within six months of the entry into force' of the Omnibus (recital 18) was met on 3 July 2026. No date for sector guidance is stated anywhere in the texts read.

implications: Close out any workstream preparing for mandatory sector datapoints and redirect the effort to entity-specific disclosures.
Document how you identified sector-relevant material matters, since the entity-specific duty is now the only sector mechanism.
Watch for non-binding Commission sector guidance, but treat it as help with the general standards, not a new rule.

rows.new: Capped: for CSRD reporting purposes, nothing beyond the essential datapoints listed in Annex II of the voluntary small-company standard may be demanded from value-chain partners averaging 1,000 employees or fewer. The test is employee numbers alone, so a supplier can be too small to report under CSRD and still fall outside the cap. Requests for other purposes, including EU due-diligence obligations, sit outside it too. That standard (the VSRS) is no longer hypothetical — it was published Sept 21, 2026 and has been in force since Sept 24, 2026, so the cap now has a document behind it.
rows.old: No limit on what reporters could ask value-chain partners.

detail.timing: Voluntary standard in force September 24, 2026; cap article applies to financial years from January 1, 2027; national transposition of the right to decline due March 19, 2027.

sources.ref: Amended Article 19a(3) and 29a(3) of Directive 2013/34/EU (protected undertakings; right to decline; contractual provisions not binding; information duty; other purposes unaffected); new Article 29ca (voluntary standards); recitals 22–23

detail.applies_to: Companies reporting under the EU rules when they request sustainability data from any value-chain partner with 1,000 or fewer average employees; such partners worldwide gain the right to decline.

sub_changes.new: Protected: any company in your value chain that did not exceed 1,000 average employees in its previous financial year, whatever its turnover and wherever it is based. It may decline to provide anything beyond the voluntary standard's content.
sub_changes.old: No supplier had a legal right to refuse a reporting company's data request; the only brake was commercial leverage.
sub_changes.topic: Which suppliers and customers are protected
sub_changes.specifics: Directive 2013/34/EU Article 19a(3) and 29a(3) as amended by Directive (EU) 2026/470: 'protected undertakings' are value-chain undertakings that do not exceed 'an average number of 1 000 employees during the preceding financial year'; 'Protected undertakings shall have the right to decline to provide information exceeding the information specified in the voluntary standards' and 'Reporting undertakings shall not require protected undertakings to provide information exceeding the information specified in the voluntary standards'. Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 Article 1 repeats the definition. No turnover test and no EU-establishment condition appear in the definition.

sub_changes.new: Capped at the 'essential' datapoints of the voluntary standard — a defined list drawn from both its basic and comprehensive modules, with a shorter list for partners of ten employees or fewer. Anything outside that list can be requested but not required.
sub_changes.old: Companies routinely sent long questionnaires mirroring their own full disclosure requirements, including scope 3 breakdowns and policies, to suppliers of every size.
sub_changes.topic: What the cap actually contains
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 Article 3: 'The value chain cap shall only comprise the datapoints specified in Annex II to this Regulation.' Recital 4: 'Only essential datapoints should be covered'. Revised ESRS 1 paragraph 66 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1563): the cap 'only comprises the datapoints specified in Annex II to Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560'; the Commission distinguishes undertakings with more than 10 employees from those with 10 or fewer and draws essential datapoints from 'both the Basic Module and the Comprehensive Module' (IBR-IRE, difference 4). Annex I: Basic Module B1–B11, Comprehensive Module C1–C9; items marked '[Voluntary for undertakings with 10 employees or less]' fall outside the cap for micro-undertakings. Annex II itself was not reproduced in the text read.

sub_changes.new: You may ask a protected supplier for its scope 1 and location-based scope 2 emissions and its energy use without it being able to invoke the cap, because those datapoints are on the cap's essential list; even so, the law gives it no duty to answer. Supplier scope 3 is not in the basic module, and reduction targets are a comprehensive-module item, so expect to estimate rather than demand.
sub_changes.old: Reporters asked suppliers for scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, product footprints and reduction targets with no legal ceiling.
sub_changes.topic: Greenhouse-gas data you can still demand
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 Annex I, disclosure B3 'Energy and GHG emissions' (voluntary for undertakings with 10 employees or less): scope 1 and location-based scope 2 emissions in tonnes CO2 equivalent, total energy consumption in MWh with renewable/non-renewable split where obtainable. Scope 3: not mandatory in the Basic Module; may be added as sector- or undertaking-specific information (paragraph 12; guidance paragraphs 49–52 name manufacturing, agrifood, real estate and packaging as sectors where scope 3 is 'appropriate'). Disclosure C3 'GHG reduction targets and climate transition' (Comprehensive Module): absolute scope 1 and 2 targets, optional for significant scope 3 categories. Annex II (Council transmission ST 11697/26 ADD 1) lists B3 paragraph 32 (total energy consumption in MWh) and paragraph 33 (estimated gross scope 1 and location-based scope 2) among the cap datapoints, with separate columns for more than 10 and for 10 or fewer employees; no scope 3 datapoint and no C3 row. The Official Journal Annex II was not readable.

sub_changes.new: Unenforceable beyond the cap: any contractual clause requiring a protected company to provide information above the voluntary standard is not binding. If you ask for more anyway, you must tell the partner it has the right to refuse.
sub_changes.old: Supplier codes and master agreements could oblige suppliers to provide any sustainability data the buyer specified.
sub_changes.topic: Contracts that demand more
sub_changes.specifics: Directive 2013/34/EU Article 19a(3) as amended by Directive (EU) 2026/470: 'Any contractual provision contrary to point (a) shall not be binding'; where a reporting undertaking requests information, directly or indirectly, from protected undertakings for the purpose of sustainability reporting and 'some or all of that information exceeds the information specified in the voluntary standards, that reporting undertaking shall ensure that protected undertakings are informed of' their right to decline. The cap does not affect requests 'for purposes other than sustainability reporting' (for example due diligence) and creates no obligation on value-chain undertakings to provide any information.

sub_changes.new: Permitted and expected: use estimates, sector averages or proxies where protected partners do not supply data, explain your efforts for the first three years, and improve coverage over time. Only gross greenhouse-gas totals must still cover the full scope rather than a defined part.
sub_changes.old: The 2023 standards expressed a preference for primary data from value-chain partners, pushing companies to collect supplier-specific figures.
sub_changes.topic: Filling the gaps with estimates
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 Article 19a(3): after the three-year transition, reporting is done 'by using information directly obtained from undertakings in its value chain or estimates for that information, as appropriate'. Revised ESRS 1 paragraph 33 (materiality assessment without direct value-chain input), paragraph 91 (partial-scope relief except for E1-8 gross GHG emissions), paragraph 123 (first three financial years: explain efforts where value-chain information is unavailable), paragraph 95 (reassess undue cost or effort each period). ESRS 2 AR 2 (per EY paragraph map): disclose actions to increase coverage and quality and progress versus the prior period.

sub_changes.new: The voluntary standard has been in force since September 24, 2026 and its cap article applies to financial years beginning on or after January 1, 2027. The right to decline sits in the directive and takes legal effect through national transposition, due by March 19, 2027.
sub_changes.old: No cap existed for FY2024 and FY2025 reports.
sub_changes.topic: When the cap bites
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 Article 4: entry into force on the third day following publication in the Official Journal of 21 September 2026 (24 September 2026); 'Article 3 shall apply from the financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027'. Recital 5: Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/1710 (the earlier VSME recommendation) 'should be considered as no longer producing any legal effects' from entry into force. Directive (EU) 2026/470: protected-undertaking rights sit in Directive 2013/34/EU Article 19a(3)/29a(3), transposition deadline 19 March 2027 (Latham & Watkins; Council press release 'within one year'). Member States may transpose earlier.

implications: Screen your supplier and customer master data for partners under 1,000 employees and flag them as protected before the next data campaign.
Cut supplier questionnaires to the voluntary standard's essential datapoints; move everything else to optional questions with a stated right to decline.
Amend supplier codes and contract templates, since clauses demanding more than the cap will not be enforceable.
Build estimation methods for supplier scope 3 now, and plan to explain data-gap efforts for three years.
Keep due-diligence information requests on a separate legal footing, because the cap covers reporting requests only.

rows.old: Transitional phase: quarterly reporting only, no cost.

detail.timing: Definitive regime since January 1, 2026; verifier registration from September 2026; certificates on sale from February 1, 2027; first annual declaration and surrender by September 30, 2027 for 2026 imports.

detail.applies_to: Importers into the EU of cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen and listed precursors; small importers at or below 50 tonnes a year are exempt, except for electricity and hydrogen.

sub_changes.new: Required since January 1, 2026: importers of cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen must be authorised, declare embedded emissions annually and buy and surrender certificates that price those emissions at the EU carbon price.
sub_changes.old: From October 2023 to the end of 2025 importers of covered goods filed quarterly emissions reports and paid nothing.
sub_changes.topic: From reporting to paying
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2023/956 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2025/2083: definitive period applies from 1 January 2026 (Commission: 'As of 1 January 2026, CBAM is applicable under its definitive regime', introducing 'authorisation requirements, reporting obligations and the purchase and surrender of CBAM certificates'). Covered sectors: 'cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen' (Annex I goods). Transitional period: 1 October 2023 to 31 December 2025, quarterly CBAM reports without financial adjustment. Regulation (EU) 2025/2083 published 17 October 2025, entry into force on the third day after publication (recital 38).

sub_changes.new: Required: only an 'authorised CBAM declarant' may import covered goods above the small-importer threshold. Importers who applied before March 31, 2026 could keep importing while their application was processed.
sub_changes.old: Any importer could bring in covered goods; the only duty was the quarterly report.
sub_changes.topic: Who may import covered goods
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2023/956 Article 5(1) as amended: authorisation as a CBAM declarant is required 'prior to importing goods into the customs territory of the Union', applicable from 1 January 2026. Implementing rules adopted 17 December 2025 simplify the procedure; 'importers who have applied for authorisation before 31 March 2026 can provisionally continue importing CBAM goods' (Mayer Brown summary of the Commission package; the implementing act itself was not read). Authorisation is per Member State through the CBAM Registry.

sub_changes.new: Exempt: importers whose covered goods total 50 tonnes or less per calendar year have no CBAM obligations; electricity and hydrogen imports do not count toward or benefit from the threshold. The EU estimates this removes most importers while keeping at least 99% of embedded emissions in scope.
sub_changes.old: A 150-euro-per-consignment exemption left many occasional importers in scope and generated most of the filing burden.
sub_changes.topic: The 50-tonne small-importer exemption
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2025/2083 inserts Article 2a into Regulation (EU) 2023/956: a 'single mass-based threshold' of 50 tonnes cumulative net mass per calendar year per importer; Article 2a(4) excludes electricity and hydrogen from the threshold. Recital 5: 'at least 99 % of emissions embedded in imported goods remain within the scope'. Recital 2 notes that 'only a small proportion of those importers account for the vast majority' of emissions. Importers near the threshold must monitor cumulative mass; crossing it mid-year triggers authorisation for the remainder of imports.

sub_changes.new: Required from February 1, 2027: certificates go on sale and must be bought for emissions embedded in goods imported from 2026 onward. For 2026 imports the price is the quarterly average EU carbon price of the quarter of import; from 2027 it tracks the weekly average. Carbon prices paid in the country of origin are deducted.
sub_changes.old: No certificates existed; the price was zero.
sub_changes.topic: Certificates and what they cost
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2023/956 Article 20(1) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2025/2083: certificate sales 'From 1 February 2027'. Article 21(1a): for 2026 imports the certificate price is the 'quarterly average of the closing prices of EU ETS allowances' for the quarter of import; Article 21(1): from 2027 the weekly average closing price. Article 9: deduction for carbon price effectively paid in the country of origin. Free-allocation adjustment reduces the number of certificates to surrender in line with the EU ETS phase-out of free allowances (Commission Guidance No. 4, 14 August 2026). Implementing act on certificate pricing adopted 17 December 2025.

sub_changes.new: Required: the first annual declaration, covering 2026 imports, is due by September 30, 2027, and certificates are surrendered at the same time. Separately, from January 1, 2027 you must hold certificates covering at least half the emissions embedded in goods imported since the start of the year at each quarter end - the first test is March 31, 2027, before the first declaration falls due.
sub_changes.old: Quarterly reports were due one month after each quarter; nothing was surrendered.
sub_changes.topic: Deadlines: declare and surrender
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2023/956 Article 6(1) as amended: annual CBAM declaration 'By 30 September of each year, and for the first time in 2027 for the year 2026' (originally 31 May). Article 22(1): surrender of certificates by 30 September each year. Article 22(2): at the end of each quarter the declarant must hold certificates corresponding to 'at least 50 %' of embedded emissions in goods imported since the beginning of the year (originally 80%). Commission Guidance No. 1 (14 August 2026) sets out the full compliance cycle, roles and deadlines.

sub_changes.new: Required if you use actual emissions data: an accredited verifier must verify installation-level figures, with an on-site visit in the first year and at least every two years after. Verifiers register from September 2026 and can issue reports from January 2027; default values need no verification.
sub_changes.old: Transitional reports needed no independent verification; from mid-2024 actual installation data were required but unverified.
sub_changes.topic: Verifying the emissions figures
sub_changes.specifics: Commission CBAM verification page: annual declarations use 'either on actual verified emissions data or on default emissions values'; accreditation by 'EU countries' national accreditation bodies' under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2551; verifiers register in the CBAM Registry from September 2026; verification reports can be issued and shared with declarants from January 2027; certificates can be purchased from February 2027. Guidance on CBAM verification and accreditation published 24 August 2026. Mayer Brown summary of the December 2025 implementing act: on-site inspection required in the first year of verification, then 'at least every two years'. The ISO standard referenced for accreditation is not stated on the Commission page.

sub_changes.new: Permitted: you may declare with default values set per product code and country of origin, but they are set at the average of the ten highest-emitting exporting countries plus a mark-up that rises over time, so actual verified data will usually be cheaper.
sub_changes.old: Transitional defaults could be used freely until mid-2024, then only for a minority of emissions.
sub_changes.topic: Default values when suppliers will not share data
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2025/2083 recital 35: default values for goods based on the '10 exporting countries with the highest emission intensities' where actual data are unavailable. Implementing act of 17 December 2025 (Mayer Brown summary): default values set 'by Combined Nomenclature code and country of origin' with a gradual introduction of the mark-up 'to mitigate any immediate and disproportionate impact'. Commission Guidance No. 3 (14 August 2026) covers calculation methods and the use of defaults; sector guides 5a–5f cover cement, hydrogen, fertilisers, iron and steel, aluminium and electricity.

sub_changes.new: Different measure: the levy uses installation-level embedded emissions per tonne of product, calculated with the EU emissions-trading method, including specified precursors and, for some goods, indirect electricity emissions. A supplier's company-wide scope 1 and 2 total does not satisfy it.
sub_changes.old: Companies sometimes assumed their supplier's corporate footprint could stand in for CBAM data.
sub_changes.topic: This is not your corporate inventory
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2023/956 Article 7 and Annex IV: embedded emissions determined per installation and per product using actual emissions of the production process, including relevant precursors; indirect (electricity) emissions included except for the goods listed in Annex II (iron and steel, aluminium, hydrogen), for which only direct emissions count. Commission Guidance No. 2 (14 August 2026) gives non-EU operators a 'roadmap for emissions monitoring'; Guidance No. 3 sets 'CBAM methods for the calculation of emissions embedded in goods'. Corporate inventories under the GHG Protocol or the EU sustainability standards are organisation-level and are not a substitute; the texts read do not provide any equivalence between the two.

implications: Confirm every EU importing entity holds authorised declarant status or is reliably under 50 tonnes a year.
Secure verified installation-level emissions from suppliers of covered goods, because the first declaration on 2026 imports is due September 30, 2027.
Model the certificate bill for 2026 and 2027 imports at quarterly, then weekly, EU carbon prices and reserve cash before February 2027.
Check that your verifier is accredited and booked, since reports can only be issued from January 2027.
Keep CBAM product data separate from your corporate greenhouse-gas inventory; the two methods are not interchangeable.

rows.new: That proposal stalled and was never adopted — the Commission signalled withdrawal but never completed it, and the file is still listed as pending. Instead, the consumer-protection directive bans offset-based 'carbon neutral' product claims and vague green labels, and those rules have applied since Sept 27, 2026.
rows.old: Green Claims Directive proposed to police all environmental claims.

detail.applies_to: Any trader making business-to-consumer environmental claims, labels or future-performance promises about products or services sold in the EU, regardless of where the company is headquartered.

sub_changes.new: Banned outright for consumer-facing claims in the EU since September 27, 2026: saying a product has a neutral, reduced or positive greenhouse-gas impact on the basis of offsetting is an unfair practice in all circumstances, with no case-by-case defence.
sub_changes.old: Companies could label a product climate neutral, carbon neutral or net zero on the strength of purchased carbon credits, subject only to the general ban on misleading advertising.
sub_changes.topic: 'Carbon neutral' claims built on offsets
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2024/825 Article 1, point (4), inserts point 4c into Annex I of Directive 2005/29/EC (practices considered unfair in all circumstances): 'Making a claim based on the offsetting of greenhouse gas emissions that a product has a neutral, reduced or positive impact on the environment in terms of greenhouse gas emissions.' Transposition deadline 27 March 2026; measures apply from 27 September 2026 (Article 4). Offset-based claims about the company rather than a product fall outside point 4c and under the general misleading-practice test (though generic and whole-business claims about a trader are caught by points 4a and 4b); the directive is silent on business-to-business claims.

sub_changes.new: Banned since September 27, 2026 unless backed up: a generic environmental claim is an unfair practice when you cannot demonstrate recognised excellent environmental performance relevant to the claim. A claim about the whole product is also banned when it concerns only one aspect of it.
sub_changes.old: 'Eco-friendly', 'green', 'climate friendly' and similar words were judged case by case under the misleading-practice rules.
sub_changes.topic: Vague green words
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2024/825, Annex I of Directive 2005/29/EC points 4a and 4b: 'Making a generic environmental claim for which the trader is not able to demonstrate recognised excellent environmental performance relevant to the claim' and 'Making an environmental claim about the entire product or the trader's entire business when it concerns only a certain aspect of the product or a specific activity of the trader's business'. Definitions inserted into Article 2 of Directive 2005/29/EC: 'environmental claim' (point (o)), 'generic environmental claim' (point (p), a claim not on a clear and prominent label), 'recognised excellent environmental performance' (EU Ecolabel, national EN ISO 14024 type I labels, or top performance under Union law).

sub_changes.new: Banned since September 27, 2026: displaying a sustainability label that is not based on a certification scheme or established by public authorities. A certification scheme means third-party verification with open, transparent and fair conditions.
sub_changes.old: Self-made eco-logos and private 'sustainable' badges were lawful unless shown to mislead.
sub_changes.topic: Sustainability labels and logos
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2024/825, Annex I of Directive 2005/29/EC point 2a: 'Displaying a sustainability label that is not based on a certification scheme or not established by public authorities.' Article 2 of Directive 2005/29/EC new point (q) 'sustainability label' and point (r) 'certification scheme' (third-party verification scheme open under transparent, fair and non-discriminatory terms to all traders willing to comply, with monitoring of compliance by a third party). Labels covering social characteristics are included in the definition of sustainability label.

sub_changes.new: Restricted since September 27, 2026: an environmental claim about future performance is misleading unless it rests on clear, objective, publicly available and verifiable commitments in a detailed and realistic implementation plan, with measurable targets and regular verification by an independent third-party expert whose findings are made available.
sub_changes.old: Net-zero-by-2040 style marketing claims were not specifically regulated.
sub_changes.topic: Promises about future performance
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2024/825 Article 1, point (2)(b), amends Article 6(2) of Directive 2005/29/EC by adding point (d): making an environmental claim related to future environmental performance 'without clear, objective, publicly available and verifiable commitments set out in a detailed and realistic implementation plan that includes measurable and time-bound targets and other relevant elements necessary to support its implementation, such as allocation of resources, and that is regularly verified by an independent third party expert, whose findings are made available to consumers'. This is a misleading-practice test (Article 6), not a blacklist item, so it applies where the claim is likely to affect a consumer's decision.

sub_changes.new: The rules apply from September 27, 2026 to products already on the market; the directive contains no stock-clearance grace period, so existing packaging and listings with banned claims are an enforcement exposure in every Member State that has transposed, and national practice on remediation varies.
sub_changes.old: No transition problem existed because there were no new blacklist items.
sub_changes.topic: Products already on shelves
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2024/825 Article 4: Member States adopt measures by 27 March 2026 and 'shall apply those measures from 27 September 2026'; Article 5: entry into force 20 days after publication in the Official Journal of 6 March 2024. No sell-through or grandfathering clause exists in the directive. Enforcement is national under Directive 2005/29/EC Article 11–13 (penalties up to at least 4% of turnover for widespread infringements under the Omnibus consumer rules). The Commission must report on application by 27 September 2031. Whether every Member State had transposed by the application date is not confirmed in the texts read.

sub_changes.new: Not law and not withdrawn: Parliament adopted its position in March 2024, the final trilogue set for June 23, 2025 was cancelled after the Commission said it intended to withdraw the proposal, and the Commission then said it had not formally withdrawn it. The file still sits at 'awaiting Council's first-reading position' and the 2026 work programme lists it as ongoing.
sub_changes.old: The 2023 proposal would have required pre-approval of explicit environmental claims by accredited verifiers before use, with substantiation on a life-cycle basis.
sub_changes.topic: The separate Green Claims Directive
sub_changes.specifics: Legislative Observatory 2023/0085(COD): proposal COM(2023) 166 of 22 March 2023; Parliament first-reading position 12 March 2024 (T9-0131/2024); 'Committee decision to enter into interinstitutional negotiations announced in plenary' 16 December 2024; status 'Awaiting Council's 1st reading position'. June 2025: a Commission spokesperson said the 'Commission intends to withdraw the Green Claims proposal' (20 June 2025), the 23 June 2025 trilogue was cancelled, and the Commission later said the proposal 'has not been formally withdrawn' (ESG News; secondary). Linklaters on the Commission 2026 Work Programme: 'The proposal for a Green Claims Directive remains listed among ongoing files' (secondary). No Council position has been published.

implications: Sweep live consumer packaging, websites and advertising in the EU for offset-based neutral, reduced or positive climate claims and remove them now.
Replace generic words like 'green' or 'eco-friendly' with specific, substantiated statements or a recognised label.
Retire any self-declared sustainability logo that is not backed by a third-party certification scheme or a public authority.
Back every public net-zero or emissions-reduction promise with a published, time-bound plan that an independent expert verifies regularly.
Monitor the stalled Green Claims proposal, but do not wait for it: the consumer-law bans already apply.

rows.new: A dedicated, lighter standard (ESRS 40a) is proposed for the non-EU parent itself. Exposure draft consultation closed Oct 31, 2026; EFRAG's advice to the Commission is due January 2027, so the content is not yet settled.
rows.old: Non-EU groups above the EU-turnover threshold were to report through an EU subsidiary or branch using the full ESRS.

detail.timing: Consultation closed October 31, 2026 (cost-benefit survey closed October 18, 2026, extended from October 11); EFRAG advice January 2027; Commission delegated act and scrutiny to follow; first reports on FY2028, published in 2029 — the start date is law, the standard's content is not.

detail.applies_to: Non-EU parent companies whose group net turnover in the EU exceeded 450 million euros in each of the last two financial years and that have an EU subsidiary or branch with more than 200 million euros of turnover; the report is published by that EU entity.

sub_changes.new: Required from FY2028 for a non-EU parent whose group made more than 450 million euros of net turnover in the EU in each of the last two financial years and that has at least one EU subsidiary or branch with more than 200 million euros of turnover. Groups below either test are out of the parent-level duty.
sub_changes.old: Non-EU parents with more than 150 million euros of EU turnover for two years and an EU subsidiary that was large or listed, or a branch above 40 million euros.
sub_changes.topic: Which non-EU groups are caught
sub_changes.specifics: Directive 2013/34/EU Article 40a(1) as amended by Directive (EU) 2026/470 (recital 26): third-country undertaking threshold raised 'from EUR 150 million to EUR 450 million' net turnover in the Union; subsidiary and branch thresholds 'EUR 200 million'. EFRAG ESRS-40a project page: 'Net turnover in the Union exceeding EUR 450 million in each of the last two consecutive financial years' and EU branches with net turnover exceeding EUR 200 million or 'ultimate parent of EU subsidiaries with net turnover exceeding EUR 200 million in the preceding financial year'. ESG Today (secondary): the narrowed scope reduces affected groups from roughly 10,000 to around 1,200. Original thresholds: Directive (EU) 2022/2464 Article 40a (EUR 150 million; EUR 40 million branch).

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: the first parent-level report covers the financial year beginning on or after January 1, 2028 and is published in 2029, within twelve months of year-end.
sub_changes.old: FY2028 was already the start year in the 2022 directive.
sub_changes.topic: When the parent-level report starts
sub_changes.specifics: EFRAG, July 2026: 'The first sustainability reports prepared under the future ESRS-40a are expected to cover financial year 2028, with publication in 2029.' Directive (EU) 2022/2464 Article 5(2), as retained by Directive (EU) 2026/470, applies Article 40a 'for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2028' (Deloitte, secondary; the enacting article was truncated on EUR-Lex). Publication within 12 months of the balance sheet date (Directive 2013/34/EU Article 40d). EFRAG technical advice due January 2027; Commission delegated act adoption expected mid-2027 (Conventus Law), then Parliament and Council scrutiny.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: an EU subsidiary or branch of the group — in practice the largest — publishes the report covering the whole non-EU group, together with an assurance opinion or a statement that none was obtained. The report follows the parent's standard, not the EU subsidiary's own local filing.
sub_changes.old: The EU subsidiary or branch was to publish the parent's report; if the parent did not supply the information, the subsidiary had to report what it had and say so.
sub_changes.topic: Who publishes it and signs for it
sub_changes.specifics: Directive 2013/34/EU Article 40a(2)–(3) (inserted by Directive (EU) 2022/2464): the subsidiary or branch publishes the sustainability report of the third-country undertaking at group level, drawn up under the Article 40b standards or in an equivalent manner, accompanied by an assurance opinion issued by a person or firm authorised under the third country's or a Member State's law, or a statement that no assurance opinion was provided; where the parent does not provide the information, the subsidiary publishes what it has and states that the parent did not make it available. Conventus Law on the exposure draft: 'An EU entity... bears the reporting obligation on behalf of the wider group. Generally, this will be the group's largest EU-based entity.'

sub_changes.new: Proposed: the draft standard requires reporting only on your impacts on people and the environment. Financial risks and opportunities, resilience and dependencies are left out, though you may add them voluntarily. Four social and nature topics may be omitted for the first two years.
sub_changes.old: The 2022 directive asked the Commission for a non-EU standard on 'impacts' only, but no draft existed and many assumed the full EU standards would be applied in practice.
sub_changes.topic: A standard built on impacts only
sub_changes.specifics: EFRAG ESRS-40a Exposure Draft (23 July 2026): reporting based on 'a single materiality assessment (impact materiality) only'; 'Companies that choose to identify financial material impacts are... not prevented from reporting these, but this is not required' (Conventus Law quoting the draft). Risks, opportunities, resilience and dependencies disclosures are removed (ESG Today). Transitional omission for two years of biodiversity (E4), workers in the value chain (S2), affected communities (S3) and consumers (S4). The draft is marked up against the revised ESRS of 3 July 2026 and 'contains no sector-specific standards'. EFRAG approved a 'mixed approach' (project page). Datapoint counts are not stated in the draft.

sub_changes.new: Proposed option: for topics other than climate, you may limit disclosures to 'EU-related impacts' — impacts from your activities in the EU and from products or services sold or expected to be sold there — topic by topic, provided you show the narrower boundary gives a complete and reliable picture. EFRAG itself flags comparability and assurance concerns.
sub_changes.old: No boundary choice existed in the 2022 directive beyond 'group level'.
sub_changes.topic: Global or EU-only reporting boundary
sub_changes.specifics: ESRS-40a Exposure Draft 'mixed approach': EU-related impacts defined as 'impacts arising from the group's activities in the EU; and impacts linked to products or services sold, provided or reasonably expected to be sold or provided in the EU' (National Law Review quoting the draft); 'A single report could therefore combine global and EU-related reporting across different sustainability matters'; the boundary choice must give 'a complete and reliable picture of their EU-related impacts'. EFRAG 'has expressed reservations about its practical application, its effect on comparability and the challenges it may create for assurance'. The consultation asks whether the mixed approach should survive; gender pay gap disaggregation between EU and non-EU workforces is a specific question.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: climate change must be reported on a global basis whenever it is material — the EU-only option does not apply. If material, you disclose your transition plan with its targets, levers, investments, board approval and alignment with 1.5°C, or state explicitly that you have no plan.
sub_changes.old: Nothing specific; the full EU climate standard would have applied via an EU subsidiary.
sub_changes.topic: Climate: always worldwide, plan or say you have none
sub_changes.specifics: ESRS-40a Exposure Draft: 'Climate-related impacts would still have to be reported globally' (National Law Review); climate change 'always requires global reporting' when material; where material, 'either disclose their transition plan in full or explicitly state that no plan exists', with plan components 'reduction targets, decarbonisation levers, investment needs, board approval, and Paris alignment' (Conventus Law). The climate section tracks revised ESRS E1 as adopted on 3 July 2026 (E1-1 paragraphs 12–13; E1-6 targets; E1-8 gross scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions), which EFRAG marked up to produce the draft; the exact E1 paragraphs retained in ESRS-40a were not readable because the EFRAG PDF was not fetchable. Content remains subject to consultation until 31 October 2026.

sub_changes.new: Two routes remain and they stack. An EU subsidiary or EU sub-group above 1,000 employees and 450 million euros must report from FY2027 under the revised standards unless it is covered by the parent's consolidated report prepared under the EU standards or deemed-equivalent ones. Separately, if the group clears the 450 million / 200 million EU tests, the parent-level impact report under the 40a standard starts with FY2028. Reporting at parent level does not by itself exempt the subsidiary's FY2027 duty.
sub_changes.old: Three overlapping duties loomed: each large EU subsidiary reporting from FY2025, an EU sub-group consolidation, and the parent-level report from FY2028, all under the full EU standards.
sub_changes.topic: US-headquartered group with EU subsidiaries: which route
sub_changes.specifics: Directive 2013/34/EU Articles 19a(1)/29a(1): EU undertakings and parents above EUR 450 million and 1,000 employees, FY2027 start (Directive (EU) 2022/2464 Article 5(2)(b) as amended). Articles 19a(9)/29a(8): exemption where included in a parent's consolidated management report — third-country parents included — drawn up under ESRS or 'in a manner equivalent' per a Commission equivalence decision; none exists for any non-EU framework in the texts read (1 October 2026). Article 40a: parent-level report from FY2028 where EU net turnover exceeds EUR 450 million in each of the last two years and an EU subsidiary or branch exceeds EUR 200 million; being impact-only, it differs in content from the subsidiary's ESRS report, and whether it can later exempt EU subsidiaries is not stated.

sub_changes.new: The comment window closed October 31, 2026, with a separate EFRAG cost-benefit survey that closed October 18, 2026 after an extension from October 11 and jurisdiction outreach sessions including a United States session held on September 17, 2026. EFRAG advises the Commission in January 2027; the Commission then runs its own consultation before adopting a delegated act, which Parliament and Council may still block.
sub_changes.old: No standard, no timetable.
sub_changes.topic: What happens next and when to speak
sub_changes.specifics: EFRAG: 'Public consultation period: 23 July – 31 October 2026 (100 days)'; technical advice to the Commission 'in January 2027'; the Commission 'will subsequently launch its own public consultation before adopting the delegated act'. Cost-benefit survey deadline extended to 18 October 2026 (originally 11 October) and US outreach session 17 September 2026 are confirmed by BDO's note on the EFRAG survey (published 18 September 2026, deadline 11 October 2026) and EFRAG's outreach schedule (United States session with AmCham EU, 17 September 2026, one of seven jurisdiction sessions 14–29 September 2026). Directive 2013/34/EU Article 40b: Commission delegated act for third-country standards; scrutiny by Parliament and Council under Article 49. Commission adoption 'mid-2027' per Conventus Law (secondary, not an official date).

implications: Run both tests now: EU net turnover above 450 million euros for the last two years, and any single EU subsidiary or branch above 200 million euros.
Decide which EU entity will publish the parent-level report and whether you will seek assurance on it, since both must be stated.
Keep the FY2027 subsidiary-level program running; parent-level reporting from FY2028 does not cancel it.
Build a global climate dataset regardless of the EU-only option, because climate must be reported worldwide under the draft.
The comment window closed October 31, 2026 - track EFRAG's January 2027 advice and comment in the Commission's own consultation instead.

rows.new: A proposal would extend CBAM to the finished goods made from those materials. The European Commission proposed 180 product categories in December 2025, the Council's June 2026 mandate keeps the Commission's annex and adds about 200 further codes, giving just over 300 in total, and the European Parliament on September 15, 2026 backed a list reported at around 457. Trilogue negotiations will settle the final list.
rows.old: CBAM covers raw and simply-processed materials only: iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen and electricity.

detail.timing: Commission proposal December 17, 2025; Council mandate June 12, 2026; Parliament position September 15, 2026; first political negotiation October 20, 2026 with no provisional agreement. The Council's ad hoc working party on CBAM met on this file on October 2, 23 and 30 and again on November 13, 2026, confirming it is actively negotiated at working level. A further negotiating meeting reported for November 30, 2026 rests on trade press only and has no institutional confirmation. Proposed application from January 1, 2028 — all proposed, nothing adopted. Note that the European Parliament's legislative observatory records no event on this file after September 15, 2026 and serves a stale page, so silence there is not evidence of a stalled file.

sources.ref: Procedure 2025/0419(COD): COM(2025) 989 of 17 December 2025; ENVI vote 6 July 2026; report A10-0201/2026 of 9 July 2026; plenary 15 September 2026 (T10-0276/2026), referred back for negotiations
sources.title: European Parliament Legislative Observatory — procedure file 2025/0419(COD), CBAM downstream extension

sources.ref: General approach 12 June 2026: refined product list, annual review, pre-consumer scrap, deceptive practices, objective criteria for exemptions, agreement sought before end of year
sources.title: Council press release, 12 June 2026 — general approach on strengthening CBAM

sources.ref: Impact assessment summary: downstream steel and aluminium-intensive sectors; pre-consumer scrap as precursor; costs EUR 8–43 million yearly plus EUR 31 million one-off

detail.applies_to: Importers into the EU of finished or semi-finished goods made predominantly of steel or aluminium, and users of pre-consumer metal scrap; the exact product list is under negotiation.

sub_changes.new: Proposed, not law: about 180 additional downstream product categories made mainly of steel or aluminium — fabricated metal goods, machinery, vehicles and parts, instruments, metal furniture and prefabricated buildings — would carry a CBAM charge on the embedded emissions of their metal content from January 1, 2028.
sub_changes.old: Only basic materials and a few precursors were covered; a car part or a steel cabinet imported into the EU paid nothing.
sub_changes.topic: What the Commission put on the table
sub_changes.specifics: COM(2025) 989 of 17 December 2025, procedure 2025/0419(COD): 'Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism: extension of its scope to downstream goods and anti-circumvention measures'. Approximately 180 goods in six groups — iron and steel products; fabricated metals (netting, fencing, nails, furniture fittings); machinery and equipment (engines, pumps, motors, transformers, welding equipment); vehicles (motor vehicles, chassis, gearboxes, wheels, trailers); medical instruments; metal furniture and prefabricated buildings — applying from '1 January 2028' (Mayer Brown summary; the proposal PDF returned 403). Impact assessment SWD(2025) 989: recurrent business costs 'EUR 8 to 43 million yearly' plus one-off 'EUR 31 million'. Accompanied by a proposed Temporary Decarbonisation Fund (Akin).

sub_changes.new: Open: the Council's June 2026 mandate adds some 200 metal-intensive industrial, construction and electrical goods such as forklifts and conveyor machinery; the Parliament's September 15, 2026 position reaches about 457 products including solar panels, kitchen utensils, heat pumps and electric-motor materials. The final list is whatever the trilogue agrees.
sub_changes.old: There was one list, the Annex I of the 2023 regulation.
sub_changes.topic: Three lists: 180, about 200, 457
sub_changes.specifics: Council general approach, 12 June 2026: 'refined the list of new products' with an 'annual review on future downstream products' (press release gives no count); Akin: 'some 200 metal-intensive industrial, construction, and electrical equipment goods, such as forklifts, conveyor machinery, and electric motor components'. Parliament: ENVI vote 6 July 2026, report A10-0201/2026 tabled 9 July 2026; plenary position adopted 15 September 2026 (T10-0276/2026), 'Matter referred back to the committee responsible for interinstitutional negotiations' (Legislative Observatory). Vote 464 in favour, 50 against, 159 abstentions; product count 'around 457' per several outlets, a figure the adopted text will confirm (CBAM Guide, secondary). Items named: 'solar panels, kitchen utensils and materials for electric motors and washing machines, as well as heat pumps' (Akin).

sub_changes.new: All three institutions propose January 1, 2028 for the new goods. Pricing would follow the emissions of the steel or aluminium content, with default values by product and country where producers do not supply data; whether a reporting-only run-in applies to the new goods is not stated in the texts available.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Start date and how new goods would be priced
sub_changes.specifics: Application date '1 January 2028' in COM(2025) 989 (Mayer Brown), the Council general approach and the Parliament position (CBAM Guide: all three institutions). Embedded emissions for downstream goods based on precursor metal content using the Annex IV methodology; default values by CN code and country (implementing act of 17 December 2025 for existing goods). Trilogue target: Council 'with a view to finding an agreement before the end of the year'; Commissioner Hoekstra 'well before the end of the year' (CBAM Guide); Akin expects adoption 'late 2026 or early 2027'. No reporting-only period for new goods is described in the sources read.

sub_changes.new: Proposed and backed by the Council: pre-consumer steel and aluminium scrap becomes a covered precursor, authorities may demand proof that goods were produced at the declared installation, and the Commission may restrict the use of claimed actual emissions where deceptive practices are detected.
sub_changes.old: Scrap was outside the mechanism and importers were taken at their word on where goods were made.
sub_changes.topic: Closing the loopholes
sub_changes.specifics: COM(2025) 989: 'preconsumer aluminium scrap and preconsumer steel scrap' added as CBAM precursors; authorities may 'request the authorised CBAM declarant to provide evidence that the imported goods were produced in the declared installation'; Commission empowered to require that 'actual emissions values be used only if additional supporting documentation is provided' (Mayer Brown). SWD(2025) 989: 'inclusion of pre-consumer scrap as CBAM precursor'. Council general approach: bring 'pre-consumer metal scrap into CBAM's scope' and empower the Commission to act on 'deceptive practices' by high-risk companies. Parliament (ENVI, 6 July 2026): burden-of-proof shift and disallowance of international carbon credits (Akin).

sub_changes.new: Open: the Commission proposed a mechanism to suspend or soften the levy in serious circumstances, the Council kept it with objective criteria such as exposure to severe price increases, and the Parliament deleted it in favour of temporary support for affected sectors paid from CBAM revenue. This is the main unresolved point for trilogue.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: The safety valve dispute
sub_changes.specifics: Council general approach, 12 June 2026: exemptions for serious circumstances require 'clear and objective criteria, including EU exposure to severe price increases'. Parliament position, 15 September 2026: 'rejected the Commission's safety valve' and replaced it with 'temporary support for affected sectors funded from CBAM revenue'; one exemption kept for electricity flows from non-EU grid operators for network stability (CBAM Guide). ENVI report also deleted the exemption article (Akin). Export solution for EU producers: not addressed in the Council press release or the impact-assessment summary read here.

sub_changes.new: In trilogue preparation: Parliament's position is adopted and referred back to committee for negotiations, the Council has its mandate, and the first political negotiation was held October 20, 2026 with no provisional agreement, and a second is reported for November 30, 2026 without institutional confirmation. Nothing is binding on importers until a text is adopted and published. Confirmed active: the Council's ad hoc working party on the carbon border tax met on this file on November 13, 2026, with three earlier meetings in October 2026. The Parliament's public procedure tracker shows nothing after September 15, 2026, but that page is stale rather than telling.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Where the file stands
sub_changes.specifics: Legislative Observatory 2025/0419(COD): Commission proposal 17 December 2025; rapporteur appointed 23 February 2026; ENVI vote 6 July 2026; plenary 15 September 2026, first-reading position adopted and matter referred back for interinstitutional negotiations. Council: negotiating mandate 12 June 2026; 'Negotiations between the Council presidency and the European Parliament are expected to start as soon as possible after the Parliament adopts its own position, and with a view to finding an agreement before the end of the year.' Status label on the Legislative Observatory as fetched (1 October 2026) still reads 'Awaiting Parliament's position in 1st reading' despite the 15 September adoption; no trilogue dates listed there, though the first negotiation is reported as held on 20 October 2026 and a second provisionally set for 30 November 2026. Council Ad Hoc Working Party on CBAM met Friday 13 November 2026 at 10:00 (Lex building, Brussels, '2+2' format), convening notice CM 4916/26 of 6 November 2026; provisional agenda: exchange of views on the proposed amendment to Regulation (EU) 2023/956 extending CBAM to downstream goods and adding anti-circumvention measures, then a German delegation presentation on abusive practices, then AOB. The same meeting page records earlier meetings of the working party on 2, 23 and 30 October 2026. The European Parliament legislative observatory for the file records no event after 2026-09-15 and its status line contradicts its own event list, so an absent event there is inconclusive. Not institutionally confirmed: the 30 November 2026 negotiating meeting.

implications: Map every EU import of finished metal goods to its customs code and test it against all three lists, not just the Commission's 180.
Ask suppliers of finished goods for the steel and aluminium content and its production installation, because that is what the levy would price from 2028.
Model 2028 landed-cost scenarios at the Commission, Council and Parliament scope levels before fixing long-term contracts.
Treat pre-consumer scrap flows as potentially covered and check origin evidence, since all institutions back the anti-circumvention package.
Do not act on any list until the agreed regulation is published; follow the trilogue, expected to conclude around the end of 2026.

rows.new: Climate stays the most demanding topic. If material, you must still disclose gross scope 1, 2 (both methods) and significant scope 3 emissions with no phase-in and no partial-scope relief, absolute reduction targets for all three scopes, and either a transition plan or an explicit statement that you have none and whether you will adopt one. Reporting boundary may now follow financial control, operational control or equity share.
rows.old: ESRS E1 (2023): transition plan, targets, energy, scope 1-2-3 emissions, removals, carbon pricing and financial effects — nine disclosure requirements, scope 3 deferrable one year for smaller first-wave reporters.
rows.topic: Climate reporting (ESRS E1) under the revised standards

detail.timing: Revised standards published September 21, 2026, in force November 10, 2026; optional for financial years beginning in 2026, mandatory from financial years beginning January 1, 2027; no phase-in for gross emissions.
