detail.applies_to: Every company reporting under the revised standards for which climate change is material; a conclusion that climate is not material must itself be explained in the general disclosures.

sub_changes.new: Not compulsory to have one, but compulsory to be clear. Required if you have a plan: describe its key features — reduction targets, decarbonisation levers, key actions, investments and funding — plus fossil-fuel capital spending, key assumptions and dependencies, locked-in emissions and progress. Required if you do not: say so and state whether and when you expect to adopt one.
sub_changes.old: The 2023 standard required disclosure of your transition plan if you had one, with a long list of required contents, and a statement of whether and when you would adopt one if you did not.
sub_changes.topic: Is a transition plan compulsory?
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS E1-1 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 Annex; Knowledge Hub text) paragraph 12: (a) 'description of its key features. This includes GHG emission reduction targets, the decarbonisation levers, key actions, investments and funding needed'; (b) CapEx in 'coal, oil and gas economic activities'; (c) 'key assumptions used and dependencies'; (d) locked-in GHG emissions; (e) progress. Paragraph 13: 'If the undertaking does not have in place a transition plan for climate change mitigation which includes the key features listed in paragraph 12(a), it shall disclose this fact and indicate whether and, if so, when it expects to adopt one.' Financial resources may be indicative ranges for approved and announced key actions (EY, AR 2(c)).

sub_changes.new: Required to be transparent, not required to comply: state whether your targets are science-based and compatible with 1.5°C and name the framework used; if they are not compatible, you must explain that, including how your target values compare with the reference values. The EU does not say which science-based framework to use.
sub_changes.old: You had to explain how your targets were compatible with limiting warming to 1.5°C and state whether they were science-based.
sub_changes.topic: Must the plan line up with 1.5°C?
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS E1-6 paragraph 24(c): 'statement on whether the GHG emission reduction targets are science-based and compatible with limiting global warming to 1.5°C. The undertaking shall state which framework and methodology has been used'. E1-1 AR 2(a): where a transition plan's targets lack 1.5°C alignment the undertaking must 'explain that in the statement, in particular by explaining how its target value(s) compare with the reference value(s)'. Commission explanatory memorandum p. 4: 'The text requires undertakings that report transition plans with targets that are not compatible with 1.5C target to be transparent about this' (a Commission addition relative to EFRAG's advice — IBR-IRE difference 10). No validation by any external target-setting body is required by the standard.

sub_changes.new: Required if you have targets: absolute reduction targets for scope 1, 2 and 3, separately or combined, intensity values where relevant, the share of each scope covered when the target boundary differs from the inventory, and the science-based statement. Targets must be gross — removals, carbon credits and avoided emissions cannot count toward them. Fixed milestone years and the five-year update rule are gone.
sub_changes.old: Absolute targets for scope 1, 2 and 3, with a base year not older than three years before the target period, five-yearly milestones from 2030, and a required update at least every five years.
sub_changes.topic: Which emissions targets you must disclose
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS E1-6 paragraph 24: (a) 'absolute GHG emission reduction targets for scopes 1, 2 and 3, either separately or combined, and where relevant, in intensity value'; (b) where target scope diverges from the inventory, 'the percentages for scopes 1, 2 and 3 covered by the target'; (c) science-based and 1.5°C statement with framework. AR 12: 'The GHG emission reduction targets shall be gross targets, meaning that the undertaking shall not include GHG removals, carbon credits or avoided emissions as means of achieving the GHG emission reduction targets'. Adopted E1-6 AR 14: select 'a recent and representative base year', which may be the base year of existing targets or the first year of application; no fixed three-year rule in the adopted text. Prescribed horizons and five-year update removed (EY).

sub_changes.new: Required whenever climate is material, for everyone: absolute gross scope 1 (with the share under the EU emissions trading system), scope 2 on both the location-based and market-based methods, and scope 3 for each significant category, all in tonnes of CO2 equivalent, plus your measurement approach. No phase-in exists and the partial-scope relief that applies to other metrics is expressly switched off for this one.
sub_changes.old: Scope 1, 2 and 3 were required when climate was material, with a one-year deferral of scope 3 for first-wave reporters under 750 employees.
sub_changes.topic: Gross emissions: scope 1, 2 and 3 are all required
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS E1-8 paragraph 30(a): 'disclose absolute gross GHG emissions generated during the reporting period, expressed as metric tonnes of CO2eq classified as: (i) scope 1 GHG emissions, including the percentage of scope 1 GHG emissions from the EU Emission Trading System (EU ETS)...; (ii) scope 2 GHG emissions (location-based and market-based); and (iii) scope 3 GHG emissions from each significant scope 3 category'; 30(b) 'disclose the approach it uses to measure its GHG emissions'. Paragraph 31: biogenic CO2 separate from scope 1. AR 20(b): seven gases incl. NF3; AR 20(d): no netting of removals or credits. ESRS 1 paragraph 91: relief 'Except when reporting ESRS E1-8 metrics Gross scope 1, 2, 3 GHG emissions'; paragraphs 125–127: no E1-8 phase-in.

sub_changes.new: Required: you decide which of the fifteen value-chain categories are significant, mainly by estimated size of emissions, but also spend, influence, related transition risks and stakeholder views, and you report each significant one. Immaterial categories may be left out, with the reasoning kept for your assurance provider.
sub_changes.old: Companies had to report significant scope 3 categories judged on magnitude and other criteria, and the 2023 standard listed all fifteen categories as a checklist.
sub_changes.topic: Which scope 3 categories count as significant
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS E1-8 AR 24: the undertaking shall 'identify and disclose its significant scope 3 categories based on the magnitude of their estimated GHG emissions and other criteria... such as financial spend, influence, related transition risks and opportunities or stakeholder views'. The fifteen categories follow the GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard, which AR 20 directs undertakings to consider. Significance thresholds (for example a percentage of total scope 3) are not stated in the standard. For protected value-chain partners (1,000 employees or fewer) supplier data cannot be demanded beyond the voluntary standard, so significant categories will often rest on estimates (ESRS 1 paragraphs 33 and 123).

sub_changes.new: Choice, now explicit: your organisational boundary is financial control by default, but you may instead use the equity-share or operational-control approach from the GHG Protocol. Whichever you use, scope 1 and 2 must be split between the consolidated accounting group and other emissions, and the EU rules on leases and joint operations override the chosen method.
sub_changes.old: The 2023 standard tied the inventory to financial control, the same perimeter as the consolidated accounts, with operationally controlled assets outside the group added as a separate line.
sub_changes.topic: Whose emissions are inside your boundary
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS E1-8 AR 19: 'Chapter 5 of ESRS 1 General Requirements defines the reporting boundary to be applied, corresponding to financial control as per the GHG Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (2004). Alternatively, the undertaking may use the equity share or operational control approach as defined in the GHG Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (2004)'. Paragraph 30(c): scope 1 and 2 disaggregated between '(i) the consolidated accounting group' and '(ii) other emissions'. Source-conflict note: the Commission explanatory memorandum (p. 4) names only 'the financial control approach or the operational control approach', while adopted AR 19 also names equity share; the standard text governs. EFRAG's advice allowed operational control only as a supplementary disclosure (IBR-IRE difference 9).

sub_changes.new: Unchanged and required: report scope 2 on the grid-average (location-based) method and the contract-based (market-based) method side by side. The standard does not pick one for targets; your target disclosure must say which scope and method it covers.
sub_changes.old: Both location-based and market-based scope 2 figures were required, with contractual instruments meeting the GHG Protocol quality criteria.
sub_changes.topic: Scope 2: both methods, every year
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS E1-8 paragraph 30(a)(ii): 'scope 2 GHG emissions (location-based and market-based)'. E1-6 paragraph 24(b): where the target's scope diverges from the GHG inventory, disclose the percentages of scopes 1, 2 and 3 covered. AR 20(a): consider the GHG Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (2004); the Scope 2 Guidance quality criteria for contractual instruments are carried through the GHG Protocol reference. The revised text read here contains no hourly-matching or deliverability requirement; it does not address the GHG Protocol's pending scope 2 revision.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: you 'consider' the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard and may use the EU environmental-footprint recommendation or the international organisational standard instead, but where any of them differs from the EU standard — notably on boundaries — the EU standard wins. Removals and purchased credits may not be netted off, and biogenic CO2 is kept out of the scopes.
sub_changes.old: The 2023 standard asked companies to consider the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard and allowed the international organisational standard as an alternative, with the EU text taking precedence.
sub_changes.topic: Which accounting rules win if they conflict
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS E1-8 AR 20(a): 'consider the GHG Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (2004). The undertaking may also consider Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 or EN ISO 14064-1:2018. In all cases, the requirements of ESRS take precedence over the above-mentioned GHG accounting standards (e.g. regarding reporting boundaries)'. AR 20(d): 'not include any removals, any purchased, sold or transferred carbon credits'; AR 20(e): no biogenic CO2 from biomass combustion or biodegradation in scopes 1, 2 and 3. The reference is to the 2004 GHG Protocol edition; the standard does not address the GHG Protocol's in-progress revision or any future ISO consolidation.

sub_changes.new: Required if applicable: describe removal and storage projects you have implemented and the amounts removed; disclose credits you have financed or intend to finance and the verified credits cancelled in the year; and explain whether and how you use an internal carbon price and the average price per tonne. None of it may be used to reduce gross emissions or targets.
sub_changes.old: Separate disclosures covered removals and storage in own operations and value chain, carbon credits cancelled and planned, and internal carbon pricing.
sub_changes.topic: Removals, carbon credits and internal carbon prices
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS E1-9 paragraphs 33–35 (GHG removals and GHG mitigation projects financed through carbon credits): projects implemented, amounts removed and stored, carbon credit quality and credibility standards, credits verified and cancelled in the reporting period. E1-10 paragraph 37 (internal carbon pricing): whether and how carbon pricing is applied in decision-making and the average price per metric tonne for each scheme. E1-6 AR 12 (gross targets) and E1-8 AR 20(d) (no netting of removals or credits). Numbering per the Knowledge Hub Delegated Act text; the EFRAG November 2025 draft used paragraphs 35–36 for the same content.

implications: Decide whether to keep financial control or switch to operational control or equity share, and prepare the group-versus-other split either way.
Lock down a full scope 1, 2 and 3 inventory for every reporting year; no phase-in or partial-scope relief will cover gaps.
If you have no transition plan, draft the required statement on whether and when you will adopt one and get leadership sign-off on it.
Benchmark your targets against 1.5°C reference values now, because a shortfall must be explained in the report.
Keep removals, credits and avoided emissions out of target progress and gross totals; disclose them separately.

rows.new: Removed by Omnibus I: the obligation to adopt and implement a transition plan is deleted. What remains is disclosure — under the revised ESRS, companies describe the plan they have or state that they have none. The due diligence law itself now applies only above 5,000 employees and 1.5 billion euros, from July 26, 2029.
rows.old: The 2024 due diligence directive required in-scope companies (from 1,000 employees and 450 million euros) to adopt and put into effect a climate transition plan compatible with 1.5°C, with supervisory authorities able to enforce it.
rows.topic: Due diligence law: climate transition plan duty

detail.timing: Transition-plan obligation deleted on March 18, 2026 with the Omnibus directive; due diligence duties apply from July 26, 2029 after transposition by July 26, 2028.

detail.applies_to: Companies formerly in due diligence scope at 1,000 employees and 450 million euros; now only groups above 5,000 employees and 1.5 billion euros (or non-EU companies above 1.5 billion euros of EU turnover). Transition-plan disclosure continues for all ESRS reporters.

sub_changes.new: Repealed: there is no EU-law obligation to adopt or implement a climate transition plan. Having one is a business decision; describing it, or the absence of one, is a reporting matter under the sustainability standards.
sub_changes.old: In-scope companies had to adopt a transition plan for climate change mitigation aimed at compatibility with the 1.5°C goal and the EU's 2050 climate-neutrality target, update it yearly and describe progress; adopting it was deemed to satisfy the duty if the plan met the reporting-standard contents.
sub_changes.topic: The duty to have a plan
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2024/1760 Article 22 (as adopted 13 June 2024) required a transition plan for climate change mitigation with time-bound 2030 and five-yearly targets, decarbonisation levers, investments and the role of the administrative body. Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 47: 'It is necessary to repeal those provisions in order to streamline obligations'; the Article 22 obligation is deleted (Council press releases of 9 December 2025 and 24 February 2026: 'the obligation for companies to adopt a transition plan for climate change mitigation ... has been removed'). The amended article text itself was beyond the readable portion of the Official Journal page; the recital and both Council statements are consistent.

sub_changes.new: Required under the reporting standards, not the due diligence law: if you have a transition plan, disclose its key features; if you do not, say so and whether and when you expect to adopt one. If your targets are not compatible with 1.5°C, you must explain that. Non-EU parents reporting under the proposed 40a standard face the same disclosure.
sub_changes.old: Companies in both laws were double-covered: a plan was required by the due diligence directive and described under the reporting standards.
sub_changes.topic: What still has to be said about climate plans
sub_changes.specifics: Revised ESRS E1-1 paragraph 12 (key features: targets, decarbonisation levers, key actions, investments and funding; fossil CapEx; assumptions and dependencies; locked-in emissions; progress) and paragraph 13 (no plan: 'disclose this fact and indicate whether and, if so, when it expects to adopt one'); E1-1 AR 2(a) (explain where a transition plan's targets are not 1.5°C-compatible). Latham & Watkins on Directive (EU) 2026/470: 'The requirement for in-scope companies to adopt and implement a climate transition plan has been removed from the CSDDD, though CSRD requirements to disclose information about transition plans, where a company has one, remain in force.' ESRS-40a exposure draft: where climate is material, disclose the plan in full or 'explicitly state that no plan exists' (Conventus Law, secondary).

sub_changes.new: Required only for EU companies above 5,000 employees and 1.5 billion euros net worldwide turnover, and non-EU companies above 1.5 billion euros of EU turnover; franchising thresholds rise to 75 million euros of royalties and 275 million euros of turnover.
sub_changes.old: EU companies above 1,000 employees and 450 million euros worldwide turnover, and non-EU companies above 450 million euros of EU turnover, in phases from July 2027.
sub_changes.topic: Who the due diligence law now covers
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 amending Directive (EU) 2024/1760: employee threshold raised 'from 1,000 to 5,000'; turnover threshold 'from EUR 450 million to EUR 1 500 000 000'; non-EU companies at 'EUR 1.5 billion in turnover in the European Union' (Latham & Watkins); franchising/licensing royalties EUR 75 million (from EUR 30 million) and turnover EUR 275 million (from EUR 150 million). Council press releases of 9 December 2025 and 24 February 2026: '5,000 employees' and 'EUR 1.5 billion'. Due diligence is focused where impacts are most likely; information from partners under 5,000 employees requested 'only where the information cannot reasonably be obtained by other means' (recital 41).

sub_changes.new: Postponed to July 26, 2029 for everyone, with national transposition by July 26, 2028. Penalties are capped at 3% of net worldwide turnover and the EU-harmonised civil liability regime is deleted, leaving national liability law.
sub_changes.old: Application in three steps from July 26, 2027 for the largest companies to July 26, 2029 for the rest (later pushed to 2028 and 2029 by the stop-the-clock law), with penalties of at least 5% of worldwide turnover and an EU-wide civil liability regime.
sub_changes.topic: When it applies and what it costs to miss
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2026/470 recital 46: 'application deadline for Directive (EU) 2024/1760 for all companies should be postponed to 26 July 2029', two years after Commission guidelines due 26 July 2027; CSDDD transposition deadline 26 July 2028 (Council 24 February 2026: Article 4 'due by 26 July 2028'). Article 27 as amended: uniform maximum penalty '3% of net worldwide turnover' (previously a minimum maximum of 5%). Recital 49: Union-wide liability regime removed; the Council notes 'a review clause on the need for an EU harmonised liability regime'. Directive (EU) 2025/794 had earlier moved application to 26 July 2028 and 2029 in two waves; Omnibus I unifies it at 2029.

implications: Remove any compliance item that treats a climate transition plan as a legal requirement; recast it as a disclosure and strategy decision.
Prepare the plan-or-no-plan statement for the sustainability statement, since that is now the only EU hook.
Re-test due diligence scope at 5,000 employees and 1.5 billion euros and reset the program clock to July 2029.
Align supplier engagement so that due diligence information requests are proportionate and separate from capped reporting requests.

frameworks.title: EU — original CSRD/ESRS (2023) → Omnibus + revised ESRS (2026)

frameworks.note: Two opposite directions: the federal rule is being withdrawn while California's regime comes into force.

rows.new: Full rescission proposed May 2026, no replacement; back to the pre-2024 materiality-based regime. The SEC's own agenda sets no date for final action.
rows.old: SEC 2024 climate rule: material climate risk + scope 1/2 disclosure for large filers (never took effect — stayed in court).

detail.applies_to: All SEC-registered companies; the 2024 emissions and assurance items would have hit only large accelerated and accelerated filers. Today no company has any obligation under the 2024 rule.

sub_changes.new: Not required. The rule never took effect, and the SEC has proposed to repeal it outright with nothing in its place. Listed companies disclose climate matters only where they are material under the ordinary rules that applied before 2024.
sub_changes.old: The 2024 rule would have made large and mid-sized listed companies publish their scope 1 (direct) and scope 2 (purchased energy) emissions in SEC filings when those emissions were material, starting with fiscal years beginning in 2026.
sub_changes.topic: Is any federal emissions disclosure required today?
sub_changes.specifics: 2024: Regulation S-K Item 1505 required scope 1 and/or scope 2 emissions, if material, from large accelerated filers (fiscal years beginning 2026) and accelerated filers (fiscal years beginning 2028); smaller reporting companies, emerging growth companies and non-accelerated filers were exempt; scope 3 was dropped from the final rule (89 FR 21668, March 28, 2024; Release 33-11275). Now: the Commission stayed the rule on April 4, 2024 before any compliance date; on May 29, 2026 it proposed rescinding all of Subpart 1500 and Regulation S-X Article 14 (91 FR 33296, June 3, 2026; Release 33-11421; File S7-2026-19). No replacement is proposed.

sub_changes.new: All of it is proposed for removal, for every filer. The SEC's stated view is that the package exceeded its legal authority, abandoned a principles-based materiality approach, imposed costs that outweighed benefits, and touched a divisive social and political topic outside the securities laws.
sub_changes.old: Beyond emissions, companies would have described material climate risks and their financial effects, board and management oversight, any transition plan, scenario analysis or internal carbon price they used, climate targets, and, in a new audited financial-statement note, the costs of severe weather events above a one percent threshold.
sub_changes.topic: What the 2024 rule would have asked for
sub_changes.specifics: 2024: Items 1500–1508 of Regulation S-K (governance, strategy, risk management, targets and goals, GHG emissions, attestation) and Regulation S-X Article 14 (severe-weather and natural-condition costs, carbon offsets and renewable energy credits, subject to a one percent and de minimis threshold); forward-looking statements on transition plans, scenario analysis, internal carbon pricing and targets carried a PSLRA-style safe harbor. 2026 proposal: rescind amendments to 17 CFR Parts 210, 229, 230, 232, 239 and 249 in full; reasons set out in Sections III.B (statutory authority) and III.C.1–III.C.4 (materiality, divisive topic, cost, capital formation) of 91 FR 33296.

sub_changes.new: No compliance date ever arrived for anyone. The stay froze every date in the table, and the rescission would delete them. Companies do not need to unwind anything because nothing was ever filed under the rule.
sub_changes.old: Every SEC registrant, with a phase-in by size: the largest filers first for fiscal years beginning in 2025, mid-sized filers from 2026, and the smallest from 2027, with emissions and audited weather costs a year or more later.
sub_changes.topic: Who was covered and when it would have started
sub_changes.specifics: 2024 phase-in (SEC fact sheet, Release 33-11275): large accelerated filers — all Subpart 1500 and Article 14 disclosures for fiscal years beginning (FYB) 2025, financial-statement effects audit and GHG emissions FYB 2026, limited assurance FYB 2029, reasonable assurance FYB 2033; accelerated filers — disclosures FYB 2026, financial-statement audit FYB 2027, GHG FYB 2028, limited assurance FYB 2031, no reasonable assurance; smaller reporting companies, emerging growth companies and non-accelerated filers — disclosures FYB 2027, financial-statement audit FYB 2028, no GHG disclosure; electronic tagging FYB 2026/2026/2027. Effective date was May 28, 2024; stayed April 4, 2024.

sub_changes.new: The SEC itself paused the rule on April 4, 2024 pending the court case, then voted on March 27, 2025 to stop defending it. The court declined to rule and instead told the SEC to decide whether to repeal, change or defend the rule.
sub_changes.old: Adopted March 6, 2024 by a 3–2 vote, the rule was challenged within days and the cases were consolidated in a federal appeals court.
sub_changes.topic: Why the rule never took effect
sub_changes.specifics: Adopted March 6, 2024 (3–2); petitions consolidated in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit on March 21, 2024 (Iowa v. SEC, No. 24-1522 and consolidated cases); Commission stay order April 4, 2024; SEC letter of February 11, 2025 noted the change in Commission composition; vote to end the defense March 27, 2025; SEC status report July 23, 2025 asked the court to decide the case; on September 12, 2025 the Eighth Circuit instead held the petitions 'in abeyance until such time as the Commission reconsiders the challenged Final Rules by notice-and-comment rulemaking or renews its defense' (recounted at 91 FR 33296).

sub_changes.new: Proposed, not final. The SEC published the repeal proposal on June 3, 2026 and took comments until August 3, 2026. Its regulatory agenda still lists the item at the proposal stage with no date for final action, and in late August the SEC told the court the rulemaking 'remains underway'.
sub_changes.old: Before May 2026 the rule was stayed but still on the books, and the SEC had told the court in July 2025 that it did not then intend to reconsider it, and the court had parked the case until it either repealed or defended the rule.
sub_changes.topic: The rescission proposal and where it stands
sub_changes.specifics: Press release 2026-49 (May 29, 2026); Federal Register publication June 3, 2026 at 91 FR 33296 (Document 2026-11091; RIN 3235-AN76); 60-day comment period closing August 3, 2026. The Regulatory Flexibility Agenda published August 14, 2026 (91 FR, Document 2026-16619) lists RIN 3235-AN76 at the Proposed Rule Stage with only NPRM 06/03/26 and comment close 08/03/26 in its timetable. A law-firm summary (September 8, 2026) reports the SEC's August 31, 2026 status report to the Eighth Circuit said 'the rulemaking remains underway' and that over 19,000 comments were received — secondary source, not independently verified. No final rule as of October 1, 2026.

sub_changes.new: The case is parked. The court is holding it until the SEC finishes the repeal; challengers asked in May 2026 to restart it and have the rule struck down, and the court said no.
sub_changes.old: The appeals court had the case fully briefed and could have ruled on the merits at any time.
sub_changes.topic: What the court case is doing meanwhile
sub_changes.specifics: Eighth Circuit order of April 24, 2025 granted intervenor states' abeyance motion; order of September 12, 2025 continued the abeyance pending reconsideration; SEC letter May 7, 2026 informed the court of the rescission proposal sent for regulatory review; petitioners' consolidated motion to lift abeyance May 8, 2026 (arguing the proposal concedes an Administrative Procedure Act violation); intervenor states' opposition May 18, 2026; motion denied May 21, 2026; SEC letter June 1, 2026 on publication of the proposal. Docket chronology per the Sabin Center climate litigation database (secondary tracker; court docket not fetched).

sub_changes.new: The ordinary rules remain and still reach climate matters when material: the 2010 interpretive guidance on climate disclosure, the general requirements to describe the business, risk factors and management's discussion of results, financial-statement standards, and the anti-fraud provisions. Nothing new is proposed.
sub_changes.old: The 2024 rule layered prescriptive climate items on top of the general disclosure rules.
sub_changes.topic: What still applies after a repeal
sub_changes.specifics: 91 FR 33296 Section III.C.1.a: 'existing disclosure requirements and anti-fraud provisions already elicit information about the effects of climate-related matters in a way that is tailored to reflect registrants' particular circumstances.' The proposal names the Commission's 2010 interpretive guidance on climate-related disclosure, Regulation S-K items on description of business, risk factors and MD&A, financial-statement requirements under applicable accounting standards, and Securities Act Sections 11 and 12 and Exchange Act Section 10(b)/Rule 10b-5 as the framework that would remain.

sub_changes.new: No federal assurance requirement of any kind is in force or proposed. Assurance demands now come from California (limited assurance proposed from 2027) and from non-US regimes, not from the SEC.
sub_changes.old: Large accelerated filers would have needed limited assurance over scope 1 and 2 from fiscal years beginning 2029 and reasonable assurance from 2033; accelerated filers limited assurance from 2031.
sub_changes.topic: Assurance that would have been required
sub_changes.specifics: 2024: Item 1506 attestation phase-in — large accelerated filers limited assurance FYB 2029, reasonable assurance FYB 2033; accelerated filers limited assurance FYB 2031, no reasonable assurance; no attestation for other filers (SEC fact sheet, Release 33-11275). 2026: entire Subpart 1500 including Item 1506 proposed for rescission (91 FR 33296). For California's assurance schedule see the 'Assurance (California)' row.

implications: Plan on no federal climate-disclosure rule; treat the 2024 requirements as a dead letter unless a final rule surprises everyone.
Keep your climate-risk materiality assessment current under the ordinary disclosure rules, because the anti-fraud provisions still apply to what you do say.
Redirect the budget you had earmarked for SEC assurance toward California's limited-assurance requirement, which is proposed to start with 2027 reports.
Watch for a final rescission order and the court's next step; neither has a published date.
Investor-facing climate disclosure outside SEC filings remains voluntary at federal level; align it with California and ISSB-based regimes you face instead.

rows.new: SB 253: >$1B-revenue companies doing business in CA report scope 1 & 2 publicly — first reports were due Nov 10, 2026 under a regulation in force since Oct 12, 2026 (good-faith year one), and an appeals court upheld that duty on Nov 9, 2026. The scope 3 requirement that was to begin in 2027 was struck down in the same ruling.
rows.old: No mandatory US corporate GHG reporting.

detail.timing: Statute in force since 2023; the initial regulation was approved by the state's regulation-review office and took effect October 12, 2026, codified at Title 17 of the California Code of Regulations, Article 6, sections 96070 to 96077; the first scope 1 and 2 report fell due November 10, 2026 and that deadline passed with the obligation intact, one day after the appeals court upheld it; fee notice December 10, 2026 with payment within 60 days; the scope 3 requirement for 2027 was struck down on November 9, 2026 and is now before the trial court on severability (see the scope 3 row).

detail.applies_to: US-formed companies with more than one billion dollars of annual revenue (lower of the last two fiscal years) that are organized in California or sell above a small indexed threshold there; tested entity by entity, with optional parent-level consolidation; non-profits, government-owned entities, regulated insurers and telework-only presences are exempt.

sub_changes.new: Required for any US-formed business with more than one billion dollars of total annual revenue (worldwide, not California-only) that does business in California. 'Doing business' means being organized or headquartered in California, or making California sales above a modest inflation-indexed amount; owning property or having payroll there does not by itself count. You use the lower of your last two fiscal years' revenue. Non-profits, government-owned entities, regulated insurers, companies whose only California presence is teleworking staff, and wholesale-electricity-only traders are exempt.
sub_changes.old: No US company had to report corporate greenhouse gas emissions; the only mandatory programs were facility-level (EPA and California's facility rule).
sub_changes.topic: Who must report
sub_changes.specifics: Statute (HSC 38532(b)): a business entity formed under US, state or DC law 'with total annual revenues in excess of one billion dollars ($1,000,000,000) and that does business in California'. Regulation (17 CCR 96071–96072, modified July 27, 2026): 'doing business' follows Revenue and Taxation Code 23101(b)(1)–(2) only — organized or commercially domiciled in California, or California sales above the indexed threshold ($735,019 for 2024, CARB Nov 18, 2025 slides) — excluding the property and payroll tests in 23101(b)(3)–(4); 'taxpayer' read as 'business entity'; revenue per RTC 25120(f)(2), tested on the lesser of the two prior fiscal years, intercompany transactions excluded; 96071(b) exempts tax-exempt non-profits, regulated insurers, government and >50% government-owned entities, telework-only presence and interstate wholesale electricity.

sub_changes.new: The test is applied company by company, not to the group: a parent is not caught just because a subsidiary qualifies, and vice versa. Any qualifying subsidiary can be covered by one consolidated report (and one fee payment) filed by its parent, so it need not file separately. Consolidation is optional. A 'subsidiary' is one controlled through more than fifty percent ownership, voting power or board control.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable — no mandatory regime.
sub_changes.topic: Which entity in a group files — parent or subsidiary
sub_changes.specifics: HSC 38532(c)(2)(A)(iii), as amended by SB 219 (2024): 'Reports may be consolidated at the parent company level. If a subsidiary of a parent company qualifies as a reporting entity, the subsidiary is not required to prepare a separate report.' Regulation (15-day notice, July 27, 2026): applicability evaluated at the individual-entity level (96072(a)(8), (a)(13)); reports and fee payments 'may be consolidated at the parent company level'; 'subsidiary' (96072(a)(16)) uses the direct corporate association provisions of 17 CCR 95833 (more than 50% control indicia). CARB Nov 2025 slides: 'A subsidiary may request for a parent to report on the subsidiary's behalf.' The intake platform lets one filer cover several entities with combined or individual fee payment.

sub_changes.new: Required for year one: your scope 1 and scope 2 emissions for the prior fiscal year — nothing else is mandatory. There is no mandatory template: you may upload an existing annual or sustainability report that contains the figures, re-use data already filed with another program, or fill in CARB's optional spreadsheet template. If you were not collecting scope 1 and 2 data as of December 5, 2024, you may instead file a short statement of non-reporting on company letterhead. Submissions go through CARB's online intake platform or by email, and everything submitted is made public.
sub_changes.old: Nothing was required; companies published inventories voluntarily, if at all.
sub_changes.topic: What goes in the first report and in what format
sub_changes.specifics: CARB Guidance (Sept 1, 2026), p. 2–3: report 'Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions for the applicable preceding fiscal year, as determined under section 96076'; formats — 'an existing annual report including Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions', 'existing Scope 1 and 2 data reported to other programs/voluntary initiatives', 'CARB's Draft Scope 1 and 2 Template' (voluntary for 2026), or a 'statement of non-reporting (on company letterhead)' if not collecting data as of December 5, 2024; submit via https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/climatedisclosure or climatedisclosure@arb.ca.gov. Methodology, GWP values, emission factors, boundary and gas breakdown are optional. No scope 3 in 2026 (15-day notice, 96074(a)). HSC 38532(c)(2)(D): public digital platform posts disclosures within 90 days of receipt.

sub_changes.new: Required: the fiscal year that ended most recently with at least about six months to prepare. If your fiscal year ended between January 1 and February 1, 2026, you report that 2026 fiscal year; if your fiscal year ends later in 2026 (as it does for a December year-end company), you report the fiscal year that ended in 2025 — calendar 2025 for calendar-year companies. Reporting more recent data than required is allowed.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Which year's data the first report covers
sub_changes.specifics: 17 CCR 96076 (CARB ISOR p. 14; Nov 18, 2025 slides 10–11; March 23, 2026 slides): companies whose fiscal year 'ends on or before February 1, 2026 ... would report data based on the fiscal year ending in the current calendar year (in this case, FY 2025-26 data)'; those ending after February 1, 2026 report 'the fiscal year ending in the previous calendar year (in this case, FY 2024-25 data)'; a minimum six months after fiscal year-end to submit; voluntary submission of more recent data permitted. The July 27, 2026 modifications changed 'fiscal year 2026' to 'calendar year 2026' in 96074(a) for the 2026 cycle. CARB's July 21, 2026 workshop said a similar fiscal-year approach is under consideration for 2027 onward (secondary account).

sub_changes.new: November 10, 2026 is legally final. CARB moved it from August 10 in July 2026 and resubmitted the regulation on September 21, 2026; California's Office of Administrative Law approved it on October 12, 2026 and it took effect the same day, codified at Title 17 CCR sections 96070 to 96077. No procedural step now stands between you and the deadline, and CARB's guidance and intake platform assume it. Outcome: the deadline passed on November 10, 2026 with the obligation intact. The appeals court had affirmed the denial of an injunction against scope 1 and 2 the day before, and CARB published no statement, filer count, enforcement notice or extension before or after the date.
sub_changes.old: The statute said reports start 'in 2026' on a date CARB would set; CARB first proposed August 10, 2026.
sub_changes.topic: The November 10 deadline — and what happened on it
sub_changes.specifics: HSC 38532(c)(2)(A)(i): scope 1 and 2 'starting in 2026 on or by a date to be determined by the state board'. Timeline: 45-day notice Dec 9, 2025 proposing August 10, 2026 (96076); Board approval Feb 26, 2026; submitted to the Office of Administrative Law (OAL) May 20, 2026; withdrawn June 24, 2026; 15-day modifications July 27–Aug 11, 2026 'change the reporting deadline from August 10, 2026, to November 10, 2026'; resubmitted Sept 21, 2026 as OAL file 2026-0921-06 ('Regular Resubmittal'), requesting effect on filing with the Secretary of State. OAL approved the resubmittal on October 12, 2026 and the regulation took effect the same day on filing, codified at Title 17 CCR sections 96070-96077, so the November 10 deadline is set by text in force. The Sept 1, 2026 guidance condition - deadline applies 'if approved by the Office of Administrative Law' - is satisfied.

sub_changes.new: Year one is a good-faith exercise: CARB has said it will not penalize incomplete first reports from companies that make a good-faith effort and that report with the data they already had or were collecting in December 2024. The statutory cap remains five hundred thousand dollars per year; for scope 3, penalties between 2027 and 2030 apply only to failing to file at all, and good-faith scope 3 estimates with a reasonable basis are shielded from misstatement penalties.
sub_changes.old: The statute allows fines of up to five hundred thousand dollars per reporting year.
sub_changes.topic: Good faith in year one, and penalties
sub_changes.specifics: CARB Enforcement Notice, Dec 5, 2024: 'CARB will not take enforcement action for incomplete reporting against entities, as long as the companies make a good faith effort to retain all data relevant to emissions reporting for the entity's prior fiscal year' (confirmed verbatim via Sidley Dec 2024 summary; CARB PDF returns 403). Sept 1, 2026 guidance p. 1: first reports may use 'information they already have or were collecting when the December 2024 Notice was issued'. HSC 38532(f): penalties not to exceed $500,000 in a reporting year; scope 3 penalties 'between 2027 and 2030, shall only occur for nonfiling'; none for scope 3 misstatements 'made with a reasonable basis and disclosed in good faith'. 96075: late fees; each noncompliant day a separate violation.

sub_changes.new: Struck down. On November 9, 2026 an appeals court held the scope 3 requirement is not commercial speech and likely unconstitutional, so nothing is required of companies on scope 3 in California and the five-category proposal is moot unless the provisions are revived. The separate scope 3 row sets out what the court held and what happens next.
sub_changes.old: The statute requires scope 3 (value-chain) reporting starting in 2027, on a schedule CARB sets, without saying which of the fifteen categories.
sub_changes.topic: Scope 3 from 2027: which categories
sub_changes.specifics: HSC 38532(c)(2)(A)(ii): scope 3 'starting in 2027 and annually thereafter' on a schedule set by CARB (SB 219 removed the fixed 180-day lag). CARB March 23, 2026 workshop slides offered three options (all 15 categories; sectoral phase-in; category phase-in). CARB July 21, 2026 workshop (per law-firm accounts; CARB July slides returned 403): phase-in limited to GHG Protocol Categories 1 (purchased goods and services), 3 (fuel- and energy-related activities), 5 (waste generated in operations), 6 (business travel) and 7 (employee commuting); remaining ten categories voluntary; staff declined to give a timeline for adding categories. Sector listening sessions ran Aug 5/12/19/26 and Sept 2/9, 2026. The 45-day notice for this 'Subsequent Regulation' had not been published as of October 1, 2026. Superseded November 9, 2026: Chamber of Commerce v. Sanchez, Ninth Circuit No. 25-5327, reversed as to the scope 3 provisions, applying strict scrutiny, and remanded for the district court to decide severability in the first instance. The five-category proposal was never formally issued and no 45-day notice was ever published.

sub_changes.new: Required: every covered company pays an annual flat fee to fund CARB's program, with a written fee notice due December 10, 2026 and payment within 60 days. CARB has not published the per-company amount; CARB estimates the program will cost about twenty-one million dollars a year for the first three years and about fourteen million a year after that; the regulation sets a formula, not a dollar cap. Companies over one billion dollars pay both the emissions-law and climate-risk-law fees; parents may pay once for their subsidiaries.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Fees: how much and when
sub_changes.specifics: HSC 38532: fee 'in an amount sufficient to cover the state board's full costs', paid into the Climate Accountability and Emissions Disclosure Fund. 17 CCR 96073 (ISOR p. 5, 19; Nov 2025 slides 13–17): flat fee per entity = annual program cost / number of regulated entities; highest estimated annual cost $20,800,000 in FY 2026-27 through FY 2028-29 (ISOR p. 19); ongoing about $13.9 million (Nov 2025 slides 15–17) / 'approximately $14 million ... and ongoing' (ISOR p. 4). July 27, 2026 modifications: fee notice moved 'from September 10 to December 10'; payment within 60 calendar days; 'fee payments may be consolidated at the parent company level'. $500M–$1B revenue pays the SB 261 fee only; above $1B pays both. Per-entity amount unpublished; a $3,000–$4,000 figure in secondary sources is labelled preliminary.

implications: Decide now which entity files: run the revenue and doing-business tests company by company, then choose whether the parent consolidates subsidiaries into one report and one fee payment.
Assemble scope 1 and 2 figures for the correct fiscal year, choose a format — existing report, other-program data or CARB's optional template — and book sign-off before November 10.
If you were not collecting scope 1 and 2 data in December 2024, prepare the letterhead statement of non-reporting instead, and start collecting for 2027.
Treat November 10 as fixed - the regulation took effect October 12, 2026 - and budget for the annual fee, invoiced December 10 with 60 days to pay.
Start scoping the five proposed scope 3 categories and supplier, travel, commuting and waste data flows now; the 2027 report is expected to require them.

rows.old: SB 253 required large companies to report their Scope 3 (value chain) emissions in California from 2027, a year behind Scope 1 and 2.
rows.new: Struck down on appeal. On November 9, 2026 a federal appeals court held that Scope 3 disclosures are not commercial speech, applied the strictest constitutional test and found the requirement likely unconstitutional. Nothing is required of companies on Scope 3 in California while this stands, and whether the rest of SB 253 survives without it has been sent back to the trial court.

detail.applies_to: The same companies the emissions law covers — US-formed companies with more than one billion dollars of annual revenue doing business in California. The ruling removes a prospective obligation; no company has yet had to file a California Scope 3 report.
detail.timing: Statute required Scope 3 from 2027 reports on a schedule CARB would set. CARB's July 2026 workshop proposed five mandatory categories but never issued a formal rulemaking notice. The appeals court reversed on Scope 3 on November 9, 2026 and remanded; no date is set for the trial court's severability decision, no mandate-issuance date is published, and one legal commentator does not expect a trial-court ruling before 2027.

sub_changes.topic: What the court actually held
sub_changes.old: The trial court refused to block any part of the emissions law, and the appeals court was asked to step in.
sub_changes.new: The appeals court reversed as to Scope 3. It held these disclosures are not commercial speech, because they describe diffuse conduct by third parties rather than the company's own commercial activity, so the strictest constitutional test applies and the requirement likely fails it.
sub_changes.specifics: Chamber of Commerce v. Sanchez, Ninth Circuit No. 25-5327, published opinion filed November 9, 2026 (argued January 9, 2026; D.C. No. 2:24-cv-00801-ODW-PVC, C.D. Cal.). Panel: Nguyen and Bennett, Circuit Judges, with Matsumoto, District Judge (E.D.N.Y.), by designation; opinion by Nguyen. Quoted: 'Scope 3 disclosures do not qualify as commercial speech.' Strict scrutiny applied; the court found irreparable harm on the Scope 3 provisions (loss of First Amendment freedoms) and that the equities favour relief. Contrast the same opinion's treatment of Scope 1 and 2, affirmed as commercial speech under intermediate scrutiny, citing Pharm. Rsch. & Mfrs. of Am. v. Stolfi, 153 F.4th 795 (9th Cir. 2025). Bennett, concurring in part and dissenting in part, would have applied strict scrutiny to both laws and enjoined SB 253 and SB 261 in full.

sub_changes.topic: Does the rest of the emissions law survive?
sub_changes.old: Not in issue — no part of the law had been struck down.
sub_changes.new: Undecided, and this is the open question. The appeals court sent the severability question back to the trial court to decide in the first instance: whether SB 253 still works with the Scope 3 provisions removed. The law contains a severability clause, which usually favours keeping the remainder.
sub_changes.specifics: Quoted from the opinion: 'we remand to the district court to determine, in the first instance, whether those provisions are severable.' The opinion notes SB 253's severability clause at California Health and Safety Code section 38532(i). Not stated: any date for the remand decision, or the mandate-issuance date. Secondary commentary (Morrison Foerster, November 11, 2026) does not expect a trial-court ruling before 2027 and describes an injunction against all of SB 253 as a remote possibility. The challengers' remaining non-First-Amendment claims are still pending before the trial court.

sub_changes.topic: What companies must do on Scope 3 now
sub_changes.old: Prepare to report five Scope 3 categories in 2027 under a rulemaking CARB had not yet proposed.
sub_changes.new: Nothing, for now. The requirement is held likely unconstitutional and no California Scope 3 report is due. Treat any Scope 3 work as voluntary or as preparation for other regimes — the EU rules, the ISSB standards and SBTi targets all still require value-chain emissions.
sub_changes.specifics: No California Scope 3 filing obligation has ever come due: the statute set 2027 as the first reporting year and CARB never issued a rulemaking notice for it. Not stated anywhere in the opinion: any direction to CARB about its 2027-and-later rulemaking. Independent of this ruling, Scope 3 duties remain under ESRS E1 (revised ESRS, FY2027), IFRS S2 as amended (effective January 1, 2027) and the SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2.0.

sub_changes.topic: Which categories had been proposed
sub_changes.old: The statute named no categories, leaving the choice to CARB.
sub_changes.new: Five of the fifteen categories would have been mandatory from 2027 — purchased goods and services, fuel- and energy-related activities, waste from operations, business travel and employee commuting — with the other ten voluntary. That proposal was never formally issued and is now moot unless the provisions are revived.
sub_changes.specifics: CARB July 21, 2026 workshop, per law-firm accounts (CARB's own July slides returned a server error): phase-in limited to GHG Protocol Categories 1, 3, 5, 6 and 7; remaining ten categories voluntary; staff declined to give a timeline for adding categories. CARB March 23, 2026 workshop slides had offered three options (all fifteen categories; sectoral phase-in; category phase-in). No 45-day rulemaking notice has ever been published for the 2027-and-later requirements.

sub_changes.topic: Could Scope 3 come back?
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.new: Possibly. What issued is preliminary relief, not a final judgment, so rehearing by the panel, review by a larger panel and a petition to the US Supreme Court all remain available, and the case continues in the trial court. California could also legislate differently.
sub_changes.specifics: Not stated: whether any party will seek rehearing, en banc review or certiorari; no such petition is reported as filed as of November 16, 2026, and roughly a dozen law-firm alerts report none. Nixon Peabody (November 13, 2026) flags the pending certiorari petition in PhRMA v. Stolfi, No. 25-1018, filed February 24, 2026, as the relevant Supreme Court vehicle on the commercial-speech question. The mandate-issuance date is not published.

implications: Stop budgeting for a California Scope 3 filing, but do not dismantle the data collection you built for it.
Keep value-chain emissions work running for the EU rules, the ISSB standards and SBTi targets, which are unaffected.
Watch the trial court on severability — it decides whether the rest of SB 253 keeps working.
Record that your Scope 1 and 2 duty was upheld; only Scope 3 and the climate-risk law were struck.
Do not treat this as final — rehearing and a Supreme Court petition remain available.

sources.title: Sidley: CARB Workshop Gives Glimpse of Possible Future for SB 253 Reporting (July 2026)

detail.applies_to: Every company covered by California's emissions law (more than one billion dollars of revenue, doing business in California); assurance covers the scope 1 and 2 submission including biogenic carbon dioxide, with scope 3 assurance only from 2030.

sub_changes.new: Not in practice for the November 2026 report. CARB has said it will accept 2026 submissions whether or not they have been assured, as part of its first-year enforcement discretion, and the detailed assurance rules are being written for 2027 onward. Companies that already obtain assurance may simply include it.
sub_changes.old: The statute's text says limited assurance over scope 1 and 2 begins in 2026.
sub_changes.topic: Do we need assurance in year one?
sub_changes.specifics: Statute (HSC 38532(c)(2)(F)): limited assurance for scope 1 and 2 beginning in 2026, reasonable assurance beginning 2030. CARB Guidance (Sept 1, 2026), p. 4: 'given first-year enforcement discretion, CARB will accept submissions whether or not assurance has been obtained for the 2026 cycle.' CARB Dec 9, 2025 notice: the Initial Regulation 'is not intended to establish other program requirements, including, but not limited to, reporting and assurance requirements and enforcement provisions. These elements will be developed and adopted through a subsequent rulemaking.' March 23, 2026 slides: limited assurance for scope 1 and 2 'Starting in 2027'. Conflict: statute says 2026, regulator says not enforced for 2026 — the regulator's position governs the November 10, 2026 filing.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: limited assurance over the whole scope 1 and 2 submission (including separately reported biogenic carbon dioxide) is required for reports filed in 2027. Reasonable assurance from 2030 and scope 3 limited assurance from 2030 remain statutory but are not part of the current rulemaking.
sub_changes.old: The statute fixes the ladder: limited assurance over scope 1 and 2 first, reasonable assurance from 2030, and limited assurance over scope 3 from 2030.
sub_changes.topic: The schedule after year one
sub_changes.specifics: Statute: scope 1 and 2 limited assurance 2026–2029, reasonable assurance 2030 onward; scope 3 limited assurance beginning 2030 (HSC 38532(c)(2)(F)). CARB March 23, 2026 slides: limited assurance for scope 1 and 2 starting in 2027; 'SB 253 assurance requirements slated for 2030 are not part of this rulemaking'. CARB July 21, 2026 workshop (law-firm accounts): assurance applies to the entire submission — scope 1, scope 2 and biogenic CO2; scope 3 assurance level and timing not specified. Statute 38532(c)(2)(F)(ii) also lets CARB, by Jan 1, 2027, review and set a scope 3 assurance requirement (reproduced statute text).

sub_changes.new: Proposed: five recognized frameworks — the international sustainability assurance standard (for engagements from December 15, 2026, with its predecessor pair accepted before that), the US accountants' attestation standard, the AccountAbility standard, and the ISO greenhouse gas verification standard provided the verifier is accredited. Full conformance with the chosen standard is required, and the report must name it.
sub_changes.old: The statute only says the assurance provider must be independent and experienced; it names no standard.
sub_changes.topic: Which assurance standards count
sub_changes.specifics: CARB March 23, 2026 slides: 'AA1000 Assurance Standard (AA1000AS v3), AICPA (AT-C Section 210 or AT-C 205), ISAE 3000 (Revised) and ISAE 3410, ISSA 5000 (effective December 2026), ISO 14064-3:2019'. July 21, 2026 workshop (law-firm accounts): ISAE 3410 with ISAE 3000 (Revised) for engagements before Dec 15, 2026, ISSA 5000 for engagements on or after Dec 15, 2026; ISO 14064-3:2019 'with additional accreditation requirements'; AICPA AT-C Section 210; AA1000AS v3; the assurance report must identify the standard applied, the emissions covered and the provider's conclusion, and the engagement must be 'conducted in full conformance with all requirements of the applicable standard' (engagement scope, methodology, qualifications, evidence, independence, oversight, reporting). Not yet in a published regulatory text.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: on top of the statutory independence and experience test, verifiers using the ISO route would need accreditation from a recognized accreditation body under the ISO verifier-competence standards. Rotation and other independence mechanics have not been stated.
sub_changes.old: The statute requires an independent third party with significant experience in measuring or attesting greenhouse gas emissions.
sub_changes.topic: Who may be the assurance provider
sub_changes.specifics: Statute 38532(c)(2)(F)(iii)–(iv): assurance by 'an independent third-party assurance provider' with 'significant experience in measuring, analyzing, reporting, or attesting to the emission of greenhouse gasses'. CARB March 23, 2026 slides: 'ISO 14065 / ISO 14066 – provider qualifications' through accreditation bodies (ANAB, DAkkS, JAB, etc.). July 21, 2026 workshop: independence and oversight mechanism required under the applied standard; rotation requirements, named accreditation bodies and conflict-of-interest mechanics not stated.

sub_changes.new: Still a staff proposal. CARB has previewed the assurance rules in workshops in March and July 2026 and plans a formal 45-day proposal for a 'Subsequent Regulation' covering 2027 and later reports, but no notice had been published as of October 1, 2026.
sub_changes.old: No regulation on assurance existed; CARB's first regulation deliberately left it out.
sub_changes.topic: Where the assurance rules stand
sub_changes.specifics: CARB Dec 9, 2025 notice: assurance deferred to 'a subsequent rulemaking'. Pre-rulemaking workshops March 23, 2026 (comments to April 13, 2026) and July 21, 2026; sector listening sessions Aug 5–Sept 9, 2026. Staff indicated a 45-day public comment period before Board approval; dates for the notice, Board hearing and effective date not given (law-firm accounts of the July 21 workshop). CARB's July 21 slides could not be fetched (HTTP 403) — details rely on two consistent law-firm summaries.

implications: Do not delay the November 2026 filing for assurance; file what you have and keep the evidence trail an assurer will later ask for.
Select an assurance provider in early 2027 for the first limited-assurance report and confirm which recognized standard they will apply.
If you want an ISO-route verifier, check their accreditation status now, since accreditation is proposed as a condition.
Plan data systems for reasonable assurance by 2030; the step up from limited to reasonable is the largest cost jump.
Watch for the formal proposal on 2027 rules and comment if the standards list or scope of assurance would be a problem for you.

detail.timing: Statutory GHG Protocol anchor in force; edition pinning and detailed method rules previewed at CARB workshops on March 23 and July 21, 2026 for 2027+ reports; formal proposal not yet published as of October 1, 2026.

detail.applies_to: All companies covered by California's emissions law; the edition pinning, dual scope 2 methods and disclosure list are proposals for reports filed from 2027 onward, while 2026 filers may re-use existing inventories.

sub_changes.new: Proposed for 2027 onward: CARB would write the specific current editions into the regulation — the corporate standard, the 2015 scope 2 (purchased energy) guidance and the scope 3 standard — so the rule refers to fixed texts. For the 2026 report CARB accepts existing inventories and has not specified editions.
sub_changes.old: The statute itself requires inventories 'in conformance with' the GHG Protocol's corporate standard and its scope 3 (value-chain) standard, without naming editions.
sub_changes.topic: Which accounting standards the law names
sub_changes.specifics: HSC 38532(c)(2)(A)(i)–(ii): reporting entities measure and report 'in conformance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol standards and guidance, including the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard and the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard', with CARB able, starting in 2033, to adopt a globally recognized alternative accounting and reporting standard (38532(c)(2)(A)(iv)). July 21, 2026 workshop (law-firm accounts): inventories under the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard, Scope 2 Guidance (2015 edition explicitly) and Scope 3 Standard; edition years for the Corporate and Scope 3 standards were not stated in the accounts read. 2026 guidance (Sept 1, 2026) names no GHG Protocol edition and accepts existing reports.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: California's requirements would not move automatically. CARB staff said the rule 'would not dynamically update' to follow future GHG Protocol revisions without a separate CARB action, so companies could face one method for California and another for the revised Protocol until CARB catches up.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable — no state rule existed.
sub_changes.topic: What happens when the GHG Protocol changes
sub_changes.specifics: July 21, 2026 CARB workshop, staff response quoted by two law-firm summaries: requirements 'would not dynamically update to incorporate such future changes in the GHG Protocol without additional action by CARB' (Sidley); 'SB 253 will not dynamically update to reflect GHG Protocol developments' (Ropes & Gray). Another summary (K&L Gates) records that reporting entities 'will not need to comply with the Scope 2 GHG-P currently being updated'. CARB's own July 21 slides returned HTTP 403 and could not be read; no regulatory text yet exists.

sub_changes.new: Proposed for 2027 onward: both numbers are required — the location-based (grid-average) figure and the market-based (contract-and-certificate) figure — broken down by electricity, steam, heating and cooling, by individual gas, with documentation where factors are missing.
sub_changes.old: Not stated for the 2026 report: CARB's guidance does not say which scope 2 method to use, and its optional template simply asks for scope 2 figures plus a separate section for emission reductions from renewable electricity and gas contracts.
sub_changes.topic: Scope 2: grid-average or contract-based numbers?
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: Sept 1, 2026 guidance — scope 2 method not specified; emission factors may be 'the most recent official U.S. EPA eGRID release (eGRID 2023) or, if preferable, the eGRID 2024 dataset published by the Cornerstone Sustainability Data Initiative' or other credible sources; Oct 10, 2025 draft template includes an 'Emission Reductions' section for 'direct contracts of renewable electricity and renewable gas'. 2027+ (July 21, 2026 workshop, law-firm accounts): market-based and location-based methods both required; emissions by source type (electricity, steam, heating, cooling) and by gas (CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6, NF3) plus CO2e totals; documentation required if factors are unavailable for a region or source.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: you choose equity share, financial control or operational control, consistent with the GHG Protocol, and must disclose the approach and your consolidation choices in the report. The choice is yours; there is no mandated approach.
sub_changes.old: Not stated; CARB's draft template asks which of the three GHG Protocol approaches you use.
sub_changes.topic: Organizational boundary and consolidation approach
sub_changes.specifics: Oct 10, 2025 draft template memo: inventory boundary section asks entities to 'specify whether they use the equity share, financial control or operational control approach', reflecting GHG Protocol guidance. March 23, 2026 slides: 'Equity Share: Account for emissions based on company's percentage ownership' and 'Control: 100% of emissions from operations over which it has control (financial or operational)'; staff propose disclosures 'about entities' organizational boundary selection, emission factors, and accounting methods'. July 21, 2026 workshop: disclosure of consolidation approach for organizational boundaries required. Note the regulatory applicability test (entity by entity, with optional parent consolidation) is separate from the inventory boundary.

sub_changes.new: Proposed for 2027 onward: you would report gross emissions in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, name the global-warming-potential values and their vintage, give each emission factor's source, vintage and representativeness, state whether figures were measured or calculated, give confidence intervals where possible, and document any missing or substituted data. Biogenic carbon dioxide is reported separately; voluntary credits and removals are reported apart from the inventory.
sub_changes.old: For 2026, CARB only encourages you to identify the emission factors and sources used.
sub_changes.topic: Emission factors, gases and data quality disclosures
sub_changes.specifics: 2026 guidance p. 3–4: methodology, data sources, GWP values, emission factors and organizational boundary 'encouraged' but optional; eGRID 2023 or 2024 datasets acceptable. March 23, 2026 slides: proposed factor sources include EPA eGRID, IPCC EFDB, EPA Emission Factors Hub and US EEIO. July 21, 2026 workshop (law-firm accounts): gross emissions in metric tons CO2e; GWP values with assessment-report vintage; emission-factor source, vintage, geographic/technical representativeness and uncertainty; quantification method (direct measurement or calculation); confidence intervals where applicable or qualitative assessment; missing/substitute data documented with basis and assumptions; biogenic CO2 from combustion or biodegradation reported separately, biogenic CH4 and N2O inside scopes 1/2/3; carbon credits, offsets and land-management removals reported separately from scopes 1–3.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: you may leave out sources only where omitting or misstating them could not reasonably influence a reader's decisions, assessed on quantity and quality, and you must disclose each exclusion and its estimated size. Your first reporting year becomes your base year; if structural or method changes cumulatively move it by more than five percent, affected prior years must be recalculated and explained.
sub_changes.old: Not stated; CARB's draft template has a section for de minimis or minor sources excluded under a materiality-type threshold.
sub_changes.topic: Exclusions, method changes and base-year recalculation
sub_changes.specifics: July 21, 2026 workshop (law-firm accounts): exclusion permitted where 'the omission, misstatement or obscuring of the information could not' reasonably influence users' decisions about the inventory; both quantitative and qualitative factors; basis and estimated magnitude disclosed per exclusion; CARB seeking feedback on adequacy of factors. Methodology changes from the prior year disclosed with reasons and may require recalculation. Base year = first reporting year; if cumulative effect of structural or methodological changes exceeds 5% of base-year total emissions, all affected prior years recalculated and reported with explanations. Oct 10, 2025 template memo: 'De Minimis / Minor Sources' section for emissions excluded under specific materiality thresholds.

sub_changes.new: From 2027, only if it follows the editions California pins and carries the extra disclosures above. CARB has said it aims for interoperability with the ISSB climate standard and the EU sustainability standards, but the binding reference is the pinned GHG Protocol text, so differences could emerge once the Protocol's revision lands.
sub_changes.old: For the 2026 report, yes: CARB expressly accepts an existing annual report or data already reported to another program.
sub_changes.topic: Can we re-use an inventory built for other regimes?
sub_changes.specifics: 2026: Sept 1, 2026 guidance accepts 'an existing annual report including Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions' or 'existing Scope 1 and 2 data reported to other programs/voluntary initiatives'. 2027+: July 21, 2026 workshop — primary alignment with the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard and Scope 2 Guidance, with a stated goal 'to promote interoperability with IFRS S2 and EU's CSRD' (K&L Gates account); requirements fixed to the pinned editions and not updated automatically (Sidley, Ropes & Gray accounts). The GHG Protocol's own revision of the Corporate Standard, Scope 2 Guidance and Scope 3 Standard is in progress (see the GHG Protocol block), creating the dual-methodology risk noted in the row text.

implications: Build the California inventory on the current GHG Protocol editions and keep a change log so you can run a parallel method once the revised Protocol publishes.
Prepare both location-based and market-based scope 2 figures, split by energy type and by gas, with factor sources and vintages documented.
Record your boundary approach, every exclusion with its estimated size, and your global-warming-potential vintage now; these are proposed mandatory disclosures from 2027.
Lock a base-year policy: your first California report becomes the base year, with recalculation when cumulative changes exceed five percent.
Map differences between California's pinned methods and your ISSB or EU inventory so one dataset can serve all three.

No mandate-issuance date is published, no replacement reporting deadline has been set, and no source states a next SB 261 deadline. Voluntary docket open since December 1, 2025.

detail.applies_to: US-formed companies with more than five hundred million dollars of annual revenue doing business in California, excluding regulated insurers; parent-level reports may cover subsidiaries.

sub_changes.new: The law covers US-formed businesses with more than five hundred million dollars of total annual revenue that do business in California — a lower bar than the emissions law — but regulated insurers are excluded. Subsidiaries can be covered by a parent's report. Enforcement is currently suspended by a court order.
sub_changes.old: Climate-risk reporting in the US was voluntary, usually following the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures framework.
sub_changes.topic: Who the climate-risk law covers
sub_changes.specifics: HSC 38533(a)(4): 'covered entity' is a corporation, partnership, LLC or other business entity formed under US, state or DC law 'with total annual revenues exceeding $500,000,000 and that does business in California', excluding insurance businesses regulated by the Department of Insurance. Same regulation (17 CCR 96070–96077) supplies the 'doing business' (RTC 23101(b)(1)–(2)), revenue and subsidiary definitions as for the emissions law; parent-level consolidation permitted. Ninth Circuit injunction pending appeal, Nov 18, 2025 (No. 25-5327), bars enforcement.

sub_changes.new: Required (once enforceable): a report on your climate-related financial risks — the material risk of harm to near- and long-term financial outcomes from physical and transition risks — and the measures you take to reduce and adapt to them, written to the Task Force framework, the ISSB climate standard, or an equivalent regulatory requirement. If you cannot complete every element you report what you can and explain the gaps. The report goes on your own website.
sub_changes.old: Voluntary reports followed whichever framework the company chose.
sub_changes.topic: What the report must contain
sub_changes.specifics: HSC 38533(a)(2): climate-related financial risk is 'material risk of harm to immediate and long-term financial outcomes due to physical and transition risks', spanning operations, supply chains, employee safety, investments, borrowers, shareholder value and consumer demand. 38533(b)(1): report 'in accordance with the recommended framework and disclosures contained in the Final Report of Recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures' or an equivalent requirement including IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards; where incomplete, 'provide the recommended disclosures to the best of its ability, provide a detailed explanation for any reporting gaps'; post on the entity's website. CARB Nov 18, 2025 slides 34–36: name the framework applied and which disclosures were compiled or omitted, covering governance, strategy, risk management, metrics and targets.

sub_changes.new: Decided, against the law. Enforcement was first blocked by an appeals court order of November 18, 2025, and on November 9, 2026 the same court decided the appeal and reversed: the climate-risk reports compel noncommercial, subjective speech and fail the strictest constitutional test, with the court noting the state all but concedes it cannot meet that standard. The case returns to the trial court for relief consistent with that ruling.
sub_changes.old: Business groups sued in January 2024; the trial court refused to block either law, and the appeals court was asked to step in.
sub_changes.topic: Where the court case stands
sub_changes.specifics: Chamber of Commerce v. Sanchez, Ninth Circuit No. 25-5327: injunction motion Sept 15, 2025; referred to merits panel Oct 23, 2025; order Nov 18, 2025 — 'The motion for injunction pending appeal (Dkt. No. 6) is GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART' — granted as to SB 261 (HSC 38533), denied as to SB 253 (HSC 38532). Oral argument Jan 9, 2026. No merits decision as of Aug 19, 2026 (Jones Day, Sept 8, 2026) or a Sept 11, 2026 tracker update; docket not fetchable. Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Sanchez, E.D. Cal. No. 2:25-cv-03104 (filed Oct 24, 2025; First Amendment claims against both laws plus securities-law preemption of SB 261) is effectively on hold pending the appeal; the state requested a stay. A Supreme Court emergency application noticed Nov 12, 2025 was withdrawn after the Nov 18 order (Sabin Center tracker; application number not verified). Decided November 9, 2026 (published opinion, No. 25-5327): 'Because SB 261 does not regulate commercial speech, it is subject to strict scrutiny'; the court found the law compels subjective, 'politically fraught' assessments, fails tailoring, and that the State 'all but concedes it cannot satisfy' strict scrutiny; irreparable harm found. Disposition 'AFFIRMED IN PART, REVERSED IN PART, and REMANDED' — affirmed as to SB 253 scope 1 and 2, reversed as to SB 253 scope 3 and as to SB 261. Bennett, concurring in part and dissenting in part, would have enjoined both laws in full. Not stated: the mandate-issuance date, any replacement CARB deadline, or any rehearing or certiorari petition (none reported as of November 16, 2026).

sub_changes.new: Suspended. On December 1, 2025 CARB said it will not enforce the January 1, 2026 deadline while the injunction stands and will announce further information, including an alternate reporting date as appropriate, after the appeal is resolved. No replacement date has been set.
sub_changes.old: The statute set the first report for January 1, 2026, and CARB had planned a docket where companies would post links by July 1, 2026.
sub_changes.topic: The January 1, 2026 deadline and what CARB said
sub_changes.specifics: HSC 38533(b)(1): 'On or before January 1, 2026, and biennially thereafter'. CARB Enforcement Advisory, Dec 1, 2025: 'CARB will not enforce Health and Safety Code section 38533 against covered entities for failing to post and submit reports by the January 1, 2026, statutory deadline'; 'CARB will provide further information—including an alternate date for reporting, as appropriate—after the appeal is resolved.' Pre-injunction plan (Nov 18, 2025 slides 34, 37): post on website by Jan 1, 2026; submit link to CARB docket by July 1, 2026; docket open Dec 1, 2025–July 1, 2026. The Initial Regulation's applicability, definitions and fee sections (96071–96074) also cover climate-risk covered entities, but it sets no climate-risk reporting deadline; section 96077 is only a severability clause.

sub_changes.new: Optional. CARB opened a public docket on December 1, 2025 where companies may post their climate-risk reports voluntarily, and many have. Doing so carries no legal obligation, but the docket is public.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: Voluntary posting while the law is paused
sub_changes.specifics: CARB Enforcement Advisory, Dec 1, 2025: 'For entities that may choose to report voluntarily at this time, CARB will open a docket starting December 1, 2025'. Docket URL: https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/public-comments/climate-related-financial-risk-reports-sb-261-docket (not fetched; CARB web pages blocked). About 94 reports were on the docket as of January 30, 2026, 91% of them TCFD-structured (PwC analysis of the docket); CARB publishes no running count itself; secondary trackers describe submissions as ongoing.

sub_changes.new: Every two years once enforceable, with fines capped at fifty thousand dollars per reporting year — a tenth of the emissions law's cap. Companies are also charged an annual fee to fund the program.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: How often, and penalties
sub_changes.specifics: HSC 38533(b)(1): biennial reporting. 38533(f)(2): administrative penalties not to exceed $50,000 in a reporting year; 38533(c)(2): annual fee into the Climate-Related Financial Risk Disclosure Fund. Regulation 96073: entities with $500M–$1B revenue pay the SB 261 fee only; those above $1B pay both fees (CARB Nov 18, 2025 slides 13–17); the fee notice for 2026 moved to Dec 10, 2026 (15-day notice). Whether a 2026 climate-risk fee will be charged while enforcement is enjoined is not stated in the documents read.

sub_changes.new: No. The same court order refused to block the emissions law, so the November 10, 2026 scope 1 and 2 deadline is unaffected by this case. A ruling on the merits could still change either law.
sub_changes.old: The challengers asked the court to block both laws together.
sub_changes.topic: Does the injunction affect the emissions law?
sub_changes.specifics: Ninth Circuit order, Nov 18, 2025 (No. 25-5327): injunction pending appeal granted as to SB 261 and 'denied the appellants' motion as to enforcement of Senate Bill 253'. The merits appeal covers both statutes (First Amendment compelled-speech claims); outcome and timing unknown as of October 1, 2026.

implications: Keep a Task Force- or ISSB-aligned climate-risk report ready; the obligation is paused, not repealed, and a new deadline could follow the ruling with limited notice.
Decide whether to post voluntarily on CARB's public docket, weighing peer practice against the permanence of a public filing.
Confirm which group entities exceed five hundred million dollars and do business in California; the parent can cover them in one report.
Do not let the climate-risk pause slow the emissions report; the court left the November 10 deadline in place.
Monitor the appeals court decision and CARB's follow-up notice, which will set the alternate reporting date.
