detail.applies_to: Companies with more than one billion dollars of revenue doing business in New York (bill passed one chamber) or New Jersey (committee stage); Illinois, Colorado and Washington bills are dead for now. No state other than California has an enacted mandate.

sub_changes.new: Proposed, not law. A renumbered Senate version passed the New York Senate on February 10, 2026 by 40 votes to 22 and went to the Assembly, where the companion bill was amended the same day and remains in the Codes Committee. Nothing becomes binding unless the Assembly passes it and the Governor signs; otherwise it must be reintroduced in 2027.
sub_changes.old: New York's bill had been introduced in every session since 2022 without passing either chamber; the 2025 Senate version sat in the Finance Committee.
sub_changes.topic: New York: where the bill stands
sub_changes.specifics: S9072A (Sen. Harckham), Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act: passed Senate Feb 10, 2026 (40 Aye, 22 Nay), delivered to Assembly Feb 10, 2026; same-as A4282A (M. of A. Glick), referred to Environmental Conservation Feb 4, 2025, reported to Codes May 13, 2025, referred to Codes Jan 7, 2026, amended and recommitted to Codes Feb 10, 2026 (print number 4282a). The earlier Senate bill S3456 (Sen. Hoylman-Sigal; prior versions S897/A4123 in 2023–24) was reported to Finance on April 2, 2025 and has not moved; the Senate site lists both S3456 and S9072 as same-as A4282. New York's two-year session ends December 31, 2026.

sub_changes.new: If enacted, companies with more than one billion dollars of revenue in the prior fiscal year that do business in New York would report scope 1 and 2 from 2028 and scope 3 from 2029, using the GHG Protocol corporate standard, with limited assurance over scope 1 and 2 from 2028 and reasonable assurance from 2032. Regulations would be due by the end of 2027.
sub_changes.old: No New York requirement.
sub_changes.topic: New York: what it would require
sub_changes.specifics: S9072A text: revenue 'in excess of $1 billion in the preceding fiscal year'; doing business in New York with receipts within the state per Tax Law 209; scope 1 and 2 beginning 2028, scope 3 beginning 2029; reports in compliance with the 'Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard'; limited assurance for scope 1 and 2 2028–2031, reasonable assurance from 2032; Department of Environmental Conservation to review scope 3 assurance by Jan 1, 2029; regulations by December 31, 2027; Department to create or contract an emissions reporting organization and a Climate Accountability and Emissions Disclosure Fund.

sub_changes.new: Yes, as drafted: the bill lets companies satisfy it with reports prepared for other state, national or international requirements, including the ISSB sustainability standards — a clause modelled on California's own, which likewise accepts reports prepared for other national and international requirements, with New York adding other states' requirements and naming the ISSB standards; in both cases the report must still satisfy every requirement of the law.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: New York: can other reports be re-used?
sub_changes.specifics: S9072A: permits use of 'reports prepared to meet other State, national, and international' reporting standards, including the ISSB Sustainability Disclosure Standards, to satisfy the New York requirement. HSC 38532(c)(2)(D)(i) (California) contains the parallel clause for 'other national and international reporting requirements, including any reports required by the federal government, as long as those reports satisfy all of the requirements of this section'; New York adds 'State' requirements and names the ISSB standards. Both are conditional on satisfying all requirements of the act.

sub_changes.new: If enacted, fines of up to one hundred thousand dollars per day, capped at five hundred thousand dollars per year — the same annual cap as California. Penalties would be sought by the state's Attorney General in court. Scope 3 penalties in the first years would apply only for not filing, and good-faith scope 3 estimates with a reasonable basis are protected, as in California.
sub_changes.old: Not applicable.
sub_changes.topic: New York: penalties
sub_changes.specifics: S9072A (as passed by the Senate Feb 10, 2026): civil penalties of up to $100,000 per day, sought by the Attorney General in a civil action, capped at $500,000 per reporting year; scope 3 penalties between 2029 and 2032 'shall only occur for nonfiling'; no civil action 'for any misstatements with regard to scope 3 emissions disclosures made with a reasonable basis and disclosed in good faith'. Compare California HSC 38532(f): penalties not to exceed $500,000 per reporting year, scope 3 penalties for nonfiling only between 2027 and 2030, and the same safe harbor for scope 3 misstatements made with a reasonable basis and in good faith.

sub_changes.new: Proposed. A Senate committee advanced an amended bill on February 12, 2026 that removes scope 3 entirely: companies over one billion dollars would report scope 1 and 2 to the state three years after enactment and publicly four years after, with graduated fines of ten, twenty and fifty thousand dollars. It has not passed either chamber.
sub_changes.old: New Jersey's bill as introduced mirrored California, including scope 3.
sub_changes.topic: New Jersey: scope 3 dropped in committee
sub_changes.specifics: NJ S679 (2026–2027 session), Senate Environment and Energy Committee statement, Feb 12, 2026: applies to entities with 'total annual revenues in excess of $1 billion' doing business in New Jersey; reporting to the Department of Environmental Protection three years after enactment, public disclosure four years after; committee amendments eliminated scope 3 requirements, clarified that subsidiaries need not file separately where the parent includes their emissions, and allowed use of the NAIC Climate Risk Disclosure Survey; penalties $10,000 first offense, $20,000 second, $50,000 third and subsequent; DEP may contract a nonprofit to manage reports and an academic institution to analyze them. Assurance and GHG Protocol references not described in the committee statement.

sub_changes.new: None is moving. Illinois's bill died in the Rules Committee in March 2025; Colorado's was killed in committee in February 2025; Washington's earlier bill failed. No state other than California has enacted a corporate emissions-disclosure mandate as of October 2026, and no state bill has passed more than one chamber.
sub_changes.old: Copycat bills were introduced in 2024–2025 in several states.
sub_changes.topic: Illinois, Colorado and Washington: stalled or failed
sub_changes.specifics: Illinois HB 3673 (Climate Corporate Accountability Act): filed Feb 7, 2025; reporting entity >$1,000,000,000 revenue doing business in Illinois; scope 1 and 2 from Jan 1, 2027, scope 3 within 180 days; GHG Protocol Corporate and Scope 3 standards; re-referred to Rules Committee (Rule 19(a)) March 21, 2025. Colorado HB25-1119: >$1B revenue; scope 1 and 2 from Jan 1, 2028, scope 3 from Jan 1, 2029, third-party verification, penalties up to $100,000 per day; House Energy & Environment Committee 'Postpone Indefinitely' Feb 27, 2025. Washington: earlier bill failed (Jones Day, Sept 8, 2026 — secondary; bill text not fetched). Jones Day: no state bill outside California has 'passed more than a single chamber in five years'.

implications: Treat New York as the only live second-state risk: map which group entities exceed one billion dollars with New York receipts, and pencil in 2028 scope 1 and 2 data.
Build one GHG Protocol inventory that can serve California, New York and future states; every bill anchors to the same standard.
Note New York's reciprocity clause: an ISSB-aligned report may satisfy it, so keep that option open in your reporting architecture.
Do not plan resources around New Jersey, Illinois, Colorado or Washington until a bill passes a chamber.
Re-check state trackers in January 2027 when new sessions open and stalled bills are reintroduced.

sub_changes.specifics: 40 CFR Part 98 applies to facilities emitting 25,000 metric tons CO2e or more per year from covered sources (98.2(a)(2)) plus suppliers and CO2 injection sites — about 8,200 reporters across 47 source categories. Final rule 'Extending the Reporting Deadline Under the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Rule for 2025', 91 FR 9712 (Feb 27, 2026; effective same day): RY2025 deadline moved from March 31, 2026 to October 30, 2026 to allow time to finalize the reconsideration. Sept 17, 2026: EPA delivered an interim final rule further extending the RY2025 deadline to OMB; the OMB summary does not state the new date (trade-press report, Sept 23, 2026 — secondary).

sub_changes.new: Proposed: reporting would end for 46 of the 47 categories after the 2024 data year; oil-and-gas systems would stop reporting from 2025 through 2033 and resume in 2034, and natural-gas distribution would be removed for good. EPA says it no longer needs the data to implement the Clean Air Act and estimates savings of about three hundred million dollars a year.
sub_changes.old: Forty-seven source categories reported, from power plants and refineries to landfills, chemicals and fuel suppliers.
sub_changes.topic: What EPA proposes to remove
sub_changes.specifics: Proposed rule 'Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program: Reconsideration', 90 FR 44591 (Sept 16, 2025; Document 2025-17923; comments to Nov 3, 2025): remove reporting for all non-Subpart W source categories after reporting year 2024; suspend Subpart W (Petroleum and Natural Gas Systems) for reporting years 2025–2033, resuming 2034; remove the Natural Gas Distribution segment permanently (Congress excluded it from the waste emissions charge); authority under Clean Air Act section 114 — 'the Administrator no longer believes the information collected under the rule is necessary to implementing relevant provisions of the CAA'; estimated cost savings $303 million per year, about $256 million from the Subpart W suspension.

sub_changes.new: If finalized, that verified federal data source disappears for most industries, so companies will have to maintain the same measurements internally for California and other corporate reporting. California's emissions law does not depend on the federal program: it references the GHG Protocol, and its own facility rule continues separately.
sub_changes.old: Many companies lifted facility-level scope 1 figures, and verified fuel and process data, straight from their federal filings.
sub_changes.topic: Why it matters for corporate inventories
sub_changes.specifics: HSC 38532 references the GHG Protocol Corporate and Scope 3 standards, not 40 CFR Part 98; CARB's Oct 10, 2025 draft template has a separate 'California MRR Fields (if applicable)' section for facilities under California's Mandatory Reporting Regulation (17 CCR 95100 et seq.), which is unaffected by the federal proposal. The federal proposal itself acknowledges that alternative datasets such as the Manufacturing Energy Consumption Survey do 'not provide the same level of detail' (90 FR 44591). Whether EPA's eGRID electricity factors, which CARB's 2026 guidance points to, would be affected is not stated in the documents read.

sub_changes.new: Not final. Comments closed in November 2025; EPA said in February 2026 it intended to finalize the rest 'in one or more subsequent final actions', but as of October 1, 2026 no final rescission has been published and EPA's own rulemaking page lists only the proposal and the deadline extension.
sub_changes.old: The program had run continuously since reporting year 2010.
sub_changes.topic: Where the proposal stands
sub_changes.specifics: 90 FR 44591 comment period closed Nov 3, 2025. 91 FR 9712 (Feb 27, 2026): EPA 'intends to separately consider all other aspects of the GHGRP Reconsideration Proposal in one or more subsequent final actions', with completion then anticipated by July 2026. EPA 'Rulemaking Notices for GHG Reporting' page (checked Oct 1, 2026) lists the Sept 16, 2025 proposal (status: proposed) and the Feb 27, 2026 extension (status: final) as the most recent actions; no final rescission rule. Trade press (Sept 23, 2026): 'The agency has not yet taken final action on its proposal to cancel the GHGRP.'

implications: Work 2025 facility reports to the new March 10, 2027 deadline set by EPA's October 14, 2026 interim final rule, and comment by November 30, 2026 if the timing matters to you.
Preserve the facility-level fuel, process and monitoring data you now compile for EPA; you will need it for California scope 1 regardless of the federal outcome.
Check whether any of your scope 1 or supplier emission factors are sourced from federal program data that may stop updating.
Watch for the final reconsideration rule and the further deadline extension sent for review in September 2026.

detail.applies_to: Any organization making or verifying a carbon neutrality claim against an ISO standard — a methodology reference, not a reporting obligation.

sub_changes.new: Required if you cite ISO: the 2026 edition is the only one in force, and the 2023 edition was withdrawn the same day. ISO calls it a minor revision: the title changed and the part number was dropped, nothing else. Whether certification bodies re-issue existing certificates is not stated.
sub_changes.old: The 2023 edition was the ISO reference for demonstrating that an organization or product is carbon neutral. It was numbered as part one of a planned 'transition to net zero' series.
sub_changes.topic: Which edition to cite from now on
sub_changes.specifics: 2023: ISO 14068-1:2023 'Climate change management — Transition to net zero — Part 1: Carbon neutrality', published 2023-11-30, 44 pages; stage 90.92 'to be revised' 2026-05-08; stage 95.99 'Withdrawal of International Standard' 2026-09-11. 2026: ISO 14068:2026 'Climate change management — Carbon neutrality', edition 1, 38 pages, stage 60.60 'International Standard published' 2026-09-11, ISO/TC 207/SC 7, ICS 13.020.40. Foreword: 'This first edition cancels and replaces ISO 14068-1:2023, of which it constitutes a minor revision. The changes are as follows: the title has been updated; the part number has been removed.' Verification bodies are accredited under ISO/IEC 17029:2019 (UKAS bulletin, 30 July 2024, PAS 2060 removed from schedules 31 December 2025).

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: the subject can be an organization or a product, where 'product' includes goods, services, buildings and events. The standard is a method for making and supporting a claim, not a reporting obligation; the clause structure is identical to the 2023 edition.
sub_changes.old: An organization, or a product including goods, services, buildings and events, could be the subject of a claim.
sub_changes.topic: What can be declared carbon neutral
sub_changes.specifics: 2023 and 2026 abstracts match in substance: the standard 'specifies principles, requirements and guidance for achieving and demonstrating carbon neutrality' and 'provides a standardized approach to quantifying, reducing and offsetting the carbon footprint of organizations and products, including goods, services, buildings and events'. Clause structure (both editions): 6 Commitment to carbon neutrality; 7 Selection of the subject and its boundary; 8 Quantification of GHG emissions and removals; 9 Carbon neutrality management plan; 10 GHG emission reductions and removal enhancements; 11 Offsetting the carbon footprint; 12 Carbon neutrality report; 13 Carbon neutrality claims; Annex A pathway (informative), Annex B additional requirements for specific cases (normative), Annex C comparison with other standards, Annex D ambition.

sub_changes.new: Unchanged: the same hierarchy applies. You must commit at senior level, keep a management plan with targets, make reductions against your baseline, and use credits only to offset the remaining footprint. Credit quality rules carry over: real, additional, measurable, permanent, with safeguards against double counting.
sub_changes.old: Required: cut your own and value-chain emissions and enhance removals first; buy credits only for the footprint left over, backed by a management plan with short- and long-term targets.
sub_changes.topic: Reductions first, offsets only for what remains
sub_changes.specifics: Introduction (both editions): 'The hierarchy approach presented in this document prioritizes actions to reduce the direct and indirect GHG emissions and enhance GHG removals of the subject, with offsetting used only for the carbon footprint remaining after these actions'; the document 'is designed to build upon existing International Standards addressing GHG quantification, reporting, validation and verification, such as ISO 14064-1, ISO 14064-3 and ISO 14067'. Management plan (clause 9, per the BSI briefing on the 2023 edition — secondary): short- and long-term targets, planned reductions and removal enhancements, selection of carbon credits, monitoring indicators, resources. Credit hallmarks (same source): real, additional, measurable, permanent, safeguards against double counting. ISO's clause text on credits was not read directly.

sub_changes.new: Not to consumers: from September 27, 2026 EU law bans claiming that a product has a neutral, reduced or positive climate impact on the basis of offsetting, whatever standard the claim follows. The ISO standard still governs how a claim is built and verified, but it does not override the ban.
sub_changes.old: EU consumer law had no specific rule on offset-based neutrality claims; the ISO standard was the main reference for substantiating them.
sub_changes.topic: Can you still market a product as carbon neutral in the EU
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2024/825 (Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition) adds point 4c to Annex I of Directive 2005/29/EC: 'Claiming, based on the offsetting of greenhouse gas emissions, that a product has a neutral, reduced or positive impact on the environment in terms of greenhouse gas emissions' is a commercial practice regarded as unfair in all circumstances; Article 4: Member States adopt measures by 27 March 2026 and apply them from 27 September 2026; recital 12 gives the rationale (offsetting occurs outside the product's value chain). ISO 14068:2026 published 2026-09-11, sixteen days earlier. Point 4c sits in the business-to-consumer unfair-practices framework; the ISO standard is silent on consumer law.

sub_changes.new: No. The 'transition to net zero' wording and the part number were removed, so carbon neutrality now stands alone. ISO's net-zero definition is a separate draft that failed its ballot in September 2026 and is not published; the 2022 ISO net-zero guidelines remain the only ISO text on net zero.
sub_changes.old: The 2023 title placed carbon neutrality as 'part one' of a 'transition to net zero', implying a net-zero part would follow in the same series.
sub_changes.topic: Is this ISO's net-zero standard
sub_changes.specifics: 2023 title: 'Climate change management — Transition to net zero — Part 1: Carbon neutrality'. 2026 title: 'Climate change management — Carbon neutrality' (Foreword: 'the title has been updated', 'the part number has been removed'). Net zero: ISO/DIS 14060 'Net zero aligned organizations', stage 40.60 'Close of voting' 2026-09-10; ISO statement reported 23–24 September 2026: the draft 'did not receive the level of approval required to advance in its current form'. ISO/DIS 14060 Foreword: 'This document was developed from the ISO Net Zero Guidelines IWA 42:2022'; the project page lists IWA 42:2022 as the document it will replace.

implications: Update methodology and assurance references from the 2023 part-one edition to the 2026 carbon neutrality edition; the content is a minor revision, so no method change is needed.
Check consumer-facing claims separately: the EU banned offset-based carbon-neutral product claims from September 27, 2026, sixteen days after this standard published.
Do not read this as an ISO net-zero standard — that is ISO 14060, which has not been published.
Ask your certification body whether certificates issued against the 2023 edition will be re-issued or simply re-referenced; ISO has not stated a transition.

rows.new: Still nothing published. The draft standard (ISO 14060) failed its first international ballot, which closed September 10, 2026, and went back to committee with no revision date disclosed. SBTi remains the working benchmark.
rows.old: No international standard defined what a net-zero aligned organization is — only ISO's non-binding Net Zero Guidelines (IWA 42:2022), which ISO 14060 would turn into a standard; SBTi criteria filled the gap in practice.

detail.timing: Draft International Standard ballot ran twelve weeks from June 17, 2026 and closed September 9/10, 2026 (ISO records differ by a day); failure reported September 23–24, 2026; committee next step (refer back or new ballot) not decided publicly; finalisation anticipated 2027 at the earliest by trade press, no date published by ISO.

detail.applies_to: Anyone relying on an external definition to support a net-zero claim, or planning to cite one; the draft covers organizations only, not products or territories.

sub_changes.new: Still no. National standards bodies voted on the draft over twelve weeks ending in September 2026; it did not reach the approval level ISO requires (two-thirds in favour and no more than a quarter against) and has gone back to the committee. ISO has published no vote tally and no date for a revised draft. The 2022 guidelines remain the only ISO text until a new ballot passes.
sub_changes.old: No standard. ISO's 2022 net-zero guidelines, a non-binding workshop agreement, were the only ISO text, and SBTi criteria filled the gap in practice.
sub_changes.topic: Is there an ISO net-zero standard you can cite
sub_changes.specifics: ISO/DIS 14060 'Net zero aligned organizations', 85 pages, edition 1, ISO/TC 207/SC 7, will replace IWA 42:2022. Stages: 40.20 DIS ballot initiated 2026-06-17 (12 weeks); 40.60 close of voting 2026-09-10; DIS cover: 'Voting terminates on: 2026-09-09' (one-day discrepancy). Next: 40.92 referred back, 40.93 new DIS ballot, or 40.99 approved for FDIS — none recorded as of 1 November 2026. Approval needs two-thirds of participating members in favour and no more than one quarter of votes cast negative. ISO statement (via Trellis 23 Sept, ESG Dive 24 Sept 2026): 'did not receive the level of approval required to advance in its current form'. Trellis and Enviliance both report 88 countries taking part and roughly 5,000 comments; ESG Dive's 177 is ISO's total membership, not the number voting. ISO publishes no tally.

sub_changes.new: Organizations only, of any size or sector: the draft sets requirements for a company's net-zero strategy, targets and progress, and excludes products, services and territories. It recognizes four claim stages: aspiration, aligned transition plan, aligned progress, and achievement.
sub_changes.old: The 2022 guidelines addressed states, regions, cities and organizations alike, and were guidance rather than requirements.
sub_changes.topic: Who the draft would apply to
sub_changes.specifics: IWA 42:2022: 'a common reference for collective efforts, offering a global basis for harmonizing, understanding, and planning for net zero for actors at the state, regional, city and organizational level'. ISO/DIS 14060 Clause 1 Scope: 'specifies principles, requirements and guidance for organizations to develop, implement and communicate a net zero aligned pathway'; applies to organizations claiming a net zero aspiration, a net zero aligned transition plan, net zero aligned progress or net zero achievement; excludes territories and products/services. Project page: 'The scope would be limited to organizations, not including their products, in line with the scope of IWA 42'. Clause 16: four claim stages. ISO press release 17 June 2026: 'organizations of all sizes and sectors'.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: separate targets for direct emissions, purchased energy, and all significant value-chain categories; a long-term net-zero date set by the chosen pathway; a first interim target within five years and later ones at most ten years apart. No fixed percentage cut: the residual emissions you may leave are derived from the pathway and a company-level carbon budget.
sub_changes.old: Nothing binding from ISO; in practice SBTi's criteria set the near-term and long-term target architecture.
sub_changes.topic: What targets the draft would require
sub_changes.specifics: ISO/DIS 14060 Clause 10.1: long-term target 'by the date required in the chosen net zero pathway'; 'the first interim target shall be no more than 5 years from the target setting year'; 'Subsequent interim targets shall be set at intervals of no more than 10 years'; 'separate targets for each scope' — scope 1, 2 and 3 'covering all significant indirect GHG emissions categories' (significance per ISO 14064-1:2018 Annex H or GHG Protocol; no numeric threshold). Clause 8.2: base year per ISO 14064-1:2018 clause 6.4.1 or GHG Protocol. Definition 3.2.11: residual emissions remain 'at the net zero target date, after implementation of all technically and economically feasible activities'; Clause 10.1: residuals derived from the pathway; 3.1.4 'organizational greenhouse gas budget' (cumulative base-year-to-target-year emissions); 4.3 front-loading.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: credits could not be used to claim progress toward interim or net-zero reduction targets. Removal credits could prepare for, and at the net-zero date counterbalance, residual emissions if they meet durability, additionality and no-double-counting tests. Any credit type could fund contributions beyond the value chain, remedial action or historical emissions, reported separately.
sub_changes.old: No ISO rule on credits in a net-zero claim.
sub_changes.topic: Whether carbon credits could count
sub_changes.specifics: ISO/DIS 14060 Clause 5.4: 'Carbon credits shall not be used to claim progress towards interim or net zero GHG emission reduction targets'; 'removals credits may be used to achieve the milestones that organizations set ... to prepare for counterbalancing all residual emissions at organizational net zero'; 'all types of carbon credits may be used' for contributing to global net zero, remedial action and historical emissions as high-ambition activities. Clauses 12.3–12.4: counterbalancing residuals with carbon dioxide removals meeting quality criteria — durability, additionality, quantification, no carbon leakage, no double-counting, credible accounting; 12.4.2 durability. Definition 3.1.1: residual emissions 'counterbalanced by anthropogenic carbon dioxide removal'. Reported opposition (Trellis, anonymous sources): credit-use rules; unconfirmed.

sub_changes.new: Proposed: a public transition plan built on quantified data, integrated into business and financial planning, covering every scope and expected residual emissions, updated at least every five years; top management accountable and reviewing it annually; annual public reporting on progress, with remedial action if a target is missed.
sub_changes.old: No ISO requirement for a public transition plan or for board-level accountability.
sub_changes.topic: Transition plan, governance and annual reporting
sub_changes.specifics: ISO/DIS 14060 Clause 9.1: plan 'based on reliable, quantified data', integrated into core business and financial planning, addresses all scopes and anticipated residuals, timelines, monitoring/reporting/verification approach (9.1(k)), stakeholder participation, social and environmental risk assessment, carbon-credit use, 'publicly available', updated 'at least every five years'; assess 'locked in emissions' and potential stranding. Clause 6 and 9.2.2: top management shall 'demonstrate leadership and commitment', annual review of pathway and plan, align strategy 'including investments, divestments and asset management' with net zero targets, 'publicly and regularly communicating transition plans and reporting progress'. Clause 14: annual reporting on scope, progress against targets, remedial action, achievement and maintenance of net zero; Principle 4.10 public availability of information.

sub_changes.new: Not mandatory in the draft: companies would have to set out an approach to validating the plan and verifying results, but first-, second- or third-party checks would all be allowed, with third-party noted as more credible. That is looser than SBTi, which requires independent limited assurance for its larger-company category.
sub_changes.old: No ISO requirement.
sub_changes.topic: Would third-party verification be mandatory
sub_changes.specifics: ISO/DIS 14060 Clause 9.1(k): the plan 'establishes an approach for any validation of the plan or verification of its results'; Introduction: validation and verification 'may be undertaken on a first-, second- or third-party basis', third party 'generally recognized to deliver greater credibility'; Clause 14: claims supported by 'validated' assumptions and 'verified' results. Comparison: SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2.0 Criteria (June 2026) CNZS-C7 — Category A 'shall obtain independent third-party assurance at a minimum level of limited assurance' over base-year scope 1, 2 and 3, 'conducted by an accredited independent third party in accordance with internationally recognized assurance standards'; Category B optional.

sub_changes.new: Keep using the 2022 ISO guidelines and SBTi's 2026 net-zero standard. The ISO draft was written to replace the guidelines; the committee may refer it back for rework or run a new ballot, and no ISO date exists. Trade reports expect finalisation no earlier than 2027.
sub_changes.old: In practice SBTi's criteria defined 'net-zero aligned'; ISO's 2022 guidelines were a secondary reference.
sub_changes.topic: What to rely on while ISO revises
sub_changes.specifics: IWA 42:2022 Net zero guidelines: launched at COP27 (November 2022), free of charge; ISO/DIS 14060 'will replace IWA 42:2022' (project page). SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2.0 (June 2026; dates in the SBTi block). Committee options after a failed DIS vote: stage 40.92 (referred back to TC/SC) or 40.93 (new DIS ballot). ESG Dive (24 Sept 2026): finalization expected 2027 depending on revisions; development began 2022. Trellis (23 Sept 2026): ISO general assembly 28 September–2 October 2026 in Paris — no decision published as of 1 October 2026.

implications: Keep net-zero claim language anchored to SBTi V2.0 criteria rather than a forthcoming ISO definition.
Expect substantive change in the next draft: close to 5,000 comments, from a reported 88 voting countries, go back to committee.
Treat any date you hear for publication as speculation until ISO publishes one.
Stress-test your plan against the draft's architecture — separate targets per scope, a first interim target within five years, a public plan refreshed every five years.
If you hold removal credits for future residual emissions, document durability and double-counting safeguards now; the ISO draft and SBTi point the same way.

sub_changes.new: Yes. The 2018 edition remains in effect; ISO lists it as 'to be revised', not withdrawn, and both organizations state that existing standards remain in effect until new ones are published with transition information. No withdrawal date exists.
sub_changes.old: The 2018 edition was in force, and ISO had already decided in October 2024 to revise it on its own track.
sub_changes.topic: Is the current ISO inventory standard still valid
sub_changes.specifics: ISO 14064-1:2018, edition 2, 47 pages, published 2018-12-19; stage 90.92 'International Standard to be revised' since 2024-10-14; 'will be replaced by ISO/WD 14064-1.2' (under development, edition 3; stage 20.20 working draft 2025-06-28, 20.60 close of comment 2025-08-26, 20.20 again 2026-04-01, 20.60 close of comment 2026-05-12). Partnership FAQ (23 September 2025): 'The existing standards of both organizations remain in effect, until new standards are published with additional information on transition periods.' Consolidated Standard Development Plan (29 July 2026): no withdrawal or transition provision for ISO 14064-1:2018.

sub_changes.new: One jointly published, dual-logo corporate standard replacing both. GHG Protocol's working title is Corporate Standard Version 3.0, in two parts: general requirements and the physical inventory, then actions and market instruments. Whether the result will also carry an ISO number is not stated.
sub_changes.old: Two rulebooks for the same inventory: ISO's standard and GHG Protocol's corporate, purchased-energy and value-chain documents, revised on separate timetables.
sub_changes.topic: What the merged standard will be
sub_changes.specifics: SDP p. 1: partnership scope for entity-level accounting 'includes ISO 14064-1 and the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard, Scope 2 Guidance, and Scope 3 Standard, and the new Actions and Market Instruments workstream'. SDP section 6 p. 10: 'Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (Corporate Standard), Version 3.0' — Part 1 'General Requirements and Physical GHG Inventory', Part 2 'Actions and Market Instruments'; 'The part structure is subject to change'. SDP p. 16: 'Adopted standards will be published under a dual logo.' FAQ 29 July 2026 Q1: consolidates Corporate Standard (2004), Scope 2 Guidance (2015), Scope 3 Standard (2011), AMI workstream 'and ISO's 14064-1 standard'. ISO numbering: not stated; ISO/WD 14064-1.2 (edition 3) is listed as replacing ISO 14064-1:2018.

sub_changes.new: Both must approve. GHG Protocol's Independent Standards Board approves the draft; then its Steering Committee ratifies and ISO's climate subcommittee votes through the normal ISO enquiry stage, needing two-thirds in favour and no more than a quarter against. ISO experts have sat in GHG Protocol's working groups since early 2026 and ISO observes the board.
sub_changes.old: ISO standards were approved by ISO national member bodies alone; GHG Protocol texts by its own board and steering committee.
sub_changes.topic: How ISO approves the joint text
sub_changes.specifics: SDP pp. 15–16: 'members of ISO WG4 joined the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard TWG, Scope 2 TWG, Scope 3 TWG, and Actions and Market Instruments TWG' in Q1 2026; during public consultation 'ISO/TC 207/SC 7 is invited to review ... through its committee draft (CD) stage'; after ISB approval the draft goes concurrently to the Steering Committee for ratification and 'to ISO/TC 207/SC 7 for approval through the ISO enquiry stage'; approved 'if a two-thirds majority of permanent members of ISO/TC 207/SC 7 are in favor and no more than one quarter of the total number of votes cast are negative'; ISO follows 'the ISO/IEC Directives'. FAQ (Sept 2025): ISO is an Observing Entity on the ISB.

sub_changes.new: No date is set. The published plan is a consolidated draft for consultation estimated in Q2 2027 and publication estimated in Q4 2028, later if pilot testing is added. Neither body has published an effective date or a transition period.
sub_changes.old: No change was scheduled; the 2018 edition had only just entered ISO's revision cycle in October 2024.
sub_changes.topic: When companies would have to switch
sub_changes.specifics: SDP section 9 p. 13: 'Consolidated draft standard for public consultation (estimated Q2 2027)'; 'Published revised standard (estimated Q4 2028)'; 'If a pilot testing phase is added, the timeline would be extended'; 'The need for a pilot testing phase will be determined based on needs identified during the standard development process'; p. 14: 'The workplan and timeline are subject to change during the standard revision process'. Guidance documents 'expected to be published after publication of the consolidated standard'. COP30 Action Agenda announcement (11 November 2025): by 2028 the parties will have 'established the standards infrastructure required for harmonized emissions reporting, functioning carbon markets, and interoperable regulation'. Effective date, transition period and withdrawal of ISO 14064-1:2018: not stated.

sub_changes.new: Nothing changes yet. Statements against the 2018 edition stay valid because the standard stays in force; ISO's verification standard is confirmed and not under revision, and the partnership documents do not say whether it will be co-branded. How verifiers transition to the new text is not stated.
sub_changes.old: A verification statement against the 2018 ISO inventory standard, issued by an accredited body, was the ISO route to a checked inventory.
sub_changes.topic: What happens to ISO-verified inventories and verifiers
sub_changes.specifics: ISO 14064-1:2018 remains published (stage 90.92). ISO 14064-3:2019 stage 90.93 'International Standard confirmed' 2024-08-01; not in the ISO/TC 207/SC 7 work programme as of 1 November 2026 (programme lists ISO/DIS 14060, ISO/WD 14064-1.2, ISO/WD 14064-2.2, ISO/WD 14067.2, ISO/DIS 14070-1, ISO/AWI 14070-2, ISO/AWI TR 14082, ISO/CD 14094). ISO 14065:2020 confirmed 2026-03-18 (90.93). Partnership FAQ names the 'ISO 1406X family' without listing 14064-3; the SDP never names ISO 14064-3; it lists verification/assurance as a Corporate Standard TWG topic and (p. 20) says 'Consider introducing a verification or assurance requirement or recommendation to the Corporate Standard'. Transition for verified inventories: not stated.

sub_changes.new: The substantive proposals — mandatory value-chain emissions, dropping equity-share consolidation, caps on exclusions, separate physical and market-based statements — are being decided in GHG Protocol's working groups with ISO experts inside them. See the GHG Protocol block for each; ISO has published no separate content positions.
sub_changes.old: Content differences between the two rulebooks were a known source of divergence; each was revised on its own.
sub_changes.topic: What content is actually changing
sub_changes.specifics: Content decisions sit with the GHG Protocol TWGs (Corporate Standard, Scope 2, Scope 3, Actions and Market Instruments) to which ISO WG4 members were added in Q1 2026 (SDP pp. 15–16; Scope 3 Phase 1 Progress Update, March 2026, section 1.2: 'Members of ISO's technical community will join GHG Protocol's existing Technical Working Groups ... in Q1 2026'). ISO/WD 14064-1.2 comment rounds closed 2025-08-26 and 2026-05-12; working drafts are not public and ISO has published no summary of changes. SDP Q3–Q4 2026 workplan: 'The Scope 2 TWG engages with both public consultation feedback and feedback from ISO WG4, at the direction of the ISB.' Cross-reference: GHG Protocol block rows on boundaries, scope 3, completeness, scope 2 and market instruments.

implications: Keep verifying against the 2018 ISO edition or the current GHG Protocol texts; nothing is withdrawn and no switch date exists.
Plan one methodology change after the consolidated standard publishes rather than two; it is the single successor to both rulebooks.
Track the Q2 2027 consultation through both GHG Protocol and your national standards body, since ISO members review the same draft.
Ask your verifier how they will treat the transition and whether accreditation scopes need updating; neither body has stated this.
Follow the content debates in the GHG Protocol block; ISO is not running a separate content track.

EU sustainability-report assurance must come from auditors or accredited providers under national, then Commission, standards, and SBTi requires limited assurance under 'internationally recognized' standards without naming ISO.

detail.applies_to: Companies using ISO-accredited verifiers for inventories that also feed California emissions reporting, EU border-levy filings, EU sustainability statements or SBTi validation.

sub_changes.new: No. ISO confirmed the verification standard in 2024 and the standard for verification bodies in March 2026; neither is in the committee's work programme. Competence requirements for verification teams are under review. Whether verification will be folded into the ISO–GHG Protocol partnership is not stated.
sub_changes.old: The 2019 verification standard was reviewed and confirmed in 2024; the standard for verification bodies was under review in 2025–26.
sub_changes.topic: Is the ISO verification standard itself changing
sub_changes.specifics: ISO 14064-3:2019 'verification and validation of greenhouse gas statements', edition 2, 54 pages, published 2019-04-15; systematic review 90.20 2023-04-15, 90.60 2023-09-03, 90.93 confirmed 2024-08-01; 'GHG programme neutral'. ISO 14065:2020, edition 3, 31 pages, a sector application of ISO/IEC 17029:2019; 90.20 2025-10-15, 90.93 confirmed 2026-03-18. ISO 14066:2023 competence requirements: 'under review by ISO/TC 207/SC 7/JWG 6' (committee page). SC 7 work programme (1 October 2026) lists no 14064-3 or 14065 project. Partnership FAQ: 'ISO 1406X family' unspecified; the SDP lists verification/assurance as a working-group topic (p. 8, p. 12) and p. 20 says 'Consider introducing a verification or assurance requirement or recommendation to the Corporate Standard', but never mentions ISO 14064-3.

sub_changes.new: Proposed, with a catch: ISO's 2019 verification standard is one of five standards California proposes to accept for limited assurance over direct and purchased-energy emissions from 2027, but only 'with additional accreditation requirements'; the March 2026 version pointed to provider qualifications under the ISO verification-body and competence standards, and staff have not finalised the wording. Three of the other four are accountancy-profession standards (AICPA AT-C 210, ISAE 3410 with ISAE 3000, ISSA 5000); the fourth, AA1000AS v3, is a sustainability assurance standard. Formal rulemaking has not started.
sub_changes.old: California's air regulator first floated a list of five acceptable assurance standards, including the ISO verification standard with provider qualifications under the ISO verification-body and competence standards, at a March 23, 2026 workshop; nothing had been formally proposed.
sub_changes.topic: Will California accept an ISO verification
sub_changes.specifics: CARB workshops 23 March 2026 (ISO entry then read 'ISO 14064-3:2019 (with provider qualifications under ISO 14065/14066)', per Sullivan & Cromwell) and 21 July 2026 (per Jones Day and Deloitte; CARB pages not fetchable): five proposed standards — AA1000AS v3; AICPA AT-C Section 210; ISAE 3410 with ISAE 3000 (Revised) for engagements commencing before 15 December 2026; ISSA 5000 from 15 December 2026; 'ISO 14064-3:2019 (with additional accreditation requirements)'. Limited assurance for scope 1 and 2, including biogenic emissions, beginning 2027; the report must identify the standard, level, emissions covered, provider name and contact; engagements 'in full conformance with one of the proposed assurance standards'; rules to cover 'engagement scope, methodology, provider qualifications, evidence gathering, independence, oversight mechanism and reporting'. Next: proposed regulation, 45-day comment, Board approval. Accreditation detail: not stated.

sub_changes.new: No, not on its own. From 2026 embedded emissions must be verified by a verifier accredited by an EU national accreditation body under the generic validation-and-verification body standard and its environmental application; the Commission's guidance says the ISO GHG verification standard is 'applicable to GHG emissions in general, but not specific enough', so only the levy's own methodology rules apply.
sub_changes.old: Verification of embedded emissions was not yet required under the levy.
sub_changes.topic: Does ISO verification satisfy the EU border carbon levy
sub_changes.specifics: European Commission, DG TAXUD, 'Guidance on CBAM verification and accreditation for verifiers and national accreditation bodies' (24 August 2026): the AVR-DA 'prescribes the application of a harmonised standard in the accreditation of verifiers ... EN ISO 17029'; 'the sector-specific application of this broader generic standard must also be applied by the verifier: EN ISO 14065'; 'ISO 14064-03 is applicable to GHG emissions in general, but not specific enough for the CBAM. Instead, only the requirements of the Methodology Regulation apply'; verification required from 1 January 2026 (definitive period); accreditation by national accreditation bodies that are EA members. Commission page: first verifiers accredited around September 2026, registry registration from September 2026, reports from January 2027.

sub_changes.new: No. Assurance of the sustainability statement must be given by the statutory auditor or, where a member state permits, an accredited independent assurance provider, applying national standards until the Commission adopts its limited-assurance standard, now due by July 1, 2027. The requirement for the Commission to adopt reasonable-assurance standards by 2028 has been removed, so no step-up beyond limited assurance is scheduled. An ISO verification report can support that work but does not replace it.
sub_changes.old: EU rules required limited assurance of the sustainability statement by the statutory auditor, or an accredited independent provider where a member state allows, using national standards until the Commission adopted its own by October 2026.
sub_changes.topic: Does ISO verification count for EU sustainability reports
sub_changes.specifics: Directive (EU) 2022/2464 inserting Article 26a into Directive 2006/43/EC: Member States apply national assurance standards, procedures and requirements until the Commission adopts Union standards; Commission to adopt limited assurance standards by 1 October 2026 (original). Accounting Directive Article 34(1) second subparagraph: opinion based on a limited assurance engagement; Article 34(3)–(4): Member States may permit independent assurance services providers accredited under Regulation (EC) No 765/2008. Directive (EU) 2026/470 of 24 February 2026: Article 26a(3) now 'no later than 1 July 2027'; reasonable assurance standards requirement removed, recital 5: 'To avoid an increase in the costs of assurance for undertakings'. ISO 14064-3 is not named in either directive.

sub_changes.new: Not named, not excluded: SBTi's 2026 standard requires its larger-company category to obtain at least limited assurance from an accredited independent third party 'in accordance with internationally recognized assurance standards', and the inventory itself must follow GHG Protocol rather than the ISO inventory standard. Whether an ISO-standard engagement qualifies is not stated.
sub_changes.old: ISO verification bodies issued statements against the ISO verification standard with no SBTi role.
sub_changes.topic: Does SBTi accept an ISO verification
sub_changes.specifics: SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2.0 Criteria (June 2026): CNZS-C7 — Category A (Category B optional): 'Companies shall obtain independent third-party assurance at a minimum level of limited assurance' over scope 1, 2 and 3 for the target base year, low-carbon electricity calculations and significant emissions-intensive activities, 'conducted by an accredited independent third party in accordance with internationally recognized assurance standards'; CNZS-C8.6: recalculated inventories assured (Category A). CNZS-C5.1: inventory 'in accordance with the GHG Protocol Standards and Guidance, using the most recent and effective versions available' — ISO 14064-1 not offered as an alternative. ISO 14064-3 is not named in the Criteria; footnote 16 to CNZS-C7.3: the SBTi 'will develop criteria and processes for recognizing third-party frameworks, standards, and programs'.

implications: Map every jurisdiction's assurance rule before contracting one verifier: California (proposed), the EU border levy and EU reporting each name different standards and accreditations.
If you rely on an ISO-accredited verifier for California, confirm with them what extra accreditation the regulator will demand once the draft rule publishes.
For EU border-levy filings, use a verifier accredited by an EU national accreditation body under the levy's own rules; an ISO statement alone will not be accepted.
Have your statutory auditor or accredited provider cover the EU sustainability statement; hand them the ISO verification as evidence, not as a substitute.
For SBTi, check that your provider is accredited and the standard internationally recognized; the inventory must follow GHG Protocol.

sub_changes.new: Either, unchanged. ISO's standard is listed as 'to be revised' and GHG Protocol's remains available; both bodies say existing standards remain in effect until the joint text publishes with transition information.
sub_changes.old: Either ISO's 2018 product carbon footprint standard or GHG Protocol's 2011 Product Standard; they overlapped but differed.

sub_changes.specifics: ISO 14067:2018, edition 1, 46 pages, published 2018-08-20; stage 90.92 'to be revised' 2024-10-14; 'will be replaced by ISO/WD 14067.2'; scope: quantification and reporting of the carbon footprint of a product 'in a manner consistent with International Standards on life cycle assessment' (ISO 14040, ISO 14044); 'only a single impact category: climate change'; excludes offsetting. GHG Protocol Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard (2011) remains downloadable; GHG Protocol nominated its Joint Working Group participants on 9 February 2026. Partnership FAQ (September 2025): existing standards 'remain in effect, until new standards are published with additional information on transition periods'.

sub_changes.new: One harmonized product carbon footprint standard built on both current documents, written by an ISO working group expanded into a joint group with GHG Protocol experts, intended to serve corporate, investor and regulatory needs including border carbon adjustment mechanisms such as the EU's.
sub_changes.old: No joint product work existed; ISO's product footprint work sat in its own working group.
sub_changes.topic: What the joint product standard will be
sub_changes.specifics: GHG Protocol announcement 27 October 2025: ISO/TC 207/SC 7 Working Group 8 'will expand into a Joint Working Group under agreed Terms of Reference'; builds on 'ISO 14067 and the GHG Protocol Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard' to 'maintain continuity with existing frameworks'; supports decarbonization strategies and 'Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism implementation'; expressions of interest due 30 November 2025. ISO/TC 207 plenary, Toronto, 25 October–1 November 2025: JWG formally announced. 9 April 2026: JWG finalized after 'more than 450 submissions, including applicants from 50+ countries and over 410 organizations'. ISO work item: ISO/WD 14067.2, edition 2, stage 20.60 close of comment period 2026-05-25, will replace ISO 14067:2018.

sub_changes.new: Not stated. The ISO working draft finished a comment round in May 2026; no public consultation date, publication date or effective date has been announced by either body.
sub_changes.old: ISO's revision was registered in October 2024 with no public timetable.
sub_changes.topic: When a draft will appear
sub_changes.specifics: ISO/WD 14067.2 stage 20.60 close of comment period 2026-05-25 (working draft, not public). GHG Protocol JWG announcement (9 April 2026): no timeline; second COP Action Agenda webinar 24 April 2026. Partnership FAQ (September 2025): 'The teams are currently discussing the timelines and integration of processes'. The Consolidated SDP (29 July 2026) covers the corporate standard only. GHG Protocol blog index as of 1 October 2026 shows no product-level post after 9 April 2026.

sub_changes.new: Still no under ISO's working draft, whose scope keeps the exclusion of offsetting and the single climate-change impact category. How the joint standard will treat market instruments is not stated; the corporate-level work proposes separate statements rather than netting.
sub_changes.old: Not under ISO: the 2018 standard covers one impact category, climate change, and excludes offsetting from the footprint.
sub_changes.topic: Can offsets be netted into a product footprint
sub_changes.specifics: ISO 14067:2018 abstract: addresses 'only a single impact category: climate change'; excludes carbon offsetting, social and economic aspects and other environmental impacts. ISO/WD 14067.2 abstract (project page): same scope — consistent with ISO 14040 and ISO 14044, single impact category, offsetting excluded. Joint Working Group position: not published. Corporate-level interim guidance (GHG Protocol FAQ, 29 July 2026, Q3): report physical inventory emissions, market-based emissions and impacts of climate actions 'separately and transparently, without netting between categories'.

implications: Keep issuing product footprints under whichever of the two standards your customers specify; neither is withdrawn and no switch date exists.
Flag long-lived product declarations and labels for re-baselining once the joint standard publishes; expect method changes, not just a renumbering.
If you file under the EU border levy, watch the joint product work: it was launched partly to support that mechanism.
Do not net credits into product footprints; ISO's current and draft texts exclude offsetting.

sub_changes.old: Published March 2023 as a new standard replacing an earlier ISO workshop agreement.

sub_changes.specifics: ISO 14083:2023 'Quantification and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions arising from transport chain operations', edition 1, 117 pages; stage 60.60 'International Standard published' 2023-03-20; revises IWA 16:2015 (withdrawn); CD approved 2021-07-21, DIS registered 2021-11-23, FDIS approved 2022-10-03. ISO/TC 207/SC 7 work programme (1 October 2026) lists no 14083 project. Partnership FAQ (September 2025): scope is 'corporate carbon footprint (CCF), product carbon footprint (PCF), and project-level accounting standards'; ISO 14083 is not named in any partnership document read.

sub_changes.new: From December 2, 2030 in the EU: anyone who calculates and discloses emissions of a transport service starting or ending in the EU — under a contract, voluntarily for commercial purposes, or because another law requires it — must use the ISO method. The regulation does not force disclosure; it governs how disclosure is done.
sub_changes.old: No legal requirement to use it anywhere.
sub_changes.topic: When EU law makes it mandatory
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2026/1030 of 29 April 2026 'on the greenhouse gas emissions accounting of transport services', OJ L 12.5.2026. Article 1: rules for transport services 'that start or end on the Union territory, where disaggregated information on those emissions is calculated and disclosed' on a contractual or voluntary basis for commercial purposes, or where required by Union or national law. Article 3(1): emissions 'shall be calculated on the basis of the common methodology within the meaning of EN ISO 14083:2023'. Article 20: in force on the twentieth day after publication; 'shall apply from 2 December 2030' (listed empowerment provisions apply from entry into force). Entities: transport operators, service organisers, hub operators, data intermediaries, tool and database developers, conformity assessment bodies.

sub_changes.new: Under the EU regulation, companies other than small and medium-sized enterprises that calculate these emissions must have their output data verified by an accredited conformity assessment body; SMEs may opt in. Frequency will be set by implementing acts.
sub_changes.old: No verification rule attached to the ISO method.
sub_changes.topic: Who must have transport figures verified
sub_changes.specifics: Regulation (EU) 2026/1030 Articles 12–13: transport and hub entities and data intermediaries calculating emissions must have output data verified, 'except SMEs', who may request verification voluntarily; verifiers are conformity assessment bodies accredited under Regulation (EC) No 765/2008; implementing acts set the 'appropriate frequency of that verification' considering the nature and scale of services and avoiding disproportionate burdens; proof-of-compliance documentation required. Article 3: the Commission assesses EN ISO 14083:2023 by 3 December 2033 and may by delegated act prohibit application of amendments 'creating a manifest risk of incompatibility' with the regulation's objectives.

implications: Align logistics emissions data with the ISO transport method now; from December 2030 it is the only EU-acceptable basis for disclosed transport-service figures.
If you buy transport services, ask carriers whether their figures already follow the ISO method; your value-chain inventory will inherit them.
Larger transport providers: budget for accredited verification of output data; frequency rules are still to come.
Do not expect the ISO–GHG Protocol merger to change transport accounting; it is out of scope.

rows.new: Convergence confirmed, no draft public: ISO's project standard is being revised in an ISO working group with GHG Protocol experts, toward a co-branded project standard. Both current texts remain in force; ISO's working draft closed a comment round in June 2026 and no consultation or publication date exists.
rows.old: ISO's 2019 project standard and GHG Protocol's 2005 Project Protocol ran in parallel for quantifying reductions or removals from a project.

detail.timing: ISO revision registered October 14, 2024; working-draft comment round closed June 6, 2026; GHG Protocol experts seated in the ISO working group; no consultation or publication date; both current texts in force.

detail.applies_to: Project developers, credit buyers and programs quantifying reductions or removals from a defined project; not the corporate inventory itself.

sub_changes.new: Both still apply. ISO's 2019 project standard is listed as 'to be revised', not withdrawn, and GHG Protocol says its 2005 Project Protocol 'remains in force until the revised, co-branded Project Standard is published'.
sub_changes.old: Both current texts; ISO decided in October 2024 to revise its project standard.
sub_changes.topic: Which project standard applies today
sub_changes.specifics: ISO 14064-2:2019, edition 2, 26 pages, published 2019-04-15; stage 90.92 'to be revised' 2024-10-14; 'will be replaced by ISO/WD 14064-2.2'. GHG Protocol Project Protocol page: 'GHG Protocol's Project Protocol is currently being updated as part of the ISO-GHG Protocol partnership for standard harmonization'; 'GHG Protocol's Project Protocol (Copyright © 2005) remains in force until the revised, co-branded Project Standard is published.' ISO 14064-2 scope: quantification, monitoring and reporting of 'activities intended to cause greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions or removal enhancements'.

sub_changes.new: ISO's project working group, with three GHG Protocol-appointed experts, is the vehicle; the result is to be a co-branded project standard. The working draft is not public and closed its latest comment round in June 2026.
sub_changes.old: ISO's working group alone revised the project standard; GHG Protocol had not revised its Project Protocol since 2005.
sub_changes.topic: Who is writing the joint project standard
sub_changes.specifics: GHG Protocol Project Protocol page: three experts appointed to 'ISO TC 207/SC 7/Working Group 5' to support the development. ISO/WD 14064-2.2, edition 3, stage 20.60 close of comment period 2026-06-06; will replace ISO 14064-2:2019; scope covers 'planning a GHG project, identifying and selecting GHG sources, sinks and reservoirs (SSRs) relevant to the project and baseline scenario, monitoring, quantifying, documenting and reporting GHG project performance'. GHG Protocol blog (2 December 2025): the Toronto plenary 'launched parallel work to align corporate and project-level accounting standards, including those from the ISO 1406X family and the GHG Protocol corporate suite'. Consultation and publication dates: not stated.

sub_changes.new: Still separate tracks. Project-level quantification feeds credit programs; how a company reports purchased credits or removals in its own inventory is being set by GHG Protocol's land, removals and market-instruments work, which sits outside the ISO partnership for now.
sub_changes.old: Project accounting and corporate inventories were separate documents with their own rules for removals.
sub_changes.topic: How this relates to removals and credits in your inventory
sub_changes.specifics: Partnership FAQ (September 2025): 'Other documents, such as the GHG Protocol Land Sector and Removals Guidance, fall outside the co-development scope' but may be proposed later. GHG Protocol LSR FAQ Q14: the LSR Standard and forthcoming Guidance 'is currently outside the scope of the GHG Protocol and ISO partnership but may be brought into this partnership in the future'; Q7: 'The LSR Standard goes into effect on January 1, 2027'. ISO/DIS 14060 (net zero, failed ballot) would govern how an organization counterbalances residual emissions with removals, separately from project quantification under ISO 14064-2.

implications: Keep developing and validating projects under the current ISO or GHG Protocol project texts; neither is withdrawn.
If you develop or buy credits, expect the co-branded project standard to reset baseline and monitoring rules; avoid locking long contracts to today's wording.
Treat project accounting and your own inventory's removals as separate questions; the removals rules sit in the GHG Protocol block.

frameworks.title: ISO — existing GHG standards (2018–2023) → merged and new standards (2026 onward)

updates.headline: ISSB staff propose keeping the duplicate Scope 1 industry metrics — and set April 2027 for the digital tagging rules
updates.detail: Agenda papers for the ISSB's November 18-19, 2026 meeting are published and readable, though the papers themselves carry no posting date beyond "November 2026". Paper AP7 records that the balloting process for the taxonomy update covering the amended GHG disclosures begins at the end of November 2026 with a pre-ballot review, and that publication is planned for April 2027 — neither date appears on the public project page. AP7 also says the narrative explaining how a company limited its Category 15 disclosure will change so the full passage can be tagged as a block of text, and that financed emissions are a subtotal within Category 15 rather than an additional component. Separately, paper AP6E recommends retaining the Scope 1 metrics in the industry-based materials, on a design principle that duplication with IFRS S2 is not by itself a reason to exclude content.
updates.so_what: Do not plan on the duplicate Scope 1 industry metrics disappearing — staff are recommending they stay — and pencil in April 2027 as the date the digital tagging rules for the amended GHG disclosures land.
updates.source_title: ISSB November 2026 agenda paper AP7 — Feedback on Proposed IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Taxonomy Update: Amendments to Greenhouse Gas Emissions Disclosures

updates.headline: SBTi reclassifies its automotive standard as an add-on to V2.0 and reopens it for comment until December 6
updates.detail: SBTi revised its draft automotive standard and reclassified it as a sector specification — an extension of CNZS V2.0 rather than a standalone standard — and opened an additional public comment period running November 13 to December 6, 2026, 11:59 PM Pacific. Two new drafts were published: an automotive sector specification at version 0.2 and automotive sector pathways at version 0.1, both marked draft for public comment, with release and effective dates listed as to be determined. The specification states it must be used with CNZS V2.0 and that it updates relevant sections of the March 2024 land transport guidance. The sector page now says final publication is expected no sooner than Q1 2027, which removes the lapsed Q3 2026 date it had been carrying and aligns it with SBTi's work plan.
updates.so_what: If you set targets covering vehicle manufacturing or a large owned fleet, read this draft as an add-on to V2.0 rather than a separate rulebook, and comment by December 6.
updates.source_title: SBTi — Automotive and land transport sector

updates.headline: The EU's downstream carbon border tax file is confirmed live at Council working level
updates.detail: The Council's ad hoc working party on CBAM met on November 13, 2026 for an exchange of views on the proposed amendment extending the carbon border tax to downstream goods and adding anti-circumvention measures, plus a German presentation on abusive practices. The meeting page records three earlier meetings of the same working party, on October 2, 23 and 30, 2026. This matters for how the file should be read as much as for its substance: the European Parliament's legislative observatory still records no event after September 15, 2026, so that silence reflects a stale page rather than a stalled negotiation. A further negotiating meeting reported for November 30, 2026 still has no institutional confirmation.
updates.so_what: Treat the downstream expansion as actively negotiated rather than stalled, and keep collecting supplier emissions data for finished steel and aluminium goods you import into the EU.
updates.source_title: Council of the EU — Ad hoc Working Party on the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), 13 November 2026

updates.headline: The European Commission opens consultation on the assurance standard every EU sustainability statement will be checked against
updates.detail: On November 12, 2026 the Commission opened a targeted consultation on the EU limited assurance standard, running to January 18, 2027 at 23:59 Central European Time, through an online questionnaire only. The standard will be set out in a delegated act built on technical work by CEAOB, and the consultation states that it does not reopen three settled choices: that assurance is required, that limited assurance is the level, and the content of ESRS. Reported coverage of the draft says it is based on ISSA 5000 with EU-specific departures — treating the EU Taxonomy as applicable assurance criteria, adding procedures for digital tagging, and setting rules on the use of third-party verification reports — and that the consultation asks whether the standard should become mandatory from 2027, 2028 or later. A national standard-setter's note states the delegated act is due by July 1, 2027 at the latest; the Commission's own page does not state that deadline.
updates.so_what: This decides what your EU assurance provider will actually test and from which reporting year, so get their read on the draft and respond by January 18, 2027 — above all on the mandatory start year, which could be FY2027.
updates.source_title: European Commission — Targeted consultation on limited assurance standard

updates.headline: GHG Protocol's standards board adds two members weeks before it decides three open questions
updates.detail: On November 11, 2026 GHG Protocol announced two new members of its ISB — Ming Xu of Tsinghua University and Steve Davis of Stanford — along with two-year renewals for six existing members. The release gives no total board size and says nothing about verification, land-sector scope or the corporate standard timeline. It is recorded here only because of what this board is about to decide: the Scope 2 proposal on December 15, 2026, whether third-party verification will be required in the merged corporate standard, and whether land-sector content stays inside the GHG Protocol-ISO partnership.
updates.so_what: Nothing to do — noted because the body that will settle the Scope 2 and verification questions has just changed composition.
updates.source_title: GHG Protocol welcomes new members to its Independent Standards Board

updates.headline: ISO and GHG Protocol restated the Q2 2027 consultation date at COP31 — but said only "2028" for publication
updates.detail: At a COP31 session on November 11, 2026, GHG Protocol's chief executive and an ISO representative discussed harmonisation between the two bodies under the COP30 action agenda. A trade-association daily report of that session states that the planned co-branded corporate standard is up for consultation in Q2 2027, with the aim of publication in 2028. This is a secondary source reporting what the two organisations said rather than an ISO or GHG Protocol publication, and it is the only restatement found in the week. It partly repairs last week's finding that neither date could be re-verified on any readable page: the Q2 2027 consultation is restated and the publication year is corroborated, but the Q4 2028 quarter is not.
updates.so_what: Keep planning to the Q2 2027 consultation, and treat the Q4 2028 publication quarter as a July 2026 estimate that still has not been reconfirmed.

updates.headline: GHG Protocol published its Scope 2 workshop outcomes — one proposal, hourly matching but not 24/7, and a December 15 board decision
updates.detail: The outcomes of the Scope 2 TWG's October 20-22, 2026 workshop in Washington DC were published, the newest document dated November 10, 2026, closing a five-week gap in which the workshop could not be confirmed to have happened at all. The group will develop a single proposal rather than competing alternatives, and the proposed market-based method uses hourly matching but explicitly not 24/7 certificate matching, with deliverability defined as a plausible physical connection and incrementality recommended but not required — though companies would have to disclose their incremental share. Whether market-based reporting is required or optional remains open, reporting would be optional below a size or load threshold, and the ranking order of the location-based emission-factor hierarchy is unresolved with votes split evenly. The documents are marked draft and subject to change, and they set out the decision calendar: subgroup recommendations on November 23-24, materials to the ISB by December 1, and the ISB considering the secretariat's recommendations on December 15, 2026.
updates.so_what: Your existing annual certificate contracts are not safe yet, but they are not dead either — the live question is whether hourly matching becomes required or optional, and the board that decides meets on December 15.
updates.source_title: GHG Protocol — Scope 2 Workshop Outcomes Overview (November 10, 2026)

updates.headline: The first mandatory US corporate emissions reports came due — and California has said nothing since
updates.detail: The November 10, 2026 deadline for Scope 1 and Scope 2 reports under SB 253 passed with the obligation intact, one day after the appeals court upheld it. CARB published no post-deadline statement, bulletin, question-and-answer update, filer count, enforcement statement or extension: its climate-disclosure program page still frames the deadline as forthcoming, and the newest dated item on it is from July 21, 2026. One correction to last week's record: the OCC's October 29, 2026 letter asking California to exempt federally chartered banks is in fact published, as news release 2026-95, and was recorded as unpublished only because the release numbers had been walked upward from 97 rather than in both directions. CARB has still published no response to that letter, and the OCC has taken no further action through news release 2026-100 of November 13.
updates.so_what: If you filed, keep your submission evidence and watch for fee notices from December 10; if you did not, nothing in the record suggests California has relaxed the duty.
updates.source_title: OCC Raises Concerns with California's Climate Disclosure Laws (news release 2026-95)

updates.headline: The revised EU reporting standards entered into force — with no official word marking it
updates.detail: Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 entered into force on November 10, 2026 under its own Article 3, making the revised ESRS law. No Commission or EFRAG communication marked the date: the Commission's corporate sustainability reporting page was updated on November 12, 2026 but does not mention the regulation by number and does not note the entry into force, and the newest implementation materials on it remain a CSRD question-and-answer document from August 2024. No corrigendum appeared in any Official Journal edition read during the week. One correction for precision: 2026/1563 is a Commission delegated regulation of 3 July 2026, not a co-legislated Omnibus amending regulation — the Omnibus directive is a separate instrument.
updates.so_what: The revised standards are now law and first apply to FY2027, so stop planning against the 2023 version — and expect no transitional guidance, because none has been issued.
updates.source_title: European Commission — Corporate sustainability reporting (page updated 12 November 2026)

updates.headline: Appeals court upholds California's Scope 1 and 2 reporting, strikes down its Scope 3 requirement and the climate-risk law
updates.detail: On November 9, 2026, one day before the first reports were due, the Ninth Circuit decided the preliminary-injunction appeal in Chamber of Commerce v. Sanchez, No. 25-5327, affirming in part, reversing in part and remanding. It held that SB 253's Scope 1 and Scope 2 disclosures are commercial speech, reviewed them under intermediate scrutiny and found they are likely to survive, so the denial of an injunction stands and the reporting duty remained in force. It held that Scope 3 disclosures are not commercial speech, applied strict scrutiny, found them likely unconstitutional, and remanded for the district court to decide in the first instance whether those provisions are severable. It also reversed on SB 261, holding that the climate-risk reports compel noncommercial, subjective assessments that fail strict scrutiny, noting that the state all but concedes it cannot meet that standard; one judge would have enjoined both laws in full.
updates.so_what: Keep reporting Scope 1 and 2 to California, but pause spending on a California Scope 3 filing and on SB 261 climate-risk reports until the district court rules on severability.
updates.source_title: US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit — Chamber of Commerce v. Sanchez, No. 25-5327 (November 9, 2026)

updates.headline: Commission carbon-market reports confirm the ETS2 surrender duty slips to 2028, with the first surrender in 2029
updates.detail: The Commission adopted two reports on November 9, 2026: its annual report on the functioning of the European carbon market in 2025, and its 2026 climate action progress report. The carbon-market report states that the ETS2 surrender obligation is postponed from 2027 to 2028, that the 2028 cap is to be set by June 2027, and that the first ETS2 surrender falls due on May 31, 2029. It records emissions covered by the main trading system down about 2% on 2024, an average allowance price of EUR 73.43, auction revenues of EUR 43.2 billion, and a compliance rate of 99.5% on monitoring, reporting, verification and surrender. The progress report confirms that the EU's 2040 target of a 90% net cut became legally binding in April 2026 and that net emissions are 39% below 1990.
updates.so_what: If your EU operations buy fuels covered by ETS2, you have a year longer than previously planned before the surrender obligation bites — the first surrender is 2029, not 2027.
updates.source_title: COM(2026) 596 final — Report on the functioning of the European carbon market in 2025 (Council cover note ST 15651/26)

updates.detail: On November 5, 2026 SBTi published four proposed interpretations and limited-scope revisions to the electricity criteria in CNZS V2.0, with a public comment period of at least 30 days. The most commercially significant is a legacy clause confirming that power contracts fully executed and legally binding before February 1, 2027 keep their eligibility regardless of when delivery starts. A new interim interpretation of 'deliverability regions' would require the generator behind a contract or certificate to sit in the same wide-area synchronous grid as the facility consuming the electricity, with a proposed region list open to comment. SBTi says the changes will be implemented in January 2027 through a Basis for Conclusions and take effect immediately on publication — one month before V2.0 validation opens.
updates.so_what: If you are negotiating power purchase agreements or certificate contracts intended to support an SBTi target, execute them before February 1, 2027 to keep them eligible under the legacy clause, and re-check cross-region certificate purchases against the proposed same-grid test.
updates.headline: SBTi opens public comment on the electricity rules in its new target standard — and sets a contract cut-off of February 1, 2027
updates.source_title: Clearer electricity rules for the Corporate Net-Zero Standard Version 2.0: SBTi opens public comment

updates.detail: On November 4, 2026 EFRAG released an updated digital template for the voluntary standard (VSME) together with an updated XBRL taxonomy and a converter, all under an open-source licence. The release is aligned to the voluntary standard adopted in July 2026 and reflects every change made since the earlier recommendation. New features include side-by-side comparative-period reporting, DOCX files for narrative disclosures, a merge function that combines the inline XBRL report with PDFs, and per-disclosure footnotes. It is available in 11 languages with more to follow, and no deadline attaches to it.
updates.so_what: This is the format in which value-chain data requests will realistically be answered, so have the team that collects supplier emissions data test the template and converter now rather than during the FY2027 reporting cycle.
updates.headline: EFRAG ships the machine-readable template for collecting sustainability data from suppliers
updates.source_title: EFRAG Releases the Voluntary Standard Digital Template and XBRL Converter

updates.detail: The European Parliament's environment committee is reported to have approved the provisional agreement with the Council on the EU ETS market stability reserve on November 4, 2026, by 49 votes to 12 with 20 abstentions. That is the committee confirmation step following the member states' endorsement of the same compromise on October 28, 2026, and it would put the file on course for a plenary first reading scheduled for November 23 to 26, 2026. The compromise raises the threshold above which surplus allowances are permanently cancelled from 400 million to 700 million once the amendment enters into force. This report comes from trade press and could not be corroborated on any institutional source: the Parliament's legislative observatory has recorded no November event and serves a cache predating the vote, and the Parliament's own press room listed no release on this file that day — so treat it as reported rather than verified, and as a procedural step rather than formal adoption.
updates.so_what: Nothing to do on reporting — this is carbon cost, not disclosure; if you hold EU installations, note that the surplus-cancellation threshold is on track to loosen and watch the plenary vote in late November for the figure that actually becomes law.
updates.headline: European Parliament committee reported to have endorsed the carbon-allowance cancellation deal, clearing the way for a plenary vote
updates.source_title: MEPs on environment committee endorse agreement with EU Council on ETS market stability reserve (Europe Daily Bulletin No. 13975)
